en: Oṃ.
Chapter One: The Section on Ritual Action (Kriyādhikāra).
Salutations to that Vikhanas, whose father was Nārāyaṇa, whose mother was Haripriyā, and whose disciples were the sages Bhṛgu and others. || 1 ||
The sages said:
[They addressed] the sage who was seated properly in the hermitage, striving for the welfare of all, in response to the questions of the sages.
All the sages, having arrived, prostrated themselves and spoke as follows: || 2 ||
"O Blessed One, by what path do they worship which deity?
O virtuous Brahman-sage, explain all of this to me in detail. (3)
Bhṛgu said:
O best of all sages, that which has been asked by you, I shall speak;
listen with attentive minds to what is being explained by me.
Situated within the heart is the square, golden seat,
radiant and auspicious, difficult to behold due to the blazing flames of various clusters of jewels.
One should meditate upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa, free from all affliction, situated in its center—
resembling pure crystal and bearing the conch and the discus.
One should mentally contemplate for him the services beginning with the seat;
this is indeed mental worship (mānasī pūjā), while the worship of the image (berapūjā) will now be described.

Having established an image according to the aforementioned proportions and the supreme procedure for gold and other materials, one should worship it; this is indeed enjoined as the "bera-pūjā" (image worship). 8.
Having meditated upon the circle of fire, one should meditate upon auspicious radiance in its center;
within that radiance, one should meditate upon Janārdana seated there.
Resembling molten gold, it had four horns and two heads;
it possessed seven arms, three feet, was difficult to behold, and had seven tongues.
In his right hands, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a rosary, and a spear;
in his left hands, he holds a chowrie, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.
Having meditated, one should perform that worship with oblation as prescribed;
and because it is possible to employ them according to need, one may also perform worship with flowers and other offerings.
From that which brings delight to the eyes, the mind, and the heart, devotion is born through that joy; for the devotee, Hari is easily attained.
Therefore, among these three, the worship of the image (bera-pūjā) is distinguished as superior. The worship of the image is twofold:
domestic worship (gṛhārcā) and temple worship (ālayārcā); thus, that worship of the image is of two kinds. || 14 ||
Because it is complete through all its forms by means of divine offerings such as the *bali* and festivals, it continues uninterrupted even when the patron has passed away. || 15 ||
Because it is common to all the inhabitants of that village and its surroundings, Brahmā declared in ancient times that the worship of the Liṅga in a temple is the primary [duty]. (16)
The worship of the Ālaya [temple image] is of two kinds;
that procedure for the worship of Viṣṇu’s Ālaya is also proclaimed to be twofold:
the Vaikhānasa and the Pāñcarātra, which are respectively Vaidika and Tāntrika. (17)
The ritual procedure (vidhi), however, is rooted in the Veda; when conjoined with initiation (dīkṣā), it is Tantric.
It yields results solely for the next world and promotes both the Veda and the Vedas. || 18 ||
One should cause it to be built according to the Vedic rites in villages and other such dwellings,
on a riverbank, a mountain peak, in a forest, or elsewhere in a secluded place.
One should never worship them in a village or similar place using only Tantric rites;
one should worship them using only Tantric rites in dwellings that follow the natural order. || 20 ||

One should not worship the Viṣṇu idol with either [of these two types of cloth]: that worn by a Vrātya or one from the intermediate castes, nor that worn in the reverse order; such is the instruction of the Elder Brother.
When the characteristics of the preceptor had thus been considered in his mind, the sacrificer, filled with joy,
performed the rites beginning with conception according to the Vaikhānasa Sūtra.
A Brahmin who is devoted to his private Vedic study, who perceives the true meaning of the Vedas, who is gentle, has conquered his senses, is pure, and is intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu. || 23 ||
One whose mind has had its doubts destroyed by the process of reasoning and refutation, who is accompanied by wife and children, who is tranquil, habituated to bathing, and righteous; || 24 ||
Having summoned him and honored him like a god, one should choose a teacher who instructs in all matters; then, one should perform everything as instructed by him.

Therefore, one should perform the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the ninth day prior to that [day], or on the seventh, or on the fifth day, or on the third; such is the offering of the sprouts. || 26 ||
Alternatively, if constrained by haste, one may perform it immediately;
or, on the day immediately following the new moon (Amāvāsyā), one should perform the immediate sowing of the sprouts.
Some maintain that even when there is an interval caused by a transition [to another state], the result occurs immediately;
for when actions are fully infused with their latent potency, they bestow their fruit instantly. (28)
However, before the time of commencement, one should determine the east and have it constructed;
or else, even before the time of installation, one may do so with haste. || 29 ||
Having immediately performed the unbinding of the eyes and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water and other elements,
and having performed the rites beginning with the pouring of oblations into the fire, he should invoke [the deity] as before.
Some say that one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite according to the rules and then perform the worship;
however, when many rites are to be performed on a single day, there is only one offering of the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
For that purpose, one should bring small bowls, jars, and even shallow dishes—
sixteen, twelve, eight, and four respectively, each set being separate.
For all the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, there are four,
or nine, or five, or even one [day] for the immediate offering of the time-seeds.
Some of the best of sages say that they should be fashioned according to their capacity, following the sequence of the number of days and endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics.
Either in the house of the sacrificer, or in the northeast, or in other places, or in another pure location, or in a house built by a village-dweller. || 35 ||
Having smeared a four-cubit square in the four directions with cow dung,
one should apply six lines from east to west and from south to north.
One should designate one square for the *upapīṭha* and [another] for the *brahmapīṭha*;
eight squares around it are for the purpose of movement (*caryā*), and the remaining sixteen are for the rows (*paṅkti*).
One should fashion the Brahma-pīṭha within that square in a row; likewise, one should fashion the pīṭhas of Śeṣa and the others in a row as well. || 38 ||
And Marīci also spoke of their seats,
which are six finger-breadths in height and sixteen finger-breadths in length, even though they are outside the Caṅkhi.
One should fashion six separate pedestals, each provided with three threads, for the image in the house of the patron or likewise upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 40 ||
Having worshipped the God of gods with twenty-seven forms,
and having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should worship Brahmā in the center.
To the north of the eastern gate is Śeṣa, while Vakratuṇḍa is to the south;
one should worship Garuḍa to the east of the southern gate.
One should worship Sudarśana in the west according to the prescribed rite,
and Ṣaṅktīśa to the south of the western door according to the injunctions.
Having worshipped the Sustainer of Beings (Bhūtabhartṛ) in the north according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship the peaceful Soma through the northern door in the east.
One should worship those beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, as well as the Apsarases such as Jayā and others;
for each of them, there is a separate and excellent oblation consisting of sacrificial offerings.
That [offering] is proclaimed as the middling for the six beginning with Brahmā;
however, for the remaining ones including Brahmā, the bali alone shall be the lowest. || 46 ||
One should fill the small vessels (pālikās) and other such items with either clay or sand;
in their midst, one should surround them with either kuśa grass or thread.
Facing the east and becoming purified,
he should indeed place [the syllables] in sequence while muttering the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī in the row surrounding Brahmā.
One should meditate upon the goddess Medinī and worship her in all [vessels],
namely in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of bell-metal.
Having lifted out the seeds submerged in water and washed them with milk, and having filled [the vessel] with them, one should worship Soma there. || 50 ||
At that time, having had it proclaimed with the sounds of musical instruments, he, being composed,
put on a new garment along with an upper cloth and a ring.
The preceptor or the sacrificer should cause auspicious sprouts to be sown, reciting "O King Soma" and muttering the Viṣṇu-sūkta. (52)
If a woman or a Śūdra should perform [the rite], one should not have them perform the sowing;
rather, having recited the Vāruṇa mantra, one should have them perform the sprinkling with water. || 53 ||
Having covered it with a new cloth, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
one should constantly sprinkle it with water and protect the lamp.
Just as one would carefully protect a well-developed sprout, so too should one guard those that are dark-green, red, or even those that have turned horizontal. 55.
Sprouts that have not yet emerged must be carefully avoided;
if they are green, there will be loss of wealth, and if they are red, there will be strife. (56)
If the lines are curved, there will be disease; if they are not well-formed, death indeed occurs.
If they are yellow or white, straight, and rising upwards, they indicate auspiciousness.
It certainly comes to pass for both the doer and the instigator; of this there is no doubt.
In this very same sequence, the sowing of the seed of auspiciousness occurs.
On the fifth day, if it falls on an odd-numbered day, the performer, being in a hurry, should immediately offer the sprouts;
or likewise, he may do so on the third day.
If one is unable [to do so], one should fill the *pālikā* vessels and the like with pure rice that has immediately sprouted auspicious shoots,
or alternatively, with five-colored powders.
Having adorned it with lotuses and other flowers, or having filled it [with water], one should place it there;
one should perform all the rites mentioned for the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) using those very same materials.
The Moon is declared to be the presiding deity of all sprouts;
the Blessed One is not pleased if the offering of sprouts is not made on that day.
Therefore, with every effort, the planting of the sprouts should be done specifically at night.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Meditation on the Fire, the Selection of the Preceptor, and the Planting of Sprouts," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The second chapter: Examination of the Ground.
After the rite of planting the sprouts, one should properly examine the ground;
[one should worship] the deity in the house of the patron with twenty-seven forms. || 1 ||
Having performed worship and reciting [the mantra] before him, saying "O Blessed One, be favorable," he should bow down to the Lord of the gods and seek his favor, saying "Be gracious. || 2 ||
Having adorned a maiden of the same caste as is appropriate, having had her eat milk-rice (pāyasa), and having dressed her in white garments and anointed her with unguents; || 3 ||
One should lead the one whose hand holds a lotus-lamp forward with all auspicious rites, reciting the Śākuna Sūkta while pronouncing the Svasti Sūkta. || 4 ||
The preceptor and the sacrificer, preceded by a stream of water,
went to the designated ground and ascended it, which was covered with trees inhabited by living beings.

Having thoroughly examined the earth according to the prescribed rules by means of its fragrance, color, shape, taste, and omens, one should recite the Bhūsūkta, which has the Earth as its presiding deity.
Having taken possession of the beautiful land of Japan, which is free from defects, [he said]:
"May all beings, as well as the gods, asuras, and others, depart! (7)
Saying, "O Viṣṇu, this earth has been accepted for the sake of a celestial mansion," he should dismiss all the deities and worship the earth there.
Having determined the temple together with the artisan, including the principal pavilion and the surrounding enclosures, one should clear away the grass and shrubs.

One should have the rites beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration performed by that very preceptor who has been duly examined and chosen according to the prescribed rules. || 10 ||
In his absence, however, [the king shall take] his son, grandson, or even great-grandson;
likewise, a brother, a disciple, a grand-disciple, or even a preceptor. || 11 ||
In the absence of the former, he should likewise employ the latter fellow-celibate, or another person authorized by him, for the sake of the teacher. || 12 ||
Otherwise, there is great calamity; the king destroys his kingdom, the duties of the social classes perish, and the intermixture of castes arises. (13)
The sacred fires will not be maintained, Vedic study will not proceed,
and other things will become inverted, with the low becoming high and the high becoming low.
Therefore, having performed an expiation according to all ancient rites as prescribed in the Khila,
one should have all ritual acts performed by that very same person.
One who initiates various specific locations is called a "Guru" everywhere;
however, if he is somehow unfit, one should have it performed by another who is liberated.
At the conclusion of that rite, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to him;
the presiding teacher (sthānācārya) shall be the principal recipient, or it may be someone else appointed by him.
Or one born into that same lineage may perform all the rites.
Regarding the characteristics of artisans: artisans are said to be of three kinds, those who subsist by their respective crafts. || 18 ||
The potter, the carpenter, and likewise the Pāraśava—these are the threefold enmities; and above the mountain is the work of painting.

The whitewashing of the upper part of the temple, the painting on the walls and so forth—thus the mason should perform whatever work pertains to plastering, such as for monasteries and other structures. (20)
A Pāraśava should perform all that work for him—the carpenter shall do it all: working with iron, stone, wood, and bamboo, as well as the tasks involving the eight types of binding and so forth.
The layout of villages and other settlements, the construction of houses for the various social orders (varṇas), and the planning of palaces, pavilions, gates, and walls. || 22 ||
The carpenter shall perform it; indeed, all artisans should do that.
Otherwise, if he does not, that village, the king, and the kingdom will perish. || 23 ||
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme characteristics of ploughing;
on a day that has been declared auspicious, pure, and favorable to the performer. (24)
During the six months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should properly carry out the plowing;
for the purpose of preparing the pair of oxen and the plow, one should procure the wood of the trees previously mentioned. (25)
Having cleansed the foot of the tree and smeared it with cow dung,
[he should worship] Rudra, the Bhūtas, Indra, Kīnāśa, the Mothers, Soma, and Vīraka.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings and having presented the bali-oblation in that forest,
he should likewise worship Rudra, Indra, Yama, and the lord of trees at the foot of a tree.
Having said "To the lords of the forest," and having proclaimed it to the young maidens,
and having said "To the kings of trees," one should offer the sacrificial oblation all around.
And after [granting] all desired objects, one should perform the fire-oblation for Agni Vanarāja, Soma, and Yama. (29)
To the branch, to the one with coarse vision (the hunter), to the hunter in the form of a deer, to the lords of the forest, to the young maidens, to the creepers, and to the flower. || 30 ||
To Śalāṭava, Bṛhattvacas, Puṇya, Amṛtatejas, Sūrya, Harirūpa, Śṛṅgin, and Bhūtarūpin. || 31 ||
Having invoked Nāgahasta, Divya, and likewise Trihasta, as well as Vighna, Vighnarūpa, and Vināyaka; || 32 ||
Uttering "to Prasārin, to Muruṇḍa, to Nyarṇeya," and saying "to the Nāgas, to the kings of spirits (bhūtarāja), and to the Cāraṇas," [he offered oblations]. || 33 ||
To those who roam by day and by night, to the twilight deities (saṃdhyās), and likewise to those who move during the twilights, and having thus spoken, [he offered] to the Apsarases as well. || 34 ||
And likewise to the yakṣīs, the kumārīs, and the āsurīs;
to the rākṣasīs, the piśācas, and to the forest and the land-dwellers. || 35 ||
One should offer oblations to the deities of the trees and to the deities of the sacred sites;
one also offers to the embodied ones, to the couples, and to the blissful ones.
Having likewise offered the Vyāhṛtis and reciting "anirdagdham," and having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), he should again exert himself regarding the tree. || 37 ||
Having offered oblations to Sarveśvara, the Mothers, and Vakratuṇḍa with their respective forms, one should likewise worship the Mothers, Soma, and Vakratuṇḍa. || 38 ||
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day and likewise tied on the protective amulet (pratisara), he then spent the remainder of the night;
thereafter, having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rule—
Having properly cut down the tree, one should fashion the yugas and other parts;
as for the characteristics of the yugas and so forth, one should perform them according to the procedure stated in the Khila.
Standing in the east or the north, one should properly arrange [the offerings] in the directions starting from the east;
having offered the bali-oblation and gathered [the materials], one should consecrate them with scented water.
One should worship the God of gods with twenty-seven forms,
within a square enclosure measuring twenty-four [units] in length, possessing excellent characteristics.
A pedestal (pīṭha) with a height of six aṅgulas, a width of one cubit (ratni), and three tiers (mekhalā) is likewise prescribed for worship elsewhere as well. (43)
And also from the gods, the spirits, the nāgas and yakṣas, the piśācas, the svabhūtas, and likewise the rākṣasas. || 44 ||
One should scatter the bali offering all around to the hosts of Vairocana;
having quickly presented the nāga-bali in the center and performed the rite for the auspicious day, one should proceed without delay.
Having adorned two bulls with auspicious silver horns and hooves,
one should tie a protective amulet (kautuka) on their two front right legs.
Having passed the remainder of the night, he should bathe according to the prescribed rites in the morning and worship that God of gods in the western part of it.
Together with the Cakravīśas and others, having worshipped them with offerings ending in the ritual rinsing (ācamana),
he said, "May [this] be dear to me," to the five deities of the earth.

Having prostrated to the Lord of Gods upon the ground, and having likewise offered salutations and obtained his permission, he established the boundary with water while reciting, "Salutation to Varuṇa. (49)
Having said, "Do not play with dice," he should sprinkle the plowman again;
saying "Thou art a bull" on the right, and "O descendant of Surabhi" on the left.
Having tied the yoke with a rope of *kuśa* grass while reciting "yu-yuga," and having fastened the yoke at the distance of three finger-breadths with the *kuśa* rope while remembering Hari; 51.
Having visualized the Ṛṣis, one should take hold [of the thread] with the mantra "Iṣe tvā gṛhṇāmi," and while reciting the mantra "Viṣṇur mā," one should perform self-protection.
Reciting "ye'smin deśe," he should have the plowing performed there;
and having brought all the seeds, he should touch them while reciting "ime bījāḥ. (53)
With the mantra "O Goddess, you... while performing circumambulation, one should sow all the seeds and cause them to be sprinkled with water. || 54 ||
One should give the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the prescribed rule for the dakṣiṇā.
If one is unable to perform it in this manner through immediate ploughing, one should perform it immediately with haste. || 55 ||
Having examined the ground and immediately ploughed it according to the prescribed rite, and having gathered the seeds and bestowed them upon the Brāhmaṇas; || 56 ||
Having spread straw or chaff everywhere,
he should bring the herds of cows there and offer them to the herds.
Having said, "May the gods eat," one should offer the bali there;
having presented the arghya to the god, and having bowed and sought his permission. (58)
Having laid out the eighty-one squares and worshipped the deities of the squares,
one should lead the square of the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) toward the inner sanctum.
These deities, beginning with Nāga and ending with the five elements, are each worshipped at five points; they are situated at the junctions where the five lines run eastward and northward.
Having worshipped Śeṣa and the others outside, facing westward and so forth,
Kusturuṇḍa and the others are to be worshipped starting from the southeast (āgneya) in a clockwise direction.

Having worshipped Kiṣkindhā and the others ending with Hitā, as well as those in the directions starting from the east in the middle, one should offer an oblation of groats and cakes upon the courtyard.
Having offered an oblation accompanied by water to the Piśācas and the Bhūtas,
and having performed the ritual of the Brahma-lotus, he should examine the auspicious and inauspicious omens.
At the conclusion of the pacifying oblation for inauspicious rites, one should perform auspicious acts;
having determined the layout and measurement of the village, and having conducted an examination of the income and so forth, one should establish the village.
Having laid out sixty-four squares, each multiplied by four, according to the prescribed rule using ten threads increased by seven, facing the northeast; || 65 ||
Having abandoned the Brahma and Paiśāca [portions], one should designate the area for the residence of the Brahmins;
in the north-western part of the Brahma portion, however, there should be the temple of Viṣṇu facing east.
One should construct the assembly hall, the cow-pen, and the marketplace respectively in the northeast, southeast, and southwest;
likewise, if one should build them in the west or north from the Brahma-thread.
Having set aside the portion for the Piśācas, whether outside or even inside, one should orient the pavilion facing the east; such is the instruction of the Elder Brother.
If the temple of the God of gods is situated in the portion belonging to the Piśācas, all those dwelling on the site are afflicted by mental anguish, physical disease, and other such ailments. (69)
In the sixty-four-fold division, likewise in the outer enclosure,
one should place Bhadrakālī and Hara, as well as the Teacher (Śāstṛ), in the outer sector.
One should gradually make them face outward; all others are situated outside of that.
Having planned a row of houses within the human interior in the half-portion, || 71 ||
In the Paiśāca region, one should fashion the channel of the house at the outer half;
having thus determined the site, one should design the temple.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Ploughing and the Laying Out of the Footprints," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The Third Chapter:
The Rules for the Vimāna.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the celestial chariot (vimāna).
From the primary foundation, it should be placed in the northeast, the north, or the northwest.
Having first established a small shrine and consecrated Keśava,
one should then construct the temple while performing uninterrupted worship. || 2 ||
And one desiring to perform a festival in the first instance should perform the festival after hoisting the banner atop the Bālālaya (the temporary or childhood abode). || 3 ||
Having dug the ground on all sides down to the water level or to the level of a stone,
one should fill it with sand and gradually moisten it with water.
Having made it firm everywhere with pestles, elephant feet, and large wooden mallets, one should fill it completely with water.
Having established a stake there as a means for determining the east, one should perform the delimitation of the directions;
by means of that stake or by means of an ear-whistle, one should ascertain the eastern direction.
Having laid the first brick there according to the prescribed rule,
one should begin the temple structure in sizes starting from five cubits and so forth.

The characteristic of measurement is as follows: a paramāṇu, an aṇu, a reṇu, a keśāgra, a likṣā, a tila, and a yava—each subsequent being eight times the size of the preceding—are declared to be the constituent units of the measuring finger (mānāṅgula). || 8 ||
The middle person (madhyamapūruṣa) is indeed eight tālas in height by his own hand;
[the measurement] is from the middle of the middle finger of his right hand.
Whether it is long or even extended, it is declared to be a *mātrāṅgula*;
these two measurements of the *mātrāṅgula* are proclaimed as the best. (10)
That which is one-eighth less than that is proclaimed as the medium size;
that which is one-seventh less is declared to be the smallest finger-breadth. || 11 ||
Twenty-four finger-breadths are known as a hasta (cubit) and a kiṣku;
twenty-five finger-breadths are declared to be a prājāpatya.
The handle of the bow is twenty-six [finger-breadths] and the grip of the bow is twenty-seven;
the measurement for the earth, temples, and so forth, is indeed by means of the *mānāṅgula*.

One should indeed construct the house, bed, seat, vehicle, bowl, and weapon, as well as the fuel-sticks, the *sruc*, the *sruva*, the *juhū*, and so forth, according to the measurement of one's own finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*).
The division of the *mātrāṅgula* itself is called the *śākhāṅgula*; it should be measured by the middle of the fist when constructing fire-pits and other such structures. (15)
Based on that very *mātrāṅgula*, one should design the temple (*vimāna*) according to the middle or lowest proportions, ensuring it is not less than five cubits (*hasta*). || 16 ||
The one who knows the ritual rules should fashion the height as twice the width;
its divisions up to the end of the neck consist of one part, eight parts, and ten parts respectively.
The artisan should fashion the temple with two parts for the base and one part for the pinnacle;
the various types of ornaments and other features should be as described in the section on the abode of the deities.
One should perform the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa) according to the method prescribed for the deposition of the embryo;
and when the temple (vimāna) is completed, one should again place the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā).

The method for fashioning the permanent image (dhruvabera) is as follows: having installed either a pillar (śūla) or a stone according to the prescribed procedure by way of the installation of the pillar, one should fashion the permanent image.
One should fashion the *kautuka* (the portable image) in accordance with the *dhruvabera* (the permanent image),
and then perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) once again according to the procedure prescribed for consecration.
If one wishes to act quickly, then immediately— by means of contemplating the impermanence of the body and so forth—
one should worship either an image made of metal or even one made of wood.
Having prepared the sacrificial hall and arranged the five fires,
and having appointed an Ācārya for the purpose of the installation of the shrine for the deity, || 23 ||
For the purpose of establishing the abode of the Child (Bāla), for the sake of the bricks,
and likewise for the installation of the trident (śūla), one should appoint separate officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having gathered all the necessary materials, as well as stakes and bricks,
one should especially perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) during the first part of the night.
And then, in due order, one should perform the *āghāra* oblation in the *gārhapatya* and other sacrificial pits;
having performed this, one should carry out the opening of the eyes and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) for the mobile image (*jaṅgamabera*).
Having prepared the pitcher according to the rite with seven jars,
and having bathed [the deity] along with the subsidiary baths, one should also worship the pitcher.
Following the sprinkling with the waters emerging from that pitcher according to the prescribed rite,
one should praise the office of the Hotṛ priest, invoke the deity, offer the portions of clarified butter, and perform the oblations.
First, one performs the oblation prescribed for the consecration of the foundation of a temple;
then, one should likewise bathe the bricks or the stones with water from ritual jars.
Having consecrated the bricks separately upon the altar according to the rule,
one should complete the fire-oblation (homa) in the manner prescribed for the laying down of the bricks.
Likewise, one should bathe either the trident or the stone image with water-pots;
having bound a protective cord (pratisara) around it in the same manner, one should place it separately upon a bed.
Having passed the remainder of the night with dances, songs, and instrumental music,
he should bathe at dawn according to the prescribed rules and likewise recite the hymns (sūktas).
When the auspicious moment had arrived, having first examined the ground, having ploughed it, having spread grass upon it, and having offered it to the cows; || 33 ||
Having established [the image] in the chamber for the child, one should again lay down the first brick;
having determined the sanctum (garbhageha), its solid mass, and its firm floor. || 34 ||
Having indeed fashioned the foundation up to its conclusion there, the wise one should install either a trident or a stone image according to the previous [prescribed] method. || 35 ||
Having constructed a cage all around, one should fashion the celestial chariot (vimāna) outside;
or else, within the sacrificial hall, one should fashion them separately, each shining brightly.
Likewise, for the purpose of laying the bricks and the sacrificial posts (śūla) in the chambers of the children,
one should construct a separate sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at the entrance of each of them, including the assembly hall (sabhya).
Having consecrated the pitcher, bathed [the deity], and offered oblations, one should install [the image] in due order.
If one is unable to act in this manner, [one may install] both the permanent image (dhruvabera) and the portable image (kautuka).
Having installed either a stone image, a fixed (dhruva) image, or a mobile (bera) image, one should worship it;
one should then sequentially deposit the yogas and other elements within the [mandala] squares, beginning with Brāhma and ending with Paiśāca.
Having fashioned an image beautiful in all its limbs according to the prescribed method,
one should perform the opening of the eyes and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in accordance with the ritual rules.
Having first established [the image] by means of the method for fixing the pin (śūlasthāpana) through the artisan,
one should then perform the consecration again according to the procedure for the Great Consecration (mahāpratiṣṭhā).
And if one wishes to perform the consecration of a single liṅga immediately,
having completed the fire-oblation at night by the very path previously described, || 42 ||
In the morning, having examined the ground and likewise ploughed the earth,
and having constructed thick walls, one should then perform the ritual consecration (saṃkalpa) there once again.
Having constructed a cage all around, one should fashion a celestial palace (vimāna) outside;
this excellent central pavilion (agramaṇḍapa) should be equal in extent to the celestial palace.

Half of that is declared to be the middle [measurement]; when the distance between the two [extremes] is divided into eight parts, the face-pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) is ninefold, increasing by one part for each successive type. || 45 ||

One should determine the space between the three [measures], beginning with the best; having constructed a pavilion there, enriched with the various classes [of deities], according to the prescribed rule. (46)
The first enclosure is known to be equal in extent to the vimāna;
from that, it is doubled in front, extending eastward from the front of the central pavilion.
Some of the best of sages desire that the outermost [gate] be double [the size];
the first enclosure is known as the gate of the directions for the gates of the celestial chariots (vimāna).
Otherwise, if the king should act differently, the kingdom will perish; there will be great calamity for the village and for the sacrificer. (49)
Therefore, with every effort, one should first perform the sequence of the enclosure,
including the gate of the celestial chariot and the gates of the directions, with a height equal to half that of the temple.
According to the available space, there should be a second enclosure and so forth for the central sanctum of the celestial mansion, the bathing area, and the temple. 51.
In the same way, one should know that among the enclosures of the sacrificial hall and the kitchen,
the door for those [within] faces inward, while the doors for others face outward.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Immediate Procedure for All Rites," beginning with the examination of the ground and ending with the installation, within the section on ritual action (*kriyādhikāra*) of the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium (*saṃhitā*) proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The Fourth Chapter: The Construction of the Root House.
Having designed the celestial mansion (vimāna) according to its nature as a house for a child, with dimensions such as five cubits and so forth, one should provide it with all ornaments.
When the stars are divided into seven parts, [the result] is increased by six, five, and four;
above the double [of that], it follows the sequence of eight and five.
The height is prescribed as five cubits according to the sequence beginning with pacification (śāntika):
namely, pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), victory (jayya), the marvelous (adbhuta), and that which fulfills all desires (sārvakāmika). || 3 ||
The sum of the longitudes, divided by three and then by eight, is known as the nakṣatra; the remainder indicates the birth sign, the sex organ, and so forth.
When the arc is multiplied by nine and divided by seven, the result gives the day of the week, beginning with Sunday.
When the height is multiplied by eight and divided by twenty-seven, the result is the number of days;
when the circumference is tripled and divided by thirty, it is declared to be the number of lunar days (tithis). || 5 ||
One should determine the life span by multiplying the height by eight and dividing by twelve;
when the number of stars is multiplied by nine and divided by eight, the remainder shall be the expenditure (vyaya).

By means of the [planetary] qualities, one should determine the birth sign, the excess of expenditure, the number of days for Mars, Saturn, and the Sun; as well as the eighth house (Vaināśika), the Moon, the Vipat and Pratyaraṇa yogas, and the eighth house (Nidhana).
One should diligently avoid the conjunctions of the *martya*, *asura*, and *ṛkṣa* yogas;
otherwise, one should calculate [the yoga] ending with the *kartṛ* or ending with the *vāstu*.
Even those [planets] that are to be avoided become auspicious through excellent yogas with perfected nectar-like substances.

On a single square, one should offer the previously mentioned portion for the characteristics of pacification (śāntika) and so forth; specifically, in the case of pacification, one should present a portion of seven and a half [squares]. || 9 ||
The sages have likewise declared that the temple of the Universal Teacher (the Buddha) should be built in the same manner;
in the case of the height for prosperity, the base should be one and a half parts of the ninth division.
Two parts shall be the height of the base (caraṇa), and four times one and a half parts shall be the height of the neck (gala);
one part shall be the measurement of the neck, and two parts shall be the elevation of the pinnacle (śikhara). || 11 ||
One part shall be the height of the *sthūpikā* (finial); such is the arrangement for the *pauṣṭika* [temple].
In the case of the *jayada* [temple] with a ten-part height, the *sthūpikā* and the *prastara* (cornice) are likewise [one part each].

One part for the neck, one and a half for the eye, one quarter for the foot, and three for the pinnacle; the height of the throat is one and a half parts—thus is the "Victory-giving" (Jayada) style described.
In the Rudra-portion, at the height of the base, the elevation of the plinth (tala) shall be one and a quarter parts;
the height of the pedestal (aṅghri) shall be two and a half parts, and the elevation of the entablature (prastara) shall be one part. || 14 ||

The height of the neck (grīvā) is one and a half parts, the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) is one and a half parts, and the elevation of the pinnacle is one and a quarter parts; thus has this wonderful [structure] been described. || 15 ||
On the high mansion at the portion of the element (dhātu), the base (tala) shall be two parts;
the height of the spire (śikhara) shall be three parts, and the elevation of the finial (sthūpikā) one part. || 16 ||
This [temple] fulfills all desires, especially when built on a single storey;
for a two-storeyed temple, rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others are performed,
and when the height of the two-storeyed pacification temple is divided into fourteen parts, [the proportions are determined].
The āyiṣṭhāna is three parts; the wheel is six parts according to the fires (three);
the foot-rising is five parts; and the pedestal is said to be two parts. || 18 ||
The *vitardikā* (balcony) is one part, the neck (*grīvā*) is two parts, and the emergence of the pinnacle (*śikhara-udaya*) is two and a half parts;
the dome (*stūpikā*) shall be four and a half parts, with an additional half-part for its finial.
In the case of an edifice for prosperity (pauṣṭika), which is twice the height of the base and divided into thirty-four parts,
the plinth (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one and a half parts, and the rise of the base (caraṇodaya) shall be double that.

The portion containing the fire-altar should have a height equal to the *prastara* (the sacrificial grass-bundle); one-sixth of that should be the height of the base (*caraṇa*), half of that again should be the height of the seat (*mañca*), and the altar (*vedī*) is fashioned with one part. || 21 ||
The height of the neck should be three and a half parts, the rise of the pinnacle five parts, and the height of the stūpa one and a half parts;
this brings all happiness.
In the thirty-third part of the Jayada [mandala], the earth is one and a half fire-units (three and a half);
the pedestal (talama) is seven parts; the platform (mañca) is six parts; and [the remaining] by fire (three).
One part for the railing, one and a half parts for the neck, five parts for the head, and one and a half parts for the height of the stūpa; thus is the Jayālaya temple described.

In a [pedestal] with a height divided into six parts, the height of the base (tala) shall be four parts, the height of the plinth (caraṇa) seven parts, and the height of the dais (mañca) three parts. || 25 ||
The vedikā (moulding) is one part, the neck (gala) is three parts, and the height of the śikhara (spire) is five parts;
the stūpikā (finial) should be one and a half quarters; thus is the wonderful [temple] described.
On the forty-fold height of the palace, there are four stories; on the ground level, there is a couch with eight legs.
One leg is half of seven parts, and the floor is fire.
The altar is formed by two fires, and the neck is elevated. || 27 ||

The height of the pinnacle (śikhara) should be seven parts, and the elevation of the finial (sthūpikā) one and a half parts; the master of all regions should employ this measurement for the pacificatory rite in the Adbhuta temple.
In a three-tiered [temple], for the rites of pacification and so forth,
when the height of the pacificatory tier is divided by twenty-four, the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of two parts,
and the emergence of the plinth (padodaya) shall consist of four parts.
The height of the pedestal (prastara) shall be one part; the [height of the] fire-altars (agni) shall be one and three-quarters parts, and the feet (aṅghri) shall be one and a half parts.
The platform (mañca) shall be one and a half parts, and the elevation of the feet (caraṇodaya) shall be two and a half parts.
The height of the throne (mañca) shall be one and a quarter parts, the terrace (vitardikā) three parts;
the height of the neck (grīvā) shall be one part of Śiva (i.e., eleven parts), and the pinnacle (śikhara) shall be three and a half times that. || 31 ||
One part shall be the height of the pinnacle; thus is the peaceful [temple] with three tiers.
In the case of a prosperous [temple], the height of the building is divided into twenty-four parts. (32)
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of two parts, and the emergence of the plinth (caraṇodaya) one part;
the height of the entablature (prastara) shall be eight parts, with three-quarters being the fire-altars (agni) and one-quarter the legs (aṅghri).

The bedframe (mañca) should be one and a half parts, the leg (pāda) one part, the base (tala) one and a half parts, the height of the altar-molding (vedikā) one part, and the measurement of the neck (grīvā) likewise. || 34 ||

In the case of the Jayada temple type, when the height of the edifice is divided into twenty-seven parts, three parts constitute the height of the pinnacle (śikhara), and one-quarter of a part is the elevation of the crest (śikhodaya).

The elevation of the face (mukhodaya) is two parts, the floor (tala) is two parts, the elevation of the base (caraṇodaya) is two parts, the height of the entablature (prastara) is two parts, and the elevation of the base (caraṇodaya) is four parts. || 36 ||

The height of the pedestal (prastara) is desired to be one and a half parts, less than a quarter; the height of the base (pāda) is two and a half parts, while the throne (mañcaka) is one and a quarter parts.
The measurement of the Soma-portion is the size of the altar; the measurement of the neck is two parts;
the height of the spire (śikhara) is four parts, and the elevation of the crest (śikhā) is one and a quarter parts. || 38 ||
In the Adbhuta [plan] on a sixty-four-fold grid, the base (adhiṣṭhāna) occupies three and a half units, while the emergence of the column (caraṇodaya) consists of seven units. || 39 ||
The platform (mañca) is equal to the base (adhiṣṭhāna), with a height of six and a half parts;
the height of the lintel (prastara) is one-third of that, and the measurement of the pillar (pāda) is six parts. || 40 ||

The *prastara* (pedestal) shall be one and a half parts, the height of the altar (*vedī*) one part of Soma (two parts), the measurement of the neck (*grīvā*) two parts, and the height of the spire (*śikhara*) five parts. || 41 ||

The master of all regions should determine the measurement of the spire (stūpī) as one part of the wing (pakṣa), and the measurement of the halls (śālā) and other parts when the height of the palace intended for all desires is divided into six or eight parts.
The height of the base (dharā) should be one-eighth of the foot (pāda);
the mañca should be equal to the base, and from that, the caraṇa should be one-eighth [of the total]. || 43 ||
The bed (mañca) should be three-quarters of a quarter-part [of the base], with its legs being one-quarter more than a mountain-part [one-and-a-half units];
the corner-posts (karṇa) should be one and a half fire-parts [three units], and the altar (vedikā) should be eleven parts. || 44 ||
The neck should be two parts, the pinnacle five parts, and the ground for the stūpikā [the finial] one part;
if these are counted as being mutually overlapping, it causes the destruction of the village and its builder.
The width should extend beyond the base by one quarter, and it should be elevated from the top of the plinth (khura) to the end of the neck (stūpī).
Alternatively, it may be one part out of six parts, or one part out of five parts.
In the case of a division by seven, one should take five parts; in a ninefold division, one part;
in a division by eleven, one part; and in a sixteenfold division, eight parts. (47)
In a single-storey vimāna, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be one-ninth of the half-diameter of the width divided by seven; the remainder shall be the thickness of the wall. 48.
In the nine-part division of the temple's width, the necklace (hāra) shall occupy one part;
the space between necklaces likewise one part, and the thickness of the wall one part. || 49 ||
In a two-storied temple, the inner sanctum (garbhageha) should consist of three parts;
when the width is divided into six parts, the width of the spire (kūṭa) should be one part.
The *śālātāra* should consist of two parts, while the remainder is for the *pañjarahāraka*.
Thus is the arrangement of the two-storied structure; now hear separately concerning the three-storied one.
One part is for the Rudra-section, likewise a necklace and the space between the pearl necklaces;
one part equal to the wall shall be the remainder, which becomes the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). || 52 ||
Some of the best of sages desire the *ādibhūmighana* [style];
in the *tāra* [measure], the *karṇakūṭa* is one-eighth part, and the *śāla* is said to be one-ninth part.
The lattice-work (pañjara) occupies one and a half parts, and the remainder is likewise for the necklace (hāra);
above that is the nose-arch (nāsikā), the mouth (oṣṭha), or the interior chamber (nīḍa) of the lattice-work.
In the upper level, however, the *rasāṃśa* (six-part) section shall consist of a *kūṭa* occupying one part;
two parts shall be the *koṣṭha*, the *śiva*, and the *nīḍa*; and the remainder shall be the space between the *hāra*s. || 55 ||
In the middle of the portion belonging to the fire of the upper level, however, is the auspicious portion of Śiva.
Thus, the arrangement of the three levels has been described according to its general outline.
Whatever has been stated regarding the authority of the site-plan (vāsādhikāra) and whatever remains unstated according to the treatises on architecture (śilpaśāstra),
[should be applied] at the emergence of the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), when it is divided into six parts consisting of the elemental portions (bhūtabhāga).
In the Sādhāraṇa style, the height is five, six, three, two, four, five, six, seven, and nine parts respectively;
however, from that point onward, it is endowed with the first half of this [measurement].
One should not construct that [pedestal] beneath the floor in an upapīṭha or in a jāṅgala region;
rather, one should construct the vedikā below the neck of the foot-path.
Some indeed say that the group of bases (pādavarga) is devoid of a railing (vedikā);
others say that the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) possesses straight walls and a fillet (paṭṭikā).
That pavilion should be enriched with the three categories (of deities), or it may have straight walls;
on the surface of the straight walls, there should be a base-platform alone, provided with a central opening.
The pavilion should be devoid of a central pillar and covered with wooden beams;
in its center is the pit for the ceremonial bathing, according to the prescribed rite for removing obstacles.
In the third part of the third [section], one should construct the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa),
either in the fourth enclosure or else in the fifth enclosure.
In the second portion, one should, endowed with devotion, construct a pond and a pavilion to its north, and plant flowering trees all around them.
One should perform daily dancing in the perpetual bathing pavilion, as well as in the assembly pavilion and the bathing pavilion. (88)
One should arrange the southern face toward the northeast or the north;
one should also fashion Śrī, Bhūta, and Garuḍa in the pavilion of the steps.
One should construct a bathing pavilion provided with four staircases;
one should perform the worship of the water-pot on the eastern staircase, the fire-oblation (homa) on the southern, and the oil-rite on the western.
Having performed the pouring of oil toward the north, the one who knows the ritual should place it in the center of the pit and bathe it.
From the sacrificial fire or from the eastern foot [of the altar], the space inside the wall is the best;
the middle of the wall is the middling; and outside the wall is the lowest. || 99 ||
One should construct a base (śilā) enriched with the three-fold purpose (trivarga), or one with straight walls;
it should be equal in height to the temple (vimāna), or its elevation is considered to be three-quarters [of that]. || 92 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Peaceful Rites and the Ornamentation of the Vimāna," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the illustrious Vaikhānasas.
Oṃ.
The Fifth Chapter:
The Installation of the First Bricks.
I shall describe the laying of the primary bricks in the construction of temples and other edifices;
at the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, one should arrange five fires.
At the conclusion of the Āghāra offerings, one should worship those [deities] while meditating upon the Vaiṣṇava deity;
the Puruṣasūkta and the Aindra hymn are to be offered into the Āhavanīya fire.
And according to the prescribed rule, one should separately recite the Āgneya hymn ending with the Vyāhṛtis,
as well as the Viṣṇusūkta, the Yāmya, and the Nairṛta, at the Anvāhārya offering.
The oblation for Viṣṇu is offered in the Gārhapatya fire; that for Varuṇa and Vāyu is offered in the Āhavanīya;
and that for Soma and Īśāna, along with the Vaiṣṇava, is offered in the Āvasathya fire.
O assembly member, having established those stones in a pit to the east of the Āhavanīya fire, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta, which is dedicated to all deities and belongs to Viṣṇu. || 5 ||
Having first worshipped the four Vedas in those [vessels],
he should bathe each of those bricks individually with seven jars of water before beginning the work.
Then, from west to east, one should place heaps of grain in those cities;
having spread five cloths over them, one should wrap them with a garment.
Having installed them there, one should worship the presiding deities of the four Vedas;
having tied the protective thread (pratisara) for them, one should lay them down separately, each one by one.
Having covered [the vessel] with flowers and clothed it above with garments at the entrance of the door,
one should bathe according to the prescribed rite in the morning during an auspicious moment when strength is present.
Taking those various [images], the installers should go to the village or the temple itself,
reciting the Śākuna Sūkta together with the Svasti Sūkta.
Having circumambulated and entered within, while indeed meditating upon the deity,
one should place bricks or stones on the southern side of the door.
From the single-syllable mantra at the end of the hymn, and from the mantras beginning with the four Vedas,
[one should place] the grass with its tips pointing north in the east, and with its tips pointing east in the south.
In the west, it should have its tip pointing north; in the north, its head facing east.
One should place a gem or gold in the center while muttering the Dhruva-sūkta.
Then, from the bed, toward the east, at the Āhavanīya fire,
one should recite the Pauruṣa hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the supreme Vaiṣṇava hymn.
Having likewise offered oblations ten times with the hymn beginning with "Ekākṣara" along with the deities of the directions, one should perform everything else as previously described. || 15 ||
In the same way, for the gate-towers (gopuras), the placement of the deity is especially recommended on the right side of the exit and on the right side of the entrance. 16.
One should construct the chamber for the ritual bathing of the bricks (iṣṭakā) either in the northeast or the southwest of all the enclosures, or to the south of the eastern gate.
One should place the first brick for the assembly hall and other structures in the northeast;
if there is no wall there, one may instead place it in the northeast of that wall.
One should not lay the first brick for any of those structures that depend on a hall;
rather, one should prepare the first brick to the southeast of the kitchen.
For all [structures] such as the Śālā and others, one should worship either the Sabhya or the Āvasathya fire;
and within the enclosures, one should worship the respective presiding deities of the retinue.
One should worship the mantras of the gatekeepers at the gates, and the mantras of the Gopuras;
one should worship the mantras beginning with the four Vedas and the Varuṇa mantra in the bathing hall.
One should worship with the Śrībhūmisūkta mantras in the assembly hall;
the deity who protects the sacrificial oblation (havis) is to be worshipped with the Śrībhūsūkta in the kitchen.
One should place a single stone in all the enclosures and other parts, reciting the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the fire with the respective mantras of the attendants, including the Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should place four bricks in the foundation.

This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as described for the Khila type. Regarding the method of laying the foundation (garbhanyāsa): one should arrange the laying of the foundation for all parts except the gateway (gopura). || 25 ||
Some lords of sages say that one should even place [the deities] within the interior of the kitchen;
however, one should install the golden door-deities within the interior of the gopura.
In the center of the kitchen, one should place five fires as protectors of the oblation;
and the vessels for the cooked food (garbhāṇi) should be placed in the waste-basket (phelā) as previously described. || 27 ||

Having prepared the womb for its fruit by means of the very path described above, and having brought the substances for the womb, one should deposit them there with the recitation of mantras. || 28 ||
Having covered it with a lid, one should place it upon a heap of grain;
it should be deposited only at night, during an auspicious lunar portion and when the moon is in a fixed sign.
If the face is turned upward, joined with auspicious [planets], and the eighth or twelfth house is pure, a Brāhmaṇa [is indicated] by a tablet above, while a king is indicated by sandals above. (30)
Likewise, for the Vaiśya and Śūdra, one should install [the image] with a reduction of one finger-breadth each;
on the southern side of the door, within the middle of the wall, at the third part.
"It must be placed near the relic; this is the firm conclusion of the scripture.
There, while recollecting Viṣṇu with the intellect, one should perform the ritual bathing as well as the worship. (32)

One should perform the ritual of acceptance (adhivāsa) and the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed for the "Khila" texts. When the temple is completed, one should again place the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā). || 33 ||
Having taken stones endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, or five bricks, as well as the *sthūpī* and the *śūla*, one should perform everything just as described for the first brick.
One should worship Adhivāsa, Homa, Snāpana, Arcanā, and so forth,
as well as Nyakṣa and the others upon the grain-seat (dhānyapīṭha), beginning with the preliminary rites.
On the foundation brick of the stūpa,
the Guru— having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite and being adorned with garlands, garments, and ornaments— should worship the Supreme Prakṛti.
One should place the bricks upon the head [of the structure] with the very mantras previously mentioned;
having recited the Bhūmisūkta, one should set down the brick at the base of the spire (sthūpī).
With the hymn beginning with "ā tvā harṣe," one should again place the pinnacle and the trident;
then, having invoked the lords of the respective directions within the temple, one should worship them once more. || 38 ||
One should worship the Vimāna-devatās and Kalpanas at the southern gate and in front of the gate; by their authority, one should arrange all the others, ensuring that they all face outward. || 39 ||
Having assigned the gatekeepers to the doors and having invoked them, one should worship them;
one should appoint the gatekeepers as those who look after the doors to some extent.
If there should be an intermediate space on both sides in succession, one should fashion Vakratuṇḍa and Durgā on the outer wall. || 41 ||
Or one should arrange the group of four [deities] on the wall of the front pavilion;
likewise, the group of four should be arranged around the neck of the temple, proceeding in order.
One should arrange the previously mentioned [deities] beginning with Prāga in the group of quarters;
one should arrange the lords of the vimānas by means of a measure of half a unit of the base (upāna). || 43 ||
One should arrange these— Indra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Nārasiṃha, and Pitāmaha—
in the directions starting from the east, endowed with their respective characteristics at the throat.
Alternatively, one should fashion the forms of Puruṣa and so forth, or the Varāha, Nārasiṃha,
or Hayagrīva, seated comfortably upon the neck.
The height of those [shrines] is said to be either equal to the fixed image (dhruvabera), or less by one-quarter, or half, or one-third. || 46 ||
Likewise, one should fashion Garuḍa upon the lintel in the corners; in the shrines of other deities, one should fashion their respective vehicles.
Or one may fashion a lion (mṛgendra) in all the temples of the gods;
likewise, one should construct an Āvasathya fire-pit facing them.
Having prepared the pitcher and sprinkled it with seven jars of water,
one should praise the office of the Hotṛ priest according to the rule, reciting each respective mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should indeed offer oblations joined with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, ending with the Vyāhṛtis;
having bathed in the morning, having invoked [the deity], and having worshipped, one should present the offering.
Worship with twenty-seven offerings is considered the highest;
worship with thirteen services is known as the middling. || 51 ||
One should offer the lowest bali-oblation combined with flowers and food;
or wherever devotion arises in the sacrificer, there he should offer it. || 52 ||
Having installed them, one should indeed perform worship there constantly;
one should arrange the lords of the gates within the groups of pillars at the gate-towers.
Having fashioned those deities upon the neck of the chariot, one should worship them;
or else [one may worship] Nārasiṃha, or Durgā, or Sudarśana.

Having performed the visualization and invocation, one should worship [the deity] eternally as before; likewise, if one desires to perform the *kautuka* (auspicious thread-binding) for these [deities], it should be done in that same manner. || 55 ||
Having installed the *kautuka* (the marriage-thread), one should worship it daily before that [image];
or, having prepared a pedestal, one should worship it on its respective side. || 56 ||
One should worship the four Vedas, starting with the East, in the bathing hall,
as well as in the sacrificial hall and in the assembly pavilion for Indra.
One should worship Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, in the pavilion for water-sports, or in other pavilions associated with their respective world-protectors (dikpālas). || 58 ||
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena according to one's capacity, one should present the offerings;
and when these [rites] are completed, at the conclusion of the Vāstuhoma.

Having prepared the pitcher according to the rite with its respective Vaiṣṇava mantra ending in the Vyāhṛtis, and having performed the sacrifice, one should again invoke [the deity] and worship him. || 60 ||
Having established the Lord of Gods in the pavilion and other structures at an auspicious moment,
and having worshipped the twenty-seven lunar mansions, one should cause him to enter within.
Having established the sacrificial fire in the sacrificial hall at an auspicious moment,
and having offered a hundred oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should perform the regular daily oblation.
One should worship the protector of the oblation in the southeast within the kitchen;
having duly honored the God of gods, one should thereafter perform the act of cooking.
Upon the walls of the pavilions and other structures, after the application of whitewash,
one should depict the forms of the Lord’s victorious sports according to one's preference.
Whatever the agent desires to create, having fashioned it as exceedingly beautiful and endowed with all characteristics by means of the action of manifestation, [he brings it forth]. 65.
At the conclusion of opening the eyes without mantras, he performs the Vāstuhoma sacrifice;
likewise, having performed the opening of the eyes according to the previously stated procedure.
Having performed the purification of the fixed point (dhruva-śuddhi), one should place the aupāsana fire-pit;
then, having prepared the water-jar according to the rite, one should sprinkle it with seven jars of water.
Having placed the water-pot upon the altar and likewise the *pratisara* therein,
and having performed the *aupāsana* rite, one should indeed praise the office of the *hautra*.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta, as well as the mantras prescribed therein, one should worship him one hundred and eight times.
Having invoked [the deity] in the morning and performed worship, one should present the sacrificial offerings;
one should arrange a seat accompanied by the three Vedas before each [deity].
Having invoked [the deity] there and worshipped it thoroughly, one should dismiss it at the conclusion of the worship;
in this very same manner, the installation and worship of images reflected in cloth or mirrors are performed.
When the laying of the crown-bricks for the temple has been performed in this manner,
one should then take up the *śūla* (the ritual stake) here, having grasped it with the *śūlagrahaṇa-mantra*.
Having installed the trident according to the prescribed rite, one should fashion the permanent image (dhruvabera);
or, having properly taken up a stone slab, one should install it as described therein.
One should have the permanent image (dhruvabera) fashioned according to the distinctions of yoga, enjoyment, and so forth;
it is of three types: seated, reclining, and standing. || 74 ||
Each of those—yoga, bhoga, as well as vīra and viraha—is fourfold; this has already been explained by me previously. (75)
One should fashion the god who bears the discus and conch as both engaged in yoga and in enjoyment;
one should fashion him endowed with the discus, conch, and mace according to the path of heroes.
One should indeed fashion a mace in the left hand and the gesture of granting boons (vara) in the right for the sake of victory;
likewise, one should visualize the God as being without weapons and free from passion.
If the permanent image (dhruvabera) is made of copper, having had it fashioned so that it is clearly beautiful in all its limbs,
one should install it on every auspicious festival day (parvan).
Having consecrated [the image] with pure water, one should also adorn it with garments and other ornaments;
if there is no established single deity, [one may use] an image made of stone that is devoid of color.
Alternatively, having placed the iron image in the portion belonging to Brahmā, one should worship it;
for when an iron image has been consecrated, the procedure is according to the rite for a single image (ekabera). || 79 ||
Furthermore, in a place protected from fear of thieves, enemies, and the like, which has been worshipped,
he should construct a stone [image] of that [deity] according to his available means and proportions.
Having established the mobile [deity] therein, one should perform the daily worship;
once the fear of thieves and enemies has subsided, one should remove the previous [image]. (81)
Having invited [the deity] from the stone image, one should worship it in the metal image;
or else, one may fashion a stone image according to the proportions of the metal image.
Having fashioned and consecrated the immovable [image], according to the procedure for establishing the permanent image (dhruvārcā),
one should then arrange the festivals for that very [image] which is made of metal or wood.
In accordance with the fixed position of Dhruva, one should place all those attendants in their respective enclosures;
when Dhruva is seated, they should be made to remain seated, and when he is standing, they should be made to remain standing.
One should likewise imagine them as seated, standing, or even reclining upon a bed;
namely Viṣvaksena, Vidhneśa, Rohiṇī, and the Mothers.
And Jyeṣṭhā is always seated; such is the observation of the ancients regarding the extent of Dhruva, reaching either to the armpits, or to the breasts, or to the navel.

One should fashion the Brahma, Īśa, and Sūrya [images] as measured [by the main icon], or one may arrange them to be equal to it; and one should make the Kautuka [image] with dimensions of one-third, one-fourth, or other such proportions of that.

One should not fashion the retinue according to the measurement exceeding that of the Lord of Devas. Regarding the rule for the materials used for the images: the attendants (pārṣadas) should be made from the same material as the permanent image (dhruvabera). || 88 ||
Viṣvaksena, Ravi, Skanda, Durgā, and Garuḍa—there would be no fault even on a mountain; such is the view of the ancestors. (89)
Likewise, when the assembly members are joined with constant curiosity,
one should not perform the worship of Dhruva in the worship of Dhruva in a contrary manner.

The fixed positions for the *beras* and the specific facial expressions for the various types of *beras* must be established; likewise, the gatekeepers should be appointed as observers of the entrance.
The lords of the celestial palaces (vimāna) are oriented outward, with their abodes consisting of mansions and temples. || 91 ||
Between Īśāna and Soma, Amita faces south;
likewise Śrī, Bhūta, Ari, Dhvaja, Ambhoja, Yūtheśa, and Akṣahā.
The [deities] to be visualized are indeed outward-facing, while Viṣṇu is considered to be facing inward;
one should place them before the deity, each separately in their respective enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Anapāyin and Śrībhūta, as well as Garuḍa, are stationed in the first enclosure;
Cakra, Dhvaja, Abja, and Yūtheśa are in the second enclosure and those following.
These are declared to be non-forsaking, accompanied by Viṣvaksena;
others, who dwell taking refuge in the ramparts, are the observers of the site (vāstu).
Resembling molten gold, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
she was adorned above her forehead by three flower-crests.
Her left hand ended in a lotus, her thick breasts bound by a bodice, her other arm extended, and adorned with all ornaments. (97)
In the month of Phālguna, one should meditate upon that Śrī, who originates from the north, possesses the seed-syllable 'A' as her primary mark such as the Śrīvatsa,
and flows out from the right side with the swan as her vehicle.
On his left side is Mahī, dark-complexioned and adorned with all ornaments;
born under the constellation Revatī in the month of Vaiśākha, she holds a lotus in her right hand.
With one hand extended and a face resembling the bright moon,
she was borne by a great cātaka bird and was accompanied by the syllables "Lakṣmī" as her prefix.
Some desire the two hands for Śrī and Bhūmi in reverse order;
Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu [are placed] with one knee bent, seated at the base of the southern wall.
Then, in the month of Phālguna, there was Mārkaṇḍeya, the worshipper, who wore a sacred thread and a crown of matted hair, resembled molten gold, and was the lord of Rohiṇī.
On the left side, Bhṛgu should be depicted, with the luster of vermilion;
born under Rohiṇī in the month of Vaiśākha, he is the renowned Lord Khyāti, holding a flower in his hand.
Whatever has not been stated here, all that should be understood as it was described in the Purāṇa:
Brahmā and Śaṅkara are seated upon a lotus-throne; he is golden-hued, four-faced. || 104 ||
Holding a water-pot and a rosary in his hands, with matted locks upon his head and four arms, he has a swan as his vehicle and is called the Lord of Sāvitrī. 105.
Ambarīṣa was born to Śauṣika in the month of Caitra under the asterism Abhijit;
he had a water-pot as his emblem, and the one named Brahmā was situated to the south of Dhruva.
To the north of the fixed image (dhruvabera), Hara should be depicted as resembling a coral fire, holding an axe and a trident, with four arms, and wearing a tiger-skin garment. || 107 ||
He has a crescent moon as his crest-jewel and is endowed with three tawny eyes;
he is Ārdrāja in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and Śiva is known as Caṇḍīśa and Śaiṣika.
Facing south, the Lord of Pārvatī, whose vehicle is the bull-bannered one,
who holds a trident and wields the Pināka bow, is to be worshipped here.
In the second enclosure, Kautuka, are Śiva and the others:
Śiva is Śubheśvara, dark-complexioned, holding a water-jar and a banner;
his sound is like the roar of a kettledrum, he is clad in red garments, and his vehicle is an elephant. || 110 ||
Viśva is dark-complexioned like a black antelope, has Śuddheśa as his banner, and a horse is his vehicle; his attendant Mitra is dark-complexioned and wears reddish garments.
Sruvadhvaja, Mitreśa, Atri, Śyāma, Satīśvara, Juhudhvaja—who is red in color—and Ruruvāhana; || 112 ||
In the month of Māgha, under the asterism Rohiṇī, those who were turned outward (the Bahirmukhas) were born:
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanātana, and Sananda.

Those born under Puṣya in the month of Taiṣya should be meditated upon as having a golden luster, wearing white garments, bearing the insignia of a kūrca, and all being celibate students of the Veda. || 114 ||
Dhātṛ and the others are the deities of the doors:
Dhātṛ, who resembles a bamboo leaf, rides a chariot and faces north;
Puṣpaketu, the lord of Sandhinī, wearing red garments, is on the right.
Vidhātṛ, who resembles the color of a parrot’s wing, whose hair is tied upward, who has an elephant as his vehicle,
whose banner is a serpent, and who wears white garments— these two are to be worshipped on the two door-panels.

Bhuvaṅga has his head to the south and his feet to the north; he has eyes on his forehead, is the Lord of Pleasure, has a flame-bannered fire as his emblem, and possesses the luster of the petals of a blue lotus. || 117 ||
In the month of Māgha, he is born from the hand; in the heart, he has the bull as his vehicle.
Pataṅga is downward-facing and upward-facing, with a white luster, born from the hand of Pauṣya.
The lord of Bharaṇī has his head turned upward; he possesses a horse as his vehicle and a banner.
Clinging to the upper stone of a door-panel, he is pure and should be worshipped while dressed in red garments.
The Lord has the luster of gold, is slightly mixed with silver, faces the north, wears red garments, bears the bull as his emblem, and has the elephant as his vehicle. || 120 ||
Nāgeśa is remembered as being born under the asterism Hasta in the month of Māgha;
Varaṇa has the luster of a golden lotus and is slightly mixed with silver. || 121 ||
Dharaṇīśa, born under the asterism Phālguna, whose vehicle is a chariot and who has an arrow as his banner,
is to be worshipped here on the left side of the doorway.
At each door, one should properly worship these six deities beginning with Dhātṛ.
Maṇika and the others are the door-keepers;
Maṇika is red in color and likewise wears garments of parrot-feather hue.
Resplendent with the sacred thread and deerskin, tawny-eyed and wearing matted hair, he joined his palms at his heart; he was the lord of the twilight, bearing a sacrificial ladle as his banner.
Having observed the door situated to the right of the exit from the gate, one should worship the two-armed [deity] born in the month of Caitra under the Rohiṇī asterism. || 125 ||

And on the left [shoulder], one should worship Saumyajā, born in the month of Śrāvaṇa, who is like twilight, golden-hued, with two arms, wearing garments of flowers, and joined in the añjali gesture at her heart. (126)
And on the right side outside that second gate,
[he saw] Śātātapa, Divyeśa, and Kuśadhvaja, the lord of sages.

In the month of Caitra, however, one should worship him who was born under Rohiṇī—wearing matted locks on his crest, four-armed, resembling crystal in luster, clad in blue garments, and having Ruru as his vehicle. || 128 ||

One should worship the ascetic Sandhīśa on the left side—dark-complexioned, riding a ruru deer, born under the Puṣya asterism in the month of Phālguna, and bearing a tuft of hair as his banner. || 129 ||
One should worship Śrībhūta, who wears red garments, has two arms, and matted hair,
facing outward in the middle of the staircase.
Virājeśa, Bhūtaketu, and Jyeṣṭha, born under Dhaniṣṭhā in the month of Jyeṣṭha;
Nyakṣa and others—Nyakṣa resembling a blade of dūrvā grass—and Prajñāptīśa, who is clad in crimson garments. || 131 ||
With a hawk as his vehicle and banner, holding a staff in his hand, and making a heroic roar,
he was born facing outward under the Rohiṇī asterism in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Vivasvān is red in color, and likewise Utsādinīpati;
Bhiṇḍivāladhvaja has a staff as his emblem and a gavaya for his vehicle. || 133 ||
Born under the Maghā constellation in the month of Proṣṭhapada, Mitra has two arms and wears blue garments;
he is the protector of many creatures and resembles a śarabha beast.
Kapotavāhana, Meghanādarava, Dvibhuja, Raktavarṇa, Pūpaketu, and Halāyudha. || 135 ||
One born in the month of Jyeṣṭha should worship Dhāmapāla in the west during the month of Vaiśākha;
indeed, one should worship this deity named Paṅktīśa on the wall facing him.
Kṣattṛ, Padmanibha, Vāṇīnātha, Satāmbara, Kuśadhvaja, Cakrahētu, and Sāvādrāṇākavāhana. || 137 ||
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the two-armed deity born from the Śravaṇa asterism is to be worshipped in the north;
he is Haviḥpāla, Haviḥpāla, Asita, Vidyutpati, and Kālāgni, the wielder of the trident. || 138 ||
Born under Rohiṇī in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he is likewise clad in red garments;
he is the Lord of Flowers, dark-complexioned like a flower, and yet he has men as his vehicle.
Puṣpāyudha, Mānaketu, Citra, Anūrādhaja, Balīśa, Bālikeśa, Adridhvaja, Daṇḍī, and Sitāsita. || 140 ||
In the month of Caitra, the son of Soma (Budha) has the lion as his vehicle and wears red garments.
The world-protectors, beginning with Indra, are as follows:
Indra is green like a crop, two-armed, and holds the thunderbolt as his weapon. (141)
He is the Lord of Śacī, wears yellow garments, is born of Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise in Śrāvaṇa;
he is crowned with a diadem, wears a crown, carries a staff, sits upon a peacock, and is unarmed. || 142 ||

Adorned with all ornaments, bearing a bamboo banner, sounding like a cloud, riding upon an elephant, and the lord of Śacī; joined with the seed-syllable "Ja," he is Indra, the husband of Śacī, and likewise called Puruhūta—one should then worship Purandara. Facing inward, one should worship Indra himself. In the month of Kārttika, he is born from Agni in the southeast; for he is indeed that very one. Resembling the Kiṃśuka flower, holding a spear in his hand, wearing earrings, adorned with armlets, and likewise clothed in garments of peacock feathers.

He who has the monkey as his banner, whose vehicle is the ram, who is the lord of Svāhā, or likewise the lord of chariots; who is joined with the seed-syllable *Ra*, and whose face bestows all things—having prostrated before him while he is seated, one should especially worship him. Born indeed under the asterism Bharaṇī in the month of Mithuna (Gemini), he is dark-complexioned and wears red garments. He is endowed with a serpent-banner, and his vehicle is the buffalo. His seed-syllable is the letter *Pha*. He is accompanied by the goddess Śukāṅgī, and likewise makes a sound like the ringing of a bell. He wears a diadem and a crown, carries a staff, and likewise holds a noose in his hand.
Thus the reading is seen:
"Born in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the constellation Kṛttikā in the fire [element], he resembles a heap of kiñjalka flowers, has red eyes, and has goats as his vehicle. (143)
His two goddesses are Svāhā and Svadhā; his power is indeed his weapon.
Yama, who possesses the luster of a blue lotus, was born under the constellation Bharaṇī in the month of Phālguna.
Satyavrata, Āpatin, Daṇḍin, Pāśin, Mahiṣavāhana, Ārambhādhipati, Taiṣya, Mūlaja, and Bhañjanīpati [are the lords of the asterisms]. || 145 ||
He has a tiger as his vehicle, holds a trident in his hand, and possesses three eyes;
born under the asterism Śatabhiṣaj in the month of Caitra, Varuṇa is blue in color.
Holding a staff and a noose, clad in red garments, riding upon an elephant, with golden hair and a lion-banner, he stands facing the east in the western quarter. || 147 ||
In the month of Kārttika, Vāyu is born under Svāti; he resembles clear water, holds a trident in one hand and a sword in the other, and his goddess is considered to be Añjanā.
The hero Kubera, wearing yellow garments, with a black antelope on his chariot banner and holding a staff in his hand,
has a swan-drawn chariot as his vehicle.
The Lord of the Earth, having three feet, born under Śraviṣṭhā in the month of Kārtika, is dark-complexioned, wears red garments, faces the south, and stands in the north. || 150 ||
He who was born under Ārdrā in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Īśāna;
he has the hue of the Pāṭalī flower and has the bull as his emblem and vehicle. || 151 ||
Trilocana, Ambikānātha, Śūlapāṇi, Carmadhṛt, Mārtāṇḍa, and Padmahasta, joined by the Maṇḍala on the back. || 152 ||
