Whether four-footed or two-footed, having the luster of a Palāśa flower, it is born under the asterism Hasta in the month of Śrāvaṇa; and for the Goddess, there are Reṇukā and Suvarcalā.
A chariot yoked with seven horses is called a vehicle;
Anūru is the charioteer, a serpent is the banner, and the horse itself is the steed. 154.
Viṣvaksena was seated between Śānta and Someśa, facing south;
he possessed everything like Hari, except for the śrīvatsa mark and the sacred thread. || 155 ||
The etymology of the word *pralamba-sūtra* is as follows:
during the battle with the demon Pralamba, the single thread of the sacred cord (*apavīta*) of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was severed by his weapon and thus hung down (*pralambita*). 156.
Indeed, at his request, that [sacred thread] was worn by him exactly so; from that time forth, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has maintained the state of having a hanging sacrificial thread.
That [line] is widely renowned in this world by the name "Asādhāraṇa";
that thread, having been cut, hangs down from the right breast. (158)
Having contracted his right foot and extended his left foot, he sat together with Jayā, holding a flower in his hand and resembling fire in brilliance. || 160 ||
Alternatively, for the increase of one's station, he should be worshipped holding a mace and a spear;
if he has four arms, he should hold a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
The two goddesses have the luster of green grain; everything else is as before.
Likewise, one born under Pūrvāṣāḍhā in the month of Bhādrapada [is described]. || 162 ||
They declare that the best [form of worship] is one joined with a permanent festoon;
the middling is that which consists of a single image (ekabera); and the lowest is the worship of the pedestal alone. || 163 ||
One should fashion Viṣvaksena according to the favorable measurements of the village and the patron, or else in accordance with the proportions of the primary image (mūlabera).
If [the suffixes] āya and so forth are not to be applied due to the influence of the primary form (mūlabera), then Garutmān, Garuḍa, whose form is the Veda, is like molten gold. || 165 ||
Wearing a garment of peacock feathers, equipped with a rattle-drum and a girdle, adorned with a network of tinkling bells, and wearing earrings, armlets, and necklaces; 166.
Bound upon the twenty-seven [constellations], radiant with the crown of Kubera, he was born under the asterism Svāti during the month of Taiṣya; likewise, his vehicle is the wind.
The *śiras-sāman* of the *trivṛt* is the *gāyatra*, the eye itself;
the *ātman* is the *sāman* called *stoma*, and likewise the body is the *vāmadevya*. || 168 ||
The Bṛhat and Rathantara are its two wings, the Yajñāyajñiya is its tail;
the Vedic meters are indeed its limbs, and the sacrificial formulas (yajus) are remembered as its hooves. || 169 ||
Having meditated thus, one should worship Viśa for the increase of vehicles.
Vakratuṇḍa has the luster of coral, possesses four arms, a single tusk, and the face of an elephant. (170)
In the month of Caitra, one born under the Śraviṣṭhā constellation should offer plantains, sweetmeats, sugarcane, and ghee;
Ananta is on the right outside the city gate, while Ananta of white luster is on the left.
In Vaiśākha, Āśleṣā and Aja are present, as well as the two-armed Lord of the Suras;
the Lord of Serpents stands in the midst of his circle of hoods with palms joined in reverence.
Bhauma has a spear in his hand and is likewise Bhauma, with the luster of a Kadamba flower;
his goddess is Kumudā, and his vehicle is Varāha.
Likewise, Mars arising in the month of Jyeṣṭha under the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, as well as Saturn,
the son of the Sun, would make [the person] black in appearance and likewise clothed in garments of kuśa grass and bark.
In the month of Māgha, under the asterism Revatī, he was born with a blue lotus as his banner;
his vehicle is a chariot yoked with excellent serpents.

One should visualize Bṛhaspati as golden-yellow, situated in the midst of a grove of plantain trees, bearing a banner of kuśa grass, mounted upon a swan-chariot, and resplendent in garments dark like flowers. 176.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, under the asterism Tiṣya, one should indeed fashion the goddess Tārā and Budha;
Budha should be made resembling a grain of rice and equipped with a bow and arrows.
Accompanied by the goddess Buddhā, with Vāmadeva as his mount, he is born under the asterism Śraviṣṭhā in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
he holds a mirror and a banner. (178)
Śukra is bright and of a reddish hue; he wears matted locks and garments of bark.
He is the lord of Jayantī, has the sky as his chariot, and is born of fortune in the month of Māgha.
Jāhnavī [is] Jāhnavī,
possessing a white and red luster, likewise clad in yellow garments;
she divides a single petal with her hand and smells that lotus.
In the month of Aśvayuj, on the day of the Revatī constellation, the wise man should fashion an image of Gaṅgā, adorned with all ornaments, who was born under the red banner. || 181 ||
Candra Ātreya should place [the letter] Harivat in the middle of the cool orb;
therein, that which resembles a sprout and is mixed with white is known as Āvartaka. (182)
One should depict the king with two arms, likewise as one who cherishes Rohiṇī;
born under Mṛgaśiras in the month of Caitra, he is mounted upon a vehicle consisting of a horse and a chariot.
One should likewise represent the Goddess holding a lotus, seated upon a lotus-throne within a mandala that has upward-pointing filaments and spreading petals. 84.
The wise man should have the goddess Śrī fashioned as being consecrated by the elephants of the quarters with jars made of gold, or alternatively, as sporting with Viṣṇu. || 185 ||
The seven Rohiṇīs have peacocks for their vehicles; these Rohiṇīs are fond of lizards as their banners,
wear garments of flowers, hold flowers in their hands, and are adorned with parrot-feather cloaks.
Born under Rohiṇī, they are ever devoted to their mother and bringers of grace to the world; the Earth, the sustainer,
should be made as a nurse, fierce and adorned with tusks.
She wears a child’s crown and an upper garment, holds a trident, and has six arms;
her eyes are red and fierce, her outer corners are wide, and she is formidable with a frown and a wrathful expression. (188)
One should perform the ritual with a body as fierce as that of a man or woman;
Jyeṣṭhā holds a skull in her left hand and has curly red hair. 189.
Seated upon a camel-throne, accompanied by Aṭṭahāsa, born under the constellation of Bharaṇī in the month of Caitra, and endowed with a banner marked by a meteor. || 190 ||
In the seat known as Tripīṭhaka, the wise practitioner should place Jyeṣṭhā in the position of the Prasāra posture;
she should not be placed in a divine or human portion.
Carrying a full vessel of treasures in her left hand and a flower in her right, she is auspicious and slightly pot-bellied.
She was adorned with red flowers and garments, possessing exceedingly full and swaying breasts;
and at her right side was a son, equal in height to her arm.
He is yellow in color, named Samṛṣaka, and wears white garments;
he sits upon that throne, holding a staff in his hand, and is exalted.
The head of that [liṅga] has the bull as its portion, slightly raised as previously described;
on its left is his daughter, Sumāñjalī, who is most dearly cherished.
As she sat upon half of his seat,
her body was enveloped in red and blue light, and her lotus-like hand held a red lotus.
With one leg extended and the other drawn up in a seated posture, let her vehicle be a chariot yoked with fifty donkeys. (197)

One should fashion me with four arms, bearing the banner of a black crow, born in the month of Jyeṣṭha during Mārgaśīrṣaka, and measuring nine and a half tālas, as did the seven sages headed by Bhṛgu. || 198 ||
Seated in the Brahma posture with both hands in the Brahma-añjali gesture, his left hand is placed on his lap, palm upward and extended, and [the other hand] is upon it.
Therefore, one should hold the right hand raised above that;
the gaze directed toward the tip of the nose by oneself is known as the yogic gaze (yogadṛṣṭi). || 200 ||
Bhṛgu should hold a water-pot in his upraised right hand,
and in his left hand, a purified bamboo staff (brahmadaṇḍa) provided with a sling.
One should fashion [the deity] with the luster of vermilion, radiant with matted locks and a crown, possessing copper-colored face and eyes, having a beautiful countenance, and clad in a deer skin.

Seated upon the Brahmāsana, Marīci, who possessed the brilliance of fire, was mounted on a six-legged vehicle; he held a garland as his weapon, was endowed with excellent intelligence, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
His birth occurs in the month of Āṣāḍha under the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī;
his emblem is said to be the Brahmā-flag, and everything else is like that of Bhṛgu.
This Pulastya, resembling gold in luster, is seated upon the Brahma-throne;
he is the Lord of Affection, bears the conch as his weapon, and likewise has bees as his vehicle.
Born under Anurādhā in the month of Caitra, he was named Ūrvāṇa; his emblem is a banner, and he is copper-colored like Pulaha, seated in the posture of Pulastya.
The lord of patience (the Earth), patience and fortitude, and Tulādhāra were his vehicles;
he had a son born of a hand (Hanumān) and was joined by horses in the month of Āśvayuja; everything else was like that of Bhṛgu.
In the month of Vaiśākha, the lord is Sannati, the season is Śukla, and he is born under the asterism Hasta;
his vehicle is said to be a mare, and everything else is like that of Bhṛgu.
Then Vasiṣṭha, who is yellow like turmeric, as well as Arunghatiśa, are joined with the banner of Ūrvaṇa;
their vehicle is named Vaṣaṭkāra.
Born under the Puṣya asterism in the month of Taiṣya, his weapon is the Brahmadaṇḍa;
Atri, the husband of Anasūyā, is his [son], and his vehicle is honey-colored.
And Vaṣaṭkāra, whose banner was the Urvāṇa, born from Śravaṇa, was born on the full moon day of Kārtika; everything else was just as it had been for Bhṛgu.
Marīci and the others have two arms; one should likewise place the left hand on the lap and the right hand above it, with the palm facing upwards.
Marīci, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and I myself—these are proclaimed as the seven sages (ṛṣis). || 213 ||
Sambhūti, Kṣamā, Prīti, Sannati, Ūrjā, Anasūyikā,
and Arundhatī— these should be placed in order on the seat together with them.
Gaviṣṭha is indeed a great being, possessing the luster of an indīvara petal;
he wears a crown and yellow garments, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 215 ||
He is Satyalocaneśa, the bearer of the staff (Daṇḍin), whose vehicle is the jar-born (Kumbhakavāhana);
he is proclaimed as Bheruṇḍaketu, and likewise as Mārudravara.
In Caitra, one born under the Citrā constellation shall have a woman as his face, with eyes of truth and goodness;
Vāyu shall be dark-complexioned, sword in hand, known by the name Plavaka, and having a serpent as his vehicle. || 217 ||
Śaṅkhadhvaja, Hrasvarava, Udāyinīśvara, and he who is remembered as Pītavastra were born in the month of Māgha under the constellation Svātī. || 218 ||
Agni is golden-hued, has flames for hair, and bears the Śakti;
he has the submarine mare as his vehicle, is the lord of Svāhā, and has a monkey upon his banner. || 219 ||

In the month of Proṣṭhapada, one born under the asterism Agnibhūta, as well as those wearing blue garments—these three, along with their respective goddesses, one should worship in separate locations. (220)
Water,
water, and likewise one of the color of collyrium, riding upon a bull,
and wearing yellowish-brown garments— this is the fourfold Bhūta. || 221 ||
The sage Śātātapa declared that water is neuter;
likewise, the banner called Galaka and the sound of a loud-voiced woman [are neuter]. || 222 ||
Likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, at the conjunction with the moon and the Saumya constellation,
one should worship her who is as swift as a wave, dark-complexioned like a doe, clad in white garments, and wearing a diadem.
[He saw] the goddess Kṣamā with a lotus in her hand, lotus-eyed and well-adorned;
and Sāvitrī, who possesses the Sāvitrī mantra, bearing a banner, dressed in white garments, and standing firmly composed.
One should visualize the Vidyā as four-armed, red in color, and seated upon a lotus made of nectar. || 225 ||
In his right hand he holds a rosary and in his left a water-pot;
furthermore, in his right hand he displays the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and in his left a book.
Furthermore, when the moon is in the asterism Punarvasu during the month of Taiṣya, she is to be worshipped there with special offerings.
There resides the Lord of All,
who resembles a rain-cloud and whose vehicle is marked by the six-footed bee and the banner.
Wearing white garments and carrying a staff, he likewise has the sound of a water-pot;
born under the Puṣya asterism in the month of Taiṣya, he is clad in white and has a camel as his vehicle.
The seven Mothers [should be worshipped], as well as Brahmāṇī, who is tawny, four-faced, and four-armed,
holding a water-pot and a rosary, and adorned with a mass of matted hair. || 229 ||
In the month of Caitra, one should worship her who has a banner of *darbha* grass, whose vehicle is a swan, who arises on the southern day,
who is beloved by rivers, who is dark-complexioned, and who possesses four arms with a trident in her hand.
A swan is declared to be her banner, and a cow her vehicle.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one born under the Revatī asterism is red-robed and three-eyed. || 239 ||
On her head she bears a single braid; she is of terrible form and fearsome.
She is Vaiśākhinī, golden-hued, four-armed, and holds a spear in her hand.
The goddess Guhādhipā, who has a lizard as her banner and wears red garments,
likewise arises in the month of Jyeṣṭha under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Vaiṣṇavī, dark-complexioned, bearing the conch and discus, dressed in blue garments,
born under the asterism Śravaṇa in the month of Phālguna, has Garuḍa as her vehicle and banner.
Vārāhī is black in complexion and has the face of a boar;
she holds a conch and a parasol, and her banner and vehicle are those of a boar. || 235 ||
In the month of Pauṣa, she is born under the asterism Śravaṇā; she wears red garments, has four arms, is sapphire-blue in complexion, and holds a thunderbolt in her hand. (236)
Clad in white garments, with a vehicle called the parrot-beak,
bearing a banner with the leaf of Viṣṇu, she is born under the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra in the month of Māgha.
Kālī has a terrifying face, a dark body, and rides upon a camel;
her banner bears the mark of a piśāca, and the hair on her head has the luster of flames of fire.
Born from Yama under the Proṣṭhapada constellation, she holds a trident, a noose, and a skull-cup;
her eyes and outer corners are blood-red, and her face is distorted by a frown.
Like the faces of men and women, they were adorned with fangs;
they possessed three eyes, wore crescent moons as crowns, and were equipped with serpent ornaments.
The seven Mothers are said to be seated in the prasāra posture.
Regarding the characteristics of the prasāra posture: having contracted the right foot and extended the left foot. (241)
This is called the *prasāra* posture; it is common to all [deities].
Skanda may have six arms or four arms, and his complexion is like that of a *skanda* (palāśa) flower. || 242 ||
The child [Skanda] is endowed with a crown, is likewise the husband of Devayānī, has a peacock as his vehicle, holds a spear, and has a cock as his emblem. || 243 ||
In the month of Phālguna, an elephant born under the Kṛttikā constellation shall be his vehicle;
that elephant should be nine cubits in length and seven cubits in height.
Half of the length [is the first part], then a quarter, and the remainder is declared to be the *nāha* (girth).
From that, one should know the *prādeśika* (span) for both the head and the chest. || 245 ||
The circumference of the navel is half that of the neck;
the circumference of the two limbs is one-quarter less than that of the neck; and the circumference of the upper arm is one-quarter less than that of the limb.
Therefore, from exactly one-third [of that measure], the circumference at the tip of the hand is stated; one should likewise make the base of the hand such that its tip is not raised.
The measurement of his nails is desired to be four finger-breadths;
from this, everything regarding their other limbs should be understood. || 248 ||
Except for Airāvata, the blue color is declared for the others;
the girth of the necks of these elephants is said to be twelve [units] in length. (249)
The height of the lordly elephant should be nine cubits and two spans;
its temples have the luster of coral, and its body is said to be white. (250)
Likewise, one should apply the proportions for their height according to the proper method;
thus, the Nīlahastin should be auspicious, possessing the luster of a sapphire.
The vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu in his Vārāha incarnation is proclaimed to be five cubits long, with its back covered in scales and half of its body being that of a boar. || 253 ||
Half of that should be the height of the ear-ornament (karṇa), its circumference being six finger-breadths;
at the tip, the circumference of the portion should be such that the crest (śikhā) consists of six finger-breadths.
The head of that [image] should be broad, and its beak four finger-breadths long;
the feet should be the length of one arm, and both soles should likewise be the length of one arm.
The five syllables are described as beautiful and possessing five colors;
they appear exactly like peacocks, and likewise appear as dark-blue (mecaka).
If it is divine, one should perform the ritual for the gods with an increased body;
the hand, the foot, and likewise the span—this triad is remembered as being equal [to the previous measure]. || 257 ||

The crest should be declared to be six finger-breadths in width, as prescribed by Time; likewise, the wise artisan should fashion the throat, the fleshy protuberance, and the beauty [of the face]. || 258 ||
One should fashion a discus; the discus should have a human form, with its head topped by a wheel.
One should make the discus face outward, resembling a fire-tipped arrow.
Muṣṭikeśa, Dhūmaketu, Bhānuheti,
as well as Vivṛttavāhana, and Kārtika born from the Kṛttikās.
The best of preceptors should install it in the assembly pavilion, either one foot shorter than the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa), or even one cubit shorter. || 261 ||
The Garuda is situated upon the banner;
therefore, one should fashion his image in the place of the banner according to the prescribed rite.
One should make Garuda stand upon the banner, with another [image] placed upon the seat.
Having properly contracted the left foot and extended both arms,
[he should hold] with the single right hand either a lotus or a water-lily.
Then, the stalk should be eight finger-breadths long, and the portion for the flower's mandala;
one should fashion the face in relation to the flower, joyful, smiling, and proud.
This is declared to be beneficial for the village; for the sake of victory, another method is desired:
the seat should be pressed down with the knee by either the left or the other [right] leg. 235.
One should also cause him to smell the earth and gaze upward,
seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), the imperishable abode of bliss.
For the benefit of the sages, the wise man should fashion the deity;
he should make the banner face eastward, and he should not fashion the deity looking toward the banner while standing.
If one is unable to perform the ritual for the banner in this manner within the pavilion,
one should instead draw and worship the deity of the banner, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), there.
In the constellation Śravaṇā, there was indeed a conch or a kettledrum with the wind as its vehicle;
and in Vaiśākha, under the two stars of Vāyu, the excellent sound of a bell was born. || 269 ||
One should fashion the banner as having the luster of gold and blue cloth;
the conch should be made of water-born [shell] like the moon, joined with a conch upon the crown.
[He saw] the Lord of Varuṇī, who has the luster of a conch shell and wears blue garments, with two arms;
he possesses a banner that moves through the sky, and likewise a multitude of weapons that move through the sky. || 271 ||
One should meditate upon the Being who has the form of a being, who arises from the wind, whose vehicle is a swan,
who was born under Rohiṇī in the month of Āṣāḍha, and who has his hands joined in the añjali gesture at his heart.
The arrangement of the retinue depends upon the principal image;
one should arrange the retinue according to the principal image itself—extending to the arms, or to the breasts, or even to the navel, in the case of the Dhruva [image]. || 273 ||
One should fashion the Brahmā, Īśa, and Amita [images], or the Sun, as equal in size to those;
and one should make the Kautuka [image] with a measurement of one-third of that, or one part, and so forth.
One should not arrange the retinue according to the measurement exceeding that of the Lord of Devas;
if it is the consecration of a single image (ekabera), one should establish [the attendants] in the Brahma-pada.
I shall now describe the sacrificial pedestals (balipīṭha), categorized as superior, inferior, and middling;
they are known as Padma, Śrī, Kumuda, and Bandha, and may be square, octagonal, or circular. || 276 ||
One should perform everything beginning with the secondary pedestals (upapīṭha) according to the ritual for the temple;
[one should determine] the height of the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) of the abode and the width of the offering pedestal (balipīṭha). || 277 ||
The highest measurement for that [sanctuary] should be one *tala*; half of that would be the middle;
and half of that again is declared to be the lowest, measured from the outside of the base. || 278 ||
One should make its height equal to its width, or even one-quarter greater, or half greater, in proportion to the vimāna. || 279 ||
The height of the best [type] shall be thirty-two parts; the *pādukā* (base) shall be two parts, the *gati* (projection) is said to be seven parts, and the *kumbha* (pitcher) six parts. || 280 ||
The upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭī) should be one part, and the petal (dala) should be five parts;
in the two-part ear-projection (karṇakampa), there should be a large fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) of one part.
One part shall be the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭī), four parts the hanging lotus (lambapaṅkaja), and two parts the upper lotus;
it should have four doors and four faces.
That which is described with such ornaments is called "excellent" (uttama);
and in the case of the "middling" (madhyama), its height is divided into twenty-six parts.
They know the *pāduka* to consist of two parts, the *jagatī* of six parts, the *kumuda* of five parts, and the *paṭṭikā* to be one part. || 284 ||
The *karṇa* (corner) shall be four parts, while the *paṭṭikā* (beam) shall be one part;
the *pahāpaṭṭī* shall be two parts, and the upper *paṭṭikā* shall be one part. || 285 ||
There should be two parts for the single fillet (ekapaṭṭī) and two parts for the hanging lotus (lambapadma);
the hanging lotus should indeed consist of two parts, while the top of the lotus (padmūrdhva) should also consist of two parts. || 286 ||
Thus, the middle pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be joined with these proportions;
however, in the inferior [pedestal], its height shall be twenty parts. || 287 ||
The *pādukā* shall occupy one part, the *jagatī* five parts, the *kumuda* one part for its foundation, and the *paṭṭikā* is intended to be one part. (288)
The neck is said to be three parts; the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) is one part;
the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) shall be two parts; and the hanging lotus (lambapadmaka) is three parts.
The upper lotus should likewise occupy one part; this is the characteristic of the *kaniṣṭha* pedestal. One should construct it in front of the *gopura*, situated along the central axis. || 290 ||
One should not construct a raised *balipīṭha* (offering pedestal) that is higher than the surface of the base;
rather, one should prepare a pedestal for the Lord of the Herd (*yūthādhipa-pīṭha*) dedicated to the Lord of the Herd in the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*). || 291 ||
The wise man should likewise construct the Gopura in the first enclosure with a height that is double its width and with a symmetrical projection.
One should construct the two gate-towers (gopuras) with a measurement four times that [of the central shrine];
one should properly fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) dedicated to the leader of the herd (yūthādhipa).
One should properly construct the pedestal with five parts and endowed with all its characteristic marks;
it may be placed in the second enclosure or even in the third enclosure.
One should properly prepare the pedestal (pīṭha) dedicated to Viṣṇu;
for that pedestal consists of all the gods and likewise consists of all the worlds.
For the protection of the entire world, one should have [this] constructed, endowed with the auspicious marks;
it is the subduer of Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas, and the increaser of grain. (296)
Prosperity and the increase of good fortune shall accrue to men when this is performed upon a pedestal;
indeed, one should have it made wherever—in front or even behind. (297)
The wise one should cause it to be made with eight spokes or sixteen petals;
alternatively, he should make it square or even cause it to be made circular. || 298 ||
Alternatively, the learned man should cause [the temple] to be made in proportion to the vimāna;
furthermore, he should divide the length of the vimāna into five parts.
One should cause the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) to be two parts, or even three parts;
having divided it into four parts, it should be made proportionate to the temple (prāsāda). || 300 ||
Where one should make it two-fifths, one should employ twenty-six parts;
where it is four-fifths, it is said to consist of thirty-two parts. || 309 ||
One should join part with part according to the previously stated rule,
where there is constant dancing, even at the front of the gopura.
Having drawn a cord along the sides of the gopura itself, proceeding sequentially from south to north, one should divide the portion for the house at that very spot.
One should make the pathway to the south of the thread itself, and likewise to the north of the seat, one should make it to the north of the thread itself. || 304 ||
Having divided the portion of the house starting from fourteen cubits up to whatever extent it may be wide, one should likewise designate the deities and the female slaves. || 305 ||
Within the inner path (antarvīthi), wherever the central line is situated in the middle,
the wise one should construct the pedestal (pīṭha) according to the previously stated rule.
One should fashion the form of the Bhūtas in the four directions beginning with Indra;
this should be performed with the sound of a conch shell and according to the measure of five tālas. || 307 ||
Mounted in the center of that [lotus] is the one holding a staff (Daṇḍapāṇi), facing outward;
that is the form of the Great Element (Mahābhūta) above the knees, which is non-white (black).
The region below the knees is red in color, the pair of thighs is like the hue of gold, and likewise, the area below the knees is white; thus it is endowed with these colors.
Virajeśa, whose banner is the Bhūta, has the great Cātaka bird as his vehicle;
he was born in the month of Jyeṣṭha under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śaiṣika is his minor name. || 310 ||
The supreme form is that which is accompanied by all the attendants and possesses constant festivity;
this is declared to be the middling [form]. || 311 ||
Having constructed a pedestal there, measuring one cubit in width and provided with three altars that are elevated by one part each; || 312 ||
But worship is declared to be inferior if the pedestal is based on a temple.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Rite for the Retinue, Characteristics, and the Altar of Offerings," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The Sixth Chapter.

Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of the permanent image (dhruvabera). The characteristics of the permanent image are determined by the temple, the sanctum, the base, the door, and the artisan. (1)
Having obtained the measurement of the name, the wise man should divide it equally,
avoiding the loss of a finger's breadth by means of either addition or subtraction.
One should apply and then abandon [the lunar days] in sequence by means of even and odd finger-breadths;
one should avoid the inauspiciousness of the asterisms of income and expenditure, the day of the week, the eight classes of beings, and the planetary divisions. || 3 ||

When the number of years is multiplied by eight, nine, and three, and divided by eight and twelve, the resulting values are declared as the sources of gain and loss; an excess of income brings auspicious results. || 4 ||
When the height is multiplied by eight and divided by twenty-seven, the remainder indicates the asterism beginning with Aśvinī;
likewise, when it is multiplied by four, [the remainder indicates the corresponding lunar day].
When divided by the Nandas, the resulting portion indicates thieves and so forth;
[the results] are called enjoyment, power, wealth, earth, eunuch, fear, and poverty.
And the fruit corresponding to their own names for each of those [planets] in order is as follows:
when the height (tuṅga) of the Sun and the others, multiplied by nine, is divided by seven, the remainder indicates the day of the week. (7)

That same [measurement] is declared to be ninefold within each of the three sections; the height of the pillar is, respectively, one and a quarter, one and a half, and [one and three-quarters], being the lowest [grade] in sequence.
Likewise, according to the door and also according to the base, the permanent image (dhruvabera) is declared to be equal in size to the patron (yajamāna). || 12 ||
Some say that the rising of Dhruva occurs by means of the hands and fingers;
the rising of the image [of Dhruva] lasts for one hundred and seven plus eight (one hundred and fifteen) finger-breadths.
In the other parts, during the yugas, there is the arising of stationary beings within the divisions of the asterisms;
the characteristic of mobile beings is that for mobile things, the height is proclaimed to be one part.
Having taken two parts from the portion of the fire of constant enmity, and having divided that portion into three, the whole shall become excellent. || 15 ||
Two parts are declared to be the medium size, and one part likewise the inferior;
this is indeed the measurement for the ritual worship, image worship, and festivals of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

If there is to be a single fixed image (dhruvabera), it should be considered equal to the festive image (autsavabera). One should fashion the strength-image (balibera) with a height equal to the elevation of the face of the fixed image. || 17 ||
The *baliberaka* (the base for the *kautuka*) should be one-and-a-half, three-fourths, or one-third of the *kautuka*;
the *kautuka* itself should have the same form as the source [of the image] or the fixed [archetypal] form.
Whether on a seat, or standing, or on a bed, or standing while seated—in this way the rite of *kautuka* is prescribed; for the ritual bathing (*snāpana*), one should remain standing. || 19 ||
The amulet should be an image of Viṣṇu; for those who have the Matsya and Kūrma incarnations as their fixed [deities], it should likewise be one of his other incarnations, or simply Viṣṇu himself.
One should celebrate the festivals of Viṣṇu alone as the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, Kalki, and also as the son of Jamadagni.
When Dhruva is unarmed, he would make Rāma festive with weapons;
likewise when Kṛṣṇa has chosen Dhruva, whether Kṛṣṇa is armed or unarmed.
In this case, one should create a festival image (utsava-mūrti) of the Supreme Lord holding his play-staff (krīḍā-yaṣṭi), appearing in countless dark forms, or in the form of Arjuna’s charioteer.
The bathing of all the forms should be performed while [the deity] is in the four-armed standing posture;
when the God is standing, both Goddesses are standing, and when he is seated, they are in the standing and seated postures respectively.
One should not act contrary [to this]; if one does so, one perishes.
Everywhere, one should cause the festive rites and processions to be performed in conjunction with the Goddess.

One should perform the daily worship (sadārcā) and the offering of oblations (balibera), excluding the goddesses. Regarding the images in Puranic temples, one should act according to the specific tradition of those Puranic sites as it was practiced previously. || 26 ||
That which lacks the prescribed rules, possesses inauspicious characteristics, or is improperly applied does not cause harm.
In rites such as the *kautuka* (marriage thread), the consideration of the six auspicious factors beginning with the *āya* is not required. || 27 ||
Regarding the characteristics of the attendants' images:
the emergence of the permanent image of the attendants is considered to extend from the end of the arms, or to the end of the breasts, or to the end of the navel, according to the devotees. || 28 ||
One should have various festive ornaments made according to each specific fixed rule;
the measurement for the two goddesses should be up to the limit of the ears or to the end of the arms of the Lord, as prescribed by the ritual rules.
A wise person should never perform the two measurements of the Goddess—extending either to the end of the throat or to the navel—for the purposes of the pedestal (balibera) or the image (arca). 29.
Having thus fashioned the images according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on iconography (śilpaśāstra),
one should likewise construct the pedestal-assembly (pīṭhasaṅghāta) and the pedestal (pīṭha) themselves according to their respective specified forms. || 39 ||

Having deposited the nine jewels upon the pedestal, one should perform the ritual of union (saṅghāta). Some excellent teachers maintain that the pedestal is distinct from the lotus and should be placed below it. || 32 ||
Once it has been installed, however, the wise one should not separate it again and rejoin it;
at the end of the opening of the eyes without mantras, he should perform the consecration once more. || 33 ||
Regarding the consideration of the auspicious moments for consecration: among the months, [consecration] in Phālguna, Caitra, Jyeṣṭha, Vaiśākha, and Tiṣya (Puṣya) is excellent;
in Śrāvaṇa it is middling, as is the case for Kārttika and Āśvayuja.
The wise man should avoid the month of Bhādrapada as inferior, as well as the month of Āṣāḍha, while avoiding both Mārgaśīrṣa and Māgha. || 35 ||
Likewise, during both the bright and dark fortnights, excluding three parts and one-twentieth [of a day],
the asterisms Revatī, Rohiṇī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Svātī, Śravaṇa, and Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā) [are auspicious].
The ninth lunar day of Kṛttikā is auspicious for Durgā during the month of Kārtika, as are the constellations Citrā, Aśvinī, Śatabhiṣak, Punarvasu, and those beginning with Mṛgaśiras.
The installation of the Sun-god is recommended when the sun is in Leo;
likewise, the installation for the sake of prosperity is praised during the months of Phālguna and Caitra.
The fierce [form] is prescribed for the installation of Rudra during the month of Māgha;
and the Śravaṇa [constellation] and the month of Āśvayuj are prescribed for the ritual of installing the Fish and other [incarnations]. (39)
When the asterism is Anurādhā or Aśleṣā, and the Karaṇa indicates an auspicious rising,
the consecration of the patron king should take place during his three birth-asterisms.

The wise praise the weekday, its divisions, the hora, the decan, and the sign within the life-force of the poem (kāvya-jīva), as well as the weekday, its divisions, and so forth, starting from Wednesday. || 41 ||
On lunar days such as the sixth, eighth, the parvan days, and the Riktā and Ānanda days; likewise on the movable Karaṇas, during auspicious yogas, and when Viṣṭi is not present. || 42 ||

Even when free from defects such as those pertaining to the lunar day (tithi), the weekday (vāra), the asterism (ṛkṣa), and the planetary conjunctions (yoga), all the planets beginning with the Sun [are unfavorable] if the Moon is empty (rikta) or in the eighth house occupied by planets. || 43 ||

When malefic planets are situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefic planets are placed in the angles (kendras) or the trines (trikoṇas), or when [the ascendant] is joined with or aspected by benefics—provided it is devoid of Venus and the Moon (Kāma)—[the yoga is formed]. || 44 ||
One should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the God of gods specifically during the forenoon; therefore,
with haste, one should select the preceptor and the officiating priests on the day prior to that.

One should also [honour] the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the installers (sthāpaka), who possess the previously mentioned characteristics, with white flowers, unguents, white garments, and finger-rings. || 46 ||
Having honored and paid obeisance to the preceptor and others as if they were one's own deity, one should respectfully entreat the preceptor, saying: "Please perform this rite for me. (47)
Having resolved, "So be it," and having performed the ritual sowing of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
they then caused the officiating priests to have their hair, beards, and nails shaved according to the prescribed rules.
Pure, having bathed at the three daily junctures, they were chanting the Puruṣasūkta and the Vaiṣṇavasūkta, as well as the Saṃhitā of the Yajurveda known as the Pāvamānī.
Performing the Brahma-yajña with the twelve Sūktas, he likewise recited the twelve Sūktas beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca" and "devakṛtasya. (50)
The hymn beginning with "yanme garbha," and after that the "taratsamandī" hymn, as well as those beginning with "vasoḥ pavitram" and "jātavedase. (51)
The Viṣṇornuka hymn and the Puruṣasūkta, the Ekākṣara hymn and others, and thereafter the Dhruvasūkta. || 52 ||
Thereafter follows the Rudra-sūkta beginning with "tvamagne rudra," and likewise the sūkta beginning with "pavasva"; these constitute the twelve sūktas.
Chanting the goddess Sāvitrī a thousand times every day, or else observing a fast for three nights, or even the Pādakṛcchra penance; || 54 ||
Or indeed, they all together may observe a fast for one day;
however, the preceptor, being self-restrained, must perform the kṛcchra penance for the sake of purification.
If one is unable [to perform] fasting and so forth, one should instead feed Brāhmaṇas;
or one should offer clarified butter daily with the four hymns beginning with "yad devāḥ."
Reciting the mantra "vaiśvānarāya," he should worship the purifying fire;
likewise, the sacrificer should also perform the kṛcchra penance for the sake of purification. || 57 ||
The sacrificer, devoted to nothing else, eating sacrificial food and having his senses subdued,
should collect the materials as instructed by the teacher.
Having constructed the sacrificial hall provided with sixteen pillars,
the distance between the pillars should be four cubits or three cubits, as appropriate. || 59 ||
One should construct fire-pits and an altar there according to the prescribed rule;
Atri has declared that the Sabhya fire-altar should be situated either to the north of the bed or to the east.
To the southeast of the assembly hall, Kāśyapa spoke concerning the lotus and fire; all the fire-pits were arranged in rows for the rite of the sprouts.

One should fashion the vessels for the *strūva* and other implements, the fuel and other items, the weapons, and the eight auspicious symbols according to the measurement of the middle of a closed fist; such is the instruction.
Regarding the opening of the eyes:

on the fifth day prior to the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) as previously stated, the opening of the eyes is performed in a water-shed, a pavilion, or a temple-tower facing the [deity]. || 63 ||

Having established the aupāsana fire and performed the purification of the image with the rites of circumambulation by fire and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [one should proceed]. || 44 ||
Having seated the deity upon a grain-seat measuring two ratnis in width,
and having established the aupāsana fire, he performed the āghāra oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Let the oblation of the limbs (aṅgahoma) be well-offered either in a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound, accompanied by the Vaiṣṇava mantras of the five elements beginning with earth. || 66 ||
One should likewise worship with the Puruṣasūkta, with the Jayādya hymns,
and with the names of the constituent parts beginning from the pinnacle (sthūpī) down to the base (upāna).
Standing on the right side of the deity and facing north, the preceptor should take up the pigment with a golden vessel and a golden stylus. (68)
Having covered [the image] with a brand-new garment while facing Hari, one should worship the Earth upon its color and the Sun upon its vessel. (69)
Likewise, upon the brush, one should then mutter the Candra-ātmasūkta;
then, taking up the color with the brush while reciting the Pauruṣa-sūkta.
In the right eye is the Vaiṣṇava [element], and in the left is the Aindra;
the eyelashes are the Varma, while the red, white, and black parts are composed of fire (taijasa). || 71 ||
Having meditated in sequence upon these six maṇḍalas, the five great elements, and the supreme Self (Paramātman), one should perform the ritual. || 72 ||

Having lifted the concealing cloth, one should display the objects worthy of being seen; having shown the substances to be displayed, one should then arrange a heap of grain as a heap of sesame seeds. || 73 ||
Having taken one *prastha* each of clarified butter, curd, honey, and milk, individually, in a vessel of bell-metal, together with a golden jar; || 74 ||
One should place the *Uttara* and other [Vedic texts] upon a seat of grain in the *Daṇḍaka* section;
likewise, the Sāmaveda, Yajurveda, Ṛgveda, and Atharvaveda. (75)

The deities should be worshipped in sequence; [one should give] a single cow endowed with auspicious marks, with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, covered with cloth, and provided with a bronze milking vessel.
A wise man should place a cow with her calf, its limbs full and well-nourished, before the gods;
likewise, he should place Soma upon a heap of grain and the ancestors upon a heap of sesame seeds.
Having recited the Gosāvitrī and reflecting upon it with the thought, "These [limbs] are impure," one should worship the deities mentioned therein upon their respective limbs. 78.
Having given her a handful of grass and having touched it with the *gosūkta*, [one should proceed];
here, the *gosūkta* is designated as the hymn beginning with "gāvo hima. (79)
Having recited "imā oṣadhayaḥ," he should show [the image] sesame and grain;
with the Sāman-mantra beginning with "ājyam" and the Yajur-mantra beginning with "dadhi. (80)
Reciting "agnimīle" for honey and "śanna" while speaking of milk, one should recite the Godāna Sūkta, saying, "One should recite up to the Godāna [Sūkta]. || 81 ||
Having shown a very beautiful cow with its calf, he should also show the two goddesses and various other beautiful sights, one by one.
The specific method for stone images, for stone that is devoid of color, and likewise for those made of metal, is as follows:
having fashioned a firm needle, one should [insert it] through those two [eyes] to form the circle of eyelashes and so forth. (83)

One should fashion the other [image] with mantras; it should be like that which was made for the permanent image (dhruvabera). One should arrange the ritual materials separately so that they are clearly visible. || 84 ||
Regarding the opening of the eyes of the retinue:
having offered the respective mantras of the retinue, beginning with the Sage (the principal deity), ten times each separately, the opening of the eyes is performed with those mantras. || 85 ||

One should show the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to them individually in separate vessels; however, if they are not all present together, one should not perform the oblation for them separately.
Purification from the touch of the artisan begins from the taking up of the trident until the opening of the eyes;
for the sake of purification from the artisan's touch, it occurs immediately after the opening of the eyes. (87)
One should wrap a jar filled with sixteen prasthas [of grain] with a thread;
having likewise filled it with water, one should encircle it with two cloths. || 88 ||
One should place sprouts, tips of kusha grass, tips of durva grass, as well as unbroken rice grains (akṣata), gold, and auspicious flowers, while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. || 89 ||
Facing north, he then took his place upon the external seat and [recited] the mantras beginning with the four Vedas, such as "āpa undantu," in their proper sequence.
Being composed, he should touch that water with the *kūrca* while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Puruṣa-nārāyaṇa*, and the Vaiṣṇava mantras. || 91 ||
With water contained in that pitcher using a golden brush, [he should perform the rite] with the three verses beginning with "āpo hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and "pavamānaḥ". || 92 ||

With the mantra "śanno devī" and the Puṃsūkta, as well as Vaiṣṇava hymns, one should sprinkle the image for the sake of purification; one should also cause the declaration of a "day of merit" (puṇyāha) to be recited.

Thus, one should perform [the rites] for the painting upon its installation and for the appearance of the painting; one should begin the consecration (adhivāsa) of the images, such as the *kautuka* and others. || 94 ||

Having performed the perfuming with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on the northern side of the temple, a pit is dug at the water-shed; there, the small image is placed in a wooden tub lined with the five products of the cow and other substances. || 95 ||
Having recited "ājyam aśukram asi" and taken up sixteen parts [of ghee],
and having recited "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," he should pour in twice that amount of curd.
One should take three parts of milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," and four parts of cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvārā. || 97 ||
One should pour six times the amount of cow urine into it while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra;
then, having said "Vasoḥ Pavitram," one should fill the pit again with that [mixture]. 98.
One should worship Śarva, Īśa, and Avyakta within the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having recited the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should lay [the image] there with its head toward the east.
On that past day, one should raise up the image with the Viṣṇu-sūkta,
and having recited "vārīścatasraḥ," one should consecrate it with pure waters.
Having thoroughly purified the water cistern with milk-soaking and with the mantra "śanno devī," one should fill it with milk while reciting the "Atharva-kṣīra" [hymn]. || 101 ||
Having said, "It is pure and meritorious," one should worship Atharvan with milk,
having indeed strewn lotuses, water-lilies, and other flowers there.
And having spread five beds there together with *kuśa* grass,
[he should worship] Kṣīra, who lies upon the Ocean of Milk, the one who reclines upon Śeṣa.
There, remembering the God of gods, one should shade Hari as before;
when that day has passed, one should subsequently remove the image as previously described.
Having bathed [the image] and adorned it with new garments and ornaments,
the preliminary consecration in water (jalādhivāsa) should take place in a river, a pond, or a large reservoir; in the absence of these, one may proceed in the following manner.
Having constructed a water-shed all around, one should have it surrounded by a fivefold lattice-work for the sake of protection, and adorned with canopies and other ornaments. || 106 ||
Having spread out new cloths along with darbha grass, flowers, and kuśa grass, one should worship there [the image], saying: "The sacred ford, the auspicious water. (107)
As before, one should have the deity laid upon the bed without negligence;
if unable to do so, [one should remain] for three days in pure water alone.

One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for one day, or for a single day-time period, or for a watch (yāma), or for a specific duration of time, accompanied by mantras, for the sake of purifying the image.
The impossible-to-wash-away enmity [is removed] by bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and separately with milk and water infused with kuśa grass.
Having filled one hundred and eight jars with water, and having worshipped the deities therein as before, he should perform the consecration using the very same mantras.
Regarding the preliminary rites for the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and the preceding day:
at the conclusion of the evening oblation (sāyaṃ-homa), the preceptor (ācārya) and the others should perform their respective duties individually.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and recited the hymns as before,
the preceptor then [addresses] the sacrificer who has thus completed the ritual acts.
Having said, "Smaller than the smallest," he should quickly sprinkle the twice-born;
then, having summoned those officiating priests, he should appoint them to their respective duties.
Regarding the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi):

having likewise performed the Vāstu-homa in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the north of that temple, [one should perform it] throughout the entire interior chamber and so forth. || 115 ||

One should purify [the site] by means of the circumambulation with fire (paryagni), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and an auspicious day (puṇyāha). The churning of the fire should take place in front of the temple, which is adorned with the five colors. || 116 ||
Having placed the fire-drill upon a heap of grain, being pure and facing the east,
one should meditate on Hari in the churning-stick and likewise on the Earth in the fire-drill.
While reciting the Vaiśvānara Sūkta, one should wrap the upper cord dedicated to Agni and the muñja-grass rope dedicated to Vāsuki around the churning-stick with the cord.
Having recited the "jātavedasa" mantra, the wise man should cause the churning to be performed;
having placed dried cow dung around it, he should then take it up again with that same hymn. || 119 ||
Having said, "This is your fuel," he should cast the pieces of wood [into the fire];
and having said, "O you whose face is ghee," he should kindle the fire and bow down to it. || 120 ||
With the mantra "āyurdā," one should cause it to be placed down without negligence.
If the fire produced by churning is not obtained, one should act as follows;
or else, having brought fire from the sacrificial altar of a Śrotriya, some say that one should worship Vaiśvānara with the [appropriate] Sūkta there. 122.
Having abandoned all that inauspicious action and having cast out that fire which obstructs other duties on the site, [he should proceed]. || 123 ||
Having placed either churned butter or that brought from the house of a Vedic scholar,
one should perform the prescribed oblation at the conclusion of the propitiatory fire-offering.
Regarding the five fires, after mentioning the "Gārhapatya fire," one should also mention the "sacrificial deity. || 125 ||
There, while reciting "bhūḥ puruṣam" and "acyutam," one should perform the invocation and cause the utterances of *juṣṭākāra* and *svāhākāra* to be made. || 126 ||
Therefore, having taken up the fire and subsequently into the Dakṣiṇāgni,
one should lead forth the fire according to the prescribed rule, pronouncing the mantra "O Jātavedas."
Having uttered "Anvāhāryāgni" and also "Yajñadaivata," one should perform the invocation and other rites with "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ Puruṣaṃ Satyam. || 128 ||
Having led the Gārhapatya fire into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "O Agni, come hither," he speaks of the Āhavanīya fire. || 129 ||
Having said "The deity of the sacrifice," and while uttering "Oṃ suvaḥ puruṣam," one should perform the invocation and other rites with the words "Puruṣam. || 130 ||
Having brought forward the fire for the domestic hearth (āvasathya) with the mantra "This is your womb," and having said "The domestic fire" and also "The deity of the sacrifice. (139)
Reciting "Oṃ mahaḥ puruṣam" and so forth, one should perform the invocation and other rites for the deity Aniruddha in the domestic fire (āvasathyāgni). || 132 ||

Having brought fire to the *sabhyāgni* with the mantra "I take the fire," one should likewise [worship] the *sabhyāgni* with the mantras "Obeisance to Yajñadeva" and "Oṃ, the people [adore] Puruṣa. (133)
Reciting "I invoke Viṣṇu," he performs the invocation and other rites for the members of the assembly;
and with the mantra "Ghṛtapratīkam," he brings forward the fire in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice. || 134 ||
Having uttered "Pauṇḍarīkāgni," and also "Yajñadaivata," and "Oṃ Tapaḥ Puruṣa," [he should recite] "Vāsudeva" thereafter. (135)
Reciting "Oṃ, tapas-puruṣa" and "Nārāyaṇa," and having thus performed the invocation, one should offer oblations of clarified butter after having set them aside. || 136 ||
One should perform the leading forth of all the fires from the Gārhapatya fire;
one should meditate upon the fire seated within the center of the sacrificial pit as the Brahman-mind.
Facing westward, red in color, resembling the rising sun,
seated with Svāhā and Svadhā, he is the supreme being whose essence is all the gods.
It has indeed one heart, three feet, and two heads;
it has four horns, four eyes, seven tongues, and two nostrils. || 139 ||
He has four faces, with three tongues on the right side and likewise three on the left;
one should meditate upon Agni as having seven hands and adorned with all ornaments.
Wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment, equipped with a girdle of muñja grass and a staff,
he holds in his right hands a sacrificial ladle (sruk), a dipping-spoon (sruva), a rosary, and a trident.
One should meditate thus, according to the Śruti: [holding] a chowrie, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter with the left arms, and the image of the Embodiment of Sacrifice.
The seven tongues of Agni are proclaimed as Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Vasuprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā. || 143 ||
Those situated in the directions of Īśāna, Indra, Agni, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Anila, and the center;
at the conclusion of the Āghāra oblations, the Vaiṣṇava homa is performed; indeed, at the conclusion of the Āghāra oblations, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice upon the seven tongues [of fire].

According to the distinctions of the tongues of fire: one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks into Hiraṇyā, clarified butter into Kanakā, mustard seeds into Raktā, and parched grain into Kṛṣṇā. (145)
Having meditated upon Devanta in Vasuprabhā, one offers a cake;
in Atiraktā, one should offer sesame seeds and the oblation dear to the gods.
He offers other oblations while mentally recollecting Bahurūpā. Regarding the method of meditating upon Agni during the offering of specific sacrificial materials:
when the fire is established for the offering of fuel-wood (samidh), it remains there; and it likewise rests during the offering of clarified butter (ghṛta). || 147 ||
Even when performing a caru-oblation while seated, [one should use] sesame, mustard seeds, and groats;
otherwise, whatever is offered into the fire becomes entirely fruitless.
Regarding the measurement of the oblation according to the type of offering:
an oblation of clarified butter is traditionally defined as a continuous stream four finger-breadths in length that does not break;
whereas an oblation of food is held to be the amount grasped by the size of a thumb-joint. || 149 ||
The measure for cooked rice should be one akṣa; parched grain (lāja) should be the size of a handful;
and the oblation of sesame, mustard seeds, and flour should be the size of a śukti. || 150 ||
The presiding deities of the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) have been mentioned; hereafter I shall explain the presiding deities of the oblation materials:
for sand and for clay, the Earth is the presiding deity. || 151 ||
The sacrificial mound (sthaṇḇḍila) is presided over by Soma; the pit and the altar follow in due order.
Brahmā is the lord of the upper altar, and Prajāpati is the lord of the middle altar. || 152 ||
In the Sabhya and Pauṇḍarīka fires, Soma is the deity of the lower part;
the Vasus are said to be the deities of the petals; and the Pitṛs (ancestors) are the deity of the digging.
The lines (lekhās) have Skanda as their presiding deity; the sages are those of the seven-fold sacrificial grass (barhis);
Havyavāṭ is the lord of fuel; and Vihāra has Vāyu as its deity. || 154 ||
The water-pot (karaka) is declared to have the five elements as its presiding deities;
at the tip, the knot, and the base of the grass-bundle (kūrca), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara reside respectively. 155.
The four bundles of grass used for the surrounding strewing have Viṣṇu as their presiding deity;
likewise, the western enclosing-stick is said to have Gandharva as its deity. || 156 ||
The southern enclosing stick (paridhi) is proclaimed to have Indra as its deity;
the northern enclosing stick is declared to have Mitra and Varuṇa as its deities. || 157 ||
Likewise, the divine Sun-god resides in the upper two fuel-sticks (samidh) and in the juhū and other ladles. || 158 ||
Brahmā and Soma are proclaimed to be in the vessel for the praṇidhi and the vessel for the fuel-sticks;
Agni is in the two largest fuel-sticks, and Vaṃsundharā is in the clarified butter pot.
Varuṇa is the deity of the water, and Agni is the deity of the clarified butter;
the sacrificial porridge (caru) has Indra and Agni as its deities—having thus meditated, he offers the oblation.
Regarding the specific vessels for the various materials of the oblation:
one should offer the Vaiṣṇava oblation with a *juhū* ladle using *caru* rice in all six fires;
likewise, one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) in the fire-pits using a *sruva* spoon. || 161 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Time for the Great Consecration, the Gathering of Materials, the Unveiling of the Eyes, the Threefold Consecration by Abode, the Consecration of an Image that Cannot Be Transported, the Authorization of the Preceptor, the Churning of the Fire, the Bringing Forward of the Fire, the Meditation on the Fire, the Determination of the Positions of the Fire-Tongues, and the Determination of the Quantities and Deities of the Offering Substances," in the section on Rituals (*kriyādhikāra*) within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable *Vaikhānasa* scripture of the Lord.
Oṃ.
The Seventh Chapter.
The method for the worship of the pitcher (kumbhapūjā): Fetching the water.
Being pure and facing the east, one should collect pure water from a sacred river into a clean vessel while reciting the mantra beginning with "adhārā'su. || 1 ||
Having bathed, the preceptor, with a serene mind, anointed with white perfumes and adorned with upper garments,
rings, and other ornaments, [prepared for the rite].
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), adorned with white garlands,
he should take a vessel possessing the characteristics of a *kumbha*, filled with thirty-two *prasthas*, made either of iron or of clay. || 3 ||
Having the appearance of a ripe *ālaka* fruit, free from cracks or splits, and devoid of blemishes;
while reciting the consecration formula for the jar, "For food thee! For strength thee! or alternatively, "May there be well-being! || 4 ||
One should wrap it with a thread while reciting "indraṃ naro na," and having said "śucī vo havyā," one should wash it thoroughly on all sides with water.
Having strained that water with a cloth, saying "These waters are auspicious," he should thereafter strain it again with kuśa grass, and then fill the jar with that very same water.
Reciting "āpa undantu," one should fill [the vessel] with great concentration;
reciting "āpo hi ṣṭha," one should touch it after it has been perfumed with all fragrances.
Jewels, an elephant, a mare, auspicious weapons, a golden tortoise, kuśa grass, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice. || 8 ||

One should separately consecrate the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for the sake of increasing merit, as well as a white umbrella, banners, and so forth, made of eight *niṣkas* of gold each, using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
One should place those [vessels], measuring two finger-breadths, made of gold alone,
or else with two pieces of linen or two fine cloths.
One should wrap the neck of the water-pot with garlands of flowers;
one should also place upon it a bunch of Aśvattha leaves, a tuft of grass, and sprouts of Dūrvā grass.
The purpose of casting gems and other substances into the pitcher is as follows:
bone is proclaimed to be the gem, the sinew and the tendon are the thread, flesh is celebrated as the fine clay, blood is the red clay therein, and water is likewise the fat. (12)
The brush is said to be white, and the cloth for wrapping should be of cotton;
these are the seven constituent elements to be placed within the jars and the pitchers.
If even one of these is lacking, there is no presence of Him therein;
[He resides] in a beautiful place measuring a cubit, with a height of a palm tree and three altars.
One should place the pitcher upon a pedestal of grain in front of the deity.
Having performed the placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa) and encircled it with Praṇavas in the cardinal directions, one should first place the seed-syllable in the heart.
Then, having performed meditation on the Ātmasūkta and likewise the Pauruṣasūkta,
one should meditate upon and recite the Nārāyaṇānuvāka within the heart.
One should meditate upon the mandala of Varuṇa, resembling pure crystal and shaped like a half-moon, within the purified water contained in the pitcher.
Having attained perfection through the teacher's instruction and being intent on meditation upon the Lord,
the preceptor, with a well-pleased mind, should commence the practice of meditation.
Seated in the svastika posture, with his senses conquered and facing north,
he placed his right foot upward and likewise his left foot downward.
Having properly grasped both big toes between the knees,
one should place the left hand on the lap and the other hand facing upwards above it.
With his body straight, motionless like a lamp placed in a windless spot, he sat in this manner, with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose. (23)
Having restrained the vital breaths according to the rule through exhalation, inhalation, and retention, and having withdrawn the senses from all external objects; (24)
Then, having made the mind one-pointed, he should behold [the Self] through meditative absorption within the vast abode of the universe, which resembles the interior of a lotus bud.
The Supreme Self is established within the heart, in the midst of the flames of fire,
like the steady flame of a lamp in a windless place, or like a streak of lightning in the sky.
The light of the Lord’s own mind is this imperishable Person;
that Brahman, whose nature consists of pure knowledge, is declared to be the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 28 ||
When one has properly placed within the heart that Brahman which consists of the syllable Om, and is intent upon meditating upon it—that meditation is called "offering unto Brahman. (29)
When this body has become Brahman, one should firmly effect the offering of the mind;
having made the mind steady therein and having entered into meditative concentration (dhāraṇā). || 30 ||
The God who is devoid of qualities, stainless, eternal, imperishable, and the cause of all;
who is both partless and possessed of parts, and illuminated by a blazing radiance.
Meditating upon that Viṣṇu with his mind, with supreme devotion and joy,
he beheld Him who is golden-hued, with a red face and red eyes, the bringer of happiness.
Wearing a crown, necklaces, armlets, and a long sacred thread, his chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, and possessed four arms. || 33 ||

The supreme [deity] is gentle, bearing the conch and the discus; with his right hand he bestows fearlessness, while his other hand rests upon his hip, and he is clothed in garments of parrot-feather hue.

Thus, having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) with a one-pointed mind and devotion, one should meditate upon that Supreme Self, which is imperishable and consists of the Praṇava. || 35 ||
Then, one should devoutly invoke the deity into the water within the pitcher;
thereafter, one should worship him with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the arghya and the water for sipping (ācamana).
The meaning of the word "invocation" (āvāhana) pertains everywhere to that supreme Self, which is all-pervading;
[now follow] the various methods of invocation.
That which is the recollection [of the deity] in one place is declared to be the invocation (āvāhana). || 37 ||
Just as fire pervading a forest blazes forth in one place, so too does Viṣṇu manifest in the heart of one who has performed meditation. 38.
Invoked by mantras into an image, a site, a bundle of grass, or water, the deity remains there out of compassion for devotees and, being thus worshipped, accepts the adoration. (39)
Some say that the invocation of Hari comes from the solar orb;
one should meditate upon the two goddesses together with the Lord in that jar according to the prescribed rule.
If the installation of the primary abode is to take place, one should lead Hari from the temporary abode,
worship the Lord with special honors, and duly present the sacrificial offering.
One should place the Śakti, situated within that image, into the pitcher by means of the *kūrca* [bundle of grass],
provided that the image is free from defects and conforms to the *dhruva* [fixed] form.
One should perform that very same auspicious rite, but not an ordinary worldly one;
having established the worldly deities and others, one should worship them in a place other than their usual locations.
One should discard the image, along with its defects, according to the prescribed rite into the ocean or a river;
this is for the purpose of performing the examination of the ground and other rites at a different location on the earth. || 44 ||
If it is requested, it should be given at the conclusion of the rite, just as before;
or else, one should install it in the former temple for the sake of a festival.
Some say that one should request [the ritual] for the purpose of establishing the residence of a child, provided that this is appropriate for the permanent residence in another dwelling. (46)
Some say that one should place there the amulet and the festive ornaments;
while engaged in the effort of the ritual bathing,
one should bring the water-pot and the image while reciting the Śakunasūkta.
The auspicious festive bathing of the two goddesses shall proceed in order from the east;
the preceptor, holding the pitcher upon his head, should walk in front.
Taking the image, the installers should follow that preceptor;
having placed the Lord of Gods within the cavity while reciting the Viṣṇusūkta.
To the south of the pit, on a pedestal for grain measuring one hand-span in length and six finger-breadths in height, one should place [the vessel] near the pit.
One should likewise place a row of grain, as well as the two goddesses, the festive image, and the ritual bathing;
one should arrange that row with grains in front of it, extending from the south to the north.
One should construct [the altar] measuring three cubits in length and endowed with a width of one cubit.
Therein, one should place the pitchers—wrapped with threads—beginning from the north, along with the substances for the ritual bath. || 52 ||
They were filled with milk, clarified butter, honey, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, water, kuśa grass, and sandalwood;
they were provided with sacrificial grass-bundles (kūrca) and accompanied by the preliminary ablutions (upasnāna), arranged in due order.
One should deposit siddhārtha and the other substances reduced by half a quarter [of their original amount] when an āḍhaka each of curd, clarified butter, honey, and milk is difficult to obtain.
One should install [the images] three-quarters, half, or even a quarter of a cubit, according to their height;
they should face north and likewise be oriented toward the Lord of Gods.
The placement of the auxiliary bathing jars (*upasnānakalaśa*) and the worship of the presiding deities of those jars:
one should place those respective auxiliary bathing jars upon their corresponding [main] jars.
[The deities are] the Atharvaveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Ṛgveda; likewise Āditya and Kāśyapa. (56)
The seasons, the seven sages, the presiding deities of the substances, the two Aśvins, the years, Vāyu, the Apsarases, and likewise the Maruts; || 57 ||
Takṣaka and the winds are the seven deities of the secondary ablution;
one should worship them with thirteen services, each by their respective names.
The method of bathing is as follows: in sequence, [one uses] "śanno devī," "agna āyāhi," "agnim īle," "pūtas tasyemā oṣadhayaḥ," and also "abhitvā śūra. (59)
One should bathe [the deity] while reciting "catvāri vā" seven times;
having uttered "vārīścatasra," one should perform the complete ritual bathing (upasnāna).
Having sprinkled the materials and taken them up with either the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava,
one should apply them three times or once, moving clockwise as far as one's own forehead.
At the conclusion of each respective mantra, one should bathe [the deity] with the five forms (pañcamūrti),
having first sprinkled the eastern pitcher individually with those various substances.
For all the incarnations as well as for the various assemblies,
one should perform the rites with their respective presiding mantras at the end, using their specific forms.
Reciting "iṣe tvorje tvā" and "āpohiṣṭhā," he should purify [the image] with scented water and bathe it according to the prescribed rite.
Having taken the Lord of Gods from the pit and established him upon the seat in the southwest, one should wipe him again with a cloth while reciting the mantra "amitras suparṇa. (65)
One should also adorn [the deities] with new garments, upper cloths, garlands, and ornaments;
likewise, for the goddesses during festivals and other occasions, one should adorn each respective goddess in due order.
The great seers declare that the bathing of all the attendants should be performed separately, or that the bath with warm water should take place in the middle.

Having purified the milk, clarified butter, and other substances, one should bathe [the deity] and offer ornaments. Then, beginning the consecration of the bed, one should place [the deity] in the center of the bed-altar with the mantra "vedāham". (68)
Having made a heap of sesame, rice, and śāli grain, he should spread skins, cloth, and so forth upon it with the mantra "I know" (vedāham). || 79 ||
Having spread out heaps of rice grains and whole grains of paddy,
and having likewise spread out beds one by one in due order, [he arranged them] separately.

A bed well-furnished with five types of coverlets— those made of skin, those made of hair, those made of shaven wool, those made of hemp, and likewise those made of flax— is what they call a "bed. (71)
A bed made from the skin of a tiger or other such animals is known as "made of skin" (carma-ja). That which is made from the hair of sheep and the like is known as "made of hair" (roma-ja). || 72 ||
That which is made from cotton is called muṇḍaja, while that which is made from bird feathers is proclaimed to be aṇḍaja. || 73 ||
Silk, linen, and those made from the wool of goats are said to be "left-side" (vāmaja) materials;
in the absence of skins and such, one may likewise use five types of cloth.
One should thus prepare a bed upon a heap of grain in due order,
with two separate pillows for the head and the feet for the two goddesses.
One should place full water-pots, sprouts, lamps, and auspicious items all around;
on the bed, one should worship Śeṣa, adorned with the circle of his hoods and their jewels.

Having worshipped Mitra and the others, as well as Jaya and the others, outside in the east and other directions, one should perform the preliminary consecration of the bed; then, with the Śakunasūkta, one should place the deity upon the bed.
One should place the goddess Śrī on the right and Mahī on the left;
likewise, one should assign the ritual bathing and the festival to the right and the left respectively.
One should spread separate beds for the two of them within the single altar;
and with devotion, one should place the jar of Smara before the deity as if he were a god himself.
Having worshipped the deity and the water-pot separately with the eight types of offerings,
the preceptor, joined by the installers, should also cause the proclamation of an auspicious day to be made.
One should place the vessel filled with rice, not less than one āḍhaka in measure; then, one should place a protective cord (pratisara),
either made of gold or of thread, upon it.
Having said, "Perform the protection," and having touched [the deity], and saying,
"May there be well-being," one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) on the right hand of the God of gods.
And one should bind the *pratisara* (protective cord) around the left hands of the two goddesses in sequence,
likewise for the bathing image, the festival image, and the *baliberam* (offering image).
One should first bind it to the Dhruva pole and perform the rite in the proper sequence with the mantra "Svastidā" and the mantra "Viṣṇustvām. (84)

With these two [mantras], one should bind [the thread] to the left hand of the God of gods, as well as of the Preceptor and the officiating priests, and of the two Goddesses, using their respective mantras.
One should tie the *kautuka* on the right hand of the preceptor and the officiating priests;
one should perform the tying of the *kautuka* during the consecration or the festival.
If the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) is omitted, every undertaking perishes.
Having uttered the mantra "That which belongs to Viṣṇu," one should cause the Lord to lie down upon the bed. 87.
Likewise, one should lay the two goddesses on either side with their respective mantras.
In the temple at the eastern gate, the deity should also have his head facing east;
in the southern and other directions, the head should likewise face the direction where the door is located.
One should provide an upper garment made of an unwashed cloth;
likewise, one should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon the *dhruvabera* (permanent image). || 90 ||
The kautuka, arca, utsava, and ākhyāpana rites for each of those two deities must likewise be performed individually,
with the exception of the pauṇḍarīka rite which does not involve fire.
Alternatively, for the [images of] Puruṣa and the others, or for the fire that has them as its primary focus,
after the *kautuka* has been established, there follows the bathing and the festival.
Some maintain that at their simultaneous installation, there are five fires together: the Sabhya and the Pāṇḍarīka, making two fires [in addition to the three]. || 93 ||
Having established the perpetual fires for those two and having offered oblations, at the conclusion of the sacrifice,
he should establish the Sabhya fire in the Sabhya pit as before.
But when the daily fire-oblation has been omitted, having prepared five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and having brought forth the Gārhapatya fire, he offers oblations into all the fires.
If those two are separate, one should prepare a separate fire for each;
they should perform the prescribed oblation after worshipping the water-pot as before.
Having placed [the deity] facing the god, one should invoke him from the eternal abode right there;
one should perform the bathing, the laying on the bed, the priestly office (hautra), and the fire-oblation as previously described. || 97 ||
One should not perform the invocation of deities nor the worship of all the gods [elsewhere];
rather, having invoked them into the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should then invoke them into those two [the mobile images]. || 98 ||
If, out of curiosity, the installation of those two [images] is performed later in the house of a child, the invocation is likewise prescribed; everything else shall be the same. || 99 ||
The study of the four Vedas and the praise of the office of the Hotṛ-priest:
he indeed causes him to study the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, in their proper order;
he should then adorn the Hotṛ-priest with garments, flowers, and finger-rings. || 100 ||
Having been well-honored by the members with upper garments according to their ability, that Hotṛ priest, facing westward, likewise praises the office of the Hotṛ while facing eastward.
The Adhvaryu greets the Hotṛ, saying, "O Hotṛ, hail!
and the Hotṛ replies to the Adhvaryu, "The deities, O Adhvaryu. || 102 ||
Thereafter, having drawn back and taken hold of the ritual grass-bundle (kūrca), standing with his face turned toward the west, he should loudly recite "Obeisance to the Speaker" and so forth. (103)
At the end of the mantra "evam amuḥ," the Hotṛ priest should likewise append his own name, ending in the dative case and followed by "śarma," joined with the word "amuḥ" in the accusative case. (104)
Saying "bhūte bhaviṣyati" and "hirbhuvassuvaḥ," he, facing the east, should recite the verse beginning with "pra vo vājāḥ. || 105 ||
Having recited the verse beginning with "pra vo vāja" and ending with "āvahantu," one should then recite the others three times along with the Praṇava. || 106 ||
Having heard the syllable *oṃ* uttered by the Hotṛ, the wise Adhvaryu, in particular, should offer the fuel-stick (*idhma*) smeared with clarified butter while uttering "Oṃ Svāhā. || 107 ||
The Hotṛ priest should likewise recite the seventeen Sāmidhenī verses in sequence, awakening Agni by uttering the formula ending with "O Brāhmaṇa, bear the burden. (108)
He should proclaim the lineage (gotra) and the ancestral invocation (pravara) of the sacrificer in due order;
likewise, he should repeat the formula "kindled by the gods, kindled by Manu" in the same manner.
If the village headman is the sacrificer, he should recite the Kaśyapa Pravara;
if the king is the performer, he should recite the Pravara of his domestic priest.
Some say that for all those other than Brāhmaṇas, one should choose either the Ācāryapravara or the Kāśyapapravara.
Having thus praised the office of the Hotṛ priest according to the sequence of the Hotṛ duties, he should recite the "Āyātu" mantra followed by the Mūrti-mantras in their proper order. (112)
Having addressed that deity with the words "Mā vaha," he should employ the Adhvaryu;
the Adhvaryu, in turn, at that time [should act] upon the water in the southern praṇidhi.
Then, having invoked [the deities] from Ādimūrti down to Śarva in sequence with their respective form-mantras (mūrtimantra),
