saying "I invoke you," one should then [invoke them] into the northern praṇidhi.
The wise one should invoke the deities beginning with Dhātṛ and ending with Viṣṇu;
having invoked them in that very order, he should offer oblations of clarified butter.
According to the distinction between the substances for the oblation, there is a distinction in the hand-gesture:
one should carefully grasp the *sruva* ladle with the ring finger and the thumb, and extend the index and middle fingers beneath the *sruva*. || 116 ||
Having released the little finger and grasped the sruva-ladle and other implements,
the wise one should offer oblations of clarified butter with a measure of four finger-breadths.

One should offer the sacrificial fuel (samidh), the cooked rice (caru), the cake (apūpa), sesame seeds, parched grain (lāja), and flour (saktu) mixed with clarified butter, using the thumb, the ring finger, and the middle finger. || 118 ||
The Great Peace (Mahāśānti) is declared here to be offered into all the fires;
indeed, the Mahāśānti oblation consists of the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta. || 119 ||
Having offered twenty oblations for each [deity] ending with the *vyāhṛtis* one by one, and having taken equal portions of sugar, clarified butter, curd, and milk; 120.
One should offer oblations into the Pauṇḍarīka fire with the upahuti ladle while remembering Hari,
and likewise into the pits of the world-protectors with their respective mantras in due order.
Having offered twenty oblations for each [deity] preceded by their respective names,
and having sprinkled water around the Sabhya fire, one should offer the five Vāruṇa oblations.
Having individually offered victory and other rites to the various deities ending with the Vyāhṛtis,
one should thereafter perform the worship of all the gods by honoring them all around with their respective names.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu together with Śrī and Bhūmi as before,
one should worship Mārkaṇḍeya and Brahmā on the right, and Bhava along with Bhṛgu on the left, in due order.
At the doors of the hall, one should place Dhātṛ and the others, along with Maṇika and Sandhyā;
or else, a Tāpasa who grants success, or a Śaṅkha, or even a Cakra.
One should first worship Śrībhūta while recollecting him as facing outward;
then Indra, Arka, Śrī, Havis, Pāla, and Agni, facing westward.
During the six months beginning with Caitra, one should worship the Sun in the north, and in the east, Bhauma, Guha, Durgā, Yama, and Śani, respectively.
To the south of Rohiṇī and the seven [Ṛṣis], facing northward,
[one should worship] Nīla, Bṛhaspati, Dhātrī, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Budha.
One should face east toward these: Jyeṣṭhā, Phalguṇī, and Vāyu in the west;
as well as Śukra, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), Gaṅgā, Dhanya, and likewise Candra.
One should worship the five elements, Amita, Īśāna, and [the deity] facing south in the north;
likewise, Śiva with his eight forms, Bali, Rakṣa, and Sarasvatī.
To the left of Indradvāra, facing westward in sequence, [he should worship] Nyakṣa,
Bharata, Mitra, and Kṣattṛ, beginning from the east.
Having worshipped the outward-facing deities in their entirety at the very front of the temple,
one should properly worship Garuḍa between the pedestal and the gateway.
Outside, on the right and left of the door, are Vighneśa and Nāgeśa;
and [inside] are the Discus, the Banner, the Conch, and also Yūthanātha and Akṣaha.
One should worship these, who have arrived from the east facing outward, at the front of the door;
one should worship those thirteen secondary deities individually.
Having approached the Lord as He lay there, and having prostrated and obtained His permission,
he spoke "Suvaḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Bhūḥ" while touching the head, the navel, and the feet.
Then, having sprinkled water around the assembly fire (sabhyāgni), one should offer that thousand-fold oblation with the mantras "svasti caiva iha svāhā" and also "prajāpataye svāhā."
Saying "To Agni for wisdom," and "To the Ādityas," and "To the Viśvedevas," and "To the hosts of Maruts. || 137 ||
One should sacrifice clarified butter with these mantras along with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should sacrifice with these a hundred times, and then sacrifice again with the Vyāhṛtis.
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the Śrīsūkta beginning with "aśriye jātaḥ," the Bhūsūkta, and the hymn dedicated to the Earth deity (bhūmidaivata). || 139 ||
One should sacrifice to each of the Daityas individually, ending with the Vyāhṛtis;
or else, one may follow the ninefold path according to whichever method one adopts.
On that path, one should invoke the deities of the assembly and worship them on all sides;
likewise, one should perform the sacrifice with their respective mantras, even without [the presence of] all the deities.
One should perform the principal oblation, reciting the Puruṣasūkta and thereafter the Viṣṇusūkta; then,
having offered with the Yajñadeva mantras, let the Vaiṣṇava oblation be well-offered.
One should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta in the Āhavanīya fire toward the east;
likewise, the Viṣṇusūkta should be properly offered in the Anvāhārya fire according to the prescribed rite.
One should properly offer the Vedic hymn beginning with the single syllable at the Gārhapatya fire;
one should also properly offer the hymn "tvamagne rudra" at the Āvasathya fire. 144.

O best of sages, one should offer oblations into the fire of the lotus with the Pāramātmika, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Viṣṇu-sūkta, ending each with the Vyāhṛtis. Or else [one may do so] in that manner. 145.
After the invocation of the deities in the rite of the five fires (pañcāgniṣūktahoma), one should perform the worship of all the gods.
Having strewn grass around the Sabhya fire, [one should offer] fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree soaked in clarified butter. (146)
One should offer oblations one thousand and eight times with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
using fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree, and furthermore, with six Vaiṣṇava mantras.
The wise one should offer clarified butter from the upabhṛt ladle with a Vaiṣṇava hymn;
thereafter, he should offer the oblation of cooked rice and clarified butter from the juhū ladle with a Vaiṣṇava mantra.
With the hymn beginning with "viṣṇornuka," with the Puruṣasūkta, and with Vaiṣṇava mantras;
having recited "hiraṇyavarṇā" and "bhūmibhūmne" in sequence. || 149 ||

Having offered that thousand-fold oblation with the mantras beginning with "dhātā" and the five mantras dedicated to Varuṇa, one should perform the sacrifice either once, twice, or ten times by means of the officiating priests.

Thereafter, one should offer oblations with the Jayā and other Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras in their proper sequence; likewise, one should perform the offering to all the deities according to their respective traditions.
By the Vaiṣṇavas with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, likewise with the Mindā-oblation, and also with the interrupted oblations as well as the Mahāvyāhṛtis. || 152 ||
Having offered oblations with the mantra "nārāyaṇāya vidmahe," he should worship the six Vaiṣṇava verses in the Āhavanīya fire while recollecting Hari through the Narasūkta.
While performing the *anvāhārya* rite, he should recite the *Viṣṇusūkta*, the two Brāhma mantras, and the Vaiṣṇava mantra beginning with "aśriye jāto medinī. (154)
One should offer oblations well into the Gārhapatya fire, and thereafter into the Āvasathya;
with the hymn beginning with "Ekākṣara" and the two Rudra-mantras,
one should proceed according to the injunctions with these mantras in these four fires.
One should offer clarified butter sixteen times, or twelve, or ten;
and one should offer milk, curd, and ghee as prescribed, using the upajuḥ formulas in their proper order.
One should offer oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta into the five fires using parched grain;
having taken clarified butter in the sacrificial ladle, one should indeed offer it with the Vaiṣṇava hymns as well.
One should offer the Vaiṣṇava oblation beginning with "ato devā" into the tip of a white lotus;
thereafter, the wise man should offer a white lotus smeared with ghee. || 158 ||

Or else, O Jāpava, one should properly offer oblations of red lotuses or bilva fruits with clarified butter, accompanied by the Puruṣa-sūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns, while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. || 159 ||
Meditating upon the Lord with the supreme mantras, he performs oblations;
and in the homas for Indra and the other deities, he employs their respective mantras accompanied by those of Viṣṇu.
"One should offer clarified butter twenty times with the *sruva* ladle"—thus spoke the sage Atri; "one should offer in this very manner, or indeed just so. (161)
Alternatively, at the conclusion of the recitation of the *hautra*, having offered oblations with verses dedicated to Viṣṇu, those to Varuṇa,
the *jaya* mantras and others, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras, he should honor the members of that assembly.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed method with twenty-seven forms,
or with thirteen types of offerings, one should thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having strewn grass around the sacred fire, he should offer that thousand-fold oblation;
in the water-born fire, he should offer a white lotus smeared with ghee, accompanied by the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra. || 164 ||
One should sacrifice clarified butter a hundred times, offering that which pertains to the Supreme Self;
one should sacrifice in the Āhavanīya fire while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
At the Anvāhārya sacrifice, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the Brāhma-mantra joined with the Vyāhṛtis;
at the Gārhapatya fire, the Vaiṣṇava hymn, and at the Āvasathya fire, likewise the Vaiṣṇava hymn. || 166 ||
One should offer oblations with the Rudra-sūkta while remembering the God of gods;
one should perform the sacrifice eighteen times in the four fires using that very same hymn.
Having offered the Jaya and other oblations once each into the fires of Indra and the others,
he then offers them twenty-one times with their respective mantras.
One should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantras of the Viśas and Śaiṣikas,
and one should offer oblations once into the fires with the Mūrti-mantras of these [deities].
But in the case of a member of the assembly, having offered oblations to all the deities, one should indeed worship Viṣṇu;
and one should offer the Viṣṇu-sūkta accompanied by the Mindā-hutis. || 170 ||
"Kāśyapa says that one should offer oblations with the mantras beginning with 'āśrāvita';
the teacher himself should personally perform the homa in the Sabhya fire. (171)
If one should offer oblations otherwise, everything will quickly perish;
the wise man should spend the remainder of the night with dances, songs, and instrumental music.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Bed, the Covering, the Amulet, the Praise of the *Hautra*, and the Oblations in the Āhavanīya and Other Fires," within the *Mahāpratiṣṭhātantra* of the *Kriyādhikāra* in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable *Vaikhānasa* scripture of the Lord.
*Oṃ*.
The Eighth Chapter.
Having bathed at dawn according to the prescribed rite and having recited the hymns as before, Ratnayāsa entered the sacrificial hall and prostrated before the God of gods. || 1 ||
Then, one should awaken the sleeping Hari with the syllable *oṃ* slightly;
having prostrated, one should raise Him up with the words "I take refuge in Bhūḥ" and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should remove the garments, garlands, and so forth, and adorn [the deity] again with others;
having worshipped with the thirteen services according to the prescribed rule. || 3 ||
Having taken the jewels and the seeds of the elements and entered within,
one should fashion a cavity in the pedestal of the image, as well as the position for the secondary pedestal.
Including the *upapīṭha* word, these are known as the twenty-five words.
Having recited "Tamekane" and "Mim," and having touched the jewels and other items, || 5 ||
One should place a golden tortoise with the mantra "Prajāpateḥ prathamam";
one should place a golden elephant with the mantra "Tamekanemim. || 6 ||
Having uttered "Śatadhāram," he likewise [placed] a golden Garuḍa; and in the station of Brahmā, he placed the Brahma-jewel while reciting the mantra beginning with "Brahmā devānām."
Having recited, "Indraṃ praṇayanti," one should cast a pearl toward the southeast (the direction of Agni). || 8 ||
One should cast a lapis lazuli gem in the southern direction with the mantra "yamo dādhā";
having uttered "vasavaḥ prathama," one should cast a conch-shell in the southwest. || 9 ||
One should place a crystal in the western direction with the four Vāruṇa mantras;
one should cast a topaz in the northwestern direction with the mantra "The Maruts are the Supreme Self."
Having said "Somaṃ rājānam," he should then place Candrakānta in the north;
and with the mantra "Īśānassarva-," he should place Nīla in the northeastern direction as well.
Having said, "Place [this] for our welfare," he offered the Amṛta-stone to Vāsuki;
and with the mantra, "The Ordainer of the ordainers," he offered the Lohita-stone to the Sādhyas.
With the mantra "viśve devasya," one offers an utpala lotus to the Viśvedevas;
with "adhibrahmā yata te," coral is offered to the Siddhas. (13)
Having said, "This [is for] the head," [he gives] realgar to the Gandharvas;
then, saying "Among the Apsarases," the wise one gives mother-of-pearl to the Apsarases.
Having said, "To the sons of Kadrū," he gave a stainless jewel to the Nāgas;
with the mantra "To Aryaman," he gave a *kuruṃvindaka* gem to Aryaman.
And saying "there are three of these," he [offers] the most excellent blue stone to the spirits (bhūtas),
as well as gems such as the amṛtāśmaka and others in the intermediate directions in between.
Having cast [the materials] with the mantras beginning with "śanno nidhattām" and so forth in their proper order,
one should then place the seeds and the minerals in the eight central squares.
In the center, there should be gold, red ochre, yellow orpiment, realgar,
collyrium, black iron sulfate, mercury, and likewise potassium carbonate.
One should place gorocanā in the four directions with their respective mantras;
however, one should place all perfumes and all seeds in the Brahma [quarter].
In the eastern quarter, one should place nourishing grains such as māṣa and kuluttha;
in the southern quarter, wheat and mudga; and in the southwestern quarter, sesame and tilva.
Two barley grains in the west (Vāruṇī), as well as wild rice (nīvāra) and millet (priyaṅgu);
in the north (Saumya), mung beans (mudga) and wheat (godhūma); and in the northeast (Īśānya), all kinds of seeds.
One should place these [objects] outside in sequence using the very mantras previously mentioned;
one should install the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) all around the station of Brahmā.
One should place the Śrīvatsa mark in the northeast with the mantra "bhūyāma," and a full water-pot in the southeast with the mantra "namassulomi."
One should place a drum there in the south while reciting "sa eko 'bhūt"; subsequently, one should place a mirror in the southwest while reciting "devasya tvā". (24)

Having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should place a pair of fish in the western direction (vāruṇī), and subsequently an ankusha in the northwestern direction (vāyavī), while saying, "The earth is one. (25)
Having said, "O Yaśogre," he should place the conch in the north;
and saying, "Brahmā deve," he should indeed set down the āvarta in the northeast.
Having uttered "abhūmānana" and "agra," one should then deposit a mace, a discus, a sword, a spear, and an arrow, each one in turn, in the middle and on the right.
Likewise, on the left side, one should place the conch, the Śārṅga bow, and the shield, reciting for each: "May that fame be foremost. (28)

The colors and emblems of the *sruva* ladle and other implements are for the sake of increasing their respective qualities; and one should describe the form of Śrī in her place as "born for the sake of non-glory" (*aśriye jāta*). (29)
Uttering "medinī" and so forth in place of "hariṇī," and having pronounced "Prajāpati," one should place the tortoise upon it.
One should prepare all these with gold according to one's capacity.
In the absence of [the required materials], there is a substitute:
in the absence of gems, gold; or for seeds, barley alone. || 31 ||
One may also take mercury as a substitute for the various minerals, or whatever else serves as a suitable replacement;
having covered that cavity with linen cloth, one should smear it over with lime.
First, when the pedestal has been well-established with gems and other materials, one should visualize those respective gems and so forth, and utter those specific mantras. (33)
One should sprinkle [the area] with water from kusa grass while reciting the verses beginning with "apo hiṣṭhā.
Then, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the great propitiation (mahāśānti), one should go to the sacrificial hall and bow down to the Lord of Gods.
One should offer one hundred oblations into the Pauṇḍarīka fire with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, using either a white lotus, a red lotus, or a bilva fruit, smeared with clarified butter. || 35 ||
Having offered oblations with the Narasūkta, the Vaiṣṇava hymn beginning with "yad devā," as well as the Brāhma, Aindra, and Vāruṇa hymns, together with the Rātrisūkta; || 36 ||
One should offer oblations with the Viśvajit hymn; this is known as the Mahāśānti.
In the Sabhya fire, however, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta.

Having offered oblations beginning with the single-syllable mantra and ending with the *vyāhṛtis* for each [deity], he should remember the God of gods while offering fuel-sticks and clarified butter. (38)
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him according to the prescribed rule,
and perform the circumambulation of the dwelling site from left to right.
The god, joined by the goddess, together with all his ornaments. || 39 ||
The preceptor, preceded by a stream of water, should proceed to the east while reciting the Śākuna hymn from the Ṛgveda and holding a water-pot upon his head.

Thereafter, the installers likewise lead the deity and the two goddesses [to their places]. Regarding the method of installing the image: if there is the consecration of many deities, one should lead them according to the sequence of those respective deities.
If the installation is for multiple levels, then the Buddhas, being composed in meditation,
should perform the rite on each level according to the prescribed procedure as appropriate.
Having circumambulated the temple and subsequently entered the inner sanctum, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and then install [the deity]. || 43 ||
Then, having recited the Dhruvasūkta as well as the Puruṣasūkta and the Ekākṣarādisūkta, they should install [the image] with concentrated minds.
To the right of the Brahma-sūtra, at the center of the image,
one should install Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the source of the universe, the immutable.

One should install other deities to its left; however, one should not place the central image (bera) at the junction of the threads for any of them; rather, the central image should be placed in the middle.
If it is installed through ignorance, everything quickly perishes;
likewise, if the bathing is performed on the left side when it should be on the right, whether out of festive excitement or curiosity, [the same result follows].
Some say that the festive bathing ceremony should take place on the right or the left side;
however, if there is a constriction in the inner sanctum (garbhālaya), it may instead be performed in the portico (mukhamaṇḍapa). || 48 ||
"Aṅgiras says that one should install [the deity] either in the intermediate space or worship it there;
the preceptor should place the water-pot in front on a pedestal of grain. (49)

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Vyāhṛtis and so forth, from the head to the feet of the image; one should place the three Vyāhṛtis [respectively] from the head down to the feet, place the letter *ya* between the two feet, and place the letter *a* in the heart.
Having encircled [the area] with the Praṇava, one should place the Praṇava upon the head;
then, having recited the Ātmasūkta, one should indeed take it up with the Kūrca.
The method of invocation is as follows: "May the water, joined with Śakti, come from the pitcher; O Blessed One, please come.
Reciting "I invoke Viṣṇu," one should pour [the water] upon the head of the image. || 52 ||
Having first invoked the Puruṣa, the Satya, the Acyuta,
and the Aniruddha upon the head of the Bimba, one should then invoke them in order around the pedestal.
Having invoked the deities mentioned in the *puṣpanyāsa* into their respective directions, and having placed the syllables beginning with Śrīvatsa within the heart of the Śrī-devī; 54.

One should place the mantra beginning with the syllable preceded by Lakṣmī (Śrī) upon the heart; having placed it together with the anusvāra, one should likewise place Śrī with the mantra "śriye jātā. (55)
Having invoked Medinī and the others, one should invoke the Earth in due order;
then the deities residing in the womb-chamber, the lords of the doors, and the door-keepers. (56)

Having invoked the lords of the celestial chariots (vimāneśas), the guardians of the quarters (lokapālas), and those who are never-failing (anapāyins) with their respective mantras, one should then [place them] upon the marriage-thread (kautuka) and other [items].

Having performed the placement of the mantra-syllables (mantrākṣaranyāsa), one should invoke [the deity] in sequence, beginning with the *dhruva* [liṅga]. Regarding the invocation, there is this distinction:
if it is a worldly image (*laukika-bera*) here, the *dhruvas* are the manifestations (*prādurbhāva*) and so forth. || 58 ||
Having consecrated them in sequence, one should therefore invite [the deity] from the Dhruva [image].
However, in whatever temple a Linga has been installed that is devoid of the Dhruva, [it remains incomplete]. || 59 ||
Having invoked [the deity] from that very Dhruva-vessel, one should worship each according to the prescribed rite;
or alternatively, having consecrated a separate water-pot (kumbha), one should then invoke [the deity] into it.

Having worshipped with seats and other offerings, one should also present the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi). During the festival of installation, one should perform the offering of bali; during the festival of bathing, one should carry out the ritual bath. || 61 ||
Beginning on the evening of that day, one should celebrate festival after festival during the festival;
the Elder said that one should make the proclamation right then and there. || 62 ||
Regarding the rites of consecration,
the final festival, the commencement, the hoisting of the banner, and the ritual bathing,
one should not perform the offering of sprouts for many such acts on a single day. (63)
On the very same day, however, for rites performed by different agents, the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) must be performed separately for each.
From the day of the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇaka) until the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should not perform a separate rite of sprouts for the rituals being performed. 65.
The application of the requisites already prepared:
the Guru alone shall take and utilize all those materials which are indeed intended for use in the sacrifice to the gods. (66)

The sacrificial vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, the *araṇī* wood, the eight auspicious items (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*), and furthermore, those things suitable for ritual action, as well as the vehicle and the seat. (67)

Furthermore, for the sake of ritual action, one should take hold of canopies, banners, umbrellas, chowries, fans, and so forth, as well as sacrificial offerings and vessels such as the *aharya* and others. (68)
The wise have declared that other materials which cannot be used [for the image] may also be burnt as substitutes.
If one is unable to perform the installation of a stone *bimba* in the place of Brahman, then an image made of stone of inferior quality may be used. 69.
Some say that one should install [the deity] in the Brahma-sthāna and worship it;
I shall describe that procedure for the image, which is variegated and beautiful in all its limbs. (70)
Having performed the "unbinding of the eyes" (akṣimocana) thereafter without mantras,
and having established each [image] in its respective place according to the procedure for installing stone [liṅgas],
one should indeed perform the purification there with the circumambulation of fire (paryagni) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
At the conclusion of the ritual opening of the eyes accompanied by mantras, one should place jars filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances,
joined in groups of three or eight, upon the head of the image so that they are aligned with its apertures.
Just as the stream falls from that [vessel], so having gradually renounced those [impurities],
one should perform the rite of consecration (adhivāsa) separately, accompanied by the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka).
Alternatively, having placed [the vessels] filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth in front,
one should recite the respective mantras one hundred and eight times according to the sequence.
Having sprinkled [the deity], one should bathe the Lord, meditating upon each [deity] with the respective waters;
then, according to the procedure for the Great Installation (mahāpratiṣṭhā), one should perform the installation once again.
Therefore, the invocation is prescribed for both festivals and at the single-liṅga shrine (balibera);
or else, if one wishes to perform the rite of the single-liṅga shrine quickly.
Having prepared the sacrificial cake (bera) and performed the rite until the opening of the eyes, and having consecrated it upon the products of the cow and other materials,
one should perform the rites such as the worship of the water-pot (kumbha) according to the very sequence prescribed for installation (pratiṣṭhā).
Having completed [the rites] at night according to the rules, and having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed method,
one should install [the deity] in the Brahma-sthāna, preceded by the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa).
At the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, for the sake of purifying the touch of the artisan,
the knower of mantras should perform the purification of the image as prescribed for the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Having invoked the Śakti from the pitcher and worshipped her, one should present the offering;
or else, having quickly performed the installation of gems and other items in the Brahma-sthāna.
Having had the artisan install it there using the collective ritual of the *pīṭha*, and having performed the opening of the eyes without mantras and dismissed the artisan; || 81 ||

Once the eightfold binding is firm and the image is subsequently favorable, one should perform the consecration— including the preliminary rites such as the opening of the eyes and the ritual perfuming— on an auspicious day.
Regarding the consecration of images and so forth brought from another kingdom:
if a king, having conquered another kingdom, should bring back an image, he should do so with that very image in mind within his own delightful realm. (83)
The wise man should also have a palanquin made that is stable and proportionate to it;
having established it there as before, he should perform worship there.
Some say that one should install either an occasional bathing ceremony or a festival image, provided it conforms to the permanent image or is located somewhere within the temple. (85)
Alternatively, if it is not suitable, or if it is located anywhere in the world,
one should place the three images elsewhere than their original location and perform worship there.
He obtains twice the fruit of bricks and other such materials.
If the Āgneya image is placed in a lotus-shaped pit for seven days, [the result is likewise doubled].
One should perform the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as before;
having performed these according to the ritual rule, one should then establish the worldly deity once more.

Having prepared the pitcher according to the rite and having invoked [the deity] from the solar orb, one should invoke [him] from that pitcher into [the image] and worship; such is the instruction. (89)
Having examined the ground according to the prescribed rite, one who is eager to build immediately [should do so];
however, in the case of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), this is especially necessary at the conclusion of the Brahma-padmā period.
At the conclusion of the emergence of the foundation, one should fashion a solid wall;
having constructed the fivefold enclosure outside, one should place the image there according to the prescribed rite.
Setting aside faith and devotion, those seeking the ritual objects have hastily performed various expiations by some means or other,
without conducting the examination of the ground and so forth, and without a preceptor. || 92 ||

If one should establish [the deity] during a month, lunar mansion, or other time not previously specified, one should do so according to the rules during an auspicious month, fortnight, lunar mansion, and muhūrta. (93)
For a month, a fortnight, four days, five days, or even three days,
he indeed offers the Pauṇḍarīka fire-oblation for great pacification at the three times of day.
One should perform the recitation of the respective mantras for the rites of examining the ground and so forth;
thereafter, having performed the offering of sprouts, one should likewise perform the opening of the eyes.
One should diligently perform the infusion with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth as before;
one should then carry out the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration. 96.
If one should perform the consecration after the bathing and the festival, some authorities maintain that there are two fires: the Sabhya and the Pauṇḍarīka.

In the installation of the sacrificial offerings, having brought either the Sabhya fire or the single Āhavanīya fire there, and having performed the daily fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule; || 98 ||
One should establish [the fires] at the conclusion of the installation in the permanent fire-pit as before;
however, if the perpetual fire is not present there, one should mentally arrange the five fires.
Having brought [the fire] from that pit called Gārhapatya, one should offer oblations in that manner;
for the installation of the two goddesses, the pit is as described for the Aupāsana rite.
Having performed the ritual for each [deity] individually, or having unified them as one,
one should perform the bathing, the worship of the water-pot, and the laying to rest separately for each.
One should perform a hundred sacrifices with the respective hymn (sūkta) and its mantra using Vaiṣṇava ghee;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains the same. || 102 ||
Regarding the specific procedure for the permanent image (dhruvārcā):

if the permanent worship has already been established prior to the commencement of the temple construction, one should construct a five-fold enclosure around it to prevent the touch of artisans. || 103 ||
Likewise, having invoked the deities residing in the ālaya into the cage in that very same manner,
one should quickly have a celestial chariot (vimāna) constructed all around the exterior of the cage.
For the sake of purifying the touch of the artisans, once that work has ceased,
one should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and likewise cause the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) to be performed.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should also perform the rite for the auspicious day;
then, filled with joy, one should bathe the deity with water-pots according to one's capacity.
In the vicinity of a temple, and especially at Pauṇḍarīka, one should perform a Mahāśānti rite and an Ekāha sacrifice, and then feed the Brahmins. || 107 ||

Having first performed the *āghāra* oblation in the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of the assembly hall, and having placed the deity within the water-pot (*kumbha*) at the conclusion of the night worship; || 108 ||
Having bathed the image with seven jars accompanied by the primary pitcher,
and having established the image upon a pedestal of grain, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) to the west.
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ according to the rule, the Hotṛ, indeed following the sequence of the Hotṛ’s duties, duly invoked the gods residing in that altar. || 110 ||
Having offered the oblations in the same order as the invocation, one should sacrifice with clarified butter while reciting the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
One should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite, the Śrī Mahīsūkta, together with the five Vāruṇa hymns,
as well as the Jayā and other mantras, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, and likewise one thousand oblations.
Then, for those residing in the ālaya as well as for the assemblies,
[the purification is performed] by means of the *mindāhuti* offerings, with the *Viṣṇusūkta* and Vaiṣṇava hymns that have been recited separately.
In the same manner, one performs the lotus-oblation with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
likewise, one should offer the supreme self-oblation into the fire of the lotus with the Āgneyī mantra.

Having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite and having taken up the water-pot (kumbha), one should invoke [the deity] into the image from the pot, worship it, and present the offerings. || 115 ||
Then, having invoked the deities— even those residing in the cage— into that ālaya,
and having removed the entire cage, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
The definition of *dhruvārcā* and so forth is as follows:

the *dhruvārcana* (permanent worship) consists of the *dhruva* (fixed image) conjoined with the *kautuka* (festive image). The installation (*sthāpana*) of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is said to be of two kinds according to this sequence. || 117 ||
In all cases such as falling and the like, this expiation is prescribed;
as well as the formal re-installation of both the fixed and the portable [liṅga] according to the rules. || 118 ||
The Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke that which is joined with the permanent rite of curiosity;
that which is to be established when the steps have been declared is called the *dhruvārcana* (permanent worship). || 119 ||
The *dhruva* (permanent image) and the *kautuka* (festive image) together are declared to be the *dhruvārcana* (permanent worship);
that same [arrangement], if devoid of the Goddess, is known as the *ekaberam* (single-liṅga worship). || 120 ||
And they say that one [type] yields results solely in the next world;
thus, O best of sages, has the installation been briefly described. (121)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Consecration, the Deposition of Jewels, the Invocation, the Installation of the Fire, the Installation of an Image Brought from Another Kingdom, Consecrations at Unspecified Times, Expiatory Rites, and so forth," in the section on Rituals within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the illustrious Vaikhānasas.
Oṃ.
The Eighth Chapter: Ratnayāsa.
Having bathed at dawn according to the prescribed rule and having recited the hymns as before, [he should proceed].
Having entered the sacrificial hall and having bowed down to the God of gods, || 1 ||
Then, one should awaken the sleeping Hari with the syllable "Oṃ" and slightly;
having prostrated, one should raise Him up with the words "Bhūḥ Prapadye" and the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should remove the garments, garlands, and so forth, and adorn [the deity] again with other [ornaments];
having worshipped with the thirteen services according to the prescribed rule. (3)
Having taken the jewels and the seeds of the elements and entered within,
one should fashion a cavity in the pedestal of the image, as well as the position for the secondary pedestal.
Including the *upapīṭha* word, these are known as the twenty-five words.
Having recited "Tamekane" and "Mim," and having touched the gems and other items, [one should proceed]. || 5 ||
One should place a golden tortoise with the mantra "Prajāpateḥ prathamam";
and with the mantra "Tamekanemi," one should place a golden elephant.
Having uttered "Śatadhāram," he likewise [placed] a golden Garuḍa; and at the station of Brahmā, reciting "Brahmā devānām... and so forth, he [placed] the Brahma-jewel.
Having recited, "Indraṃ praṇayanti," one should cast a pearl toward the southeast (the direction of Agni).
With the mantra "yamo dādhā," one should cast a lapis lazuli gem in the southern direction;
having uttered "vasavaḥ prathama," one should cast a conch shell in the southwestern direction. || 9 ||
One should place a crystal in the western direction with the four Varuṇa mantras;
one should cast a topaz in the northwestern direction with the mantra beginning "The Maruts are the Supreme Self."
Having said "Somaṃ rājānam," he should then place Candrakānta in the north;
with the mantra "Īśānassarva-," he should also place Nīla in the northeastern direction.
Having said, "Place [this] for our welfare," he offered the amṛta-stone to Vāsuki;
and with the mantra, "The Ordainer of the ordainers," he offered the red stone to the Sādhyas.
With the mantra "viśve devasya," one offers an utpala lotus to the Viśvedevas;
with "adhibrahmā yata te," coral is offered to the Siddhas. || 13 ||
Having said, "This [is for] the head," [he gives] realgar to the Gandharvas;
then, saying "Among the Apsarases," the wise one gives mother-of-pearl to the Apsarases.
Having said, "This for the sons of Kadrū," he gave a stainless jewel to the Nāgas;
with the mantra "To Aryaman," he gave the Kuruṇḍika to Aryaman.
And speaking thus, "Therein are these three," he [placed] the supreme blue gem among the elements,
and the gems such as amṛtāśmaka and others in the middle and in the intermediate directions as well.
Having cast [the materials] with the mantras beginning with "śanno nidhattām" and so forth in their proper sequence,
one should then place the seeds and the minerals in the eight central squares.
Gold, red ochre, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, black iron sulfate, mercury, and likewise saurāṣṭraka; || 18 ||
One should place yellow orpiment in the four directions with their respective mantras;
however, one should place all fragrances and all seeds in the Brahma [quarter].
One should place the grains for prosperity belonging to Indra in the east—namely masha and kulattha;
in the south, wheat and mudga; and in the southwest, sesame and tilva.
In the west (Vāruṇī), however, two barley grains, wild rice (nīvāra), and millet (priyaṅgu);
in the north (Saumya), mung beans and wheat; and in the northeast (Īśānya), all kinds of seeds. || 21 ||
One should place these [objects] outside in sequence using the very mantras previously mentioned;
one should install the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) all around the station of Brahmā.
One should place the Śrīvatsa mark in the northeast with the mantra "bhūyāma," and a full water-pot in the southeast with the mantra "namassulomi."
One should place a drum there in the south while reciting "sa eko 'bhūt"; subsequently, one should place a mirror in the southwest while reciting "devasya tvā". (24)
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should place a pair of fish in the western direction, and subsequently an ankusha in the northwestern direction, while saying, "The earth is one. (25)
Having said, "O Yaśograbhū," he should place the conch in the north;
and saying, "Brahmā among the gods," he should indeed set down the water-vessel (āvarta) in the northeast.
Having uttered "abhūmānana" and "agra," one should then place the mace, discus, sword, spear, and arrow individually in the center and then on the right.
Likewise, on the left side, one should place the conch, the Śārṅga bow, and the shield, reciting for each: "May my fame be foremost. (28)

The colors and emblems of the *sruva* ladle and other implements are for the sake of increasing their respective qualities; and one should speak of the form of Śrī in her place as "born for the sake of non-glory" (*aśriye jāta*). (29)
Uttering "the earth" and so forth in place of "the doe," and saying "Prajāpati," one should place the tortoise upon it.
One should prepare all these with gold according to one's capacity.
In the absence [of the required materials], there is a substitute:
in the absence of gems, gold; or in the absence of seeds, barley alone. || 31 ||
One may also take mercury as a substitute for the various minerals, or whatever else serves as a suitable replacement;
having covered that cavity with linen cloth, one should smear it over with lime plaster.
First, when the pedestal has been well-established with gems and other materials, one should visualize those respective gems and so forth, and utter those specific mantras. (33)
One should sprinkle [the area] with water from kusa grass while reciting the mantras beginning with "apo hiṣṭhā.
Then, having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the great propitiation (mahāśānti), one should go to the sacrificial hall and bow down to the Lord of Gods.
One should offer one hundred oblations in the Pauṇḍarīka fire with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, using either a white lotus, a red lotus, or a bilva fruit, each anointed with clarified butter. || 35 ||
Having offered oblations with the Narasūkta, the Vaiṣṇava hymn beginning with "yad devā," as well as the Brāhma, Aindra, and Vāruṇa hymns, together with the Rātrisūkta; || 36 ||
One should offer oblations with the Viśvajit hymn; this is known as the Mahāśānti.
In the Sabhya fire, however, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta.

Having offered oblations beginning with the single-syllable mantra and ending with the *vyāhṛtis* for each [deity], he should remember the God of gods while offering fuel-sticks and clarified butter. (38)
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him according to the prescribed rule,
and perform the circumambulation of the dwelling site from left to right.
The god, joined by the goddess, together with all his ornaments. || 39 ||
The preceptor, preceded by a stream of water and reciting the Śākuna hymn, should proceed to the east while holding the pitcher upon his head.

Then the installers likewise lead the deity and the two goddesses [to their places]. Regarding the method of installing the image: if there is the consecration of many deities, one should lead them according to the sequence of those respective deities.
If it is established on many levels, then the Buddhas, being composed in meditation,
should perform the rites on each level according to the prescribed rule as is appropriate.
Having circumambulated the temple and subsequently entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and then install [the deity]. || 43 ||
Then, having recited the Dhruvasūkta and the Puruṣasūkta,
as well as the Ekākṣarādisūkta, they should install [the deity] with concentrated minds.
To the right of the Brahma-sūtra, exactly at the center of the image,
one should install Viṣṇu, the immutable god of gods and source of the universe.

One should install other deities to its left; however, one should not place the central image (bera) at the junction of the threads for any of them; rather, the central image should be placed in the middle.
If it is installed through ignorance, everything quickly perishes;
likewise, performing the ceremonial bath on the left side when it should be on the right, whether out of festive excitement or mere curiosity, leads to ruin.
Some say that the festive bathing should take place on the right or the left;
however, if there is a constriction in the inner sanctum (garbhālaya), it may instead be performed in the portico (mukhamaṇḍapa). || 48 ||
"Aṅgiras says that one should worship [the deity] either after it has been installed or during the interval;
the preceptor should place the water-pot upon a pedestal of grain in front of himself. (49)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Vyāhṛtis and so forth, placing the three Vyāhṛtis on the image from the head down to the feet;
one should place the letter *ya* between the two feet and the letter *a* in the heart.
Having enveloped [the object] with the Praṇava, one should place the Praṇava upon the head;
then, having recited the Ātmasūkta, one should indeed take it up with the Kūrca.
The method of invocation is as follows: "May the Blessed One come with the water joined with Śakti from the pitcher";
saying "I invoke Viṣṇu," one should pour [the water] upon the head of the image. 52.
Having first invoked the Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta,
and Aniruddha upon the head of the Bimba, one should then [invoke them] in order around the pedestal.
Having invoked the deities mentioned in the *puṣpanyāsa* into their respective directions, and having placed the syllables beginning with *śrīvatsa* within the heart of the Śrīdevī; 54.
One should place the mantra beginning with the syllable preceded by Lakṣmī (Śrī) within the heart;
having placed it along with the anusvāra, one should then place Śrī with the mantra "śriye jātā". || 55 ||
Having invoked Medinī and the others, one should successively invoke the Earth, the deities residing within the womb-chamber, the lords of the doors, and the door-keepers. (56)

Having invoked the lords of the celestial chariots (vimāneśas), the guardians of the quarters (lokapālas), and those who are never-failing (anapāyins) with their respective mantras, one should then [place them] upon the marriage-thread (kautuka) and other items.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the mantra-syllables, one should invoke [the deity] in sequence, beginning with the *dhruva* [image].
Regarding the invocation of the *bhrū* [image], there is this distinction: if the image here is a worldly one (*laukika-bera*), then the *prādurbhāva* and other [manifestations] are the *dhruvas*.
Having consecrated them in sequence, one should then invoke [the deity] from the Dhruva [liṅga].
However, in whatever temple a liṅga has been installed that is devoid of the Dhruva; || 59 ||
Having invoked [the deity] from that very Dhruva-vessel, one should worship each according to the prescribed rite;
or else, having consecrated a separate water-pot (kumbha), one should then invoke [the deity] into it.

Having worshipped with seats and other offerings, one should also present the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi). During the festival of installation, one should perform the offering of food (bali); during the bathing ceremony, one should perform the ritual bath (snapana). || 61 ||
Beginning on the evening of that day, one should celebrate festival after festival during the festival; the Elder said that the proclamation should be made right then and there. (62)
Regarding the rituals of consecration,
the final festival, the commencement, the raising of the banner, and the bathing ceremony,
one should not perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for multiple rites on a single day. 63.
On the very same day,
however, for those rites performed by different agents, the offering of the single shoot must be performed separately for each.
From the day of the ritual planting of the sprouts until the day of the consecration,
one should not perform a separate rite of sprouting for the rituals being performed.
Regarding the application of the materials that have been prepared:
the preceptor alone shall take and utilize all those substances that are indeed fit for use in the sacrifice to the gods. (66)

The sacrificial vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva*, the *araṇī* wood, the eight auspicious items (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*), and furthermore, those things suitable for ritual action, as well as the vehicle and the seat. (67)
Furthermore, for the sake of ritual action, one should take hold of canopies, banners, parasols, chowries, fans, and so forth, as well as sacrificial offerings and vessels such as the *aharya*. (68)
The wise have declared that other materials which are not suitable for use may be used as fuel for cremation;
however, if one is unable to perform the installation of a stone image in the Brahma-sthāna, one may instead install a stone image devoid of color (or caste).
Some say that one should install [the image] in the Brahma-sthāna and worship it;
I shall describe that procedure for the image, which is variegated and beautiful in all its limbs. (70)
After performing the unbinding of the eyes, thereafter, without mantras,
having established [the image] in its respective place according to the procedure for installing a stone,
one should indeed perform purification there with the circumambulation by fire and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

At the conclusion of the opening of the eyes accompanied by mantras, one should place jars filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances upon the head of the image, joined in groups of three or eight, and provided with holes.
Just as the stream falls from that [vessel], so having gradually renounced those [impurities],
one should perform the rite of consecration (adhivāsa) separately, accompanied by the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka).
Alternatively, having placed [the vessels] filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth in front [of him],
he should recite one hundred and eight times the respective mantras in their proper order.
Having sprinkled [the deity], one should bathe the Lord, meditating upon each [deity] with the respective waters;
then, according to the procedure for the Great Installation (mahāpratiṣṭhā), one should perform the installation once again.
Therefore, the invocation is prescribed for both festivals and for the single-liṅga (ekabera) form;
or, if one wishes to perform the rite of the single-liṅga form quickly. 76.
Having prepared the *bera* (the image) until the opening of the eyes, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) upon the products of the cow and other materials,
one should perform the rites such as the worship of the water-jar (*kumbha-pūjā*) according to the very sequence prescribed for installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having completed [the ritual] at night according to the rules, and having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed method,
one should install [the deity] in the Brahma-sthāna, preceded by the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa).
At the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, for the sake of purifying the touch of the artisans,
the knower of mantras should perform the purification of the image as prescribed for the permanent image (dhruvabera).
Having invoked the Śakti from the pitcher and worshipped her, one should present the offering;
or else, having quickly performed the installation of gems and other items in the Brahma-sthāna.

Having had the artisan install it there according to the prescribed method for the collection of pedestals, and having performed the opening of the eyes without mantras and dismissed the artisan; || 81 ||

Once the eightfold binding is firm and subsequently favorable on an auspicious day, one should likewise perform the installation, beginning with the consecration of the eyes and the preliminary perfuming.
Regarding the consecration of images and other objects brought from another kingdom:
if a king, having conquered another kingdom, should bring back a sacred image, he should dedicate that image to his own delightful realm. (83)
The wise man should also have a palanquin constructed that is stable and proportionate to it;
having installed it there as before, he should perform worship there.

Some say that one should install either an image corresponding to the permanent icon (dhruvabera), or an image for festivals (autsavam), or a bathing image (snāpanam) in some part of the temple. || 85 ||
Alternatively, if [the image] is unsuitable or if it is found anywhere in the world,
one should install it elsewhere than the location of the three images and perform worship there.
He obtains twice the fruit of bricks and other such materials.
If the Āgneya image is placed in a lotus-shaped pit for seven days, [the result is likewise doubled]. // 87 //
One should perform the great pacification (mahāśānti) and the preliminary rites such as the consecration (adhivāsa) as before;
having performed these according to the rule, one should then establish the worldly [deity] once more.

Having prepared the pitcher according to the prescribed rite and having invoked [the deity] from the solar orb, one should invoke [the deity] into that pitcher and worship it; such is the instruction. (89)
Having examined the ground according to the prescribed rite, one who is in haste should immediately begin the construction;
this is especially so for the inner sanctum at the conclusion of Brahmā’s lotus-period.
At the conclusion of the emergence of the foundation, one should fashion a solid wall;
having constructed the fivefold enclosure outside, one should place the image there according to the prescribed rite.
Placing faith and devotion foremost, those seeking the goal have hastily performed various expiations by any means whatsoever,
without conducting the examination of the ground and so forth, and without a preceptor. || 92 ||

If one should establish [the deity] during a month, lunar mansion, and so forth that were not previously specified for the installation, one should do so according to the rules during an auspicious month, fortnight, lunar mansion, and muhūrta.
For a month, a fortnight, four days, five days, or even three days,
he indeed performs the Pauṇḍarīka fire-sacrifice and the Mahāśānti rite three times a day.
One should perform the recitation of the respective mantra for the rites of examining the ground and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform the offering of sprouts as well as the opening of the eyes.
One should diligently perform the infusion with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth as before;
then, one should again carry out the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration. 96.
If one should perform the consecration after the bathing and festival rites, some authorities maintain that there are two fires: the Sabhya and the Pauṇḍarīka.

In the installation of the sacrificial offerings (baliberapratiṣṭhā), having brought the fire—either the Sabhya or the single Eka-agni—there, and having performed the daily fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule; || 98 ||
One should establish [the fires] at the conclusion of the installation in the permanent fire-pit as before;
however, if the permanent fire is not present there, one should mentally arrange the five fires.
Having carried forth [the fire] from that pit called Gārhapatya, one should likewise offer oblations;
for the installation behind the two goddesses, the pit is as described for the Aupāsana rite.
Having performed the ritual for each [deity] individually, or having unified them as one,
one should separately perform the bathing, the worship of the water-pot (kumbha), and the laying to rest upon the bed.
One should perform a hundred sacrifices with the respective hymn (sūkta) and its mantra using Vaiṣṇava materials;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains the same.
Regarding the specific procedure for the permanent worship (dhruvārcā):
if the permanent worship has been established prior to the commencement of the temple construction, one should construct a fivefold enclosure all around it to prevent the touch of artisans. || 103 ||
Likewise, having likewise invoked the deities residing in the ālaya into the cage,
one should quickly have a celestial chariot (vimāna) constructed all around the exterior of the cage.
For the sake of purifying the touch of the artisans, once that work has ceased,
one should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and likewise cause the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) to be performed.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should also perform the rite for a day of merit (puṇyāha);
then, filled with joy, one should bathe the god with water-pots according to one's capacity.
In the vicinity of a temple, and especially at Pauṇḍarīka,
one should perform the Mahāśānti rite and likewise an Ekāha sacrifice, and then feed the Brahmins.

Having first performed the *āghāra* oblation in the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of the assembly hall, and having placed the deity within the water-pot (*kumbha*) at the conclusion of the night worship; || 108 ||
Having bathed the image with seven jars accompanied by the primary pitcher,
and having established the image upon a pedestal of grain, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) to the west.
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ according to the rule, the Hotṛ, indeed following the sequence of the Hotṛ’s duties,
duly invoked the gods residing in that altar.
Having offered oblations of clarified butter according to the very sequence of invocation,
one should worship with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.

One should perform one thousand oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Śrī Mahīsūkta, together with the five Vāruṇa hymns, as well as with the Jayā and other mantras, the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, and likewise with the Sahasra-hutis.
Then, for those residing in the ālaya and for the assemblies as well,
[the rite is performed] with the Mindā oblations, with the Viṣṇusūkta, and with Vaiṣṇava hymns that have been recited separately.
In the same manner, one performs the lotus-oblation with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
likewise, one should offer the supreme self-offering into the fire of Agni with the Āgneyī mantra.

Having bathed at dawn according to the prescribed rite and having taken up the water-pitcher (kumbha), one should invoke [the deity] into the image from the pitcher, worship it thoroughly, and present the offerings. || 115 ||
Then, having invited the deities— even those residing in the cage— into that ālaya,
and having removed the entire cage, one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
The definition of the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) and so forth is as follows:

the permanent worship consists of the permanent image (dhruva) joined with the festive image (kautuka). The installation of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is said to be of two kinds according to this sequence.
In all cases such as falling and the like, this expiation is prescribed;
as well as the formal re-installation of both the fixed (dhruva) and the portable (kautuka) [lingas]. || 118 ||
The Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke that which is joined with the permanent rite of curiosity;
when the steps have been mentioned, that which is to be established there is declared as the worship of Dhruva.
The *dhruva* (permanent) and the *kautuka* (festive) constitute the single *dhruvārcana* (permanent worship);
that very same [worship], if devoid of the Goddess, is known as *ekaberam* (the single-liṅga). || 120 ||
And they say that one [type of] consecration bestows exclusively rewards in the next world;
thus, O best of sages, has the installation been briefly described. (121)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Consecration, the Installation of Jewels, the Invocation, the Enkindling of the Fire, the Installation of an Image Brought from Another Kingdom, Consecration at Unspecified Times, Expiatory Rites, and so forth," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu in the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*.
Oṃ.
The Tenth Chapter:
The Subsidiary Services of Worship. Now, O best of sages, listen as I describe the services of worship.
They are proclaimed as "accessories" (upacāra) because they serve as the means for the service of the deities. || 1 ||
Because they are specifically grasped for the purpose of worship, they are called *vigrahas* (embodiments);
and there are sixty-four ritual services (*upacāras*), as well as fifty-five.
Forty-eight, forty-two, thirty-six, thirty-four, thirty-two, and nineteen. (3)
These twenty-seven [deities] are proclaimed in nine groups;
in the rite of worshiping the Ālaya-liṅga when offerings are absent, there are thirteen.
In the worship of the deity with material offerings, as well as in the worship of the retinue,
there shall likewise be eleven modes of service (upacāras) in the worship of Śiva and the others.
In the worship of each individual substance, eight forms are prescribed; in the ritual bathing, eight forms;
in the fire offering (homa), six forms are prescribed; and in the incarnations, sixteen.
In the house of the ignorant, during the worship of Dhruva, there are twenty-five forms;
for those who are incapable, there are two forms, or even just one form.
For all of these, the initial invocation (āvāhana) as well as the general worship at the end and likewise the dismissal (udvāsana) are prescribed.
Without those two, the seat is likewise counted as being within oneself; furthermore,
in the Uttama-kalpa, there are sixty-four services,
including the inferential offering (anumāna), the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana).
Flowers, incense, and a lamp; a lamp-offering, water for sipping, and water for bathing; a towel, a garment, an upper cloth, and ornaments. || 10 ||
The sacred thread, water for the feet, and likewise water for sipping; flowers, fragrance, incense, a lamp, and again water for sipping. || 11 ||
There should be the offering of oblations accompanied by mantras, followed again by water for sipping;
then a mouth-cloth, the eight-footed seat and so forth, a mirror, an umbrella, and chowries.
The palm-leaf fan, banners, elephants, chariots, and horses; dancing and singing;
instrumental music, the service of weapons, and the circumambulation of auspicious objects. || 13 ||

The recitation of the Vedas, the praise of the Purāṇas in all directions, the offering of the measure (mātrā), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and thereafter the oblation and the fire-sacrifice (havir-homa). || 14 ||

Then there is the sipping of water for drinking and rinsing the mouth; after that, the incense offering; then the food offering (bali) and the prostration; and after that, the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). || 15 ||
Praise, a sacrificial fee, and subsequent inference through devotion—
these constitute the sixty-four modes of service for the most excellent of supreme worship.
There were fifty-five types of offerings: elephants, banners, chariots, horses, auspicious objects, and weapons;
as well as musical instruments, inference, hymns of praise, and sacrificial fees.
Fifty-five forms are declared for the superior and middling [categories],
along with six from the south and the east, excluding the handful of flowers.
In the middle ritual manual (*madhyamakalpa*), there are forty-eight services (*upacāra*) and offerings (*bhoga*) numbering six or eight for worship of the highest and lowest [deities].
Then, by means of the mantras, oblations, and the sixfold bodily postures, [he should perform the ritual]. || 19 ||
Forty-two services have been taught for the middling and superior worship;
[there are also] thirty-six services.
And without a hymn of praise, with the Vedas, with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and in the proper measure. || 20 ||
Then, by means of the parasol and the fan, thirty-six [deities] are impelled;
these thirty-six forms are said to be in the middle-of-the-middle [kalpa].
In the middle and lower grades of worship, thirty-four services are prescribed, excluding the mirror and the fly-whisk;
likewise, there are thirty-four forms, excluding dance and song. || 22 ||
In the age of degeneration (adhamakalpa), thirty-two forms are prescribed for worship that is both inferior and superior;
these are the thirty-two modes of service (upacāra).
Or even without instrumental music and fire-oblations, and with the concluding lamp and the sipping of water (ācamana). || 23 ||
Twenty-nine services and twenty-nine enjoyments are said to be for the lowest and middle [levels],
while twenty-seven services [are for the highest].
Excluding the offerings and prostrations, there are twenty-seven forms. || 24 ||

In the lowest of low forms of worship, nine types of ritual salutations (vigrahas) are prescribed; for other offerings such as the *kautuka* and so forth, and upon obtaining sacrificial oblations (*havir-lābha*), twenty-seven types of ritual salutations are prescribed. || 25 ||
Whether in the case of an image, a festival, or even in worldly or other such matters,
the worship ordained by the virtuous is performed with twenty-seven forms.
Those thirteen forms should be employed at the offering of the oblation (havirhoma):
the forms beginning with the arghya and ending with the ācamana, as well as those beginning with the āsana. || 27 ||
These thirteen [offerings] are accompanied by the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) and prostration;
those eleven alone are devoid of the offering of a handful of flowers and prostration. || 28 ||

The six services (upacāras) prescribed for the purpose of oblation, meditation, and worship are: those beginning with water for the feet (pādya) and ending with water for sipping (ācamana), as well as those beginning with the respectful offering (arghya) and ending with flowers (puṣpa). Thus, these six have been declared. || 29 ||
Those eleven modes of worship, when combined with the four offerings beginning with *havis* and with prostration, are declared to constitute the sixteen forms [of worship]. (30)

The oblation, water for drinking, water for sipping (ācamana), a cloth for the mouth, as well as the ritual offering (bali), the fire-oblation (homa), prostration, the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and praise (stuti). || 31 ||
In the worship of a single image,
twenty-five forms [of the deity] and [their corresponding] ritual services (upacāra) have been prescribed.
There are two acts: the offering of a handful of flowers and prostration; yet prostration is of a single form. || 32 ||

For the manifestation [of the deity], there are sixteen services (upacāras): four beginning with the foot-water (pādya) and ending with the eight services, followed by the four beginning with the oblation (havir-ādi). || 33 ||
One should worship according to the previously mentioned procedure, including offerings, prostrations, hymns of praise, and handfuls of flowers, during the ritual for the worship of the temple image.
The fourfold nature of the ritual offerings consists of the tangible, the visible, the audible, and the edible;
likewise, there is the seat, the offering of water for the feet, flowers, and fragrance. (35)

The water for the guest-offering (arghya), the six [substances] beginning with the bath-water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the ritual application of handfuls of flowers, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) together with the touching [of the image]. 36.
The four offerings, beginning with the oblation (havis), are indeed designated as food; one should present them, along with water for the feet, into the right hand of the deity. || 37 ||

Song, instrumental music, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and hymns of praise are indeed prescribed as the audible offerings; these, along with the [other] visible offerings, constitute the eight modes of worship (aṣṭopacārakāḥ). || 38 ||
Some say that incense, water offerings, and honey-mixture are called "fragrant articles" (āghreya);
these are declared to be the ritual services (upacāra), along with the sequence for their application and so forth. (39)
The essential nature [of the image] has been declared in the *Khila* and should be understood by those most learned in the ritual rules.
Regarding the specific procedure for the worship of the permanent image (*dhruvabera*), if one desires to perform the worship upon the permanent image with devotion: || 40 ||
Some worship the permanent image (dhruvabera) with all the ritual forms, excluding bathing, anointing, and incense, up to the offering of mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).

Regarding the daily worship during the consecration (kautuka): the manner of preparing the offerings and the method of service. One should perform the daily worship specifically at the site of the consecration itself; indeed, at the conclusion of each respective mantra, one should perform it separately with the five forms (mūrtis).
Having joined the name of the substance and saying "I give," he should bestow the garment,
upper cloth, sacred thread, ornaments, and so forth, according to the prescribed rule.
Kāśyapa says that one should offer [the oblation] by joining it to the five forms;
this is considered the superior method for the swift accomplishment of the purposes of worship.
That which is devoid of the arcane [mantra], one should prepare with that very water.
For the morning worship, the flowers are the lotus, the palāśa, the tulasī, and the navamālikā. || 45 ||
The Nandyāvarta, Mandāra, Mādhavī, Campaka, as well as Punnāga and Ketakī—these ten [are used] for worship at the time of dawn. (46)
Flowers suitable for worship at the time of midday are the white lotus, the karavīra, the palāśa, as well as the tulasī,
the blue water-lily, the bilva leaf, or even the red lotus. || 47 ||
The *kovidāraikapatra* and the *tāpasāṅkura*—
these are declared to be the ten flowers for worship at midday.
In the evening, the flowers worthy of worship are the red lotus, the night-lotus, jasmine, Arabian jasmine, Malati,
Madhavi, Karavira, Hrivera, and Gajakarnika.
Likewise, there are ten flowers for the evening worship, including Damanaka;
these are the flowers suitable for worship at all times: Dūrvā grass, Tulasī, Bilva, Karavīra, and Campaka.
Viṣṇukrāntā and Bhadrā are worthy of worship at all times; the greatness of Tulasī is to be honored,
and one should avoid stale flowers and avoid stale water.
The tulasī leaf is not to be avoided, nor is the water of the Jāhnavī;
the kapittha leaf is praised, being equal to the bilva leaf at night—the kapittha leaf is said [to be supreme] at night. 52.
One should worship with whatever flowers have been prescribed and with their respective leaves;
the worshipper [should offer] this quartet: water, incense, a lamp, and a flower. || 53 ||
By that, the worship becomes complete in its general sense.
First is the five-limbed worship, the worship of Dhruvagiri; second is the peaceful worship (śāntapūjana). || 54 ||
Next is the adoration of the seat of the Bhūtas adorned with auspicious ornaments;
the fifth is the worship with offerings (bali). By means of these five types of worship, [the rite is completed]. || 55 ||
Complete worship is proper, while incomplete worship is improper;
through the worship of the *dhruvabera*, one attains the imperishable state of union (*sāyujya*).
Indeed, through the worship of Śānta, one attains sovereignty over all worlds and a form identical [to his];
having enjoyed everything pertaining to this world and the next, one shall attain union (sāyujya). || 57 ||
Furthermore, through the worship of the Kautuka and the worship of the Bhūtapīṭha,
there shall be victory over all enemies, as well as long life and good health.
Through the worship of Bali, one shall attain prosperity, abundance of sons, the state of Sālokya, renown throughout all the worlds, and the proximity of the deity (Sāmīpya). 59.
The specific fruits for those who perform each respective consecration have been proclaimed;
this applies to the image, the temple, and likewise to the pedestal of the spirits.
Viṣṇu is eternally present within both the shadow [of the image] and the physical form;
therefore, in the performance of circumambulation, stepping over these does not cause any fault.
One should perform an even number of circumambulations; an odd number is for malevolent rites. One should never perform circumambulation between the deity and the Śānti-pīṭha.
Some say that one should not perform [the rite] within the pedestal of the deity;
this alone is the distinction, while everything else is as described in the *Khiloka*.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Regulation for Determining the Offerings and Flowers," in the section on Ritual Practice (*kriyādhikāra*) within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable scripture of the Śrī Vaikhānasa tradition.
Oṃ.
The eleventh chapter.
The Chapter on the Ten Incarnations:
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and then the Dwarf;
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Kalki—these are the ten. (1)
There are five previous manifestations (āvirbhāvas), and likewise other appearances (prādurbhāvas).
Matsya and Kūrma are said to be of two kinds, while Vārāha is remembered as being of three kinds. || 2 ||
Nārasiṃha is fivefold, while Vāmana is remembered as twofold;
Bhārgava Rāma is singlefold, and Rāghava is remembered as twofold.
Balabhadra is of two kinds, and Kṛṣṇa possesses innumerable forms;
Kalki exists as a single form—listen now to the characteristics of these.
At the dissolution of the world of moving and non-moving beings by the great flood of waters, Matsyaka was the first to withdraw that water during the pralaya.
Within the pore of his hair is contained the ocean of dissolution,
wherein the teachings of the Vedas, submerged at the end of the eon during the final dissolution, lie hidden.
The second was the god of gods, Janārdana, in the form of a fish;
the first resembled molten gold, while the other had the luster of collyrium.
One should fashion two fish according to the prescribed rule, mounted upon red lotus seats, one span (vitasti) in width, and twice that length.

The Pauṇḍarīka is the principal fire; everything else is as described in the Khila section. Kūrma is the primordial tortoise for the purpose of supporting the earth when it has moved from its own place. || 9 ||
The second [form] is the extractor of nectar, holding Mount Mandara;
its appearance is like collyrium, and it stands upon four seats. || 10 ||

The Gārhapatya fire is the primary fire; everything else is as described in the section on the "Waste" (khila). Likewise, Vārāha was the first to lift up the earth which had sunk into the netherworld (pātāla). || 11 ||
There was one named Ādivarāha; I shall describe his characteristics:
he has the form of a man and the body of a boar, is dark like a grain-ear, and possesses four arms. || 12 ||
The right foot is firmly placed on the pedestal, while the left is bent;
at a distance of five tālas from that, he beholds the dark earth upon his thighs.
Beholding her with her two hands joined in reverence, her two feet outstretched, wearing flowery garments, and filled with both bashfulness and joy; || 14 ||
The god, having grasped the feet of the two goddesses with his right hand and having placed his left hand beneath the arms of the goddess as a support, [stood there]. (15)
Having lifted up that earth which had sunk into the netherworld (Pātāla), he rose up,
holding the supreme conch and discus with his two other hands.
Likewise, he smelled the head of the goddess, who was adorned with all ornaments;
and the two white-lotus-hued, pure-tirtha attendants of hers likewise.
The two gatekeepers, Brahman and Rājarājendralakṣmī, have white and red lusters;
the four Vedas, possessing white lusters, are stationed upon their respective vehicles. || 18 ||
He should likewise perform the rites for Pulinda, Śaiṣika, Śyāma, and Śeṣa as previously described;
and when an intermediate dissolution has occurred, he should be intent upon withdrawing them.
The Boar, known as Pralaya, appeared as before with the face of a boar;
he was like molten gold, wearing supreme blue garments.
The right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), while the left hangs down along the hip;
the upper hands hold the conch and the discus, and everything else is as described previously. || 21 ||
One should fashion the goddess Mahī on the right side of the god;
the god and the goddess are seated comfortably beneath his lion-throne.
One should fashion Nārada as red in color, with a vīṇā in his hand;
Bhṛgu and Puṇya are the two worshippers, and everything else is as before.
Having slain the asura Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of all sacrifices,
he became the Sacrificial Boar (Yajñavarāha) in order to establish the sacrifice.
His color is white, and everything else is like that of the Varāha known as Pralaya;
the Supreme Lord is seated comfortably upon a throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi. || 25 ||
The two worshippers named Kanaka and Yajña were described as being like gold;
their assembly fire was the principal one, while everything else was exactly as in the other worlds.
One should perform one hundred and eight offerings with the mantra "kṣmām ekām".
The varieties of Nārasiṃha are Girija, Sthūṇaja, and Sudarśananṛsiṃhaka. || 27 ||
Likewise, Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha and Pātālanarasiṃhaka;
thus has the Nārasiṃha [mantra] been declared to be fivefold by the wise. (28)
The [mantras] born of Giri and Jasthūṇa have been declared by me at length in the Khila section;
now the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha will be fully explained. || 29 ||
One should visualize a stainless and blazing wheel, resembling ten million suns,
with a pair of great radiant cities situated in the center of the wheel.
In its center, he beheld Nṛsiṃha seated comfortably, with a ruddy luster, possessing an exceedingly terrifying form, yet bestowing fearlessness upon his devotees. || 31 ||
One should visualize the God of gods as having four arms and bearing the discus as a weapon; beneath his lion-throne, on its right and left sides, [one should place... (32).
One should visualize Brahmā and Rudra as conversing for the sake of pacifying the anger,
while reciting "yo vā nṛsiṃha" and the two discus-mantras.
The hundred and eight oblations and all other details are like those for Nṛsiṃha.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the characteristics of Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha.
Seated comfortably upon a lion-throne, having extended the left foot and likewise placed the right foot, bent, upon the seat. || 35 ||
One should place Lakṣmī upon the lap of the God; she is beautiful in all her limbs, adorned with every ornament, and filled with both modesty and joy.
With her hands joined in reverent salutation, resembling the filaments of a lotus,
the goddess stood with her feet extended, measuring five tālas in height.
Or she may have her hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, or holding upraised lotuses with her right hand while performing an embrace with that [left] hand. (38)

Having placed [the left hand] upon the left thigh and holding the conch and discus with the other two hands, one who desires the fruits of worldly enjoyment and the hereafter should perform it thus according to the rule. (39)
One who is intent solely on the world beyond should place Lakṣmī on his left side;
indeed, if he places her on the left side, he should seat her upon his left thigh.
Embracing her with his left hand, he grants the gesture of fearlessness with his right;
likewise, with his two other hands, he holds the conch and the discus.
Having thus conceptualized him, one should worship both Brahmā and Īśa;
