and one should prepare a separate sacrificial pit for the domestic fire (aupāsana) for the Goddess Śrī.
Alternatively, some say that one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for this Lakṣmī in a single vessel, reciting the Śrīsūkta while uttering the verse "śriye jāta. (43)
Having recited, "May she bestow auspiciousness," one should worship one hundred and eight times with the [mantras] "Śrī, Dhṛti, Pavitrī, and Lakṣmī" as the [personified] forms. || 44 ||
If there should be a separate sacrificial pit accompanied by the Puruṣasūkta, one should perform everything for Nārasiṃha according to the rules, as previously described. || 45 ||
There is a specific rule for the installation of Nṛsiṃha:
one should install Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha, Sthūṇaja, and others everywhere for the sake of prosperity, including in villages and other residential sites.
If it should be in the middle of a village, there would be total destruction by its gaze;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause four gates to be made. || 47 ||
One should duly install Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha and Sthūṇaja on the left and outside, facing either toward the village or [toward the deity]. || 48 ||
And I shall describe Pātālanarasiṃha in brief:
having raised the left knee with the right knee alone. (49)
One should depict Garuḍa seated, endowed with four arms,
with both hands joined in the añjali gesture at his heart.
With his two other hands, he should hold the body of Śeṣa,
and upon his shoulder, he should place Garuḍa, who is encircled by the three coils of the serpent's body.
Having extracted the head adorned with a circle of hoods,
one should fashion the Nārasiṃha [image] beneath those hoods according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed the tip of the left foot, which is drawn up, upon the remaining coils, and having extended the right leg with its knee bent, he sits. || 53 ||
Endowed with eight arms, his right hand bestows fearlessness;
with the remaining three arms, he holds a discus, an arrow, and a sword. || 54 ||
In the left [hands], he holds a conch, a Śārṅga bow, a shield, and a mace;
the rest is prescribed as before. The wise man should cause the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) to be performed. || 55 ||
One should offer twenty-one oblations to Gārūḍa and Śeṣa as deities;
or, having uttered "Yo vā nṛsiṃha," one should worship one hundred and eight times.

In the consecration of the Nārasiṃha [image], having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest at the Āhavanīya fire, one should offer oblations of clarified butter after having identified [the deity] through that form.
Everything else is declared in the Khila; having understood that, one should practice accordingly.
Furthermore, the various Nārasiṃha-kalpas have been proclaimed in many ways. (58)
Their division according to the palm-tree measure, their mantras, their forms, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the retinue of the Mountain-born Goddess shall be as previously stated. (59)
Vāmana was born from Kaśyapa and Aditi in order to seize the world by means of a stratagem from the powerful Vairocana, the preeminent among the asuras, who was himself strong. (50)
I shall describe his installation, worship, and so forth;
he himself was Trivikrama, intent upon traversing the three worlds. (61)
Trivikrama is said to be threefold: the first, the second, and the third; the wise man should have his image fashioned according to whichever of these forms he desires.
He has eight arms or four arms according to the ten-tāla proportion;
he holds a mace, a discus, a sword, a spear, an arrow, a conch, and the Śārṅga bow.
He beheld Hari, possessing a dark-blue body and bearing a magnificent form,
standing with his right foot planted and his left leg extended.
One should fashion him with eight arms, endowed with the impulse of joy and adorned with all ornaments; now I shall describe the four-armed form.
With his two other hands holding the conch and the discus,
he took hold of the right foot while the other foot was extended.
Extending the left leg upwards while remaining well-supported by the right [leg], one should properly extend the hand above that extended foot. (67)
One should place Indra as the umbrella-bearer situated in the sky according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, one should properly place Yama at the two sides and Varuṇa at the two fans.
If the foot is raised only to the height of a span (jānu), the first [offense] is prescribed;
if it reaches the navel, it shall be the second; and if it reaches the forehead, it shall be the third.
One should visualize Brahmā above, intent on washing his feet;
from that, one should fashion the Gaṅgā flowing forth from the world of Brahmā.
One should fashion Namuci as revolving above his feet, with his hands joined in añjali up to the tips and his body extending upward from the navel.
One should fashion Śuka as a creator of obstacles to the left of the standing foot, striking with his fist; above him, one should arrange Vīśa.
To the right of that, one should place a venerable dwarf in the form of a religious student (vaṭu),
holding an umbrella and a staff, and endowed with a topknot and a loincloth.
Beside him, one should likewise place a strong man holding a water-pot;
he should be adorned with all ornaments and depicted as filled with joy. (74)
One should visualize Jāmbavān as having a blue luster and the form of a monkey;
one should make Indra resemble a dark complexion and Yama resemble collyrium. || 75 ||
One should depict Varuṇa as dark-blue in color, Bhāskara (the Sun) as resembling fire,
the Moon as white, and Brahmā as having the brilliance of gold.
One should make Gaṅgā white-rayed, Namuci dark indeed,
Śukra white-complexioned, and Yama resembling collyrium.
One should fashion Cakra as white, Varuḍa as five-colored, Vāmana as dark-blue, and Balin as having the luster of gold. || 78 ||
Thus, the wise man should have the image fashioned according to his own desire from these three types of materials;
then, during the *anvāhārya* rite, he should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the *pradhāna* fire.
Or one may worship one hundred and eight [deities] as "the one who is the triple form" (trimūrti);
all rites, beginning with the installation, should be performed with the Viṣṇu-sūkta. || 80 ||
Vāmana should not be installed separately; everything else is as prescribed for all [deities].
Paraśurāma, through the slaughter of the mighty Kṣatriyas, was the remover of the earth's burden. || 81 ||
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, was exceedingly fierce;
one should fashion the image of Rāma measuring ten tālas in height. || 82 ||
One should represent him as red in color, adorned with a crown of matted locks, holding an axe in his right hand and a staff in his left.
One should depict the god wearing blue garments, whether seated or standing; one should create that form with curiosity and draw the sages around him.
One should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire during the *anvāhārya* rite;
having uttered "Viṣṇurvariṣṭha," one should sacrifice seventy-one times. 85.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, should properly perform all remaining duties as before,
in order to slay Rāvaṇa and the other Rākṣasas who commit violence against the gods.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, was armed when his body was weaponless;
one should represent Rāghava as being seven and a half tālas in height.
One should depict him as dark-complexioned, with two arms, well-established in the *tribhaṅga* posture,
holding an arrow in his right hand and a bow in his left.
One should visualize him adorned with all ornaments, radiant with a diadem and crown, and Sītā of yellow complexion at his right side. || 89 ||
With her left hand holding a lotus and her right arm extended, her right foot is firmly planted while the left is slightly bent. (90)
One should fashion the foot and hand either in the normal way or even reversed;
one should make Lakṣmaṇa eight tālas in height, golden-hued, and positioned to the left.
On the right [should be painted] Hanumān, who possesses curly locks of hair like Rāma, and who is intent on announcing the news. || 92 ||
With his right hand covering his face, which shone like gold,
his body bent forward and his face turned upward, he held up his garment with his left hand.
Thus the armed [form] has been described; now I shall describe another, the unarmed one—the God and Goddess seated upon the throne according to the prescribed rite.
To the left, one should place Lakṣmaṇa standing well-composed with palms joined in reverence;
likewise, one should have him depicted as either seated or standing, adorned with the auspicious thread (kautuka).
In the same manner, one should perform the rite of curiosity (kautuka) with the weapons [of the deities] upon those [images] equipped with weapons;
however, one should perform the meditation (dhyāna) for all three within a single water-pot (kumbha). || 96 ||
The manner of reclining for that god and his goddess is now described;
on that same altar, the bed of Lakṣmaṇa should also be placed separately.
One should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire during the *anvāhārya* rite;
muttering the mantra "O Lord of riches," one should offer seventy-one oblations. || 18 ||
One should perform the Śrīvatsa and all other rites for Sītā through skillful means and intelligence.
Balabhadra-Rāma—I shall now speak of the one named Balabhadra-Rāma who was born in the Yadu lineage. || 99 ||
Having slain the lord of the Dānavas, he too shall be the remover of the earth's burden,
whether seated upon the back of an elephant, in a celestial chariot (vimāna), or in the Somacchanda vehicle.
One should place him seated on half of Kṛṣṇa’s throne, or even separately;
he is white as a conch, the moon, or a kunda flower, two-armed, and clad in blue garments.
One should visualize a pestle in the right hand and a plough in the left;
thus he is described as being equipped with weapons. Now I shall describe him without weapons.
Having contracted the left foot and extended the right, the right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness, while the left rests upon the thigh. 103.
On the right side is Revatī, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus;
she holds a lotus in her right hand, and the other [hand] is likewise positioned. (104)
Having seated Revatī upon his lap,
one should fashion the God together with the Goddess, adorned with all ornaments.
And thus one should perform the auspicious rite and undertake the installation;
then, in the Āhavanīya fire, one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* formulas.
One should perform one hundred and eight offerings with the mantra "kṣmāmekām," and all other particulars should be carried out specifically as for Viṣṇu. || 107 ||
One should fashion an image of Kṛṣṇa measuring nine tālas in a temple shaped like a peak, a gateway, or a water-pot, and then worship Him. || 108 ||
Dark-complexioned, with three folds on the neck, wearing red garments, and having two arms;
he is the supreme one, holding a play-stick in his right hand.
With his left hand holding a plaything, standing with a firm gait, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful, and possessing gentle eyes. || 110 ||
He placed the two queens, Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā, on his right and left;
they appeared dark and red respectively, adorned with black and yellow garments.
One should have Garuḍa made, radiant with ornaments, according to the measurement of the limit of the arms;
and there, on the left side, one should indeed fashion Viṣṇu with palms joined in reverence.
One should indeed fashion the *kautuka* (the portable image) in conformity with the *dhruvabera* (the permanent image);
it should be seated upon a throne, accompanied by two goddesses, and unarmed. || 113 ||
According to the previously mentioned procedure, [one should worship] him adorned with all ornaments, as the dancer of fresh butter, or likewise as the subduer of Kālīya. || 114 ||
Or the form of Gopāla, or indeed that of Pārthasārathi;
O best of sages, these and countless other forms belong to Kṛṣṇa.
One should fashion their respective forms according to the rules prescribed in the treatises on the arts (śilpaśāstra),
with the right foot slightly bent and the left foot firmly planted.
His foot was bent and placed upon his left heel;
with both hands he held the flute, his face applied to the holes of the flute.
One should fashion the form of a cowherd boy adorned with peacock feathers as ornaments; having gathered them together with an attentive mind, one should perform the visualization of that form. 118.
Kṛṣṇa, holding his play-staff and possessing the form of a cowherd— apart from these,
there are indeed no other forms of his that are devoid of the Goddess.
Having understood Kṛṣṇa as holding a play-stick, or Viṣṇu as being full of festivity, one should, like Hari, arrange all the attendants accordingly.

One should fashion the cowherd named Sundara, who has resorted to his station according to the prescribed rite, as two-armed, carrying flowers, and removing the remains of the offerings (nirmālya). || 121 ||
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, one should perform the recitation for the Hotṛ priest at the principal fire;
having uttered "Satyaḥ satyastha," one should offer one hundred and eight oblations.
One should have all the rites, beginning with the installation, performed as for Hari;
some excellent sages maintain that Kṛṣṇa is four-armed and that one should worship the four-armed Kṛṣṇa.
As before, the two front hands hold the conch and the discus, while the other two [hold the mace and lotus];
these are declared to be the forms of Kṛṣṇa and the others, preceded by Vāsudeva. (124)
"Everything else has been declared equal; such is the teaching of the Ancient One.
At the end of the Yuga, Viṣṇu will become Kalkī, known by the name Kalkin. (125)
Holding a sword and a shield in his hands, he will strike down the Mlecchas and others;
one should visualize him as resembling crushed collyrium and clothed in red garments. 126.
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, one should perform the recitation for the Hotṛ priest at the principal fire;
one should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Ṛtaṃ satya" (Truth and Reality). || 127 ||
In the worship of the incarnations,
[they may be placed] either in the space between [the main deity and the door], or on the right and left sides of Viṣṇu; these are the alternatives for the worship of the incarnations.
Or one should fashion Rāma and Kṛṣṇa on the face-ornament itself. || 128 ||
Alternatively, some say that one should install the *kautuka* image within the inner mandala or likewise in the pavilion of the enclosure (*āvaraṇamaṇḍapa*) and perform its worship.

Having fashioned the Nārasiṃha, Varāha, Vāmana, and Trivikrama forms—endowed with the proper characteristics and excluding the permanent image (dhruvabera)—one should perform the consecration ceremony (kautuka). || 130 ||
Having thus installed Viṣṇu, one should worship him in the front pavilion, offering water for the feet, water for sipping, a bath, and likewise ornaments. (131)
Water for the feet, water for sipping, flowers, fragrance, and incense; after that, a lamp, the arghya offering, further water for sipping, sacrificial food, and water for drinking. || 132 ||
Following that, there is sipping of water (ācamana), and after that, mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).
These are the sixteen constituent forms (vigraha) of images whose primary nature is that of another [deity]. || 133 ||
One should fashion the abode of the ten incarnations, complete with fixed and movable images, just as one does for Hari’s own principal incarnations. 134.

Some of the most excellent sages maintain that there is an intermediate state; they hold that worship should be performed for the mouth [of the deity] during its residence in the place of origin and its descent. 135.
At the end of each respective principal mantra, while reciting the corresponding form-mantra, one should perform the worship and the bathing, endowed with devotion. || 136 ||
Beyond this, I shall indeed proclaim the manifestations and descents of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow:
namely, Trailokyamohana and Hariśaṅkara. (137)
I have already described in detail in the Khila [section] the incarnations as the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and Kalki.
Lakṣmīnarāyaṇa says: I shall describe Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, the excellent bestower of all prosperity, Nārāyaṇa who is free from ailment and seated upon the shoulders of Viṣṇu. (139)
Having made everything as if it were already present, he likewise placed the goddess Śrī upon his right thigh, adorned with all her ornaments.
With her hands joined in reverence, filled with bashfulness and joy,
she was embraced by the Lord of Gods with his right hand.
Viṣṇu’s left arm is properly placed upon the thigh;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else is like that of Hari.
Some say that one should have Lakṣmī depicted on the left thigh;
others [depict her] seated thus on the throne, without the Viśa-shoulder.
In the assembly hall, at the principal fire, one should offer the two established oblations in sequence,
as well as the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka and the Śrīsūkta with the same [mantra].
One should sacrifice one hundred and eight times in other fires as before;
while reciting the mantra "śriye jāta," one should perform the lotus-oblation in the lotus-fire.
One should worship the one named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa with the primary forms beginning with Viṣṇu;
specifically, during the installation ceremony there, one should fashion the form of Viṣṇu.
Having first worshipped the festival image of Bala, Viṣṇu, or likewise [the other],
with the eightfold offerings according to the mantra, one should worship Dhruva.
One should perform worship with thirty-two forms during the consecration ceremony (*kautuka*).
Regarding the contemplation of the formless worship (*niṣkalārcā*):
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," he is proclaimed as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). || 148 ||
That which is of such a nature—supreme, subtle, imperishable, and partless—is declared to be the stable abode; yet the worship of the partless is impossible [for the uninitiated]. (149)
The worship of the physical image (bera) is considered to consist merely of the placement of those flowers;
for that which is the manifest form of Viṣṇu is gross and the cause of all.
There should be a festive rite corresponding to that [occasion], and one should perform worship there;
for by means of that, it is possible to carry out the worship with flowers and other offerings.
Worship is prescribed for the Stable One (Dhruva) because he possesses an object of perception and is endowed with all parts;
however, it is not [prescribed] for the Partless One (Niṣkala) due to the reason that he lacks an object of perception.
Because it is impossible to perform there the application of bathing, perfumes, and so forth,
that worship of Dhruva is not desired for the sake of delimiting the beginning of time.

Nevertheless, if one desires to perform worship in the permanent image (dhruvabera), it should be done according to the rules with all the utterances, except for the ritual bathing and the removal of the old cloth. || 154 ||
Some say that one should worship with the mantra "ṛtaṃ satyam";
furthermore, one should offer a handful of flowers with the Nārāyaṇānuvāka. || 155 ||
Situated in the center of a solar disc, resembling molten gold, bearing the conch and the discus, gentle, and with a face like the bright moon. || 156 ||
His right hand displays the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya), while his left rests upon his hip;
he stands in the center of a lunar disc and resembles pure crystal in appearance. || 157 ||
One should visualize [the deity] as situated in the center of the circle of fire, as previously described.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the Great Wheel (mahācakra). || 158 ||
One should never establish the Mahācakra independently;
rather, one should arrange it specifically on the right side of the deity or in the south-west (Nairṛta) direction. || 159 ||
One should establish the foundation of the temple between the directions of Yama and Nairṛti;
its temple should be circular, extending from the base of the steps to the top of the stūpa.
One should establish that permanent worship (dhruvārcana) according to the single-bera rite;
having fashioned a wheel with one hundred and eight flames, [one should place it] in its center.
One should visualize the wheel situated within a pair of fire-mandalas;
it has sixteen arms in the superior [mandala] and likewise eight arms in the middle one.
And for the lowest [form], one should fashion Sudarśana with four arms,
holding a discus, a sword, a spear, a staff, a goad, and the sacrificial fire.
Holding a dagger and a spear with his eight right hands,
and thereafter a conch, an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a plow.
Holding a vajra, a mace, and a tomara with his left arms—thus he is described as having sixteen arms; now he shall be described as having eight arms.
One should visualize the supreme Lord as having eight arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a sword, a goad, a noose, and a bow. 166.
One should fashion him as holding a conch and a discus, or as holding a mace and a lotus; he may be depicted with four arms or two arms, according to one's ability. || 167 ||
His face was terrible with bared fangs, his eyes were like the sun, the moon, and fire,
and he had a garland of small bells hanging from his shoulder down to his knees.
Resplendent with noble limbs, the destroyer of all enemies,
his chest illuminated by the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, he is affectionate toward his devotees.
It was also surrounded by flames of fire, blazing with a crown and diadem;
its arrows resembled glowing embers and fire, and its garment was like the plumage of a parrot.
Having done thus, one should undertake the installation of the great wheel;
having performed the opening of the eyes and so forth, with the two mantras of the wheel. (171)

Having performed the ritual acceptance according to the scriptures, one should sequentially prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances; then, having meditated upon the deity in the pitcher (kumbha), having invoked [the deity] therein, and likewise having bathed [the image] with the ritual jars (kalaśas).
Having properly praised the ritual of the Hotṛ priest according to the rules over the domestic fire (aupāsana), he recited the Vaṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta. || 173 ||
Having performed the oblation by repeating [the mantra] four times with the two wheel-mantras,
and having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should then offer with the three root-mantras of the wheel.
Having established [the deity] during the morning hour (prātarmuhūrta) and having invoked [him], one should worship [him].
This is declared to be the Vedic method, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 175 ||
If one desires worldly enjoyment alone, one should recite the six-syllabled mantra according to the prescribed rules, especially at the time of the fire-oblation (homa). || 176 ||
Having repeated that mantra one thousand and eight times, let it be offered;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains as in the case of the wheel.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Great Cakra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Consisting of the Ten Incarnations," in the section on Rituals (Kriyādhikāra) within the *Śrī Vairavānasa Saṃhitā*, a scripture of the Lord (Bhagavat-śāstra) proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The twelfth chapter.
Regarding the separate consecration for the bathing and festival rites:
after the bathing and festival rites, I shall now describe the consecration;
provided that there is the capacity, it should be performed again in the same manner once the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) has been previously established. (1)
Having performed the festive ceremonial bathing, one should install the image according to its wealth;
having fashioned the image with all the proper characteristics, one should carry out the ritual of the assembly according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed the consecration of the opening of the eyes for it according to the rule,
or having performed the installation in the assembly hall or the lotus-pit, one should carry out the rite as before.
One should perform the oblation prescribed for other fires in the *sabhya* fire alone;
having brought the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) there, one should carry out the rite of oblation. || 4 ||
In the event of a permanent cessation of the sacred fire, one should prepare five sacrificial pits as before;
there too, having brought forth the Gārhapatya fire, let the oblation be offered into the others.
On the preceding day, at the conclusion of the night worship,
having especially honored the God, one should properly present the sacrificial offering.
Having invoked [the deity] into the permanent image (dhruvabera), having prostrated and obtained its permission,
and having prepared the water-pot (kumbha) according to the prescribed rite, one should likewise invoke [the deity] from the permanent image into that pot.
One should place the pitcher at the side of the image in the bathing pit;
likewise, [one performs] the ritual bathing, the mounting upon the bed, and the binding of the protective thread (kautuka). || 8 ||
Having performed the *hautra* and the *homa*, and having concluded the morning rites,
he should first perform the placement of the mantra-syllables (*mantrākṣaranyāsa*) on both sides, and then invoke [the deity] into the *kautuka*.
And afterwards, having invoked [the deity] from the *dhruva* vessel into the image for worship,
one should duly honor it with a seat and other offerings, and then present the oblation correctly.
One should perform the festival for the festive image and likewise the ritual bathing for the bathing image according to one's ability, and should give the preceptor’s fee.
In the worldly installation, however, the eternal fire is not brought forth;
likewise, one should perform the invocation into the pitcher from the solar orb.
Having invoked [the deity] from the pitcher into the worldly image, one should worship it;
however, if the rite of the single image (ekabera) is performed, the formal installation (sthāpana) is not prescribed.
Having performed a festival for the image at the conclusion of the night worship,
one should worship the single form and place the Śakti within the pitcher.
Having performed the rites of installation and so forth as before according to the rules,
one should invoke [the deity] into a single image, and having invoked [the deity] from that [source], one should worship it.
If there is a separate consecration for the *baliberam*, then one should invoke [the deity] into that *kautuka* [image].
Having performed worship and offered the oblation, one should then carry out the festival; now, the specific procedure for the installation of the two goddesses will be described. (17)
After the two goddesses, the installation of the mobile images should take place; furthermore, one should fashion the two goddesses [for those images] as well. || 18 ||

Even when the Dhruva polestar is separated from the goddess (Lakṣmī), one should perform the marriage ceremony with the goddess with every effort; likewise, one should especially do so during a festival.
Having performed the consecration with the opening of the eyes and reciting that mantra,
he should establish two domestic fires on both sides of the sacrificial hall.
Having established the perpetual fire for those two, one should perform the oblation as prescribed;
and having invoked Śakti from the two images of the Goddesses of Dhruva into the two jars.
Having performed the bathing, the bed, the pitcher, and the fire-oblation separately— or indeed everything else— just as before, one should bathe in the morning according to the prescribed rule.
Having invoked Dhruva and Devī, one should invoke [the other two] by means of those two;
because their consecration is preceded by their respective powers (*śakti*), one should not perform a marriage ceremony for them.
Alternatively, one may perform the installation of those two together with the deity;
having placed the power (śakti) into the permanent image (dhruvabera) according to the rite, as if it were the marriage-thread (kautuka).
Then, having invoked the Śakti from the fixed image (dhruvabera) into the pitcher as before,
one should install the Goddess and the pitcher in the bathing pit, with the pitcher to the right.
Having separately installed the two goddesses in the two side-chambers,
one should bathe them and then lay them down upon a single altar according to the mantra.
Having performed all the rites beginning with the *hautra*, according to the previously mentioned method,
one should invoke [the deity] from the water-pot (*kumbha*) into the *dhruva* vessel, and from that, invoke it into the water.

The injunction is that one should not perform the marriage rite even here [in this case], for although the Goddess was separated from Dhruva, he was united with her by means of the churned fire alone. || 28 ||
Having performed the libation (āghāra) there according to the rules in the domestic fire-pit (aupāsana-kuṇḍa),
he should worship the two goddesses as before, either from his own heart or from the solar orb.
Having invoked the two goddesses into the two jars at the conclusion of the fire-offering rite,
one should devoutly invoke their images from the jars and worship them.
O ascetics, when the two goddesses were being established together during the festival,
Dhruva, though separated from the goddesses, prepared the ritual pitcher as before.
O ascetics, while the two goddesses were being established together with Autsava,
Dhruva, though separated from the goddesses, likewise prepared the Kumbha as before.
Then, having invited the God and the two Goddesses from the image into the pitcher,
one should likewise invite them from the heart and from the solar disc while meditating upon them.
Having performed the bathing and other rites as before,
one should indeed invoke the God of gods into the permanent image (dhruvabera) there, just as previously.
Therefore, having invoked the God, one should invoke the two Goddesses from the pitcher.
O ascetics, there is a specific distinction regarding the installation of those [images] other than the *kautuka* during the consecration that excludes the *kautuka*.
One should avoid the invocation of the deities of the assembly, as well as the worship of all the gods and the fire-oblation (homa) for the deities of the assembly; such is the injunction.
Alternatively, some say that one should perform the worship of the bed and the worship of the water-pot separately for the God of gods and for the two goddesses. || 36 ||
In the installation of a single Linga, one should not subsequently install two goddesses;
rather, at the very beginning, one should perform the worship of Dhruva accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
One who desires the fulfillment of all desires, or seeks prosperity alone,
should install Śrī alone behind a single-liṅga image.
One should perform the worship of Dhruva as Nārasiṃha without the two goddesses;
all virtuous people desire the worship of Dhruva through the path of Yoga. || 39 ||

I shall explain in brief the procedure for the installation of images on cloth, walls, and the like; having fashioned an image endowed with the proper characteristics, one should perform the rite of establishing images made of cloth, wall-paintings, or plaster. (40)
Having established the *aupāsana* fire according to the procedure for the *vāstuhoma*,
he should purify the site nearby by means of the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having performed the opening of his eyes according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should take up the water-pot as before and perform the sprinkling for the sake of purification.

When evening has arrived, having performed the *āghāra* libation according to the rules at the *kuṇḍa* and the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), and having prepared the sacrificial oblation as before; || 43 ||
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water from seven jars and likewise bound the protective thread (pratisara),
he should praise the office of the Hotṛ priest according to the rule and invoke the God as before.
Having performed the oblation of clarified butter according to the very sequence of invocation, one should sacrifice;
if it is the installation of the primary image, [one should recite] the Vaiṣṇava hymn and the Viṣṇu-sūkta. (45)
Having offered oblations with the Puruṣasūkta and likewise the Vaiṣṇava hymn, as well as those joined with the five Vāruṇa mantras, and similarly the Jayā and other [hymns]. || 46 ||

Then, having offered oblations to the gods and others accompanied by a thousand offerings, one should perform a hundred sacrifices with that mantra for the descent and consecration [of the deity]. || 47 ||
Having performed the placement of the syllables of the morning mantra and having invoked and meditated upon Hari,
one should prepare a three-tiered pedestal beneath that image.
Having placed a tuft of grass (kūrca) measuring twelve finger-breadths within that [space], which is one span in length and breadth and six finger-breadths in height; || 49 ||
Having invoked the deity into that [image] and worshipped it thoroughly, one should present the offerings;
likewise, at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana) of the image.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as before.

Thus, in the *Ārṣa* Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, within the *Kriyādhikāra*, the twelfth chapter titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Deity with the Desire for Subsequent Bathing" is concluded.
Oṃ.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
The Great Bathing Ceremony.
Hereafter, I shall describe the bathing ceremony in brief, including its auspicious and inauspicious omens.
Also during the festivals of consecration, as well as at the equinoxes and solstices. || 1 ||
One should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity during the eclipses of the sun and the moon;
provided one has the means, one should also do so on the five days of Viṣṇu.
When there is a solar or lunar transit occurring in a month other than the birth-month of the asterisms of the performer and the king;
or during planetary affliction, drought, bad dreams, or inauspicious omens.
When people are afflicted by diseases and other calamities, one should perform [the rites] for their pacification at the end of the year,
at the end of the Yuga, and during the Vyatīpāta and other such astrological periods in due order.
One should collect the necessary materials, including substances gathered from after the ritual of depositing the sprouts,
as well as the eight types of earth from rivers and so forth, and from mountains such as the Himalayas.
Likewise, grains such as śāli rice and the sprouts of those various grains, the śrīvatsa, the full vase, the kettledrum, and the mirror; || 6 ||
A pair of fish, a goad, a conch, and a whirlpool are inauspicious;
however, a pair of large suns and a whirlpool are said to be auspicious.
One should perform other rites according to the rules; first, there are indeed five substances:
the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), namely clarified butter, honey, curd, milk, and [the fifth]. || 8 ||
One should take [the earth] not less than an āḍhaka, or as much as may be available;
having filled the remainder with water, one should worship it in that very place in the prescribed manner. || 9 ||
Water scented with sandalwood, ushira root, kushtha, cardamom, cloves, and other such ingredients is called "fragrant water" (gandhodaka), provided it is at least one āḍhaka in quantity.
Barley, mustard, rice, black gram, and wild rice, combined with water and unbroken grains (akṣata) in an amount equal to one-eighth part of the water, is called akṣatodaka. || 11 ||
It was provided with plantains, mangoes, jackfruit, and coconuts,
as well as oranges, citrons, the three myrobalans, and muñja grass.
Combined with bhavya, havya, kurunda, and also kāmareṇu, it is called phalodaka; it is endowed with fruits equal to one-eighth part of water.
Water mixed with the tips of *kuśa* grass is known as *kuśodaka*;
water mixed with nine or five jewels is known as *ratnodaka*.
Having repeated three times the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" one hundred and eight times, or [having recited] the six Vaiṣṇava mantras beginning with "ato devā" just once; || 15 ||
Having recited [the mantra] over water, it is known as "japyodaka" (water consecrated by recitation);
it is infused with all those herbs whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit.
The water for all medicinal herbs is prescribed to be one-eighth the measure of the [other] liquids.
[The herbs are: bilva leaves, aśvattha, dūrvā grass, lotus, nandyāvarta, and śamī. || 17 ||
The meritorious flowers have been described; one should gather them according to availability.
At night, a leaf of the wood-apple (kapittha) is said to be equal to a leaf of the bilva.

The powder of nutmeg and other such fruits, a decoction, water from sacred bathing places (tīrtha), the powder of forest herbs and turmeric, and thereafter all types of fragrant substances (sarvagandha). || 19 ||
One should collect the cloth, the root-fragrance, and also the minerals;
likewise, one should bring the garments, the upper robe, the sacred thread, and ornaments.
Jars filled with an āḍhaka measure, platters filled with a prastha measure, bowls filled with half a droṇa, and pots as well as water-jars filled with a full droṇa.
One should bring only those [blades] that are free from being broken, cracked, or old,
joined with five or ten uncut, hollowless *darbha* grasses.
One should prepare thirty-six bundles of kusha grass, each thirty-six finger-breadths in length, for the purpose of spreading around the vessels;
twelve finger-breadths in height, they should be made for the sake of the water-pots.
With nine, or seven, or five, or even with three—
kuśa grass, kāśa grass, uśīra, dūrvā, and likewise rice.

Viśvāmitra, barley, and the seven types of darbha grass are proclaimed [as the materials]. Having worshipped the Lord of Gods during the first part of the night, one should offer the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as an ancillary part of the ritual bathing. || 25 ||
Having prepared an altar to the south of the Ālaya for the purpose of the bed,
one should spread five beds in succession upon the grain.
Having placed the deity there and likewise bound the protective amulet (pratisara), one should, with a well-composed mind, lay the deity upon the bed as before. || 27 ||
If the ceremonial bathing should take place after passing two conjunctions [of the moon], one should immediately fasten the protective thread and prepare the bed. || 28 ||
If one performs the ritual bathing when the kautuka-thread has not been tied,
or even during the bathing of the dhruvārcā, the tying of the kautuka must be performed immediately.
Having prepared [the image] and established it in a pit, one should bathe it; such is the instruction.
As for the omen for the bathing, it occurs at night before sunrise. || 30 ||
At the conclusion of the night worship, one should not dismiss Hari;
likewise, having dismissed him at the end of the bathing ceremony, one should invoke him again in the morning.
For the two [rites] other than the *kautuka* [thread], there are no two acts of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarga*).
One should construct the bathing pavilion (*snapanamaṇḍapa*) facing the temple, either in the north or the northeast.
A pavilion, or a water-shed, or a peaked roofed structure, or a bathing hall, provided with sixteen pillars and equipped with four doors. || 33 ||
One should fashion a Śrīvatsa, a lotus, or a Svastika according to the prescribed rule,
and between them, one should form a row with rice or paddy.
Its width should be two *tālas* less [than its length], and its height should be twenty-three finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*);
likewise, it should be provided with doors on the four sides, each having a width of one cubit (*hasta*).
One should draw the shape of leafy creepers in the area marked "Sumitrā," as well as for Indra and the other guardians of the directions, and for Paṅktīśa and Amita.
One should arrange the seats in rows at their respective places;
or one may also do so outside the rows, provided it is for the purpose of malevolent rites (ābhicārika).

In the midst of that, having prepared the site according to the rules for the *snapana*, *paśu*, and *aupāsana* rites, and having strewn the sacrificial grass (*paristīrya*), one should also worship the *jaya* and other deities. || 38 ||
When the pedestal has been prepared in that row according to the previously described method,
one should perform the placement of materials (dravyanyāsa), placing the substances such as clay and the rest facing toward the Lord of Gods.

Having placed a tuft of grass (kūrca) upon them, one should worship the presiding deities, meditating on them as the holders of their respective substances, in proximity to those very substances. (40)
Having lifted the Lord from the bed and placed him in the middle of the pit,
one should worship him with water for the feet and other offerings, and anoint him with oil as before.
Having worshipped once again in the same manner, one should bathe [the deity] with clay and other substances;
the procedure for bathing is as follows:
having sprinkled [the image] with the Praṇava, one should take [the clay] from the hand of the disciple.
Having lifted [the vessel] up to the forehead, and having carried it three times or once clockwise,
one should bathe the deity with the five forms in due order.

Having again sprinkled the substance and the vessel, one should place them back in their former positions, together with the primary substances and the accompanying secondary ablutions (upasnāna). || 44 ||
Likewise, one should bathe [the deity] with the previously mentioned secondary substances and mantras;
having established the God in His seat and worshipped Him thoroughly, one should present the offerings. || 45 ||

And at the conclusion of the ceremonial bath, having offered the *kautuka* at the seat of the *jīva*, and having worshipped and gratified it, one should again offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). || 46 ||
Regarding the specific procedure for the bathing of the stationary image (dhruvārcā):
one should construct a water-shed (prapā) facing the temple.
As before, one should arrange the bathing substances in a row all around it. (47)
Having placed a pitcher filled with scented water in the midst of that heap of grain,
one should worship Varuṇa there as the presiding deity.
Having taken [the image] and gone inside, one should bathe it with clay and other substances;
having adorned and worshipped it, one should also present the sacrificial offerings.

If it should be possible to perform the ritual bath at night before sunrise, one should not remove the Śakti from that image; rather, having placed it in a pit as before, [the bath proceeds]. || 50 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] at the conclusion of the ablution and having offered the oblation, one should likewise perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana).
Having dismissed the Śakti at sunrise and having seated [the deity] upon the Dhruva altar...
Having invoked [the deity] there from the *Ghṛta* [mantra], one should bathe him; such is the instruction.
This is especially so if there should be a pair of lunar mansions within a single month. || 52 ||
One should bathe Puruṣottama on that very day;
if two lunar days (tithis) should coincide, one should perform the rite for both.
If the astrological sign (nimitta) or the lunar day (tithi) persists for two consecutive days, one should perform the ritual bathing and other ceremonies on the following day. || 54 ||
On a single day, when two asterisms and two lunar days coincide,
one should first perform the ritual bath under the asterism and thereafter carry out the rite pertaining to the lunar day.
But at the conclusion of the previous ritual, having immediately performed the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and having immediately bound the protective thread (pratisara),
one should perform the second ablution.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as stated in the *Khila* [supplementary section].
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Bathing," in the section on Purchasing, within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*. Om.
The Fourteenth Chapter:
The Great Festival and the Time for the Concluding Bath (Avabhṛtha).
Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the festival of Hari.
And also on the days of the equinoxes, the solstices, the full moon, the new moon, and on the lunar mansions presided over by the founders [of the temple].
On the birth-star of the sacrificer, or on the star of the king himself, during an eclipse, on the month-star, or on the five days of Viṣṇu. || 2 ||
On the final day of the festival, one should designate those [spots] as sacred sites (tīrtha).
Among these, one day should be selected according to the desire of the one performing the rite.
During the equinoxes, the solstices, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
one should perform a bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha) at those respective times, and not otherwise.

If two days of the holy site (tīrtha) fall within the same month—either at midday, in the forenoon, or during a period of superior astrological qualities—in any of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), [one should perform the rite on both]. || 5 ||
The day preceding those two [the new and full moon] is a sacred occasion (tīrtha), according to the teaching of the ancestors;
provided that very day is not pierced by the sun during its transit and so forth.

Likewise, that which is previously described as "to be avoided" (vajranīya) is declared to be auspicious if it is joined with [the previous day] for two nights, or for one day and another [day]. || 7 ||
The conjunction of Sunday and the Arka constellation is always highly praised;
the conjunction of the twelfth lunar day and the Śravaṇa constellation bestows the fruits of all undertakings. || 8 ||

And the yogas should be highly auspicious, known by the names Siddha, Amṛta, and Vara. Festivals are traditionally said to be of three kinds, categorized as those based on time, those based on faith, and those based on specific purposes. || 9 ||
In whichever month it may be, that which is performed annually for Hari according to the established agreement shall indeed be known as the Kālotsava.
That which is performed with faith is called a festival of faith (śraddhotsava), especially during portents, omens, and such occurrences as droughts. || 11 ||
Therein, for the sake of pacification, that festival with its specific signs is performed; it is known as the "festival with signs.
Regarding the measurement of the festival days, the time is considered excellent at three weeks (twenty-one days) and middling at fourteen days. || 12 ||
They declare that the period is either nine days or, at the very least, seven;
having first performed three times as many festive days, one should carry out the proclamation.

In the middle case, it should be twice [the standard] on the first day of the festival and so forth; in the lowest case, it should be on that day. Alternatively, it may be on the twenty-first day prior to the avabhṛtha bath.
Having performed the hoisting of the banner, one should carry out the entire festival.
Regarding the characteristics of the banner-pole:
for the Brahmins and the other castes in order, they are made of bamboo, the *ujāti* tree, the *campaka*, and the *pūga* (betel nut) tree.
The flagstaffs for all [deities] are thus described;
alternatively, they may be made of sandalwood, or the heartwood of auspicious trees is desired by some.

Taking a banner cloth (dhvajavastra) whose length is equal to that of the vimāna, or three-quarters, or even half of it, one should proceed according to the method prescribed for the flagstaff. || 17 ||
In the center of that, one should draw the omnipresent Lord seated with palms joined in reverence,
endowed with five colors and measuring nine tālas in height.
Whether it be the Ākāśārohaṇa or the Vīrāsana,
their characteristics have already been described by me previously in the Khila section.
Having performed the opening of the eyes and other rites according to the path described in the *Parivāra*, one should invoke the Lord, worship him, and present the offering. || 20 ||
Having placed the drum upon a seat of grain in the southeast,
one should invoke Nandīśa there, worship him, and present offerings.
Reciting the Dundubhi-sūkta beginning with "upaśvāsaya pṛthivīm," he himself should afterwards perform the blowing of the drum with the Vyahṛtis. || 22 ||

Having offered the bali-oblation at the boundary of the village together with the powerful image of Bali and the lords of the Cakravīśas, one should cause it to be proclaimed with their respective mantras. || 23 ||
Having entered the ālaya in due order and having erected the banner as before,
one should install the flagpole during the auspicious rising of the morning.
At the conclusion of the proclamation, one should again perform the ritual, or simply the act of ascending;
at the end of the auspicious day (puṇyāha), having worshipped, one should offer food made of mung beans.
Until the lowering of the flag, he should remain constantly composed, performing [this] three times a day, twice a day, or even once a day. || 26 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] exactly according to the previously stated sequence, one should present the offering;
having performed the rites of leading forth and the release of the eyes on the previous day itself in the forenoon.
Having performed the fire-oblation and other rites at night, and having invoked [the deity] as before in the morning, one should perform the hoisting of the banner especially at midday. || 28 ||
Some say that one should make a proclamation to the gods at night,
after the raising of the banner and before the day of the festival.
At the conclusion of the night worship, at the boundary of the village,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the invited deities according to the prescribed rule, as before.
From that time forward, one should gather the materials required for the festival;
on the first day, during the forenoon, one should have all the streets cleaned everywhere.
Having uttered "O you who have shaken off all impurities" (avadhūta), one should perform the sweeping with a broom;
then one should sprinkle water with the mantra beginning with "In the ten directions" (āśāsu). || 32 ||
At midday, one should bathe Hari according to the very procedure prescribed for the *sanapana* rite;
likewise, one should bathe the Cakravīs and Amitas with fragrant water.
Having worshipped him especially, one should offer the sacrificial oblation;
then, when the afternoon has arrived, together with the lords of the Cakras.
One should take the earth for the purpose of the "sprout of the holy ford" (tīrthāṅkura) according to the previously mentioned method;
then, having circumambulated the village and entered the temple without haste, [one should proceed]. 35.
Then, on the ninth, seventh, or fifth day prior to the day of the sacred rite (tīrtha), one should perform the ritual sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) according to the prescribed rules.
When evening has arrived, or when facing the south,
one should prepare the sacrificial hall provided with sixteen pillars.
Having prepared an altar in the center, one should establish five fires in the best case,
or three fires in the middling case, and likewise only the sabhya fire in the lowest case.

The Āhavanīya fire should be the primary one; it should be located in the middle. In the other two [hearths], there should be the Sabhya fire, or it may be used for the daily oblation (nityahoma). || 39 ||
If no specific place for the fire-sacrifice (homa) has been prescribed, or if the prescribed place is cramped,
or if one is incapable or in haste, then one may arrange the place even where it was not originally specified.
One should perform all ritual actions in the cooking chamber;
however, in the absence of a specific instruction regarding the location, one should employ the aupāsana fire-altar when no particular fire-pit has been designated.
When the substance for the oblation is not specified, clarified butter from a cow is prescribed;
when no time is mentioned, it should be midday; and when no vessel is mentioned, the *sruva* ladle should be used. || 42 ||
When no specific distinction is mentioned regarding prostrations, one should perform the binding with "svasti.
Having brought nine new jars and having wrapped them with thread, [one should proceed]. 43.
Having filled them with river water, one should wrap them with a pair of cloths,
provided with the eight auspicious symbols and endowed with the five weapons.
Having set those pitchers apart, each endowed with the nine gems and provided with tufts of grass and unbroken grains, and having covered them with lids; 45.
Entering once more with a concentrated mind, he should worship the God of gods twice over and offer twice as much.
Having subsequently tied the protective amulet (pratisara) upon the deity accompanied by the goddess, and having then entered the sacrificial hall, [he should recite] "O Jātavedas... (RV 1.50.1).
Having established the perpetual fire within those sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should perform the Āghāra libation;
then, having spread grain upon the altar (vedi) and placed the jars there, indeed—48.
One should invoke them starting with Dhruva, in sequence like one lamp from another;
likewise, one should invoke Viṣṇu in the central jar, and the [forms] beginning with Puruṣa in the directions starting from the east.

Having likewise invoked Āgneya and the others, as well as Kapila and the rest, according to the prescribed rule, and having worshipped them with twenty-seven varieties of offerings and prostrated before them; || 50 ||
One should worship Vīśāna, Pāyipaṅktīśa, and Śānta in the cardinal directions in sequence;
in the evening and morning, one should worship the Lord together with these [deities] starting from Vīśāna, but without the water-pots (kumbhas).
Some say that one should establish [the fire] on the altar itself and perform the sacrifice with purified [materials];
thereafter, the performer of the daily oblation (hotṛ) should carry out the recitation of the *hautra* in the principal fire. || 52 ||
Then, having invoked the deities residing in that temple according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter and worship them in that same order.

Therein, the deities of the festivals, as well as the presiding deities (adhidevas) and their respective mantras for the specific days, lunar dates, weekdays, and vehicles, shall be declared in due order. (54)
In the first [chapter] the deity is Brahmā; in the second, it is the Ṛṣis;
in the third, the deity is Rudra; and in the fourth, likewise, it is Vāsava.
In the fifth [day] one should perform the rite dedicated to Soma; in the sixth, that dedicated to Viṣṇu;
in the seventh, that dedicated to all the gods; and in the eighth, that dedicated to Yama.
In the ninth [day] one should worship the deity Varuṇa; in the tenth, the deity Vāyu;
in the eleventh, the deity Kaumāra; and in the twelfth, one should worship the deity Nairṛta. || 57 ||
On the thirteenth day one should worship Vārāha, on the fourteenth Rauhiṇa,
on the fifteenth Gārutmata, and on the sixteenth Daurgaka.
On the seventeenth day, the best of preceptors should offer oblations to Kaumāra;
on the eighteenth, however, the Narasūkta should be offered by those most endowed with wealth.
On the nineteenth day, when the wise one performs the Narasūkta,
on the twentieth day the wise one should likewise offer oblations with the Bhūsūkta.
On the twenty-first day, one should offer the supreme self;
thus, the wise man should offer to the Daitya of the festival in due order.
In the first [section], however, Agni is the presiding deity; in the second, Prajāpati;
in the third, Kubera; and in the fourth, Viṣṇu.
On the fifth day, the deity is Śrī; on the sixth, Kaumāra;
on the seventh, Sūrya; and on the eighth, Raudra.
On the ninth day, one should worship the deity Durga; on the tenth, Yama;
likewise, on the eleventh, Indra; and on the twelfth, Viṣṇu.
Likewise, on the thirteenth day, it is dedicated to the Mothers;
and on the fourteenth day, it is dedicated to the Fire-god and the Lord (Īśa).
Likewise, on the fifteenth day, one should offer oblations to the gentle deities in sequence;
on the days of the Sun and other weekdays, one should perform the rites dedicated to their respective presiding deities.

"Oṃ agnaye kṛttikābhyaḥ svāhā"—with this mantra, the deity of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) should be offered oblations; likewise, each deity of the respective mounts should be invoked and offered oblations by their specific names.
The wise one should worship the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Nara-sūkta;
then, having offered oblations with the Śrī-bhū-sūkta, he should worship the Mahī-sūkta in due order.
One should perform the *mūrtihoma* sacrifice; this is known as the constant sequence.
It consists of the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Narasūkta. (69)

He indeed performs oblations with the deities presiding over the day, the twilight, and so forth, as well as the deities of the lunar day, the weekday, and the asterism, and with the forms of the deities residing in their respective temples.
The wise man should offer oblations with fuel-sticks and clarified butter into the Sabhya fire;
he should offer the Puruṣasūkta and the Aindra hymn into the Āhavanīya fire.
At the Anvāhārya rite, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta together with the Śrī-sūkta;
thereafter, at the Gārhapatya fire, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rites, and subsequently at the Āvasathya fire.
One should likewise worship with the Ekākṣara and other hymns, as well as the Mahīsūkta;
on the first day [one should offer] a palāśa twig, and on the second, a bilva twig.
In the third [case], however, there is the Śamī tree; in the fourth, the Nyagrodha;
in the fifth, the Audumbara; and in the sixth, the Aśvattha. || 74 ||
In the seventh [chapter] the khādira wood is mentioned; in the eighth, the ślākṣa is spoken of;
in the ninth, the āpāmārga; and in the tenth, the āmra itself.
On the eleventh day, one should offer kuśa grass; on the twelfth, dūrvā grass;
on the thirteenth, an āmalaka fruit; and on the fourteenth, a pāṭala flower.
In the fifteenth [year], one offers fuel-sticks of *panasa*; in the sixteenth, of *kovidāra*;
and in the seventeenth, of *punnāga*—thus it is offered with sacrificial fuel.
One should offer a mandāra flower on the eighteenth day, a vakula on the nineteenth,
and a campaka on the twentieth, performing the oblations in due order.
In the twenty-first [rite], one should offer the wood of the *kāpittha* tree in sequence;
thus, the wise man should offer these sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) in their proper order.
One should perform the highest oblation with clarified butter, with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru), and with fuel-sticks;
for the middle [oblation], one should perform the fire-offering with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge.
The wise man should perform the oblation with clarified butter alone, or with clarified butter together with the sacrificial porridge (caru);
or he may worship morning and evening with either clarified butter or the sacrificial porridge.
Beginning from the first festival until the conclusion at the sacred site (tīrtha), one should perform oblations in sequence;
and even without the ritual jars and the deities, one should perform the fire-oblation in the perpetual fire (nityāgni).
Together with the Cakravīśas and accompanied by Bali,
one should offer the oblation at the boundary of the village, following the clockwise sequence.
The manner of the village festival:
afterwards, having entered within and bowed to the God of gods, one should adorn him according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and earrings. || 84 ||
Carrying him in a chariot, a palanquin, or on a litter, adorned with fragrant flower garlands and delightful perfumes; || 85 ||
Furthermore, having placed the deity motionless upon an elephant-chariot, a palanquin, or a swinging-cradle, while reciting the mantra "I alone am [the deity]," || 86 ||
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings (aṣṭopacāra), and having presented seasoned parched grain, cakes, and so forth, mixed with jaggery, as well as a mouth-freshener (mukhavāsaka).
Having given [the gift] accompanied by musical instruments and endowed with all ornaments,
and having offered mouth-perfume, the wise man should lead [the image] through the processional paths.
Regarding the circumambulation and the sequences of mounting:
the sequence of mounting for the God of Gods during the festival is now described.
On the first day of the festival, one should perform the mounting of the parrot in the morning. (89)
On that night, one should perform the worship of the Laughing Vehicle (hasavāhana) of the God of gods;
and on the second day, one should perform the worship of Mṛgendra and Śarabha.
On the third day, one should perform the festival for Kapīndra and Prabhā;
and on the fourth day, one should perform the Kalpaka and Pañcaga rites.
On the fifth festival day, one should worship the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and Ardhacandramas;
when the sixth festival day arrives, one should likewise worship Gaja and Pāśin.
During the seventh festival, one should perform the Puṣpaka and Kamala rites;
and when the eighth festival arrives, one should perform the Ḍolā and Aśva rites.
On the ninth day, one should employ a celestial chariot as the vehicle;
and when the tenth festival arrives, one should perform the mounting of the palanquin.
And on that night, one should fashion the great elevation and the Gaja-lakṣmī;
on the morning of the eleventh day, one should employ the tortoise as a vehicle.
On that night, one should perform the worship of the Punnāga tree as a vehicle of great height;
then, on the morning of the twelfth day, one should perform the rite with a black antelope skin.
On that night, one should perform the ritual of the Great Form (Mahārūpa) with the Fish as its vehicle;
on the morning of the thirteenth day, one should arrange the Tortoise Yantra.
On that night, however, one should especially place [the deity] together with Śrī and Bhūmi upon a couch and perform a festival.
On the fourteenth day, at dawn, one should perform the rite of the Kautuka-ratha;
however, during that night, one should employ a tiger of great form as the vehicle.
On the morning of the seventh or eighth day, one should practice the Kuṇḍalivāhana;
on that night, however, one should practice the Śubhākāra Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa.
On the morning of the sixteenth day, one should prepare the seat of light;
however, during that night, one should fashion the great form of Indra.
On the morning of the ninth or eighth day, one should perform the ritual of the mountain-vehicle;
on that night, however, one should employ a jackfruit tree of auspicious form as the vehicle.
On the morning of the eighteenth day, one should perform the Kāliya-vāhana rite;
however, on that night, one should especially perform the Cakra-vāhana rite.
On the nineteenth day as well, one should cause the horse to graze in the sun;
but on that night, one should fashion a highly elevated Pārijāta tree.
On the twentieth day, in the morning, one should perform the rite of Dhvajavāhana;
but on that night, one should perform the rite of Mahārūpa-Śaṅkhavāhana.
On the morning of the twenty-first day, one should perform the chariot procession;
thus has the mounting been declared, and one should carry out the festival in due order.
Regarding the daily ritual options: even in the twenty-first [alternative], if one is unable, one should perform it for fourteen days;
if one is unable even for fourteen days, one should perform the festival for nine days.
On the twenty-first day, or likewise on the fourteenth,
or after nine days, seven days, or a fortnight, one should perform the chariot procession.

At the conclusion of the chariot procession, having prostrated before the Lord of Devas and worshipped him with the eightfold offerings (aṣṭopacāra), one should present the ritual food (mudrānna). || 109 ||
Having offered mouth-perfume, one should then perform the offering of a handful of flowers;
at that very moment, one should cause the Lord of Gods to descend from His chariot.
Having placed [the image] upon a vehicle and entered the sacred site (tīrtha), one should position it facing the holy water and then perform the festival of the tīrtha. || 111 ||
When you were mounted upon the chariot by the gods and it was being maneuvered through the streets,
the excellent wooden fenders of the chariot and the two wheels, which served as its supports, were then broken and shattered.
When such an obstacle had arisen, for two or three days,
Keśava remained in the chariot until the day of the expected arrival.
On the ninth day, at the time of sunset, one should perform the festival for the [deity] within the sacred precinct;
having installed the Lord upon the chariot, the wise man should enter the temple.
Having likewise brought the bathing vessel and the discus as well,
and having placed them upon the palanquin, one should cause them to enter the sacred site.
Having performed the festival of the sacred ford (tīrthotsava), the wise one should enter the temple;
having entered the sacrificial hall, he should perform the concluding oblation (antahoma). || 116 ||
Having circumambulated the pitcher, one should cause it to enter the inner sanctum;
then, taking the Śakti from the pitcher, one should install it in the permanent image (dhruvabera). || 117 ||
On that night, however, one should perform all the offerings (bali) and cause them to be made;
likewise, having taken the image of the deity (balibera), one should install it in the place of the banner.
On that very day and night, one should dismiss the deity of the banner;
having lowered that banner, one should perform the bali offering in silence.
Having dismissed all the gods, one should perform the remaining rites;
then, having gone to the place of the chariot, one should pay homage to the God of Gods.
Having firmly secured that chariot wheel as its support as before,
one should then quickly yoke it to the chariot, having led the chariot forward in due order.
Having established that deity in its proper place, one should lower it down;

having established it in the seat of the *jīva*, one should perform a brief sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*), and likewise cause the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) to be performed according to the procedure prescribed for bathing. || 122 ||
One should offer a great oblation or an abundant one to the Lord of the Gods.
Regarding the release of the protective thread:
one should release the protective thread for both the preceptor and the officiating priests. || 123 ||
Having released the binding of the God of gods,
one should prostrate on the ground during the festival of the God of gods when both fortnights have passed.
Regarding the determination of the time for the sacred ford (tīrtha):
whether two months have passed or likewise two years, no fault of duality exists in the primary lunar days, asterisms, and so forth. || 125 ||
If a festival is performed with a retinue and attendants, either twice a day or once a day,
even when the God of gods has mounted his vehicle and is being drawn along the streets; 126.
Accompanied by female slaves and musicians engaged in dance and song, it was provided with all kinds of musical instruments and adorned with every ornament.

By Brāhmaṇas and devotees of Viṣṇu who were intent on praising him in various languages, by those devoted to reciting the praises of the Purāṇas, and by those dedicated to the study of the Śāstras concerning reality; || 128 ||
Having joined all of these together, one should first perform the festival,
accompanied by a retinue of banners and the like— namely, flags, parasols, sunshades, and likewise archways.
Having taken those marks of adornment and those marks of the Lord, the pure Brahmins likewise [proceeded].
They should proceed in front of the deity, adorned with all ornaments;
behind them, however, is Keśava stationed upon his vehicle.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of finery,
he was arrayed in golden garments bound together in red, yellow, and white.
With chowries and fans provided with golden handles, as well as with female attendants or devotees of Viṣṇu, one should fan [the deity] on both sides in succession. || 133 ||
The Lord Hari, the God of gods, should be carried in a vehicle by sixteen, eight, or four Brahmins and others, as is appropriate.
Pure Brāhmaṇas and others of the same caste, having bathed and assembled together,
should place the vehicle upon their shoulders and proceed very slowly.
Regarding the specific mode of mounting the elephant-king as a vehicle: one should especially adorn the God of gods with garments,
ornaments, flowers, and other such items, according to what is appropriate.
Having first placed the Lord of the Gods upon the back and side of the elephant,
the preceptor takes up the goad and sits down upon the elephant's back.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, the priest, taking up the parasol adorned with pearl ornaments,
sits on the western side of the deity.
Seated upon vehicles such as the Garuḍa-palanquin or likewise on litters, the foremost of guides sits in the eastern part while the disciple sits in the south. || 39 ||
Meditating upon the Lord of Gods in one's mind and reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra, one should simply sit;
otherwise, if one should act differently, all of that would become fruitless.
One should especially perform the study of the Vedas and other auspicious recitations of praise on the western side of the deity. || 141 ||
Brahmins devoted to Viṣṇu, led by the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu priests and intent upon the study of the Vedas, should follow the Lord of Gods.
But on the subsequent part of this, specifically for the deity,
having mounted upon the back of an elephant, [one should play] the dundubhi drum as well as the jhallarī cymbal.
Having made the proclamation, the reciters of firm speech should follow;
thus, having performed the circumambulation, they proceed through the first enclosure and the others.
Or else, one should construct the village by circumambulating it from the outside;
at the junctions, there should be special worship, worshipping the Lord of Gods at every junction with the eight forms using water for the feet and other offerings. || 145 ||
Having honored [the deity] with equal devotion, one should offer mouth-fresheners accompanied by mantras;
then follows the presentation of offerings, including uncooked foods brought even by Brāhmaṇas. 146.
One should offer uncooked foods as well as cooked food brought by a Brahmin;
having sprinkled it with pure water, one should present it after consecrating it with the *amañca* mantra.
When the Lord of Gods has been brought a long distance on the road during a festival,
there is a special rule regarding this long journey:
whether it is two krośas, three krośas, or even when he has gone to another village.
Some say that the rites of fire-oblation, bali-offering, and worship should be performed on the following day;
others say that having performed them on the preceding day itself, one should depart.
One should always visualize the musicians, dancers, and others as Gandharvas, and likewise visualize Jayā and the other Apsarases as celestial women. 150.
One should meditate on the two women, Māyā and Saṃhrādinī, as chowrie-bearers;
or, if one meditates on those two as men, they are Kiṣkindha and Sundara.
One should remember all the drivers of the chariot, the mechanism, and so forth, as being like Garuḍa.
Upon returning, there is a special worship;
thus, having performed the circumambulation, one should enter inside once again.
Having seated the deity upon a seat provided with an upper cover,
and having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
The method for the lustration rite (nīrājana):
A vessel containing water, along with cooked rice and flowers, [is prepared];
and the preceptor, standing in front, [performs it] over the head of the God of gods. || 154 ||
One should slowly rotate the vessel three times clockwise around the edge of the feet;
[the offering consists of] water mixed with turmeric, rice, and flowers. || 155 ||
Having filled a bronze vessel [with water], one should cause it to be carried around by female servants;
thus Aṅgiras says that one should carry it around from the crest of the head down to the feet.
Having dismissed [the attendants] outside the door and performed protection on his forehead,
he established the Lord upon a seat covered with an upper cloth in the assembly hall.
Having given water for sipping (ācamana) and the water from a coconut fruit, as well as various kinds of edible foods such as cakes, parched grain flour, and fried rice grains; 158.
Having offered [the food], one should offer mouth-perfume with the eight-syllable mantra itself.
Then, at the conclusion of the lustration rite (nīrājana), there should be the recitation of hymns of praise by those proclaiming the victory of the Lord. || 159 ||
One should compose various hymns of praise using compositions in diverse languages;
thereafter, one should sequentially display the Mārga dance performed by celestial nymphs.
Having bathed [the image] according to the procedure prescribed for the pure bath,
and having worshipped it and offered [the oblation], one should then install it in the seat of the soul (jīvasthāna).
In this regard, some praise [the practice of saying]: "Exert yourself, O Name," while [the deity] is on a great throne either to the right or in front of the god. || 162 ||
Having constructed a beautiful temple with firmly fixed doors, and having placed mirrors and other such objects all around the interior of the house; || 163 ||
Having installed the God of gods in the center of that [mandala], one should worship him;
all things not mentioned here should be performed according to the procedure stated in the Khila. 164.
In this very manner, the festival is prescribed for the first and last days;
on the other days, the festival may be performed twice a day or once a day.
If an eclipse of the sun or moon occurs at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
or if the night of an eclipse falls upon a sacred ford,
one should likewise perform the concluding festival on the day of the sacred ford.
From the second day onwards, one should perform the festival twice a day, beginning with the morning twilight (saṃdhyā) and concluding at midday. || 167 ||
Regarding the duration of the festival:
this morning festival should take place after the evening worship;
the evening festival, once commenced, is concluded before one watch (yāma) has passed. || 168 ||
Whether in the evening of one's work, in the morning, or even at evening, there is always an excellent festival at all times together with the Goddess. (169)
The middling [rite] should take place at dawn, while the lowest occurs on the fifth day;
if it is a festival with a single session, the bali offering and the homa sacrifice should be performed at midday.
"Aṅgiras declares that one should perform the festival at the end of the day;
when the previous day has concluded, the festival is completed in the morning after the pilgrimage. (171)
Regarding the festival of the hunt:
having specially adorned the God of gods for the sake of hunting, he should lead him followed by goats, monkeys, tigers, elephants, and horses. (172)
The wise man should also cause the two goddesses to be brought, mounted upon a lion and accompanied by attendants equipped with various weapons.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should quickly cause a festival to be held outside in a delightful place, except for those who are lords of the circle (cakravīśas). 174.
One should also arrange for various kinds of pleasure-gardens and diversions;
some say this should be done at the descents [of the deity] or in worldly temples. 175.
One may also perform the rite of worship on other days as well, at pavilions on the banks of ponds or in well-arranged gardens. (176)
The consecration for the bed:
then, on the night preceding the day of the pilgrimage site,
having specially worshipped the deity and offered the oblation, one should also bind the *pratisarā* amulet.
One should cause [the deity] to lie down together with the wheel according to the very sequence prescribed for the installation ceremony;
and having performed worship with the eight forms in the morning, one should offer the oblations even without [the wheel]. || 178 ||
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) and offered the ritual oblation (bali), one should conduct the morning festival.
Having installed the deity facing east in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa), one should proceed with the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) in due order. || 179 ||
One should place the discus facing outward upon a pedestal of grain in front of the deity;
with a concentrated mind, one should place Viṣvaksena on its northern side.
One should place turmeric upon a grain-seat at the front of the wheel;
having thus consecrated it, one should sprinkle the powder as before.
And when the wheel has been pacified, having bathed and consecrated it as before, one should circumambulate the village and enter the sacred site (tīrthasthāna). || 182 ||
The method for bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha):
Having installed the deity and the discus on its bank as before,
one should duly arrange five water-pots (kalaśas) in front of the deity according to the prescribed rite.

Having filled [the vessels] with earth, kuśa grass, scents, flowers, water, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having placed them in order from the center to the northeast (saumya) and worshipped the deities; || 184 ||
Having quickly sprinkled the Lord of Gods with the mantras prescribed for the ritual bathing, [he worshipped] Bhūmi, the Earth, the Seasons, Dhātṛ, Kāśyapa, and Prajāpati.
Having consecrated the discus with the remaining water from the pitcher, he should then immerse the deity within the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 186 ||
Having again established [the image] on the bank upon a seat covered with an upper cloth,
one should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna) according to the procedure prescribed for the pure bath.
The sacrificer, the preceptor, the officiating priests, and the attendants,
having bathed there together with the Lord, shall wear white garments as upper cloths.
The village festival:
having adorned the God of gods and placed him upon a vehicle as before, [one should worship him] with white garlands, ointments, and the like, and with golden threads and rings. || 189 ||
Adorned with ornaments, together with his preceptor and likewise with officiating priests,
he should recite the Śākuna Sūkta accompanied by the Svasti Sūkta.
Accompanied by a stream of water, one should lead [the image] clockwise around the village;
