at that time, the patron (yajamāna) should also perform the act of rising to greet it.
Having adorned the gateway of the abode with full water-jars, sprouts, and the like,
as well as many lamps, the God of gods arrived there.
Having performed the circumambulation, accompanied by showers of water, provided with many lamps,
attended by women bearing auspicious vessels, and joined by many lights;
Having taken five multicolored balls of food, one should perform a circumambulation around the head of the deity,
the Lord of the Quarters, while reciting his names preceded by the syllable Om.
One should release [the mantras] in sequence, ending with "namas" and having the fourth case endings, while placing [the seed-syllables] in the middle.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should enter once more into the interior.
One should properly perform the bathing, including the ritual bath with the removal of impurities and the offering of oblations, strictly according to the sequence of the bathing rites.
Having thoroughly honored the offering of oblations—whether it be the Great Oblation (mahāhavis) or an abundant one—one should present it [to the deity]. || 196 ||
Having entered the place where the Jīva resides and having invoked the Kumbha into that place of the Jīva, one should establish it there and prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Then, having returned to the sacrificial hall and offered oblations into the fires with mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu... (197)
Having properly established the power residing in each respective pitcher into the *dhruva* [pitcher],
and having brought the fire into the permanent hearth (*nityakuṇḍa*), one should worship the Sun.

Even if one is unable to perform it at the permanent fire-pit (nityakuṇḍa), one should follow the previously mentioned procedure on the ninth day of the festival and likewise on the fourteenth day. || 199 ||
And at the conclusion of the night worship during the twenty-first festival,
the procedure for the dismissal of the deity is as follows: having offered the village oblation at night, one should do so without the Cakra, Vīśa, and Amita [deities].
Having dismissed the deities from their own [respective] places and having returned once more to the flagstaff,
one should worship the deity of the flagstaff and offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.
Having dismissed the deity of the banner,
one should take down that banner on either the tenth day or likewise on the fifteenth day.
The Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga) is the supreme ritual procedure;
one should perform the Flower Sacrifice on the twenty-second day, provided that it is performed for the portable image (kautuka) in the absence of the festival image (autsavapratimā). || 203 ||
On that very day of the pilgrimage festival, at the conclusion of the morning twilight,
having properly bound the *pratisara* thread, one should perform the morning festival.
On the second day, one should perform the Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga) at the sacred site (tīrtha).

The festival of the Flower Sacrifice is threefold: it may be for the purpose of pacification (śāntika), for nourishment (pauṣṭika), or for the fulfillment of desires (kāmya); thus it is of three types. || 205 ||
One should perform this supreme rite characterized by its height in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon, in due order;
however, at the conclusion of the morning worship, one should adorn it as is appropriate.
Having brought the Lord into the assembly pavilion after sunrise,
one should bathe him with water from the Jāhnavī according to the procedure prescribed for the pure ritual bath.
Having adorned [the deity] with new garments, upper cloths, and ornaments, one should worship it with a great or abundant offering and present it. || 108 ||
Either in the assembly pavilion or in the bathing hall itself,
one should smear the ground for four cubits on each of the four sides with cow dung.
Having established the *upapīṭha* positions by means of six lines extending eastward and northward,
one should draw in the center a nine-square lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Or with grains prescribed for the Ratnanyāsa, or with grass, rice, or paddy;
one should worship Viśa in a single place at the front of the external squares.
Having worshipped Cakra in the south and likewise Paṅktīśa in the west,
and having worshipped Śānta in the north, [one should worship] in the remaining solar stations as well.
One should properly arrange the materials for worship, beginning with the seat;
then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) upon the eight petals of the lotus. || 213 ||
One should worship the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire in sequence upon the pericarp;
having placed a seat there, [one should worship] the lotus situated within the feet.
Having installed the deity there, one should perform worship with twenty-seven forms throughout the entire day of the festival.
With dances, songs, instrumental music, and hymns from the four Vedas,
one should offer a separate handful of flowers at the conclusion of each respective worship.
The lotus born of mud, tulasī, bilva, karavīra, and likewise utpala, nandyāvarta, kumuda, and apāmārga; || 217 ||
Viṣṇukrānta and the tips of dūrvā grass— these very items are prescribed in sequence for the offering of handfuls of flowers during worship.
One should offer all the handfuls of flowers during the worship of others;
the assembly hall should have only a single fire, and everything else is as before.
The Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga) is the third ritual procedure;

thus the middling [method] has been declared. Now I shall explain the inferior one, O Paṇu, which is performed without the deities beginning with Vīśa, but through fire-offerings (homas) and separate individual worship. || 230 ||
Having installed the deity in the mandala and worshipped according to the ritual procedure,
one should then offer the five kinds of foodstuffs as prescribed.
One should offer a handful of flowers with the mantras appropriate for the entire day;
this is remembered as the expiation for those whose faults remain unknown during festivals.
This is the declaration of the fruit of the festival:
he who performs this with devotion shall obtain all his desires;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, he shall attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. || 233 ||
This procedure for the worship of Ālaya has been briefly set forth by me;
whatever has not been stated here, one should perform all of that according to the rules prescribed in the Khila.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Festivals," in the section on Rituals within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu. Om.
Fifteenth Chapter:
The Installation of the Household Image; the Installation of Viṣṇu.
Now, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall proclaim the worship of Viṣṇu in the home, and I shall explain it to you.
Having had that image made of gold or other materials, measuring no less than six finger-breadths, one should then begin the consecration according to the prescribed path.
When the time has arrived, endowed with the previously mentioned qualities and auspiciously radiant,
one should establish the *aupāsana* fire and perform the *vāstu-homa* until its conclusion.
Having performed the opening of the eyes at the conclusion of the prescribed oblations,
and having shown the cow and other items, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water and so forth.
One should perform the purification prescribed for a permanent image (dhruvabera) even when it is a painted representation;
therefore, having performed the evening twilight worship on the previous day itself, [one should proceed].
Having established the aupāsana fire and offered oblations therein,
and having prepared the ritual pitcher (kumbha) as before, he should indeed invoke the Lord into it.
Having raised the deity who has been brought into the state of residence with the syllable Om (praṇava),
one should establish it in the bathing pit while reciting the Svasti-sūkta.
On its very southern side, one should properly place it upon a pedestal of grain,
having bathed it as before with seven jars along with the ritual sprinklings (upasna).
Having established the image of Citrā, one should sprinkle it with water from the ritual jar;
then, having placed it upon a seat of grain to the north of the fire.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day and likewise having tied on the protective amulet (pratisara),
one should cause the deity to lie down in the same manner upon a bed spread with five cloths.
Having praised the *hautra* (the office of the Hotṛ priest), at that time, while in the water of the southern ritual vessel (*dakṣiṇapraṇidhi*), he should say:
"Oṃ bhūḥ puruṣam," and likewise, "Oṃ bhuvaḥ puruṣam. || 11 ||
Oṃ suvaḥ puruṣam, and likewise bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ;
[he meditated upon] Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, and Acyuta.
Having invoked Aniruddha and Śrī with the hymn "mahīm," and having offered oblations of clarified butter while reciting the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas; || 13 ||
Therefore, one should indeed worship by reciting the mantras of the gods and others four times;
likewise, one should worship with the specific Sūkta mantras accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
And at the end of the oblations with the form-mantras (mūrtimantra), one should again offer one hundred and eight lotuses while meditating upon the Lord, using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. || 15 ||

One should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homakarma) together with the previously mentioned forms, using the respective mantras and forms for the conceptualizations of the manifestations. || 16 ||
Having completed the fire sacrifice (homakarma) and bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rules,
he should recite the hymns to be chanted during an auspicious and radiant moment.

Having installed [the deity] upon a pedestal adorned with jewels and other ornaments in the north-western part of the house, and having invoked [the presence], one should worship [it] daily according to the prescribed rite. || 18 ||
One who is like the sun should, if he so desires, constantly worship even in the house of Bhāskara the Great God Bhāskara, who has the luster of a kadamba flower. 19.
Measuring nine and a half tālas, he has two arms and holds a lotus;
he is accompanied by two goddesses and surrounded by the zodiac signs.
Having established each [liṅga] upon its own pedestal, accompanied by its respective goddess,
and having performed this according to the rule, immediately after the opening of the eyes,
one should perform the rites such as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) just as one does for Hari. || 21 ||
They declare that "udutyaṃ citram" is the root mantra;
having established the domestic fire (aupāsana) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila). || 22 ||
Having prepared the pitcher as before, provided with two red garments,
the preceptor— his soul well-pleased— [should worship] that which consists of the three Vedas and is free from ailment.
Meditating upon the Sun, whose nature is universal awakening, one should invoke him into the water;
having bathed the image along with the ritual pitcher using seven jars.
Then, having prepared a heap of grain on the northern side of the front,
and having placed a bilva-fruit slab there, he should spread out five garments.
Having placed that poison there and bound the protective amulet (pratisara),
the wise one should then have [the patient] lie down upon the bed according to the prescribed rite, covered with a red garment.
Having praised the *hautra* and invoked [the deities], he should offer the clarified butter oblations after pouring them out;
then, as the sacrificer, he should worship the sun with the *gāyatrī*, mentally visualizing the Creator.
"To Bhāskara," and "to Sūrya, Mārtāṇḍa, Vivasvat," and likewise "to the ornament of the three worlds," and also "to the one of triple form. || 28 ||
One should offer oblations with the mantra "Salutation to the Soul of All," and likewise to "Caṇḍarocis," then to "Triguṇeśvara," and subsequently to "Sarvajyotiṣmat. (29)
One should perform the sacrifice a thousand times, or a hundred times, or ten times,
having offered oblations with the two Maitra mantras and likewise with "ud vayaṃ tamasas."
Let the oblation be offered with "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam" and "citram devānām";
then, having offered with "yaccid dhi," thereafter [offer] with "yatkim ca."
Having first offered with the verse beginning "kitavāsaḥ," one should then offer with the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa," using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of arka, apāmārga, and pālāśa wood.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauruṣa, and the Sūkta dedicated to the Lokapālas,
and having then offered the Mindā oblations, one should perform the rite of Homa.
There, one should indeed offer one hundred and eight oblations with the names of the two goddesses;
having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite, one should place the jewels and other items in their proper order.
One should install the deity facing west or facing east;
the Sun-god (Bhāskara) must never be installed facing south or north.
Taking the Śakti residing in the pitcher, the Guru should invoke it into the image;
whatever has not been mentioned here, he should perform all of that as in the case of Hari.
Having recited "Udutyam Citram" and bowed to the Lord of the luminaries,
he performed the ritual sprinkling with mantras and removed the faded floral offerings.

One should offer a welcome and an inference [of his divinity] with the mantra "O Agni, you are Rudra," and then, after that, one should give water for the feet with the mantra "We rise above the darkness. (36)
He should offer water for sipping into the hand while reciting "ahiraṇyavarṇā," and having said "pavitraṃ te," he should cast a flower upon the head. || 37 ||
One should fumigate with incense using the mantra beginning with "ime gandhāḥ";
one should offer the lamp with the mantra "pravaśśukre" and present the *arghya* water accompanied by its mantra. || 38 ||
One should offer other services as well, with the hymns "ud u tyam" and "citram," or else with the ritual mantras perfected through the teacher's instruction. (39)
Some say that one should worship with offerings such as a seat and so forth;
others hold that one should always worship with the Sāvitrī mantra—such is the instruction of the ancestors.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else shall be like that of Hari:
namely, Suvarcalā, Muṣā, Śyāmalā, and Suprabhā. (41)
One should worship the goddess Reṇukā, who is red in color, on the right;
and one should likewise worship Pratyūṣā, who is clad in white garments, on the left. || 42 ||
Desiring the perpetual worship and the daily ritual for Guha, they fashioned an image according to the prescribed rules,
performing the rites such as the opening of the eyes with mantras dedicated to Skanda.
Having performed the auspicious rite and bound the thread, one should worship one hundred and eight [times];
having invoked [the deity] with that mantra, one should always worship according to the rule. || 44 ||
Whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform according to the procedure prescribed in the Khila;
for him who performs thus with devotion, his sons shall be free from disease. (45)
The venerable ones, endowed with glory, increase; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed great pleasures here, he shall attain heaven at the end.
I shall now describe the worship of Vināyaka, the constant and perfect adoration of Vakratuṇḍa;
the opening of the eyes and other rites are performed with the two mantras beginning with "Dharmaughamā. (47)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations into those two fires and having invoked [the deity] according to the rule,
one should worship daily according to the ritual using those very same two mantras.
Thus, for one who performs this with devotion, his action indeed becomes free from obstacles;
everything is quickly accomplished, and abundant prosperity shall arise. || 49 ||
Hereafter, I shall describe the worship of the Goddess Śrī, the daily ritual for the propitiation of Śrī within the home;
she who resembles the filaments of a lotus and is adorned with every ornament. (50)
Seated in the lotus posture, with two upper arms raised in the form of lotuses,
she bestows fearlessness upon her devotees with her right front hand.
Holding abundant wealth with her left hand, having thus fashioned the goddess Śrī while reciting, "Born for prosperity," [he should worship her]. (52)
Having said, "Bestow peace upon this," and likewise,
"May we be [prosperous]," he should open his eyes and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) over the water and other materials in due order.
Having thoroughly prepared the jar, bathed it, and likewise bound the protective thread (pratisara) around it,
and having laid it down and invoked the deity, [the ritual] concludes with the duties of the Hotṛ priest.
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, however, one should offer oblations with the mantra "For glory,
O born one," followed by saying "May she bestow peace upon us" and "May we be [prosperous]," in due order.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should worship once with the Śrīsūkta;
thereafter, one should worship ten times with the mantras of the Śrī-sūkta repeated one hundred and eight times.
Having offered a bountiful oblation consisting of honey and clarified butter, combined with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya),
along with bilva leaves drenched in ghee.
One should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantra "śriye jāta" (RV 10.9.4).
Having bathed in the morning, having installed [the deity], and having invoked [the presence], one should perform the worship. || 58 ||
One should worship with all the forms using that very hymn and its mantras;
whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform according to the procedure stated in the Khila.
One attains unshakable prosperity even in successive births, and those born in one's lineage shall also become prosperous; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall describe the worship of Durgā, the installation and domestic worship of Durgā;
she is indeed the manifest Māyā of Viṣṇu, therefore one should worship her constantly.
Having fashioned the four-armed goddess according to the measurement of nine and a half tālas,
she should hold a conch and a discus and be radiant with a crown and diadem.
The goddess, wearing yellow garments, with her breasts bound by a girdle,
possessing the luster of dark green grain, gentle in appearance, and adorned with necklaces and the Kaustubha gem.
Having performed the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma), one should recite the Durgāsūkta one hundred and eight times;
then, having offered oblations with the Pāñcabhautika mantra accompanied by the Vaiṣṇava mantra. || 64 ||
Having performed the ritual of opening the eyes and having consecrated it with water and other substances,
one should meditate upon [the deity] within the pitcher, invoke [him], and bathe him with the ritual jars.
Having tied the protective amulet (pratisara), he should afterwards have [the patient] lie down upon a bed;
having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest and invoked [the deity], he should offer oblations of clarified butter after pouring out the portions.
Then, in the assembly hall, one should worship the Durgāsūkta one hundred and eight times;
likewise, the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Raudra, Bhautika, and Pañcavāruṇa hymns.
The wise man should offer oblations a thousand times with the Jayā and other mantras, the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, and the Sāvitrī mantra,
up to the limit of one thousand offerings, as previously described.
Let oblations be offered with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood while reciting the *Viṣṇu-sūkta*; and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should dispel the anger of the night.
Having bathed in the morning, having installed [the deity], and having invoked [the presence], one should worship;
one should perform the worship with that very hymn beginning with "jātavedase. || 70 ||
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is just as it is for Hari.
Thus, he who performs the installation and worship of Durgā with devotion [attains the same].
Having conquered his enemies and enjoyed abundant happiness on earth for a long time,
he attains union with Viṣṇu, together with ten preceding and ten succeeding generations.
Hereafter, I shall describe the worship of Sarasvatī, the adoration of the Goddess of Speech within the home:
she is endowed with a mass of matted locks, golden-hued, and four-armed. (73)
One should represent his right hand raised and holding a rosary, while the lower hand should be formed in the *mudrā* or likewise as the boon-granting (*varada*) gesture. || 74 ||
Her left hand is joined with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and likewise raised upwards;
she is endowed with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and adorned with all ornaments. || 75 ||
Meditating on her as seated in the lotus posture, radiant with the splendor of a golden lotus, one should remember her as "Pāvakā" while recollecting the mantra "maho arṇa. (76)

With the very same mantra previously mentioned, one should perform the opening of the eyes, the consecration, the binding of the protective thread (pratisara), the ritual bathing, the placing upon the bed, and so forth. || 77 ||
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest, one should perform the invocation through his form;
having offered the clarified butter oblations, one should worship Śamī one hundred and eight times.
One should worship the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Narasūkta in due order;
likewise, one offers oblations to the Brāhma, Aindra, and Āgneya mantras, as well as the Sviṣṭakṛt.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is like that of Hari.
He who performs [this] with devotion in this manner shall attain all knowledge. || 80 ||
Thereafter, one should join the other [deity] holding a book;
then, the Brahmāsana should be performed upon the lotus-seat (padmapīṭha).
One should likewise extend the right foot;
she is adorned with all ornaments and embellished with white garments.

Having performed the opening of the eyes and other rites with the Sārasvata hymn for that girl, who was adorned with white flowers and unguents and whose breasts were bound by a cloth, [he should proceed].
Having prepared the bed in that manner, one who is composed should perform the recitation for the Hotṛ priest,
offering a thousand white lotuses smeared with ghee.
They should offer oblations with those very hymns and mantras, while mentally recollecting the Goddess;
or they may likewise perform offerings of clarified butter with these [mantras] according to their capacity.
Having bathed in the morning, one should install and invoke [the deity] with the supreme mantras, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and Vaiṣṇava hymns, and then worship it.
One should worship daily with that hymn; everything else is like [the worship] of Hari.
[It bestows] wisdom, the state of being a seer, eloquence, and likewise the power of speech.
Fame is attained here and happiness that is exceedingly difficult to find is obtained there;
therefore, that Goddess should be meditated upon and worshipped by the wise.
She is beautiful to behold and renowned, pervading the activities of the world;
[he worships] Bhadrakālī, the Teacher, Kṣetrapāla, and the other protectors.
If one desires to worship Me, having installed [the image] according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer that mantra one hundred and eight times in the aupāsana fire.
One should perform the installation, worship, and other rites using only those specific mantras.
In the home, all members of the three higher castes may worship deities such as Nārāyaṇa and others.
Having established [the deity] by this rite, they should worship according to the prescribed rule;
or else, having established [the deity] with this ritual formula (kalpamantra), one should worship.
One who follows the Tantric system should install [the image] in the direct order (anuloma) and worship it;
however, one should never worship it in the reverse order (pratiloma), even according to the Tantric system.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation and Worship of Viṣṇu, Āditya, Skanda, Vināyaka, Lakṣmī, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Bhadrakālī, and Bimbara," in the section on ritual practice (*kriyākāṇḍa*) within the *Sahitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable *Vaikhānasa-śāstra* of the Seers.
Oṃ.
The sixteenth chapter:
The separate worship of the Kṣīrārṇava (the Ocean of Milk).
Hereafter, I shall describe the separate worship of the illustrious Goddess,
who remains standing when the Lord stands, and seated upon the throne of Hari when He is seated.
One should visualize the goddess Śrī as either seated, standing, or reclining upon a bed, adorning her with all her ornaments. || 2 ||
Resembling the filaments of a lotus, wearing yellow garments, and auspicious;
she is seated upon a lotus throne with her two upper arms raised above a lotus.
With her first right hand she bestows fearlessness upon those who have offered oblations,
and with her first left hand she holds vast wealth.
Having done this and having installed the goddess Śrī,
one should worship her after constructing the sacrificial hall according to the rules, facing the temple.
Having prepared two fire-pits for the *aupāsana* fire and a bed-altar,
and having performed everything in due order with the mantra "For the sake of prosperity (*śriye jāta*)," || 6 ||
Having consecrated the jar, bathed it, and likewise tied the protective cord (pratisara),
he should cause it to lie down and invoke [the deity] into the southern ritual vessel (praṇidhi).
One should also [worship] Śrī, Dhṛti, Pavitrī, and Pramodāyinī;
or else, in the northern praṇidhi, one should worship Bhūmi and Sarasvatī.
Having invoked Rati, Prīti, as well as Kīrti, Kṣānti,
Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi— these eight are the female attendants.
And in the second enclosure, one should also worship Indra and the other world-protectors,
as well as Balākinī, Vanamālā, and Vibhīṣā, the consort of Śaṅkara.
Guggulu, agaru, damaka, and likewise śaṅkhila—these eight are specifically declared in the third enclosure. || 11 ||
At the left of the first door is Nirmālyahariṇī,
and likewise at the left [of the second] she is said to be Naivedyahariṇī.
On the left side of the second door, one should likewise worship Bhūmi,
and on the right, Sarasvatī, as the two guardians of the second door.
One should likewise assign Rati to the left of the third door,
and Prīti is said to be in the left portion during this worship.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is like that of Hari.
Having invoked these goddesses into the water of the northern praṇidhi, [one should proceed].
Having uttered "śaṃ sā niyaccha" and "bhūyāma," one should worship one hundred and eight times with the mantra "śriye jāta" in due order. || 16 ||
One should worship one hundred and eight times in the lotus-fire with the Śrīsūkta alone;
then one should assign the attendant deities, ending with Nirmālyahāriṇī.

One should perform the oblation, invocation, worship, and so forth with their respective names; all other rites should be carried out precisely according to the sequence prescribed for installation. || 18 ||

In this very manner, having installed [the image], one should worship it constantly at the three junctions of the day; having performed the service of the God of gods, one should lead the Goddess along with him.
This shall be the establishment of the limbs; it is called the independent installation.
I shall now describe this ritual procedure both in brief and in detail.
One should arrange fire-pits all around the bed-altar;
the five fires, the Pauṇḍarīka rite, and the bathing pit as before. || 21 ||
Having performed the sacrifice of the ground, one should offer the oblation (āghāra) into the sacrificial pits;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the Hotṛ priest's portion in the Pauṇḍarīka fire.
One should have the clarified butter vessel (ājyasthālī) and the dipping-spoon (sruva) fashioned out of gold;
with that spoon, one thousand oblations (āhutis) are to be offered.
Having offered a thousand oblations to Viṣṇu, one should worship the eighty-eight [deities] in sequence;
furthermore, oblations should be made ten times with the eight "Śantā" mantras of Śrī.
Having offered an abundant oblation, he performs the homa for the quarters;
he should worship in the āhavanīya fire while meditating upon Śrī with the Śrīsūkta.
He indeed offers oblations into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the mantra "śriye jāta," followed by the utterances "śaṃ sā niyaccha" and "bhūyāma" in succession. || 26 ||
Having offered oblations in the other two *kuṇḍas* separately, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should worship in the *sabhya* fire in due order with all the mantras, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*.
When the auspicious moment has arrived, one should likewise install the Goddess;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains as it is for Hara.
Having thus installed the Goddess, one should worship her daily at the three junctions of the day;
furthermore, the swan-bannered [Viṣṇu] should be the special object of veneration during the festival of the Illustrious Goddess.
One should have all other rites performed according to the very sequence prescribed for the festival;
during the festival of the God of gods, one should lead the Goddess along with him.
In this very manner, one who has taken refuge in the abode of Viṣṇu performs with devotion the festival, the consecration, the worship, and so forth. || 31 ||
He attains unshakable prosperity even in birth after birth, and those born in his lineage will also become prosperous; of this there is no doubt.
Henceforth, I shall describe the independent installation of the Goddess Śrī.
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a small market town (33).
One should install the Goddess in the center, to the right of the Brahma-sūtra,
or else in the western part, likewise to the right of that sūtra.
In a place devoid of a Viṣṇu temple, or to the north of the Brahma-thread, or in the northwest or east of the village and so forth, or to the south of the measuring-line (sūtra). || 35 ||
A wise person should perform the installation ceremony in a delightful place, or on the bank of a river, or likewise in a forest,
or on a mountain peak, or by the shore of the ocean.
In a village, the temple should be a Svastika or one established with the Śrī design;
or it may be a Viṣṇucchanda temple, or even one measuring four cubits.
One should perform all activities such as plowing and so forth using that very hymn;
while performing the worship of the temple for the child, one should fashion the vimāna.
One should then install the trident (śūla) by means of the method for establishing a trident;
the Bilva tree is proclaimed as the "trident-tree" (śūlavṛkṣa) of the illustrious Goddess. || 39 ||
Alternatively, one may install either an aśvattha tree or a stone spike (śūla), or indeed a stone image,
by means of the procedure for the installation of a stone.

Or one should perform the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) of an image endowed with all the correct characteristics, either during the laying out of the first bricks or at the time of depositing the foundation (garbha). || 41 ||
During the laying of the crown-bricks and also during the installation of the trident,
there should be one Pauṇḍarīka fire, and the mantra should indeed be the Śrīsūkta.
One should mutter the verse dedicated to Śrī, beginning with "śriye jātā," for the sake of Śrī;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else is the same as that of Hari.
And so one should have the Goddess fashioned with either two arms or four arms;
all procedures such as the binding with cords and so forth should be performed just as for Hari.
One should create a beautiful lotus in the midst of a grove of bilva trees;
in its center, one should construct a temple resembling molten gold.
With lamps, fly-whisks, pearl necklaces, two full water-jars, and sprouts;
with flowers, perfumes, incenses, canopies, and pillar-wrappings. || 46 ||
Having constructed a beautiful temple provided with four enclosures,
[one should place the deity] there upon a seat situated in the middle of the pericarp of a lotus on a lion-throne.
One should fashion the goddess with four arms, her two upper hands holding lotuses, and her front right hand bestowing fearlessness upon devotees. (48)
With her left front hand she holds abundant wealth;
she has eyes like the interior of a blue lotus, a face like the autumnal moon, and is auspicious.
Her limbs were anointed with white perfumes; she was radiant with white garlands and garments;
and she was adorned with divine ornaments shining with various jewels.
Having thus visualized the Blessed Lady, who is golden-hued, the bestower of boons, resplendent with a complexion like refined gold, and the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra; || 51 ||
One should place the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures at the feet of Śrī;
then, one should arrange Puruṣa and the others in the four directions starting from the east.
Or else, one should meditate on the supreme beings, Vāsudeva and the others, who bear the conch and discus, and are resplendent with crowns, necklaces, armlets, tiaras, and other ornaments. (53)
They had the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem upon their chests, were adorned with forest garlands,
possessed four arms, sat comfortably, were dark-complexioned, and had lotus-like eyes.
They beheld the goddess Śrī, her eyes wide with wonder,
along with guggulu, agaru, damaka, and likewise śiṅkhila.
One should visualize four white-bodied beings with four tusks in the corners:
Bhūmi, Sarasvatī, Rati, and likewise Prīti. (56)
One should assign the eight powers—fame, patience, nourishment, contentment, and the rest—and one should likewise assign the world-protectors, Indra and the others, to their respective places. (57)
And one should place Balākinī at the eastern gate, Vanamālikā in the south,
Vibhīṣikā in the west, and Śāṅkarī at the northern gate.
One should visualize these four as the Vāmanās who are the female gatekeepers;
or else, two of each may be fashioned, for these female gatekeepers have been described in the Khila.
Clad in white garments, holding lotuses in their hands, and adorned with all ornaments—
these [goddesses], beginning with Balākini, resemble the filaments of a lotus.
One should draw Mandāra and Pārijāta trees of the Kalpa-continuum in the four directions,
and bilva trees all around, along with full water-pots, in due order.
Having visualized the entire retinue as described in the scriptures in their proper order,
and having established them down to the seat of the Bhūtas, one should commence the rite of installation.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, the installation [of the deity] for the pleasure of Śrī should be performed;
sitting properly on a seat made from the root of a Bilva tree, one assumes the Vāhma posture. 64.
One should recite the Śrīsūkta one hundred and eight times and meditate upon Śrī;
on the fifth day prior to the day of installation, the offering of the vessel (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed.
After the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should prepare the sacrificial hall;
one should also arrange the bed-altar and the fire-pits all around it. || 65 ||
One should perform the five fires, the Pauṇḍarīka fire, and the bathing pit as before; likewise, the opening of the eyes, the preliminary consecration, and the purification of the Dhruva vessel.
Having performed [the rites] as before, and especially during the first part of the night,
one should perform the earth-sacrifice (bhūmi-yajña) and then carry out the foundational oblation (āghāra) in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
Having worshipped Kumṛbha, one should bathe her again with seven jars;
then, having bound the protective thread as before, one should lay Śrī upon the bed.
Then, one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* in the *pauṇḍarīka* fire;
the *ājya* vessel and the *sruva* ladle should be made of gold alone. || 69 ||
With that *sruva* ladle, one thousand oblations should be offered;
having offered one thousand oblations to Viṣṇu, one should then sacrifice eighty-eight oblations.
One should offer oblations ten times with the one hundred and eight mantras of Śrī;
having offered a full oblation, one indeed performs the Diśāhoma.
One should worship the Śrīsūkta while meditating on Śrī in the Āhavanīya fire;
and one should offer oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the mantra beginning "śriye jāta". (72)
Having uttered "śaṃ sā niyaccha" and "abhūyāma" respectively,
he should offer oblations separately in the other two pits, ending with the vyāhṛtis.
O member of the assembly, one should worship with all the mantras in sequence, ending with the vyāhṛtis;
then, when the auspicious moment has arrived, one should likewise install Lakṣmī.
This alone would be the distinction; everything else is as stated in the Khila.
If one is unable to separate [the elements] individually, they may simply take their abode in the ālayavijñāna.
One should arrange [the image] to the right of the Ālaya of the God of Gods;
one should fashion it with four arms according to the procedure previously described. || 76 ||

Alternatively, having visualized the goddess as having two arms, one should properly install her according to the prescribed rite— either as independent or as residing within a temple— just as described for the three worlds.
The worship and so forth of the Goddess Śrī, her installation, and the Śrīśatāṣṭaka are explained in detail in the Khila section; having understood each of these, one should perform the worship.
The installation accompanied by the *dhruva-kautuka* rite shall be considered the most excellent;
the worship of a single image (*ekabera*) appears as mediocre and is inferior. || 79 ||
He who, with devotion, performs the installation, worship, and other rites for Śrī, attains unshakable prosperity even in birth after birth. (80)
Those born of that lineage shall become illustrious, there is no doubt;
the sin committed in seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment. (81)
Having ascended the celestial chariot (vimāna), one shall attain the state of sharing the same world as the Goddess (sālokya).
This is the sequence of the Goddess Śrī’s celestial chariot; hereafter, the sequence of the Goddess Śrī’s celestial chariot is described.
Having fashioned the characteristic features of the celestial mansion (vimāna), one should arrange its attendants;
the sequence for the deities on the ground floor and the first level is now described.
One should arrange Puruṣa and the others in the four directions starting from the east;
on the second level as well, the array of Vāsudeva and the others is prescribed.
The sequence of the retinue as it was taught for the third level is as follows:
guggulu, kuraṇṭa, damaka, and likewise salila. || 85 ||
One should arrange elephants with four tusks and white limbs starting from the east;
O wise ones, the sequence of the retinue is also declared for the fifth level.
One should likewise arrange these four goddesses—Bhūmi, Sarasvatī, Rati, and Prīti—in the directions starting from the east. (87)
And on the sixth level as well, Kīrti, Kṣānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi are said to be located; one should arrange these starting from the east and so forth.
On the seventh floor, one should likewise arrange the deities of the directions;
on the eighth floor, one should also fashion the eight guardians of the quarters.
One should assign these deities in the four directions beginning with the east;
the sequence of deities is also stated for the ninth level.
One should likewise arrange Vāsuki, Ananta, Śaṅkha, and Gulika in the four directions starting from the east, in this very order. || 91 ||
O wise ones, the sequence of the retinue on the tenth floor is as follows:
Sarasvatī in the east and likewise Gāyatrī in the south.
In the west, one should place Sāvitrī, and in the north, Vaiṣṇavī;
now hear the sequence for the earthen mounds (pālikās) on the eleventh level as well.
In the east there was Śrī, and likewise Hariṇī in the south; Ilā in the west, and Sundarī in the north.
On the twelfth level as well, the sequence of deities is described:
Balākinī is in the east, and Vanamālikā is in the south. || 95 ||
In the western [quarter] is Vibhīṣikā, and likewise Śaṅkarī in the north;
at the section of the palace gate, however, there are four female gatekeepers.
One should also arrange these gods all around the celestial chariot (vimāna);
they are clad in white garments, hold lotuses in their hands, and are adorned with every kind of ornament.
One should place these goddesses, Balākinī and the others, who resemble the filaments of a lotus,
in each corner, visualizing them as either a lordly elephant or a lordly lion.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is like that of Hari.
On the fifth day prior to the day of installation (pratiṣṭhā), one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 99 ||
Having also prepared the sacrificial hall all around the pavilion,
one should arrange the fire-pits in the four directions of the pavilion.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should perform everything prescribed for the installation of the goddess Śrī right here. 101.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as it is with Śrī. He who performs [this] with devotion shall obtain all his desires. || 102 ||
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the world of Brahmā.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of Śrī Residing in the Temple of the Blessed One," in the section on Rituals within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable Vaikhānasa scripture of the Sage.
Oṃ.
The seventeenth chapter:
The Installation of the Threefold Form (Trimūrti).
I shall describe the installation of the Trimūrti for the prosperity of the worlds:
having established Viṣṇu in the center, one should then establish Brahmā to his right.
Having established Rudra on the left, that worship is the most excellent;
the installation of Brahmā and Rudra in reverse order is indeed the middling [method]. || 2 ||
Having installed Rudra in the center, Viṣṇu in the south, and Brahmā in the north, one should then install [the third deity] in reverse order; this is considered the lowest [method].
Or, having placed two others on the sides, or Brahmā alone in the center,
one should install Viṣṇu and the Lotus-born (Brahmā) according to this gentle ritual procedure.
The installation of Śiva should indeed be performed according to the Śaiva Tantra alone;
one should install the moon-crested Lord as either Niṣkala (partless) or Sakala (with parts).
One should arrange the respective retinues for the three [deities] as previously described;
the lords of the Anapāyinī, Gadvāra, and Vimāna [mandalas] are each distinct.
All those belonging to the enclosures and surrounding walls are considered common [to all];
the same applies to the gatekeepers of the first enclosure and the others.
One should fashion the gods according to the supreme ten-tāla measurement;
Śaṅkara according to the middle, and Viriñca according to the lowest.
One should prepare a sacrificial hall for them facing the Ālaya;
for the God of gods, there should be six fires, and likewise five fires for Brahmā.
One should likewise fashion [the image] of Rudra according to the path prescribed in that scripture;
one should perform all the rites, such as the opening of the eyes and so forth, separately, just as before.
At the time of reciting the *hautra* liturgy, one should invoke and worship the assemblies of deities such as Indra within the central altar fire-pit.
He indeed performs the *devasya tvā* oblation six times in the fires;
having performed the praise of the *hautra* in the *sabhya* pit of the Brahman priest. || 12 ||
The wise man should offer oblations as before—namely, the Prājāpatya, the Jayā and others, the Kūśmāṇḍa, the Gaṇahoma, and a thousand āhutis. || 13 ||
One should also worship one hundred and eight times with two Brahman-mantras;
then, one should worship a lotus smeared with ghee one hundred times with the Sāvitrī mantra.
One should sacrifice to Indra conjoined with Agni in the Āhavanīya fire;
one indeed offers to Yama conjoined with Nirṛti in the Anvāhārya fire.
He offers the oblation to Varuṇa and the one dedicated to Vāyu at the Gārhapatya fire;
he should sacrifice to Soma, Kubera, and Īśāna at the Āvasathya fire in due order.
One should worship one hundred and eight times with mantras beginning with the four Vedas;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains the same.
Marīci clearly proclaimed the installation of the three forms and the worship of the assembly and the attendants; one should perform whatever remains unsaid.
I shall describe the installation of two forms: having installed the immutable Viṣṇu on the right and Rudra on the left, one should worship them daily according to the prescribed rules.
Alternatively, if one should desire to establish a separate shrine for Brahmā,
it may be done in villages and the like, in their midst, in a secluded spot, or elsewhere in the forest.
One should perform all rites, beginning with the examination of the ground, using that very mantra;
having performed [the rites] such as the bringing forth and the opening of the eyes of the celestial chariot, the image, and so forth. // 21 //
The wise one should perform all the rites prescribed for the installation as before;
he should also worship daily according to the rules with the two Brahma-mantras.
In this manner, one should offer the four oblations, beginning with milk-rice;
and during the festival, one should prepare for him a banner marked with the sign of a swan.
In the festival of that [deity], the respective oblations are to be performed by Vaiṣṇavas with the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and indeed with the two Brāhma-mantras.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else shall be the same.
[The arrangement of the retinue consists of] Ravi, Guha, Vidhneśa, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Sarasvatī. || 25 ||
If one desires to perform worship separately with devotion after having established [the deity], one should carry out that which has been explained by me in detail in the Khila section. || 26 ||
If one desires the abode of the Ālaya, one should worship Viṣṇu in his temple on all sides;
if one worships him after duly arranging [the images of] Bhāskara and the others, there will be great fruit. || 27 ||
In the first enclosure, one should install Bhāskara and Bhāratī in the east,
Guha in the south, and Vidhneśa in the southwest.
One should place Jyeṣṭhā in the north-western quarter and Durgā in the southern quarter;
Bhāratī and Divākara should both be made facing westward.
"One should have others face the east; such is the instruction of the ancestors.
One should worship according to the gentle rite for the sake of all prosperity. (30)
One should not worship these [deities] who reside in a Saumya abode according to the Tantric rite;
rather, the Aupāsana fire alone should be present in their abodes.
One should perform the constant worship (dhruvārcā) according to the prescribed path; everything else should be as described for the Khila-ukta [rites].
The temple, the height of the image, and the retinue should be as stated in the Parivāra [section]. || 32 ||
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall explain the conceptualization of the foundational abode (āśrayālayakalpa) and the conceptualization of the foundational abode itself;
for it is impossible to establish an independent foundational abode elsewhere than in this foundational abode.
Having installed [the deity], he should worship it; he too shall obtain the complete fruit.
When the Lord resides in the primary abode, He remains present in the secondary shelter as well. || 34 ||
If [the teacher] is seated, one should likewise provide a seat or a standing position;
among standing, sitting, and reclining, any one of these is considered appropriate for the bed. || 35 ||
In the primary abode (mūlālaya), there is the permanent worship (dhruvārcā) and the support for the permanent worship;
likewise, in the case of one joined with both the permanent and the festive (kautuka) images, it is exactly the same. || 36 ||
If, however, it concerns the basis of the incarnations (avatāra) according to the secondary path (gauṇamārga),
then in all cases Varāha and Narasiṃha are indeed seated [upon their vehicles] in accordance with the rule.
While establishing the basis for the incarnations in the first enclosure and the others,
one should place Matsya and Kūrma to the south of the eastern gate.
One should arrange three boars starting from the southeast and ending at the south;
one should fashion a lion on the mountain situated between the south and the west.
Sthūṇaja is in the south-western region, Nīlavāruṇa is in the middle; then Saudarśana and Nṛsiṃha are in the western quarter. (40)
One should fashion Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha in the middle, Varuṇodāna in the south,
and Pātālanarasiṃha as well as Vāmana in the direction of the wind (the northwest).
One should have Trivikrama installed between Dhanada and Indra;
and Jāmadagnya in the north, between Kubera and Īśāna.
One should place Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, in the northeast; Halāyudha in the intermediate direction between Īśāna and Indra; Kṛṣṇa to the left of the door; and Kalki in the northwest.
Having established Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Rāma, and likewise Kṛṣṇa in all directions, one should worship them for the attainment of all perfections.
In Yoga, one should practice yoga within the fundamental abode (mūlālaya), which is the very refuge of the abode;
in Bhoga, one should practice either bhoga or yoga, but never anything such as separation and the like. || 45 ||
If the primary image is a trident, one should install a trident in the sanctuary;
likewise, a trident on stone or iron, or even a stone image on iron.
In all cases where there is only one *bera*, one should fashion it as a stone image;
this applies if the consecration of the *Sudarśana* is to take place in the south or likewise in the southwest.
One should conceive of Īśvara in the east; the arrangement begins from the east.
Then, one should construct a temple supported by pillars, measuring either three-quarters or half [of the original size], starting from the foundation.
In that regard, one should not fashion a superior ornament for the root-abode (mūlālaya),
nor should one ever fashion a support-abode (āśrayālaya) with more than eight stories.
Situated within the hall, enriched with the three goals of life (trivarga), and joined with a front pavilion within the inner circle—that is prescribed for the first enclosure. (50)

The deities at the doors of the celestial palaces (vimāna) and those situated within the inner sanctum (garbhālaya) are called the retinue (parivāra); their worship extends up to the entrance hall (mukhāvāsa).
If it is in the second enclosure, it should be resplendent with a peaceful assembly;
if it is in the third enclosure, one should cause the fire-offerings (homa) to be performed.
It is likewise provided with a front porch (mukhamaṇḍapa) and equipped with a discus and a conch;
if it is in the fourth enclosure, it consists of twenty-nine forms.
One should arrange for all the non-falling (anapāyigaṇa) deities a bathing hall;
above that, one should separately perform festivals and other rites with thirty-two forms.
One should not perform rituals such as the examination of the ground, ending with the Brahma-padmāvaṭa, within a temple; this is the instruction of the ancient teachers.
One should construct the temple (vimāna) beginning with the laying of the first brick;
however, there is no laying of the first or last bricks if that [temple] is within an enclosed pavilion (maṇḍapa).

If the root [mantra] is of the Paurāṇika type, then one may, according to one's desire, conceive of it as having a support that is either secondary, equal, or primary; if one does so, it does not constitute a fault.
If one should construct a subsidiary shrine within the temple of Viṣṇu, the injunction is that everything should be designed as superior to the main temple. || 58 ||
If one should construct a shelter for other deities within the abode of Viṣṇu, it should be made neither equal nor superior, but rather inferior. || 59 ||
Even when the Lord stands, Jyeṣṭhā, Vidhneśa, and Sarasvatī must be depicted as seated;
at that time, others are considered to be standing.
Thus has the conceptualization of the basis and the storehouse been briefly explained.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Planning of the Temple Based on the Rituals for the Installation of the Three or Two Forms," in the section on Rituals (*kriyādhikāra*) within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the venerable scripture of the Śrīvaikhānasas.
Oṃ.
The eighteenth chapter.

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the worship of the auspicious lunar mansions (puṇyanakṣatra). Śravaṇa, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), and likewise the five days of Viṣṇu— these indeed are the auspicious times for worship.

Among these, listening [to the teachings] is highly praised; the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is considered the most excellent. It is also meritorious during the equinoxes, solstices, the full moon, the new moon, the lunar mansions, eclipses, and other planetary transits.

Having likewise performed the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) for both the patron and the officiating priest, as well as for the village and the lunar mansion, and having similarly bound the protective amulet (pratisara), [one should proceed].
One should sleep during the first part of the night, and having bathed according to the rules in the morning,
one should recite the mantras prescribed for the day at the holy site after the morning twilight worship.
Having offered oblations into the perpetual fire-pit together with the lords of the Cakras,
one should present the bali offering at the boundary of the village according to the sequence prescribed for festivals.
Having performed the festival according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the pilgrimage as before;
thereafter, having bathed [the deity] in the manner described for the ritual bathing.
Having worshipped [the deity] and offered [the oblation], one should install it in the place of the living soul;
this rite, designated as the Peaceful Festival (śāntikotsava), should be performed during the forenoon.
A wise person should perform the festival for prosperity at midday without the offerings (bali) and oblations (homa),
but should perform the optional festival in the afternoon without visiting a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).

In the case of an image (arcā), the rite may be for pacification (śāntika), for desired results (kāmya), or indeed for a festival (autsava). Having performed the bathing (snāpana) for the festival, one should perform it during the day or at night in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa).
Having worshipped with all ritual services and offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other oblations,
one should, being free from sloth, present the food offering (naivedya) with every possible effort in this manner.
If one is unable to perform it thus repeatedly during these days,
one should bathe [the image] according to the rules with scented water, following the procedure prescribed for the pure bath.
One should worship the deity with the thirty-two forms quickly and with joy;
there too, at the time of the *balivelā*, one should place [the image] upon the vehicle as before.
One should thus lead the deity clockwise around the temple of the assembly hall;
having installed it in the place of the living soul (jīvasthāna), one should perform the remaining rites there.
For the bath on the five days of Viṣṇu, midday is said to be the prescribed time;
however, during solar eclipses and the solstices, one should perform it prior to that time.
One should perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice with cooked offerings according to the procedure prescribed for the Haviṣpāka; likewise, when various grains, diverse fruits,
all kinds of side-dishes, and new garments have been brought forth.
Having diligently gathered all [the ingredients] together, joined with every auspicious element.
One should recite the Śakunasūkta and perform a circumambulation of the village;
some say that, having adorned it, one should lead the disc (cakra) before oneself.

Next, I shall explain the supreme procedure for cooking the sacrificial oblation (havis-pāka-vidhi). For the sake of the oblation, one should procure grains as well as the various side-dishes (upadaśa). || 1 ||
Wise men know that śāli rice, vrīhi rice, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, ṣaṣṭika rice, barley, and veṣṇuka are likewise highly praised.
Among all varieties of rice, one should exclude black grain;
among all kinds of grain, śāli rice is ten times superior. || 3 ||
Priyaṅgu is a hundredfold [more effective], while nīvāra is a thousandfold;
garbhaṣaṣṭi is ten thousandfold, and barley and bamboo-seed are infinite.
Grain brought from the four castes is declared to be praiseworthy;
one should avoid blue grain brought by those of the lowest castes and those born of inverse unions.
Alternatively, one may collect pure grain acquired through trade;
however, grains that have been stored for more than three years are not commended for use in rites pertaining to the gods.
One should avoid all grains that have been stored for more than a month;
having sprinkled the grains with water while reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should then bring them forth.
Whether in a temple or in a house, in a pure place, being composed, having spread out a canopy or a mat according to the prescribed rule; || 8 ||
Having dried them thus with the sun's heat, one should winnow away the chaff of Viśvāmitra;
then, having carefully gathered the grain, one should deposit it among the straw.
Having bound him with straw and placed him upon the back of an elephant,
accompanied by all musical instruments and adorned with every ornament.
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and provided with full water-jars and sprouts,
one should adorn the entire temple with full water-jars and sprouts as well.
Having slowly led [the deity] to the temple with many auspicious lamps, as well as plantains and betel nuts, one should place them before the deity.
Having worshipped Vāyu among them with his eleven forms, and having praised the goddess Śrī with the Śrīsūkta and prostrated before her; || 13 ||

One should receive the grain without haste while reciting the mantra "śriye jāta," and then perform the threshing according to the procedure prescribed for cooking the sacrificial oblation (havis). || 14 ||
Then he should take pure rice grains and place them in a vessel;
having cooked the sacrificial offerings and the side dishes according to the prescribed rule.
Rice grains washed with water, mixed with sugar and jaggery,
as well as with black pepper, cumin, and coconut fruits.
One should offer rice mixed with ghee to the God of gods according to the mantra;
having performed the oblation with those very same grains, one should present the offering for the retinue.
Having again given water for sipping (ācamana), one should offer mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more with side-dishes and other offerings, [one should proceed]. (18)
Thereafter, one should offer the oblation (havis) and likewise perform the homa for the deities' forms;
having given the bali offering to the retinue, one should provide water for drinking and water for sipping (ācamana). || 19 ||
Having offered mouth-perfume and prostrated with the words, "Forgive me," one should thereafter present a handful of flowers at the feet of the God of gods.
On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the offering of lamps, beginning with the Kṛttikā constellation;
having thoroughly adorned the temple with cleansing, sprinkling, and smearing.
One should adorn the God of gods with ornaments and other beautiful things,
having decorated him with garments, garlands, and unguents.
One should offer a great oblation or an abundant one according to one's ability;
or else, a betel nut, a coconut, a palm fruit, or even a jasmine flower.
Having taken the lamp-stand, he should place it again before the deity;
and around the lamp-stand, he should also place three firebrands as lamps.
One should likewise have odd numbers of these made, each measuring one cubit (ratni) in length;
for the purpose of offering lamps, one should have a four-faced structure built in the shape of a peaked roof.
In all the pavilions and in all the enclosures,
one should arrange lamp-stands according to the extent of one's wealth.
At dusk, one should likewise perform the circumambulation of the temple;
then, with the mantra "uddīpyasva," one should again offer a lamp. || 27 ||
Having established [the image] on a pedestal of grain facing the Lord of Gods, one should worship Śrī there while reciting, "Born for the sake of Fortune" (Śriye Jāta). || 28 ||
O Lord of Gods, one should place a lamp on the tip of the lamp-stand for the renunciant near the presence of the deity,
and one should offer many lamps everywhere, including upon the walls and other such places.
The offering of lamps in that month of Kārtika is especially distinguished;
having established the God in his sanctuary and having worshipped him with the eight forms. (30)
One should offer cakes, parched grain, and flattened rice according to one's ability,
well-prepared with marīca, cumin, and coconut.
In the supplement (khila), the consecration of the Kṛttikā-lamp has been explained in detail, as well as Keśikā-dvādaśī and the festival of study (adhyayanotsava).
Especially during the bright fortnight of the month known as Sārgaśīrṣa. || 32 ||
Then, beginning on the eleventh day, one should perform the recitation of the Vedas (vedapārāyaṇa);
at the conclusion of the morning twilight, however, one should attend the deity in the assembly pavilion.
Establish the four Vedas and always teach them in their proper sequence;
worship that God of gods with twenty-seven forms.
Having had it fashioned adorned with all ornaments and circumambulated,
one should recite the Svasti-sūkta and place it in the seat of life (jīvasthāna).
One should practice for a fortnight, or for thirteen days, or for twelve days,
listening to the Purāṇas and Itihāsas concerning the god’s exceedingly fierce victories.
Or he should constantly cause the narrative of the God of gods to be heard in his presence;
on that very twelfth day of the month, having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rite, || 37 ||
One should discard old earthen vessels;
the others should be purified as appropriate, either with water or with the mantra "anāmā vāje". (38)

Having thus purified the temple by means of scrubbing, sprinkling, smearing with cow dung, and other such methods, one should likewise purify all the images, including those used for festivals, according to the prescribed rules.
Having bathed [the deity] with fragrant water according to the procedure prescribed for a pure bath,
one should bathe the image with the ritual pitchers according to the rules.
Having smeared a square of four cubits on the four sides with cow dung,
one should fashion a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp out of rice grains.
One should properly worship the deities seated upon that lotus as before;
having installed the Lord upon that cushion provided with an upper cover.
Having worshipped with a seat and other offerings, one should present the water for the feet and food;
having given the water for the feet and the water for sipping, one should present the mouth-perfume. 43.
One should offer many handfuls of flowers with the mantras prescribed for the flower-sacrifice;
then, at the conclusion of the circumambulation of the abode, one should place [the deity] in the seat of the living soul (jīvasthāna).
Whatever deficiency has occurred in the annual worship, or even in the daily and occasional rites,
all that shall become completely full through this worship on the twelfth day.
The sacrificer shall also attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
this is indeed for the purpose of expiating the faults incurred during the year-long worship.
Regarding the specific Śravaṇadvādaśī:
some say that one should perform the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Viṣṇu when there is the conjunction of Śravaṇadvādaśī in the month of Bhādrapada. (47)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite;
in the month of Taiṣya, one should always bathe Hari with cow’s milk.
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when the moon is in the Punarvasu constellation, is the worship of Rāghava;
on that Jayā day, having fasted, one should worship either Rāma or Viṣṇu.

Having led [the deity] around the village clockwise and having bathed him, one should present [the offerings]. This is the procedure for the Tīrtha-padmavidhi; in this month, during the bright fortnight, on the fifth lunar day known as Vijayā.
Having performed the ritual of the sesame-lotus, one should indeed offer a gift there;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods in due order during the first part of the night.
Having offered even the oblations of grain and tied the protective thread (pratisara) once more,
the wise one should cause the deity to be shaded as before and pass the remainder of the night.
At dawn, having raised the deity, one should bathe him again with water-pitchers;
then, having established the deity in the pavilion, one should bow down and seek his permission.
Having scattered grain upon a new cloth two cubits in length and breadth,
which is spread out before him and covered with a black antelope skin.
Having scattered a load of sesame seeds, or half of that, or more than that, in the shape of a mandala,
one should draw here a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having fashioned a golden lotus, one should place it upon a sesame lotus;
likewise, there should be sixteen full vessels filled with *āḍhaka* measures of śāli rice.
One should place the vessels beginning with that of Indra and ending with that of Īśāna, filled with rice, all around;
having taken one āḍhaka of oil, or likewise half of that in ghee.
Having taken an equal amount of curd and placed it in separate vessels,
one should set down oil on the right and ghee on the left.
Having placed curd in the west and bowed to the God of gods,
one should mutter the Ātmasūkta and worship Him with the eight forms.
Having prostrated before the God and invoked Him into the center of the lotus as before,
[one should worship] Puruṣa and the others starting from the east with their eleven forms.
Then, having invoked the deities of the directions beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, one should worship them;
thereafter, one should again recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta accompanied by the hymn beginning with "ato devā".
Having installed the image of the deity and gradually removed the others,
the patron (yajamāna) should then, at that time, give the teacher's sacrificial fee (ācāryadakṣiṇā).
One who is endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, self-controlled, possessed of virtues such as compassion, constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas, and complete in all his limbs; || 63 ||
Having summoned a Brahmin at that time and meditated upon that imperishable God,
one should offer a sesame-lotus to him in the presence of the God of gods.
One should offer a great oblation or an abundant one according to one's capacity;
having circumambulated the temple, one should look upon it and place it in the seat of life.
The extensive ritual procedure for the offering of incense has been fully described in the section on sacrifices;
indeed, the specific offering of incense to the God of gods is recommended during that month.
In the month of Phālguna,
having bathed Janārdana— who is with Śrī and who possesses the excellence of the supreme trees of Phālguna—
one should perform a festival, worship Him thoroughly, and present offerings. || 67 ||
Alternatively, having bathed [the deity] with pure waters, one should present [the offerings];
by worshipping Śrī on that day, one who desires prosperity shall obtain prosperity. || 68 ||
In the month of Phālguna, the offering of fragrances to the God is preeminent.
In Caitra, there is the Damanaka festival;
likewise, on the full moon day of Caitra, one should perform the Damanaka festival.
On that very same day, having adorned the auspicious temple,
one should have various beautiful garlands of *damanaka* prepared.
At the conclusion of the night worship, having worshipped the deity in the pavilion of the assembly hall, having presented the offerings, and having also bound the *pratisarā* amulet; 71.
One should visualize the heart-pleasing mandala of the three worlds before the deity;
one should place the mother of the damanaka plant upon the summit of Mount Meru.
One should place jars of scented water upon the peaks of the eight boundary mountains;
outside of that, having opened the gates in the directions within the sixteen squares, [one should proceed].
One should place the substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the remaining positions;
and having constructed a Pauṇḍarīka fire-pit before it according to the prescribed rule, || 74 ||
Having performed the libation according to the rules, one should then lay the Lord of Gods to rest;
having worshipped the presiding deities of the materials, one should worship Kāma, who dwells in the spring.
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the mantras of the Śrīsūkta and Bhūsūkta, as well as those dedicated to the various deities and so forth— || 76 ||

Having likewise offered oblations to Jayā and the other deities of the assembly, as well as to the forms and mantras, and having passed the night, one should bathe at dawn according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed the deity with water-pots and also with jars of scented water,
and having adorned him with garments and other ornaments during an auspicious moment, || 78 ||
Having accepted those offered garlands, being composed and endowed with devotion, he should offer them to the Lord while reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta. || 79 ||
For all the images as well as for the assemblies,
one should offer a garland of *damanaka* flowers with their respective mantras and forms.
Adorned with all ornaments, he should perform a circumambulation of the village;
then, having led the deity back to the temple, he should install him in the assembly pavilion.
Having bathed [the deity] with scented water and worshipped [him], one should present the offerings;
at the conclusion of the internal oblation (antahoma), let the fire be brought to the permanent sacrificial pit (nityakuṇḍa). || 82 ||
In this month, the spring festival and the offering of flowers to the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) is highly recommended;
beginning from that day until the end of Mūla in the month of Jyeṣṭha. || 83 ||
One should celebrate the spring festival with substances produced at each respective time;
having installed the deity in the assembly pavilion at the conclusion of the midday worship. (84)
Having bathed it with scented water and clothed it in a light, measured garment,
he should worship it with flowers appropriate for that season.
Having offered milk-rice and other foods, and having performed a circumambulation of the temple,
he also offered ripe fruits such as plantains, mangoes, and jackfruit.
Having offered edible foods such as cakes and the like, as well as coconut water, and having given the water for sipping (ācamana), one should offer mouth-fresheners (mukhavāsa). || 87 ||

The wise one should install the Lord of Gods upon the pedestal of the image according to the mantra; from the month of Jyeṣṭha until the end of the rainy season, he should perform this rite constantly in this manner. || 88 ||
Regarding the Vaiśākha festival: on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having performed the ritual ablutions and other rites as before,
one should install the deity in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa) according to the previous procedure.
Having worshipped with the twenty-seven forms beginning with the seat,
one should offer milk-rice and other foods, presenting them in great abundance.
One should offer abundant clarified butter prepared with marīca, jīraka, and guñjā, along with coconut juice, and a great quantity of mango pulp.
At the conclusion of the water-offering and the sipping of water, one should present mouth-perfume;
having performed the festival of the God of gods all around the temple precincts.
Having established [the image] in the Jīvasthāna, one should perform the daily worship;
in this regard, the offering of water is declared to be highly recommended. (93)
Regarding the Jyeṣṭha festival:
it is traditionally taught that in the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the Mūla asterism, one should offer garments to Hari;
and on the full moon day of that same month, having bathed Him with fragrant waters.
Having adorned [the deity] with new garments and having worshipped him thoroughly, one should present [the offerings].
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the one-day festival known as the Āṣāḍha-utsava. || 95 ||
Having bathed and worshipped him thoroughly, one should also offer oblations;
indeed, the offering of the *arghya* water to the God in the month of Āṣāḍha is highly recommended.

The Śrāvaṇa festival should be observed in the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism of Śravaṇa; the wise man should diligently perform the festive bathing and other rites for the God of gods as previously described. || 97 ||
In that month of Śrāvaṇa, specifically during its dark fortnight, the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism—or even when it is not so conjoined—is called Jayantī. || 98 ||
There, at the rising of the moon, one should worship Viṣṇu in the form of Kṛṣṇa,
or else the four-armed Viṣṇu, having likewise bathed him with waters.
Having offered abundant milk and having properly presented the oblation,
and likewise having tied the protective amulet (pratisara), one should cause Puruṣottama to be worshipped.
Having fasted for a day and night and bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform the festival of the Lord in the manner described for festivals.
Having bathed Viṣṇu with water-pitchers, the wise man should establish him in his place;
having worshipped him thoroughly, he should offer oblations of milk-rice or sweetmeats.
One should offer it at the end of the mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) and place it in the seat of the vital breath (jīvasthāna);
thereafter, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa), and he shall indeed attain union (sāyujya). || 103 ||
He obtains all desires and gains the fruit of all gifts;
thus, he who performs the worship of Viṣṇu with devotion on that day [attains these]. 104.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed at that very moment;
therefore, one should observe the festival on Jayantī with every possible effort. (105)
The offering of incense to the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow is highly praised in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
he who constantly performs the offering of incense with supreme devotion [attains great merit]. 106.
He too, for one year, attains the fruit of [giving] incense; there is no doubt.
Likewise, the Bhādrapada festival occurs when the Śravaṇa constellation is in conjunction with the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the month of Bhādrapada.
For the sake of pacifying the faults arising from the year-long worship of Keśava,
for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, and as a cause of all auspiciousness— 108.
That which was proclaimed of old by Brahmā as the pacifier of all defects—one should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa for the sake of the pacification of all defects. 109.
A wise person should perform the hearing [of this] according to the method described for festivals;
in this month, however, the offering of oblations to Keśava is highly recommended.
In this month, one should indeed begin the excellent Śrāvaṇa vow;
beginning from Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the Ekādaśī vow.
Having eaten only once on the previous day and having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rules,
one should perform an even number of circumambulations after bowing down to the God of gods.
With a one-pointed mind, one should recite the names beginning with Keśava,
starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and proceeding again in sequence through the months.
Alternatively, having fasted and observed the vow, one should perform the Pauruṣa-sūkta;
then, having bathed the Lord of Gods in the morning, worshipped him, and offered oblations. || 114 ||
Having given gifts to the best of the twice-born, one should then perform the breaking of the fast;
thereafter, throughout all the months, [one should observe care] regarding hunger, stumbling, and so forth.
One should perform the recitation while mentally remembering the Lord of Gods by means of the name of that month;
likewise, the bathing, worship, and other rites should be performed using the names beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with the five forms (pañcamūrti).
One should likewise perform it for the Brahmins using the name of that very month;
and thus, when the year is complete, one should do so in the month of Bhādrapada as well. || 117 ||

One should bathe the deity with one hundred and eight jars during the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra], or offer a great abundance of sacrificial oblations (mahāhavis) combined with milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such foods. || 118 ||
Having offered [the oblations] and provided mouth-fresheners, one should offer many handfuls of flowers;
then, having given food to the Brahmins, one should perform the breaking of the fast as before.
Having observed the Ekādaśī vow for a full year,
one should likewise perform the ceremonial bathing and other rites on the Dvādaśī of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Thus, whoever performs this with devotion is liberated from great sins; in the end, having ascended a celestial chariot, he shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
This month of Mārgaśīrṣa is declared the best among months;
on it, there is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) under the asterism Śravaṇa, as well as the new moon (amāvāsyā).
One should observe the vow of fasting on that day and perform no other rite;
the worship of Aśvayuj and the Śravaṇa constellation in the month of Āśvayuja is the best for removing all sins.
The day of the manifestation of the Fish, Tortoise, and Boar incarnations is also remembered;
on that day as well, one should perform festivals, ceremonial ablutions, and other rites for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should constantly offer mouth-perfume to Hari during this month,
and indeed perform even greater worship in all months on the lunar mansions corresponding to each month.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Rule for Worship in All Months, the Procedure for the Āgrayaṇa and Viṣpāka Offerings, and the Worship of the Auspicious Constellations," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Sahitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable scripture of the Śrī Vaikhānasa tradition.
Oṃ.
The nineteenth chapter begins.
Hereafter, I shall describe the special worship, the special propitiation of Hari;
