this worship is divided into three types: for peace (śāntika), for nourishment (pauṣṭika), and for the fulfillment of desires (kāmya). || 1 ||
For the pacification of disease, famine, bad dreams, and ill omens;
for the cessation of the affliction of enemies, and likewise for the pacification of drought. || 2 ||
That which is proclaimed as *śāntika* is for the purpose of pacifying all other defects;
that which is performed for the sake of increasing wealth, grain, and so forth is called *pauṣṭika*. (3)
Whatever object is desired is declared to be a "kāmya" (desire-based) rite;
one should perform a *śāntika* (pacifying) rite in the forenoon, and likewise a *pauṣṭika* (nourishing) rite at midday.
The rite for specific desires should be performed in the afternoon; however, one should not perform anything at night.
Having caused the sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) to be done according to the previously mentioned method, [one should proceed].
After the offering of the seed-sprouts, one should also collect the ritual materials,
and construct a pavilion, a water-shed, or a temporary shed as appropriate.
One should have it constructed in that place as prescribed for the bathing hall;
then, during the first part of the night, one should worship the Lord of Gods according to the ritual injunctions.
Having tied the protective cord (pratisara) and likewise caused it to be shadowed,
one should thereafter arrange a row of pits all around, as prescribed for the ritual bathing.
Having placed the materials such as clay and so forth there as before,
one should fashion a lotus made of *pauṇḍarīka* grass either in front of the deity or to its right.

Having established the deity in the pit and bathed him as before, one should then place either a churned fire or a common worldly fire into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as previously described. || 10 ||
At the conclusion of the Āghāra oblations, one should indeed offer well-poured oblations with the two root mantras,
using clarified butter, fuel-sticks of Aśvattha wood, Dūrvā grass, and Caru, each separately.
O best of sages, ten thousand repetitions for each [mantra] are declared to be the highest;
one thousand and eight is proclaimed as the middling.
Thus, it is declared to be of three kinds, ranging from one hundred and eight down to fewer;
with a crown blazing and ornaments resplendent.
The Lord wears dark blue garments and resembles molten gold;
his face, hands, feet, and eyes are red; he is the essence of the syllable Om and is imperishable.
Having thus meditated in the mind upon the Lord who wields the conch and the discus, the all-pervading one who is higher than the highest, one should perform the rite of oblation.
One should offer oblations once with clarified butter from the Vaiṣṇava, Viṣṇusūkta, Pauruṣasūkta, Brāhma, Raudra, and Jayādī hymns. || 16 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Śrīsūkta for the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika),
and having taken up a new pitcher filled with thirty-two prasthas [of grain], || 17 ||
Having wrapped [the vessel] with thread and filled it with water to the level of a barley grain,
one should place a golden image of Viṣṇu and separate images of Śrī and Bhūmi.
Having renounced [the world], one should perform the rite with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, offering eight niṣkas for each;
those auspicious weapons should be two aṅgulas in measure.
The wise one should deposit [the image] as before, especially with jewels;
then, with two pieces of linen, or two pieces of silk, or two fine garments.
Having wound a garland of flowers around the neck of the jar,
one should place a tuft of *aśvattha* shoots and also sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.
Having encircled [the mantra] with the *praṇava*, one should mutter the two root-mantras one thousand and eight times while mentally recollecting the Lord of Gods. || 22 ||
Having uttered "Namo vāce" and having recited "Śanno vāta," one should consecrate [the water] ten times; one should always perform it in this manner. (23)
One should install the deity upon a lotus-mandala in the assembly pavilion;
having worshipped him thoroughly, one should offer oblations of milk-rice here.
Having offered water for drinking and rinsing the mouth, and thereafter betel-leaf,
one should recite the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
Reciting the Nārāyaṇānuvāka, the Ekākṣara-sūkta and others,
as well as the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and the mantra beginning with "namo brahmaṇe" (26).

Having offered many handfuls of flowers with the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras, having prostrated with the body like a staff, and having requested forgiveness by saying "Forgive me," [he should depart]. || 27 ||
Having installed [the deity] in the image, one should perform the daily worship;
thus for a month, three weeks, a fortnight, or thirteen [days]. || 28 ||
Or likewise for eleven days, or nine days, or seven days, or five days, or three days, according to the prescribed rule. (29)

The bathing, worship, fire-oblation (homa), and likewise the touching of the jar (kumbha) constitute the highest [rite]; it is middling when performed with the jar alone, excluding the oblation and the touching.
The preceptor should thus perform this daily, completing the festival at the end of the day,
while the patron stands in the presence of the God of gods.
One should bathe [the deity] with water from a ritual jar, or sprinkle it a thousand times;
one should perform this according to the prescribed rule every month on the day of one's own birth star.
He who thus causes [this] to be made with devotion for the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, shall obtain long life, health, sovereignty, and unshakable prosperity. (33)
His diseases perish, as do afflictions from planetary influences and other calamities; ill omens, bad dreams, fear of thieves, enemies, and so forth [are likewise destroyed]. (34)
Likewise, other calamities will undoubtedly perish;
and when this is performed, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are surely accomplished.
In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) as well as in those for desired results (kāmya), there is no touching of the water-pot (kumbha).
If one is unable to do it in this manner, [one may touch it] on an odd-numbered day.
Some say that one should perform the consecration with pure water, worship, the formal entrustment, and the fire-oblation in the perpetual sacrificial pit (nityāgnikuṇḍa). || 37 ||
When the daily fire-oblation (nityāgnihotra) has been interrupted, one should perform the Pauṇḍarīka, the Śāntika, the Kāmya, and the Pauṣṭika rites in the common (laukika) fire. || 38 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Special Worship," in the section on Ritual Practice (*kriyādhikāra*) within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra* as proclaimed by Bhṛgu and compiled with the Ṛgveda.
Oṃ.
The twentieth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the examination of the ground and other such matters—the atonement for the examination of the ground and so forth.
"Prāya" refers to the arising of a fault, and "citti" is its removal. (1)
The mending of that fault is declared to be the expiation (prāyaścitta);
it should be performed starting from that very day, or on the ninth or the seventh day thereafter.
Or one should perform it on the fifth day, having first performed the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa); for if the rite of sowing the germinating seeds is omitted,
[the merit of] the rites such as the examination of the ground (bhūparīkṣā) and so forth is lost.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantras for the six beginning with Brahmā, and with the forms of the lords of the Pālikās, such as Jaya and the others; || 4 ||
Having performed the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should thereafter carry out each respective rite;
in the absence of small pots (pālikās), however, one may employ shallow bowls (śarāvas).
Some say that one should take either those [darbha grasses] which have been burnt or those already used;
however, if there has been no special worship, one should perform the worship twice over.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings, one should properly present the oblation;
O best of the twice-born, this is declared to be the "special worship" (viśeṣārcana) in all cases.
One should perform the worship with special care during the consecration of the image and the sowing of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa),
as well as during the sowing of seeds for festivals and other rites concerning the limbs and images in other temples.

One should perform that which is specifically prescribed as worship only upon the image (bera). One should worship with the forms of the Lord of the Lineage (Paṅkīśa) in a row that is devoid of [other] measurements.
If one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring seven cubits, it should be made into a square (pada);
if it measures five cubits, one should lead it into the form of a throne and its pedestal (upapīṭhapada).
If one should construct a row measuring three cubits, it likewise consists of nine squares;
in the middle of the seven-by-seven squares, one square is declared to be the Brahma-square.
Having arranged the eight [deities] beginning with Jaya around that, and outside of that in the sixteenth square,
one should then arrange [the others] in the twenty-fourth square outside of that.
There are four doors in the cardinal directions, and the remaining eight [deities] beginning with Śeṣa occupy the [surrounding] positions.
On both sides of the doors are indeed the Śeṣas for the purpose of installing the *pālikās*.
Śeṣa and Vakratuṇḍa are to be worshipped on both sides of the eastern door, on the left and right respectively; however, Cakrī and Īśa are to be worshipped on the south.
Paṅktīśa and Śaṅkha are in the western direction, while Soma and Śānta are in the northern direction;
one should arrange them in this very same manner for each of the seven sets of seven steps.
In the center of each group of five squares, one square is said to belong to Brahmā;
surrounding it are eight squares for Jayā and the others, and outside of that is the sixteenfold portion.
One should worship the four doors in the cardinal directions;
in them, one should worship Śeṣa, Vidhneśa, Paṅktīśa, and Soma, along with their respective attendants at the sides.
One should worship Viṣvaksena between Īśāna and Soma;
one should then prepare the remaining spaces for the placement of the Pālikās and other vessels. || 18 ||
In the center, within the nine squares, one [square] is proclaimed for Brahmā;
likewise, [one each] for Śeṣa and the others, for Jayā and the others, and for the pitchers. || 19 ||
And outside of that, on the eight squares, there are eight *pālikās* (small pots);
beginning with the planting of sprouts, this occurs on either the third or the fifth day.
One should perform that respective rite on the seventh or the ninth day;
thereafter, it should be performed according to the rules only on odd-numbered days.

Having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) and immediately performed the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), and having fed the Brahmins, one should then carry out each respective rite. || 22 ||
One should cause the immediate planting of sprouts for the consecrated ritual substances;
however, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) must first be performed during the preceding night.
After performing the untying of the eyes and having consecrated [the image] in water and other substances, one should perform all the rites, such as the Vāstuhoma, as previously described. || 24 ||
If [the materials] are not obtained even within two days, the performer, filled with haste,
should immediately perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and then at once the opening of the eyes (nayanonmīlana) and so forth.
Some say that having performed [the rite], one should establish it on that very day;
however, if that plowing is performed without first conducting an examination of the ground, [it is defective]. 26.

"Having offered oblations with the Bhūsūkta, which has the Earth as its deity, and having examined the ground, one should perform the plowing once again; such is the instruction of the ancient seers. (27)
At an improper time, during the examination of the ground, the wise man should likewise perform oblations;
however, he should examine the earth at an auspicious time according to the method previously described. || 28 ||
But at the time of examining the ground, if ill omens arise,
one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
Having offered oblations, one should worship with the Viṣṇugāyatrī and the Sāvitrī a hundred and eight times;
likewise, one should recite the Śākuna and the Svastisūkta ten times.
If the food of the maiden is deficient, one should offer oblations into the Daurga fire and then provide her with a meal;
likewise in the event of the interruption or the falling out of the lamp of the maiden, or of the lotus.
Having performed the oblation dedicated to the deities of the Śrīsūkta, one should thereafter perform the concluding rites;
in the absence of a lotus, one should take a fresh white water-lily (kumuda).
One should undertake all ritual actions after having worshipped Vināyaka;
if the worship of Vināyaka is deficient, one should perform a hundred oblations with his mantra.
When plowing has been performed at the proper time, or likewise when it is performed without ritual action,
and in all cases of transgression, the deity of the earth remains attached to the ground.
Having performed the oblation, one should perform each respective rite while reciting the corresponding mantra;
this applies in the event that the prescribed trees for the plow and other implements cannot be obtained, according to their sequence. || 35 ||
Having worshipped the presiding deity of that tree, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
there, one should worship the deity of Viṣṇu and the deity of the earth according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, for ploughs and other tools that fall short of the stated measurements, one must perform the Prājāpatya, Yāmya, Raudra, and Bhautika penances. || 37 ||
At the beginning and at the end, one should offer oblations ending with the *vyāhṛtis* and dedicated to Viṣṇu;
likewise in the event of breaking or cutting them, or even when their ropes are severed.
When the bull and the limb are missing, one should worship Vaiṣṇava in the lotus and fire;
likewise, one should worship Brāhma, Vīśadaivatyam, Prājāpatya, and Bhautika. || 39 ||
And one should also sacrifice with the Ṛṣi-mantras, accompanied by their respective deities,
using the clarified butter of Kapila and reciting the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should give silver according to one's means;
and at that time, if there is a wound [on the body], one should recite the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas.
Having offered the mindāhuti oblations without interruption, let a gift of gold exceeding one niṣka be given to the preceptor in the presence of the deity. 42.
When the bull is asleep, deluded, wandering, stuck in a difficult place, fallen,
or crying out, one should perform a thousand recitations of the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī over the lotus and fire.
Having performed the oblation, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) when hair, teeth, nails, and so forth,
as well as skulls, ashes, stones, husks, and thorns are present.
Having discarded all of those [impurities], one should likewise sprinkle [the site] with ritual sprinklings;
having consecrated it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should again perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.
But when the plowing has been neglected, or the sowing of seeds has been neglected, or if one is unable to perform it immediately due to fear of wasting time; || 46 ||

Having offered oblations into the lotus-fire with the Rātrisūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Vaiṣṇava hymns, as well as the Godānasūkta, he should offer the seed-syllable after performing the interrupted rite. || 47 ||
After plowing the earth, he should scatter straw and grass everywhere upon the ground and offer it to the herds of cattle.
When those seeds have been sown, have perished, or fail to sprout due to sterility,
one should perform the previously mentioned expiation and indeed spread grass upon that spot.
Having made an offering to the hosts of gods, one should subsequently perform the concluding rites;
for in the acts of plowing and sowing seeds, even a single part of the ritual may be omitted.
And for all those actions, this expiation is prescribed:
one who has accepted [an offering] for the sake of another deity should never accept it again.
If one builds out of ignorance, he will perish without a doubt;
one should not construct a temple of Viṣṇu near places where the flow of water is contrary.
One should not construct a sacrificial enclosure (raṇa) within a distance of one krośa from the settlement of Caṇḍālas;
likewise, it should be avoided from the dwellings of Pulkasas and from the quarters of carpenters and artisans.
One should not perform [the rite] even in a garment that follows the natural grain;
however, if one should perform it in garments that follow the natural grain, it must be done by a Tantrika.
If the worship of Śāntārcana is deficient, one should offer a thousand oblations to its presiding deity;
likewise, if the worship of Vīśacakrā is deficient, one should sacrifice to its presiding deity in the same manner.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with caru mixed with sesame and mustard seeds;
however, it is said that in a temple devoid of a young deity (taruṇālaya), everything becomes fruitless. || 56 ||
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, one should offer oblations with white lotuses smeared with ghee,
reciting in sequence the Rātrisūkta and the Pāramātmika hymn.
Recalling the Lord, beginning with the syllable "Iṅ," one should devoutly offer the bull;
while performing worship in the inner sanctum of the child-form, one should subsequently carry out the ritual action.
Regarding the consideration of the image for the young abode (taruṇālaya):
In the absence of metal images, one should procure whatever image is available;
or, if that is unavailable, one may procure one that is not of the proper proportions or one that has been requested [as a gift]. || 59 ||

A wise man should request worldly items from the house of a Vedic scholar or from another dwelling; however, he should not request the three items beginning with the auspicious thread (kautuka) from the temple precincts.
If a suitable [image] has been requested from the house of a Vedic scholar for Dhruva,
one should install that very object there with auspicious rites and worship it.
If it has been worshipped in another temple, then at the conclusion of that rite,
having brought it back again in due order to its original temple, one should perform the fire-oblation for peace (śānti-homa) and worship it.
If that which has been installed is not appropriate, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra and,
having offered oblations a thousand times, install an auspicious substitute for the *kautuka*.
If the Vāstu-savana and Puṇyāha rites are omitted, or if the Vāstu-homa is not performed, one should offer oblations with the five great mantras (Pañca-brahma), the Vaiṣṇava mantras,
and the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and then perform the rite again.
If the recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) is deficient, one should feed Brahmins according to one's ability.
At the site of the Brahma-lotus pit (brahmapadmāvaṭa), upon seeing a skull, bone, or similar remains therein— || 65 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations elsewhere— consisting of Vaiṣṇava, Bhūmidaivatyā, and Brāhma mantras— one should then again perform the Brahma-padmāvaṭa rite.
If that jar is broken, leaks, or causes fear among the people, one should again perform sacrifices to Viṣṇu, the Earth-deity, and Prajāpati. || 67 ||
In the event of a quarrel or the shedding of blood, one should, with a concentrated mind, worship Vaiśvaksena, Gāruḍa, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and Aindra in due order.
Having offered the Rātrisūkta together with the Prājāpatya oblation,
one should likewise offer the Vāruṇa, Vāyavya, and Bhūmidaivata oblations in a counter-clockwise direction.
If the water is turbid, one should offer oblations to Brahmā and Varuṇa;
likewise when it is agitated, moving, or covered with dust.
For its pacification, one should offer oblations to Varuṇa and Viṣvaksena;
this applies even when that lotus is positioned upside down, or when it has fallen to the side.
In the event of trembling, curling of the leaves, wilting, or splitting,
one should worship the Brāhma, Devahoma, Vāruṇa, and Bhārgava [deities].
Likewise, when the lotus is turned sideways, or when the Brahma and Āruṣa [lotuses] are misplaced,
or when the peg is set up, or when the peg is not set up at all, one should perform the *pariṣad-homa* sacrifice.
Or, without delay, one should determine the directions using pure eastern orientation;

having begun from the primary path, if one should cause the secondary one to be made, then, after giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), worshipping the deity according to one's capacity, and making the offering (nivedya). || 75 ||
One should begin as before and perform it exactly as previously done;
however, if the temple is constructed after having already laid the first brick, [the rite must be repeated]. 76.
A great calamity has befallen the village, the sacrificer, and the kingdom;
therefore, one should perform a great propitiatory rite (*mahāśānti*) for its removal. || 77 ||
Having laid down the first brick, one should then cause the temple to be constructed;
however, if there is a deficiency in the ritual of laying the first brick or in the recitation of the mantras, [the rite must be repeated].
On the tip of a brick or the edge of a stone, and likewise in cases of inversion,
as well as when the placement of jewels is omitted, one must always first perform the worship of all the deities.
One should offer oblations in sequence for the Vaṃṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the two Mindāhuti offerings, and the Mahīsūkta, whenever they have been interrupted.

"One should cause [the work] to be done according to the previously mentioned procedure; this is the instruction regarding the temple, that wooden platform, and all its ornaments in every respect. (81)
In the case of inferior seats and celestial palaces (vimānas), there is a reversal in each section;
however, in the case of palaces for peace and other rites, there is a mutual intermingling on the floor.
If the inner wall of the door is either deficient or excessive,
one should perform the sacrifice one hundred times in sequence for each of the four [measures], beginning with *nyakṣa*.
In the center, however, one should perform the lotus-oblation in the Pauṇḍarīka fire;
one should also offer the Rātrisūkta and the Puruṣasūkta. || 84 ||
The wise practitioner should perform the rite up to a thousand oblations as prescribed; in rites for pacification and the like, he should not allow any mutual confusion of the numerical sequences.
One should employ the measurement known as the *adṛbhuta* for all regions;
it is to be counted starting from the wall, excluding the bricks, and includes the presiding deity of the enclosure.
One should offer oblations ten times with the Vaiṣṇava mantra;
and in the case of a deficiency of bricks for the gate-towers and other parts, one should worship the presiding deities of the door-keepers.

One should recite the six mantras beginning with Dhātṛ ten times, along with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, during the placement of the first bricks, even if the pavilion and other structures have been deficiently constructed. || 88 ||
One should perform a hundred Vaiṣṇava sacrifices to the presiding deity of that pavilion;
if the kitchen is deficient, one should worship the deity who protects the sacrificial oblation.
One should worship that hymn dedicated to Śrī, as well as those dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu.
I shall now describe the sequence for the primary bricks in the construction of the Bhūtapīṭha, regarding the arrangement of the Bhūtapīṭha. || 90 ||

Then, having taken either a brick or a stone according to the previously mentioned number, one should perform the rites of consecration (adhivāsa) and so forth, following the path described before. || 91 ||

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the two mantras whose deities are likewise [beings] and which are joined with the Vaiṣṇava [mantra], and thereafter for the sake of the spirits (bhūtas); || 92 ||
He should offer oblations to the Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Nāgas,
and with mantras beginning with those of the four Vedas, he should establish the four bricks.
O ascetics, if even there a deficiency of bricks occurs at the beginning,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the Bhūta-mantras combined with the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
Having bathed the pedestal with water using mantras appropriate for the rite of acceptance (adhivāsa),
and having bathed it with seven jars, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before.
One should likewise recite the mantras beginning with the four Vedas in the four directions;
this is the general expiation for all ritual acts, while the aforementioned expiation applies in the event of a lapse.

Having performed the oblations, at the conclusion of those prescribed homas, one should recite the respective mantras in sequence for the abodes of the retinue and for Hari, according to the measurements prescribed.
One should perform everything, beginning with the first brick, preceded by its respective mantra;

[this applies even] when the rite of depositing the embryo (garbhanyāsa) is omitted, when the ritual for depositing the embryo is missing, when the time has elapsed, or in the event of an error. || 98 ||
One should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the hymn addressed to the Earth, and likewise the hymn addressed to Śrī; one should also offer the Viṣṇusūkta and the Puruṣasūkta.
One should worship Mindāhuti and Vicchinna, and then the Mahīsūkta in sequence;
as before, one should deposit the embryo (garbha) for each respective assembly (pariṣad). || 100 ||
If the head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) has been omitted during its placement, or if the prescribed time has passed, or if there is a reversal,
one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) and offer oblations as prescribed for the first brick.

Then, having performed the ancillary oblation (aṅgahoma), one should proceed according to the previously stated rule; however, if [the linga] is devoid of the stūpikā, the śūla, and so forth, one should recite the Dhruva-sūkta. || 102 ||
One should deposit a single brick there and place jewels within it;
having established four bricks in the cardinal directions as before, one should proceed.
Having established the stūpa in the center, one should cause it to be made firm with plaster;
and likewise for the temples of the retinue and the gate-towers (gopuras). || 104 ||
If there is a deficiency in the plastering and so forth, or if the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) is deficient, or if there is an inversion in the application of colors,
one should likewise offer a thousand oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Furthermore, one should perform the rite of purification with lime-wash and likewise apply colored coatings to a temple that has been afflicted by defects such as fire, meteors, lightning, or smoke.
For the sake of pacifying that [interruption], one should likewise offer the Īṅkāra and Īṃ offerings,
as well as the two Mindā oblations, the Vicchinna offering, and the Pāramātmika offering.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give the teacher's sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If the image is touched by fire,
or if the fire touches the image, one should perform the Mahāśānti rite for three days in a fire consecrated with water.
Having performed the fire-oblation and bathed [the deity] with one hundred and eight jars,
he should thereafter perform the consecration once more according to the very sequence prescribed for installation.

When the enclosures have been burnt by fire and the walls have been burnt by fire, having bathed and duly honored the groups of the assembly residing there, one should [teach] their mantra along with the Sāmavedic verses (Vairūpa).
Having offered oblations with mantras beginning with the four Vedas, one should feed the Brahmins;
having especially worshipped the God, one should properly present the sacrificial offering.
But at the time of taking a wife, it should be the reverse for the ascetic;
the preceptor, having performed his own ritual bath, should then prepare the fire within the lotus there.
One should offer oblations with the Rātrisūkta, the Śrīsūkta, and likewise the Vaiṣṇava;
one should also take up the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta as before for the purification.
If the temple is completed while the installation of the *śūla* (the ritual spike) has been omitted,
it shall become an abode for *piśācas*; therefore, one should perform the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice once again.
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, however, one should offer the Mahāśānti oblation in its center; having given gold, cattle, land, and other gifts, one should commence the ritual. || 115 ||
In one month it shall be thus; in two months it shall be double.
The wise man should increase it in this manner until the end of the year.
When even a year has passed, he should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) and offer oblations;
having given gold, cattle, land, and other gifts, he should feed the Brahmins.
Having thus offered oblations of bricks and other materials while recollecting their respective mantras,
and having performed the recitation of those specific mantras, he should then re-establish the trident.
For one month after twelve years have passed, he should perform the Mahāśānti sacrifice;
he should carry out all activities, such as plowing and so forth, as previously described. || 119 ||
If a fixed image (dhruvabera) is omitted and the ritual pillar (śūla) is installed instead,
one should offer oblations in the Pauṇḍarīka fire while recollecting the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Once it has indeed become interrupted, let an oblation of atonement (mindāhuti) be offered;
having offered seven fuel-sticks and paid homage to the Lord of Gods, [one should proceed].
Having given land to the preceptor, one should perform each respective rite;
thus it is declared for the first month, but in the second month, it shall be twofold.
In this very manner, he should increase [the offerings] until the end of the year;
but when the year has passed, he should perform the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
One should establish the Āhavanīya and other fires in the four directions in their proper order;
then, at the conclusion of the two libations (āghāra), the thousandfold Vaiṣṇava oblation is to be offered.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Viṣṇu-sūkta during each respective homa;
having likewise offered to the deities of the directions, one should then give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having provided food for the Brahmins and given sacrificial fees according to one's capacity,
one should double the amount on the second day, increasing it in this manner up to the twelfth day.
When twelve years have passed, one should cause the plowing and other rites to be performed;
however, in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, there is the Kūṣmāṇḍa rite accompanied by the five Vāruṇa offerings.
Thereafter, having offered the supreme *iṅkāra-anaṅga-homa*,
as well as the *puruṣasūkta* and the *viṣṇusūkta*, one should feed the Brahmins.
One should give five niṣkas of gold as the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā);
then, having performed the Vāstuhoma, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.

One should abandon a door when its panels, lintels, and pillars are displaced from their upper joints, when they have increased in size, when they are deficient in measurement, when they are decayed, or when they are burnt. || 130 ||
Having taken another [portion] conjoined with the sacred formulas (pramāṇa), one should join it again;
having sprinkled it with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should indeed offer a hundred oblations to Viṣṇu.
Having invoked the six deities beginning with Dhātṛ upon the lintel, the door-leaf, and both the door-posts, one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Wood, stone, and bricks that have been used for another dwelling, those appropriated for another purpose, or those surrounded by fire, must be abandoned.
The vimāna is ninefold on the path;
one should have a fixed image (dhruvabera) made according to that path or with a greater [proportion]. || 134 ||
Therefore, one must not perform the three [rites] beginning with the *kautuka* in a diminished manner;
likewise, when there is a reversal of the temple or a reversal of the image. || 235 ||
In the event of the displacement of the trident or the wooden [frame], or when there is a reversal in the ritual procedures and so forth,
one should recite the Brāhma, Viṣṇu, Gāruḍa, and Saumya hymns.
One should offer a thousand oblations for Prajāpati and for Rudra in sequence;
one should perform that according to the prescribed rule by the very same path mentioned previously. || 137 ||
The excellence of the celestial chariots and so forth,
the abode, the gate-tower, as well as the image and the pedestal—
these four are traditionally held to be the very body of the God. (138)
Consideration regarding the restoration of what is decayed: whether in the temple, the pavilion, or likewise in the residence of the retinue;
in the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, the pedestal, or even in the kitchen. (139)

However, if the laying of bricks, the application of colored coatings, or the commencement of new construction and similar works is performed within one or two months [of the previous], then [the same procedure applies]. || 140 ||
Having indeed removed those defects along with their characteristics for all [the images], one should perform the new rite according to the path of beauty. 141.
When the day has concluded, even on the previous day, one should likewise perform the Vāstuhoma to the north of the temple,
followed by the paryagnikaraṇa rite.

Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, the wise one should bathe it according to the very procedure prescribed for the ritual bathing. || 143 ||

To the south of the Ālaya, having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules for the domestic fire (aupāsana) and endowed with the proper characteristics, one should kindle the fire while reciting the mantras. || 144 ||
Having offered oblations to its presiding deity accompanied by the *pariṣat-mantra*,
he should then perform the *aṅga-homa* (limb-oblation) joined with the *pāramātmika-mantra*.
Then, having offered the oblations beginning with the syllable *Iṅ*, one should perform eighty-eight offerings;
therein, one should offer the Vaiṣṇava oblation accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should offer a thousand oblations for all [the deities] indeed;
having installed those various deities according to the sequence prescribed for installation. || 147 ||
Then, having performed the concluding oblation (antahoma) and having bowed down to the Lord of Gods,
one should offer a great or abundant sacrificial fee (mahādakṣiṇā) to the Lord of Gods.
Having understood the front, sides, back, top, and bottom of stone or wood, one should fashion it; for if it is made with these parts inverted, it becomes the form of a deity.
If it is established [with such intent], it is called *abhicārika* (malevolent magic);
there would be the destruction of the kingdom and the nation, as well as affliction for the subjects, fear, and death. || 140 ||
For the sake of pacifying those defects, one should quickly perform a propitiatory rite (śānti);
one should construct a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, complete with its characteristic features, to the north of the temple.

One should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Vaiṣṇava hymn beginning with "ato devā," and the oblation for the limbs beginning with the syllable "Iṃ," together with the five Vāruṇa mantras. || 152 ||

Having performed the rites as before according to the prescribed rule, including those connected with the Jaya and Abhyātāna offerings and joined with the Pariṣat mantras, the wise one should establish it. || 153 ||
Even in the case of a deficiency of limbs, there is nothing lacking nor anything redundant among the arms, forearms, hands, thighs, shanks, soles of the feet, sides, lower body, and the trunk. (154)
If it is deficient in any of the primary or secondary limbs, or even by a single finger-breadth,
it should be repaired as before with gold, or with copper colored with gold.
If the trident should break by being placed in reverse order,
one should perform the previously mentioned fire-oblation (homa) on the northern side of the temple.
Having offered oblations and recited the Puruṣasūkta, one should give the teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having taken up the trident according to the prescribed rule, one should install it in sequence as before. || 157 ||
If the image is defiled by dogs, crows, cattle, monkeys,
mice, or cocks, one should discard it and procure another according to the prescribed rite.
One should offer oblations to the deities of the earth combined with the Supreme Self;
one should perform the purificatory rites for the *iṅkāra* and other mantras, the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns, and the clay once again.
In the case of clay, unguents, powders, decoctions, and medicinal drugs, when they are deficient, lack proper preparation, or are applied incorrectly; || 160 ||

In the case of binding with cords, the eightfold binding, as well as the plastering with gravel, when these are deficient, lack the proper consecration, or involve a reversal of the ritual application; || 161 ||
The Vaiṣṇava, the Cāruṣa, and the Pāñcabhautika, as well as the Brāhma, the Aindra, and [oblations] offered to the thirty-three deities, are sacrificed. || 162 ||
One should perform each respective rite according to the previously stated procedure;
however, in the event of a confusion of castes, one should offer oblations and perform the Prājāpatya and Puruṣa rites.
One should not perform the half-image rite for a clay image, nor should one make a half-image from clay or metal;
rather, having carefully set aside the installed image, one should take up another [image]. || 164 ||

Having offered the *Brahmasūkta* and the *Vaiṣṇava* hymns beginning with "śrāvita" into the lotus-fire, and having performed the *mindāhuti* oblations, one should thereafter feed the Brahmins. || 165 ||
"One should install [the image] according to the previously mentioned procedure; this is the instruction.
Whether the image be made of stone or gemstone, or whether it be carved from stone or gemstone, or even half-carved, it does not cause any fault. (166)
One should have the permanent image (dhruvabera) made of stone endowed with color; however, if it is the worship of the permanent image, one need not have it made endowed with color.
The installation that is worthy of worship in the abode of Brahmā is the permanent worship (dhruvārcana);
one should especially perform this installation for both divine and human [images]. || 168 ||
This worship of a single Linga, when endowed with the prescribed colors, does not cause any fault.
Regarding the matter of deficiency or excess, what indeed is the reason for this that the learned know by way of measurement? || 169 ||
Whether it be a barleycorn, three barleycorns, or even half a finger-breadth;
or whether it be deficient or excessive by one, or two feet, it does not constitute a fault.
The garment, ornaments, lotus, crown, conch, and discus of the Bimba;
the sacred thread, the long necklace, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the pair of earrings. || 171 ||
One should especially fashion the image endowed with these and other such qualities;
if it should be deficient in these, it must once again be provided with them.

Having caused [the image] to be fashioned, one should indeed perform oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn joined with the Brāhma, as well as the Aindra, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Saura, the Saumya, and the Pauruṣa hymns. || 173 ||
Having fed the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite, the wise man should install [the image];
however, if through negligence he should join a statue made of artificial colors, [he must perform atonement]. || 174 ||
Having washed, wiped clean, and dried it according to the prescribed rule,
one should worship with the Vaiśvānara hymn at the Pauṇḍarīka fire-pit.
One should apply the Brāhma, Viṣṇu-sūkta, and Vaiṣṇava hymns, along with the Jayā-mantras and others,
together with a corresponding color, according to the prescribed ritual rules.
And when the release of the eyes has failed and the time has passed due to negligence, then follows the [mantra] beginning with "yad devādi," which presides over the six maṇḍalas. || 177 ||
Having offered oblations beginning with the syllable *īṃ*, and having offered for the sake of the Supreme Self,
one should then offer eighty-eight oblations and perform the opening of the eyes.
If, however, due to ignorance, [the rite] is performed at the rising of malefic planets,
then one should wash [the image], perform a fire-oblation (homa), and carry out the expiation (prāyaścitta) as previously described.
One should properly perform the opening of the eyes according to the procedure as previously described.
For the rites beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), if they are deficient, inferior, or performed in reverse order, there is a general expiation. || 180 ||
One should offer oblations in the Pauṇḍarīka fire with the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas; then, having offered with the hymn beginning "yad devādi," one should likewise offer the supreme Ātman-mantra.
Thereafter, one should offer eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable *īṃ*, as well as those dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, Indra, and Agni. (182)
One should offer oblations to Sūrya and Soma, as well as the Vaiṣṇava limb-oblation;
having offered with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas.

Having caused the Puṇyāha to be recited, one should cause the proclamation of Svasti to be made; this specific procedure for the invocation of the gods (praṇyāha) applies to all divine rites, such as the examination of the ground and other such acts. || 184 ||

When the auspicious day has been properly determined, saying "Whatever merit [there may be]," and having caused [the officiants] to pronounce "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! three times each; 185.

Having caused [the officiants] to recite "May there be well-being for us; may prosperity be ours," and having subsequently sprinkled [the materials] with water, gold, and the Pavamāna hymns at various intervals, thereafter—
Regarding the giving and not giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should act according to the procedure stated in the Sūtras;
having given the fee consisting of cows and other items, one should subsequently perform the ritual action. || 187 ||
This expiation is prescribed for all inferior rites;
it applies when a linga is fashioned from unmentioned materials, or from bricks, lime, thorns, or other such neuter substances. || 188 ||
Nor with other pieces of wood, or with trees, or even with other types of tainted timber; nor with iron, stones, or even with powders combined together. || 189 ||
When the image has been fashioned from [a mixture of] combined materials, or when it is made of baked clay, or from substances belonging to the Piśācas and Asuras, or from excess earth; || 190 ||
Or even when the permanent image (dhruvabera) is fashioned from unrefined materials such as thread,
clay, cloth, or gravel, provided it is measured using a cord.
In the case of an image made of kuśa grass that is thick, excessively worn out, or large, or one made of unmentioned materials, or likewise one made of plaster or brick; || 192 ||
If the image (bimba) is fashioned from an unmentioned material, adorned with artificial ornaments, or is possessed of such defects as these, everything perishes. || 193 ||
If one should establish this out of ignorance, the sacrificer perishes;
its pacification, its pacification, occurs when it is performed in the Pauṇḍarīka fire to the north of the temple. 194.
The supreme rite beginning with the syllable *Iṃ* consists of eighty-eight subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*), joined with the *Brahmasūkta* and accompanied by the *Śrīsūkta*. || 195 ||
One should offer oblations with the Durgāsūkta, and after that, the Viṣṇusūkta;
one should also offer the Pauruṣasūkta and the Viśvajitsūkta.
One should again offer oblations pertaining to Prajāpati, Rudra, Brahmā, and Agni, as well as those associated with Sūrya, Soma, and Viṣṇu. 197.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give the teacher's sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) after having installed [the deity] in the small shrine and having removed any defects. 198.
Then, having marked it with its characteristic features, one should install [the deity] in the same sequence as before.
Furthermore, there is the description of the dilapidated celestial palaces (vimāna) and so forth; in the central part of the group of four feet at the location of the neck of that vimāna— || 199 ||
One should have an image fashioned according to the prescribed rules, either from plaster or brick;
provided it is free from clay, spikes, gravel, fibers, or cloth, and is not deficient in its measurements.
If they are made of stone, it is said that they do not bestow defects, even when they possess artificial coloring or are joined with flaws such as thinness and the like.
One should fashion [the images] as endowed with all the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) yet devoid of color;
when the image has been made, one should omit the action of joining stones, but this applies only to a constructed body (bera), not to a stone [image]. || 201 ||
Furthermore, in the Pauṇḍarīka rite, one should perform the great pacification (mahāśānti) for a single day;
having offered the oblation for the taking of the stone, one should recite the mantra while touching it.
Having established this through ignorance and having acted thus according to the rule, one should perform the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration. (204)
One should quickly install an image that is free from defects and endowed with the proper characteristics;
for if one fails to install it out of delusion, [the patron] will be afflicted by mental anguish, diseases, and other calamities. || 205 ||
And that region is severely afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other such calamities;
therefore, having offered oblations for great peace and having fed the best of the twice-born, [one should act].
One should perform the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration,
if the image has been installed at an unmentioned time, or under an unmentioned lunar mansion such as Ārdrā, or on a weekday or zodiac sign that is censured. || 207 ||

And during the fall of meteors, fire, or lightning; during a conflagration of the quarters; when dust or blood falls from the sky; during the excessive downpour of rain; and during eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 208 ||
And likewise when a tree at a shrine falls, on a day of an earthquake, under an asterism joined with a malefic [planet], or similarly during the night. || 209 ||
If it was installed out of ignorance, one should perform the homa as before;
having offered a thousand oblations, he should likewise offer a thousand oblations to Viṣṇu.
And oblations are offered to the deities of the assembly with their respective mantras;
having established them as prescribed, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability. || 211 ||
Having omitted all rites such as the examination of the ground due to negligence, and having performed them on an unspecified seat, asterism, day, or zodiac sign; || 212 ||

If [the ritual] is performed at night, or without the proper procedure due to delusion or ignorance, then for a month, a fortnight, seven days, five days, or three days [one should perform penance]. || 213 ||
Indeed, at the three times of day, he performs the Mahāśānti oblation in the Pauṇḍarīka fire,
having performed the recitation of the respective mantras for the rites beginning with the examination of the ground.
One should perform the consecration again according to the method previously described.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Examination of the Ground and Atonement," in the section on Rituals (Kriyādhikāra) within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*.
Oṃ.
The twenty-first chapter: The Re-installation of the Moved [Image].
Now I shall explain in detail the procedure for re-installing an image that has moved from its pedestal and come to rest in a dangerous location. (1)
In another place, on a riverbank, outside a village, or on a great highway—any site that is without a dwelling and especially devoid of images. || 2 ||
An image situated in a dilapidated dwelling, one that has not been worshipped for a long time, a statue placed in an improper location, or one that has been moved through negligence; || 3 ||
The image situated in another abode is enveloped by those of the lowest castes;
it dwells in a state of inverse order, established in an empty root-abode. || 4 ||
Having moved it according to the prescribed rite, whether by means of a vehicle or even a cart,
and having placed it upon a firm spot of ground, one should cause a great temple to be constructed.
One should construct either a palace, a gate-tower, or even a celestial chariot; or, if unable to do so, one may fashion a sanctum according to whatever materials are available.
Having established that enmity toward him, one should perform the installation again;
for he who performs a great installation of Mahāviṣṇu elsewhere [commits a grave offense]. (7)
His diseases perish, as do the afflictions caused by planetary influences and other calamities; likewise, ill omens, bad dreams, and fears of thieves, enemies, and the like are destroyed.
Likewise, other calamities will undoubtedly perish;
and dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa will surely be accomplished—of this there is no doubt. (9)
The Expiation for the Auspicious Thread and Other Rites:
Hereafter, I shall declare the expiation regarding the auspicious thread and other such items, having fashioned it from mixed metal or from metal not prescribed [for the purpose]. (10)
If one should place [the vessel] containing pungent substances, one should quickly remove it and recite the assembly mantras and the Puruṣa-sūkta and Vaiṣṇava-sūkta over the lotus-fire.

One should offer oblations separately for the Śrī-sūkta, Brahmasūkta, and Rudrasūkta, ending with the Vyāhṛtis; then one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and also feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 12 ||
The *kautuka* should be made in the same form as the *dhruva*; whatever the shape of the *dhruva* is, that indeed shall be the shape of the *kautuka*. || 13 ||
Whether sitting, standing, or even lying down, there is no curiosity [regarding the posture].
It is declared that "sthānaka" (standing) refers to the standing position, while "sthānakāsana" refers to both standing and sitting during the month-long fast.
One should visualize [the deity] as seated, standing, or even reclining;
if the image is installed in the reverse manner, one should worship the thirty-three classes of deities.
One should worship the Vaidhṛna, Saura, Gāruḍa, the Pāñcabhautika Śānti,
the Durgā-sūkta, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and that Puruṣa-sūkta.

Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, he should cause them to proclaim an auspicious day; then, having performed the prescribed rite for the marriage-thread, he should again carry out the consecration ceremony. || 17 ||
Regarding the sites of descent and the regions described in the Purāṇas, the Elder (Brahmā) declared: "One may have an image fashioned according to one's desire. (18)
One should conduct oneself in ancient sites exactly as it was done before;
otherwise, one must not act, for if one does so, one perishes. || 19 ||
For its pacification, having offered oblations into the Pauṇḍarīka fire with the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas,
and having given the sacrificial fee, one should perform the rites as before.
If the eastern solar image has been established by means of the northern lunar image,
then even for the removal of that worn-out [image], one should indeed proceed exactly as before.
If an amulet made of gold is set with metal other than gold—that is, with alloyed metal—it will undoubtedly result in great harm. || 22 ||
To the south of the Ālaya, in the southeast, having offered oblations with the Brāhma, Saura, Saumya, Āgneya, and Gāruḍa hymns, as well as the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas; || 23 ||
Then, having offered oblations with the syllable "Iṃ" and having removed that image, one should fashion a new one with the aforementioned metal and install it again according to the prescribed rite.
Having consecrated and worshipped an auspicious amulet made of iron, if one discards it and installs another, that is called *abhicārika* (malevolent). || 25 ||
One should offer oblations with the three hymns to the deities of the quarters, the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and thereafter the Śrīsūkta,
the Durgāsūkta, and the Vaiṣṇava hymn.
Then, having performed the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma) as well as the Viśvajit hymn,
the wise one should first take up the Vimṛga vessel and set it down.
In that very place, having installed another new worldly image, one should worship it with whatever offerings are available; such is the teaching. (28)
When the image is discolored, cracked, rough, hollow, or worn out, and when the ritual object (kautuka) has been installed even though it is devoid of auspicious marks; || 29 ||
Having taken up another image while reciting the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas, as well as the Vaiṣṇava, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Brāhma, Aindra, and Vāyava [mantras]. || 30 ||

Having offered oblations once with the Gāruḍa mantra, and one hundred and eight times with the Vaiṣṇava mantra, and having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he should install [the image] again as before. || 31 ||

If, after having consecrated an image that was fashioned, one discards it and installs another, one should offer oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta in the northeast of the temple, at the southeast corner of the lotus. || 32 ||
One should again worship with the Daurga, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, and the Brahma Sūkta;
then, having offered oblations with the Rudra Sūkta into the Āhavanīya fire, one should proceed further.
Having offered oblations one hundred and eight times with the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he should then re-install the image.
Then, having installed a new image elsewhere, one should worship it;
or, if requested, one may give it for the sake of another temple, which yields great fruit. || 35 ||
The fault of an image being devoid of worship; the prohibition against abandoning an image that is free from defects:
"If an image is devoid of worship, it will cause total destruction;
however, one that is flawless and endowed with the proper characteristics must not be abandoned—this is the teaching. (36)
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, he bestows absolute liberation;
holding the conch and discus, he is the most excellent, granting the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 37 ||
One should worship the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace as before;
furthermore, when fashioning a physical image (bera), one should arrange it in that very same manner. || 38 ||
One should perform its installation, worship, and so forth with gentle rites;
even when a metal image has been fashioned without the application of beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa). || 39 ||
The Brāhma, Saura, Saumya, and that which is joined with the Sārasvata;
likewise the Prājāpatya, Āgneya, Vaiṣṇava, and also the Vyāhṛtis. || 40 ||
Having offered oblations and honored the Brahmins, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
In the event of an inversion of the stones,
a man's form [is established] with male stones, and a woman's form with female stones by a woman.
If it is performed by a woman or a eunuch, or even if it is performed by one in male form, it is called "malevolent" (ābhicārika); by that, everything perishes.
If, having abandoned the installed image, one should bring another;
or if a neuter or a male has fashioned an image of a goddess, one should abandon it. (43)
Having procured an image according to the prescribed stone and by another method,
and having established the six fires, one should then sprinkle the fire with water.

One should offer oblations with the Pāramātmika hymn, the eighty-eight verses beginning with the syllable *Iṃ*, and the *Jayā* and other mantras; likewise, one should offer the *Rātrisūkta* and the *Viśvajit-sūkta*.
In all [the rites], one should perform one hundred and eight recitations of the Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Nara Sūktas, along with the Rudra Sūkta and the Durgā Sūkta. || 46 ||
One should offer the lotus-oblation (padmahoma) combined with the five elements;
thereafter, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula after having fed them. || 47 ||
Having given gold, cattle, land, and other gifts, he should, filled with joy, further honor the preceptor there with garments, upper cloths, and ornaments. (48)
Having performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) in this manner, one should likewise carry out the installation;
this procedure is prescribed for all defects arising from the splitting of the stone. || 49 ||
If one should fashion a deity and two goddesses, or a divine image and a single object, from a single material,
then in that case as well, the expiation is as previously described.
Once the [new] permanent image has been installed elsewhere, then the previously installed permanent image [is to be moved] from there. || 51 ||
Having taken [the image], it must not be left elsewhere; if it has been left due to negligence, one should then perform the Mahāśānti rite and take up the image once more.
Having properly established [the image] in the eastern ālaya, one should worship it.
An image established by an improper rite is characterized by the defects of improper ritual; it is ineffective and useless. || 53 ||
Having abandoned what is deformed, discolored, or afflicted by other defects, and having prepared another according to the rules, endowed with the proper characteristics. || 54 ||
Having established [the deity] in the leaf-hut (ladālaya), the great peace-offering (mahāśānti) is offered;
to the south of the hut, in the fire of the unborn (abjāgni), let the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma) be well-offered. || 55 ||
It should be joined with the respective deities and accompanied by the *pariṣat* mantras, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Viṣṇusūkta*, and the *Brāhma* and *Puruṣasūktas*. || 56 ||
The Vaiṣṇava rite and the lotus-oblation (padmahoma) should be performed; that which pertains to the Supreme Self (pāramātmika) must be offered.
Having indeed offered the oblations and given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the installation once again.
Where there is a traditional remembrance of an author, this injunction applies.

In cases such as those concerning divine origins and the like, there is a distinction; one should act in the case of a field established by the gods or by sages exactly as was done previously. || 58 ||
That which lacks the prescribed method and is deficient in characteristics is not an invalid means of knowledge, nor does it produce a defect;
therefore, with every effort, one should act exactly as before. 59.
"Otherwise, there would be great fault; such is the instruction of the predecessors.
Regarding the installation of the *kautuka*-image elsewhere:
that image which has been installed as the *kautuka* in a single shrine," || 60 ||
If it has been placed elsewhere, however, in the northeast of the temple, that [image] belongs to Viṣṇu as its presiding deity; it should be accompanied by the ritual procedure and mantras.
Then follow the Brahmasūkta, the Rudrasūkta, and the Pāramātmika hymn,
as well as the "Īṅkārādi" and the eighty-eight-fold limb-oblation (aṅgahoma).
One should offer oblations with the Rātrisūkta and the Viśvajit-sūkta;
having taken them up as before, one should install them in their proper place with every effort. || 63 ||
Regarding the sequence of actions to be performed in cases such as fear of an enemy army:
when there is an intensification of the threat from an enemy army, or due to harassment by thieves, and the village settlement is destroyed or devoid of the movement of people; (64)

Having performed the fire oblation according to the rite in the manner prescribed for the abode of the ignorant, and having transferred the Śakti residing in the permanent image into the mobile ones; || 65 ||
If one were to lead them fearlessly to the temple and worship them, the fruit would be great;
all those images should be carried by Brāhmaṇas alone. (66)
Having approached the perpetual fire-pit and having sprinkled water around the fire,
he performs the propitiatory oblation with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter.
Having either kindled the fire within himself or having formally consigned the perpetual fire according to the rules,
he should enter a secure place, and there again into a pleasant dwelling.
Or in a temple of Agni, or in the hermitages of ascetics;
on the paths of Soma, or in the abodes and monasteries of other deities. || 69 ||
Either in the houses of householders or again in their reception halls—having entered one of these, in the absence of the former, one should likewise enter the latter. (70)
In other countries where the temples are mild, at the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa,
one should then consecrate all the images with pure waters.
Without the principal shrine and likewise the residence for the retinue, one should establish [the other structures] in spacious and delightful locations. || 72 ||
Having installed it facing either east as before or facing outward toward a wide space, one should always worship it according to the rules, using whatever materials are available.
One should worship all his attendants surrounding him;
and at the time of the fire-oblation, having placed that sacrificial fuel upon the common fire (laukikāgni), [one should proceed]. 74.
Having performed the oblation, at the conclusion of the homa, one should again place fuel-sticks upon the fire;
or else, having prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as before, one should proceed here also as previously described.
Protecting the fire so that it is never interrupted, he should perform the daily oblation (nityahoma), even without the festival of the daily procession and the festival of the year. || 76 ||
One should worship with daily, occasional, and other rites as they become available;
indeed, one should perform there whatever is appropriate until the worship of the primary shrine is completed.
"One should always worship in this manner according to what is available; such is the instruction.
When one is freed from that danger, having placed that fire back [into the hearth] as before," (78)
Having brought the images from the previous abode as before, one should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and likewise the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa). || 79 ||
Having performed the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he offers the great propitiatory oblation (mahāśānti) and,
having placed that fuel-stick in the worldly fire (laukikāgni), he should perform the foundational rite (ādhāra).
Having specially worshipped the deity at the conclusion of the night-long worship,
one should transfer the Śakti residing in the festive image back into the primary icon (kautuka).
Having invoked [the deity] from the auspicious thread (kautuka) into the pitcher (kumbha) which has been consecrated as before,
one should perform the installation once again according to the very sequence prescribed for installation.
Some say there are two fires, the Sabhya and the Pauṇḍarīka;
one who has interrupted the daily fire-sacrifice should establish five fires as before.
But at the conclusion of the *hautra* ritual, having invoked the members of the assembly and honored them with circumambulation, he offers oblations with their respective mantras.
Regarding the uninterrupted worship in the primary abode: when there is constant, unbroken worship in the eternal primary abode, this is the specific distinction. || 85 ||
Having properly established the power residing in each respective image within the *dhruva*, one should then invoke it from that [dhruva] into the image; everything else shall be the same.
If one is unable to do this, one should perform the worship of the Earth (Bhūpūjā).
Next, I shall explain the expiation for the purpose of protection from fear. || 87 ||
Or in the event of fear from thieves or enemies, or fear from a foreign army;
for the sake of protection during the consecration of auspicious marks and the like, or during the bathing festival of the image. || 88 ||
And there shall be a multitude of manifestations of various worldly forms,
as well as mobile images suitable for the practice of secret rites on the earth.
In a secret and pure place, the wise man should have a pit dug;
having poured sand into it, he should worship the goddess Earth.
Having performed the ritual sprinkling with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" according to the prescribed rule,
the preceptor, the priest, or likewise the sacrificer [should proceed] together with the patron.
Having entered the temple and bowed down together with his devotees, he said:
"O Great Lord, for as long as there may be fear, for that long [be our protection]. (92)
"O Janārdana, dwell indeed in this place with Śrī and Bhūmi"—with this mantra, he honored the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rite. || 93 ||
Having taken up the power (śakti) deposited in the images such as those of Kautuka and likewise in the attendants, the wise one should then project it into the Dhruva image.
Having carefully taken up the deity with the mantra "paraṃ raṃha," and having bowed with reverence to the deity with the mantra "pratadviṣṇustavate," || 95 ||
Having uttered "This belongs to Viṣṇu," he should likewise cause [the image] to lie with its head facing east;
then he should fill the pit with sand and earth. || 96 ||

Afterward, having caused it to be very firmly fixed and having entered the interior of the temple, one should bow to the God of gods and install [the image] in the seat of the individual soul (jīvasthāna). || 97 ||
Having worshipped the *kūrca* there, one should perform the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites;
likewise, having invoked the *śakti* from the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) into the *kūrca*, one should worship her. || 98 ||
Even there, when fear or doubt arises, or when the worship is obstructed, the officiant should go quickly, meditate upon the deity with a concentrated mind. || 99 ||
Saying "May the Blessed One come" and "O Agni,
go," he should quickly dissolve the Śakti residing in the image and Agni into his own self.
One should take refuge in a secluded place according to the *Śakunasūkta* of Japan; one should go to a spot where one may dwell at ease and free from negligence. || 101 ||
If there should be an image made of gold, one should take it and go along with it;
having invoked the deity therein, one should worship it constantly and perform festivals and other rites. || 102 ||
Devoid of both the bali-offering and the festival, one should likewise perform the daily and occasional rites,
as well as the sprinkling and bathing, according to one's ability.
One should perform everything [as prescribed] even when the pedestal is devoid of a golden image;
likewise, when the worship is ongoing, if the worshipper is afflicted by disease.
Previously, when death was imminent, he had entrusted the worship to his capable son;
at that time, he himself was also in haste regarding his own sons and brothers.
The wise man should properly install the divine power and that fire in his son or brother— even if he has passed away— having invoked it with reverence into the sacred grass (kūrca).
In this very manner, one should again propitiate [the deity] for the removal of fear,
having respectfully raised up the images at the proper time, in a healthy state, and in a suitable location.
Having thoroughly purified the entire abode, one should also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
likewise, upon contact with those who are untouchable, one should have a Vāstu-homa performed.
Furthermore, if the image is touched by Caṇḍālas or those born of the lowest castes,
one should perform the preliminary rites such as the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa) and then carry out the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once again.
One should not wait for a specific time, even after having performed the ritual planting of the sprouts;
rather, one should properly perform the consecration according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration. || 110 ||
The officiant should sequentially invoke the power residing in his heart into the water-pot;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains as before.
One should perform the worship of the ancestors according to the rules for daily worship;
having offered the daily oblation (nityahoma), one should then cause the bali offering to be presented there. || 112 ||

When festivals and such occasions have been obtained, one should perform everything during the *kautuka* [rite]; when the ritual bathing (*snapana*) has arrived there, having indeed tied the *kautuka* upon the fixed [image]. 113.
Therefore, having invoked [the deity] into the *kūrca*, one should perform the sprinkling with those substances;
having worshipped it thoroughly and offered [oblations], one should likewise dismiss it again.

Upon the arrival of the festival of Kāla, having hoisted the banner as before, one should daily perform the fire-oblation and the offering of sacrificial food according to the prescribed rules. || 115 ||
Having invoked the immeasurable lords of the Cakras into the vessels and performed worship, one should offer the bali according to the prescribed rite and then perform a circumambulation. || 116 ||
At the conclusion of the festival, having installed the power (śakti) of Bala into the permanent image (dhruvabera),
one should then invoke it into the kūrca and present abundant offerings.
Having placed [the deity] upon the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should again offer a handful of flowers;
then, when the morning festival on the day of the pilgrimage (tīrtha) has been performed.
Having performed the sprinkling with powdered *niśā* and the bathing with water-pots as well,
one should then perform the bathing again before the deity upon a seat of *kūrca* grass.

On the day of commencement, having consecrated the jar and having invoked [the deity] from the permanent image (dhruvabera) like a lamp from a lamp, one should perform the festival with that [image]. || 120 ||
At the conclusion of the sacred site (tīrtha) and at the end of the ritual bathing, one should perform the rite of re-installation (udvāsana) in the Dhruva [liṅga].
However, if the festival at the proper time is interrupted, one should perform an expiation (prāyaścitta). || 121 ||
Having extracted the image at an auspicious time, one should perform the consecration again;
having prepared two fire-pits for the assembly hall and the lotus, and having brought forth the eternal fire.

Furthermore, one should perform everything according to the rules by means of the path of re-consecration (punar-pratiṣṭhā), whether in the case of secret [images] such as the *kautuka* and others, or when the constant worship (*dhruvārcana*) has been interrupted. || 123 ||

Having performed the expiation for the omission of worship of the permanent image (dhruvabera), one should then perform the re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the portable image (kautuka) and the others. || 124 ||
In the event of touching a Caṇḍāla or other outcaste (antyaja), the penance prescribed for them is declared;
having offered oblations and performed purification, one should perform the consecration again. 125.
If the permanent image (dhruvabera) should become deficient in its limbs, it is improper to remove it for the sake of the festive bathing and processions. 126.
Having fashioned a wooden image, or having requested a [ready-made] image itself,
one should install it in the children's hall and perform the rite of consecration.
One should perform the re-consecration according to the procedure for the Great Consecration (mahāpratiṣṭhā).
Just as when a jar is broken, its space dissolves into the great space (mahākāśa), [so too does the deity merge back]. || 128 ||
Upon the destruction of the body, power likewise dissolves into this very universe—
extending eastward, westward, southward, and so forth, as well as into the intermediate directions.
Likewise, when there is a cavity in the abdomen, or it is elongated, when the sides are deficient, or the hips have wasted away;
and likewise when there is wasting of the thighs and shanks, as well as dryness of the mouth. (130)
When the crown is joined with defects, when all the secondary limbs have perished, when it is deficient in measurement, and likewise when the feet and ankles are missing; || 131 ||
In the event of damage to the ears or nose, one should also quickly perform rites for pacification;
and in the fire to the south of the temple, one should offer oblations pertaining to the Supreme Self.
One should likewise offer eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable *īṃ*,
and one should also offer one thousand and eight oblations to its presiding deity.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give the teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā);
then, having endowed [the image] with its respective characteristics, one should install it once again. || 134 ||
If one should place [the gaze] on other points than those specific locations mentioned,
such as in the defects of upward vision and so forth— namely,
in upward vision, downward vision, and likewise in sidelong vision— [the result will be adverse]. (135)
And in the case of an inauspicious or cruel aspect, one should perform an expiation:
in the west, one hundred and eight oblations into the fire of lotuses (water) dedicated to Viṣṇu, or to that deity [who aspects]. || 136 ||
Thereafter, one should offer eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable ‘īṃ’;
then, having fed the Brahmins, one should honor the preceptor and the others. || 137 ||
Having properly installed [the deity] in the prescribed location according to the correct ritual procedure, one should worship it again;
whether the seat of the fixed and movable images is deficient or even excessive in measurement. || 138 ||
One should offer oblations one thousand and eight times to that deity, and having offered with the mantras of the retinue, one should feed the Brahmins. || 139 ||
Having likewise constructed the pedestal (pīṭha) according to its specific characteristics, one should then install it;
however, this applies to the ritual procedure for determining the number of pedestals when the deposition of jewels (ratnanyāsa) is omitted.

Then, having moved [the deity] from the pedestal at the conclusion of the peace-offering (śāntihoma), and having performed the ritual placement of the mantras (nyāsa) in the same manner, one should again perform the reintegration (saṅghāta). || 141 ||
When the placement of the jewels has been performed upon the collection of lotuses, even without [the recitation of] mantras,
one should offer a peace-oblation according to the ritual procedure and mutter the respective mantra while touching it.
If the lotus-junction has been constructed solely by an artisan according to the Agni-vidhāna rite, then it should likewise be consecrated with the ritual ablutions using the water-pots (kalaśas).
Having performed the oblation, one should subsequently perform the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) and likewise recite the respective mantra;
in the same manner, when the primary image (mūlabera) has been installed in a solitary place.

Having worshipped the deity especially and having bowed down, saying "Forgive me," one should invoke the deity into the water-pot (kumbha) and prepare a pedestal endowed with the proper characteristics.
Having placed the deity upon the pedestal and performed the fire-oblation for peace according to the rule,
one should purify it with the circumambulation by fire, the five products of the cow, and the rite for a day of merit.
Having performed the preliminary rites such as perfuming with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and having bathed [the image] as before,
one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration.
Having especially worshipped the God for nine days, or seven days, or even three days, and having bowed while saying, "Forgive me," [one should conclude]. || 148 ||
"Having fed the Brahmins, one should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement regarding the Mobile Image," in the section on Rituals within the *Śrīvaikhānasa-bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
If Puruṣottama is installed by a preceptor who lacks the aforementioned qualities, or by installers and others who possess the aforementioned defects, [the result is as follows].
Oṃ.
The twenty-third chapter:
Renewal.
Henceforth, O ascetics rich in austerity, I shall describe the supreme method for the renovation of temples, gate-towers, and pavilions.
In the event of the destruction of the plaster, the cracking of whitewash, or likewise the breaking of a wall,
as well as when stones, bricks, or similar materials fall, one should perform this rite immediately.
Having brought the fire-pit of the domestic rite (aupāsana) face-to-face with the Ālaya,
one should offer oblations with the mantras of the four [deities] beginning with Nyakṣa, together with their forms (mūrtis).
Having specifically offered oblations into the fire for the deities stationed at the throat and those belonging to the group of the feet, while reciting the mantras in their proper sequence.
And having established that Śakti, who resides within its image, in the permanent image (dhruvabera),
one should [place her] in due order upon the pedestals resting on the walls in their respective directions.
Having invoked Nyakṣa and the others, and having offered the Vaiṣṇava oblation ten times,
as well as the mantras beginning with the Caturveda, he should then dismiss the fire.
Having made it firm by the casting of stones and bricks and so forth according to the prescribed rule, and having prepared the plastering with lime and the application of colors as before; || 7 ||
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), let the Vāstuhoma be well-offered;
having offered oblations into the lotus-born fire according to the Vaiṣṇava ritual, [recite] the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas.
