One should likewise offer the oblations of the *vyāhṛtis*, the limb-oblations (*aṅgahoma*) associated with the Supreme Self,
and the eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable *Iṃ*.
To pacify that fault, one should perform sacrifices up to a thousand oblations,
according to the prescribed rule and in the manner described for the installation of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Having installed those respective images and so forth, as well as the four [types of icons] beginning with the *nyakṣa*, one should cause all other rites to be performed; such is the injunction. (11)
Likewise, in the abodes of all the gods,
as well as in the dwellings of their retinues, Nyakṣa and the other lords of celestial chariots were present.
Regarding the collapse of the temple structure and similar incidents:
when the temple structure has fallen or become dilapidated, one should quickly establish a temporary shrine (bālālaya) there;
then, having installed the God of gods, one should have the temple constructed anew. || 13 ||

Whatever its measurement, whatever its form, whatever its substance, and whatever its abode may be, one should cause it to be made with that same substance, that same form, and that same measurement. || 14 ||

If it is a human image, the wise man should have it made with materials of superior quality and proportions; or, in the event of its previous destruction, he should have it restored as is appropriate.
When the enclosure wall and so forth are destroyed or when the walls have crumbled, one should offer oblations with the mantras presiding over those walls,
restore them, and perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice once again.
When the temple and its surrounding structures have fallen into decay, one should install the deities beginning with Nyakṣa and the four others upon that original central image (mūlabera),
restoring it as it was before.
Furthermore, according to the method for their consecration, one should install them in a celestial chariot (vimāna);
likewise, when the gate-towers (gopura) are dilapidated, one should install the presiding deities of those gates there.
Having invoked [the deities] upon the seats at their respective sides with great devotion,
and having offered oblations with their respective mantras, one should restore them as they were before.
Having stationed the guardians of those gates there, one should worship them; likewise, in all the pavilions and other structures, one should worship the respective presiding deities as prescribed.
Having seated [the deity] within the fixed image (dhruvabera) and having performed the ritual of bringing it down (nyāsa) as before,
one should invoke those presiding deities (adhidevas) and install Hari as previously.
In all new construction projects, such as temples and the like, purification occurs at the conclusion of the work;
this includes the general Vāstu-homa sacrifice, as well as the Puṇyāha rite.
Certain rules regarding renovation:
specifically for single-liṅga shrines (ekaberavimānas) that are human-sized, as well as for those whose images have been removed and are dilapidated, in the case of their reconstruction. || 23 ||
If one should make it larger than the previous measurement, it does not constitute a fault;
rather, one should expand it all around in accordance with the [required] dimensions. 24.
If the temple was previously made of clay, one should then construct it with bricks and other materials;
having expanded it on all sides, one should likewise fashion the temple accordingly.
Furthermore, regarding the work of repairing dilapidated walls, or likewise for those made of clay, if one desires their increase [in height or strength]: || 26 ||
One should indeed cause it to expand toward the east and the north;
or, if there is a village street ahead, one may expand it in three other directions.
One should especially perform the rite of prosperity (vṛddhi) on both sides and in front of the halls and pavilions, or likewise in the east and north.
One should construct the kitchen in the northern direction or at the front; if it is crowded on one side due to rivers, oceans, or mountains, [it may be placed elsewhere]. || 29 ||

One should cause it to increase on the other sides; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. However, one should never allow for an increase or even a decrease toward the south and the west. (30)
One should carry out the construction of walls, pavilions, and halls;
however, one should not cause the enlargement of temples dedicated to others, nor should one increase the size of Vimānas according to the Purāṇas. || 31 ||
In the construction of villages, hamlets, cities, ports, and so forth,
one should level the ground all around the site (vāstu), excluding the central womb (garbha) and the deities.

If the distinction [of the temple] is destroyed by a different arrangement [of parts], one should have the temple constructed with the same hand-measure (hasta) by which it was originally measured. || 33 ||
One should never construct enclosures, pavilions, and so forth with excessive dimensions; the supreme image (bera) should be installed in a temple of the highest, middle, or lowest class.
Otherwise, if one should act differently, the king and his kingdom will perish;
therefore, one should perform [the rites] with every effort according to the prescribed rule. || 35 ||
The Restoration of a Worn-out Fixed Image:
Hereafter, I shall describe the restoration of a fixed image (dhruvabera) when it is worn out, broken, split, cracked, or when its color has faded. (36)
One should construct the abode for the children in the southeast, or likewise in the south and southwest,
or in the west, according to the extent of one's means.
Thereafter, having installed [the deity] in the original temple according to the procedure prescribed for the installation in the original temple, one should perform the rite of renovation.
Wherever a defect is observed, there one should perform the purification;
whether in a letter or in the subsequent vowel, if a crack is seen. (39)
One should employ that specific color there using pure, skilled artisans;
however, if a defect occurs above the cloth, one should rectify it as previously described.
Or, if the cloth is defective, one should remove the entire cloth,
cover [the base] with a new cloth according to the prescribed rite, and perform the subsequent ritual action upon it.
If there is pain above the bladder and it is associated with the humors (doṣas), one should likewise purify it quickly;
[this applies when using] clay, wood, stone, or by means of sugar-pastes and similar applications.
Having performed all the ritual acts, one should properly fashion the image;
and when the earthen idol on the trident has become worn out, one should cast everything into the ocean.
Having gathered timber and erected a pillar as before, one should discard the old wooden [pillar] in the ocean and install another in the same manner. || 44 ||
Having cast that image of Śaila, which was deficient in its limbs, into the ocean, one should take a stone and fashion an image according to the prescribed rite, as before. (45)
Having established [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should subsequently fashion the bera (image) according to the rules;
for an image made of copper that is deficient in limbs, one should proceed as described in the section on the kautuka.
Furthermore, regarding the rules for the creation of an image:
one should have it made from the same material, in the same form, and of the same dimensions as the image that was previously extracted, according to its original proportions and shape. || 47 ||
If, however, the human measurement is primary, one should establish it again;
or else, one should have it made according to the dimensions and form of the principal [divine] measurement within the human scale.
Among images, there is a gradation of excellence based on the difference in material;
among those made of clay, wood, stone, and copper, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
Likewise, sitting is better than standing, and lying down is better than sitting, in that order. (49)
But if one is unable to perform it as previously described—due to fear of the destruction of the site or other such reasons—one may use stone from a mountain, or even stone from anywhere else. (50)
Some maintain that if there is a delay due to any improper cause whatsoever,
one should have [the rite] performed by means of secondary measures, such as [substituting] a likeness, a form, or a substance.
In the event of the loss of the original [vessel], it is recommended to use a secondary one according to availability;
having established it on its pedestal by means of the *dhruva* and *kautuka* rites, it is consecrated for the divine service.

Having performed the application of colors, ointments, and so forth, one should install and worship [the deity] again; this applies to all cases such as the *kautuka* thread and others, as well as when the [original] location has been destroyed. || 53 ||
Wherever a stone image or a fixed (dhruva) image is seen, one who is unable to act as before—due to fears such as the destruction of the site—[should proceed otherwise]. || 54 ||
Having performed the ritual release of the eyes, one should either install that [image] or perform the worship of the *dhruva* (permanent) image;
even if one is incapable, provided there is no fear of its destruction, it may be done as before.
One should have it constructed according to the prescribed rule, arranging it by means of the secondary method;
for if the fixed pedestal is loose, one should instantly construct a temporary abode for the child [deity]. || 56 ||
Having had it made very firm by artisans, one should perform the re-installation; and in the event of the loss of the site, having properly deposited jewels as before, [one should proceed].
One should perform the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration;
this applies if there is a consecration of many lingas, or if a single linga is associated with defects.
"Having wrapped that faultless [body] in a cloth, one should perform the purification for him who was defiled by faults as before; such is the instruction of the Elder. (59)

When the attendants are wicked, one should likewise construct a small shrine for each of them by their respective sides and offer oblations with their individual mantras, including those dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having renovated it and restored it, one should perform the re-installation ceremony;
this applies to multi-storied palaces where the ground floor is defective. (61)
Having constructed a temple for the child (Bālāgāra), one should perform [the rite] according to the rules either in the second enclosure, or in the first enclosure, or in the prescribed location.
One must never place images with flawed bases upon flawless pedestals out of delusion; if one should do so, he perishes.
Having quickly performed the oblation, one should establish great peace in the young temple;
pointing toward the upper level, [one should do so] in the western young temple.
One should properly arrange the site for its eastern part below;
however, in the case of the installation of the five forms, the temple for the child [Bāla] should be prepared according to the rules.

One should have [the images] fashioned in their respective directions, designating each according to its specific form. Regarding the materials for the icons, there is a rule concerning certain single substances:
one should have the icons of the five forms fashioned from a single material. || 66 ||
In the same way, if the positions of the five heroes, Brahmā, and Garuḍa should become reversed, that would result in misfortune for both the village and the sacrificer.
It would lead swiftly to destruction, especially for the king and the kingdom.

One should not perform a renovation without first constructing a new foundation; if one were to undertake a new construction without having established a new foundation, [it would likewise fail]. (68)
This is called the rite of exorcism (ābhicārika) for the pacification of that fault;
it should be performed for nine days, or seven days, or five days, or even three days.
Having offered oblations into the fire of the lotus and established great peace, one should worship;
having invoked [the deity] from the solar orb into the pitcher, one should worship it.
This same procedure is prescribed for other deities as well.
Regarding the method of restoration for secret images such as the *kautuka* and others:
when that secret image, such as the *kautuka*, has become worn out, [the following applies]. (71)
Having invoked Śakti into the pitcher, one should perform the rite of rejuvenation;
having invoked her from the [original] pitcher into the [new] pitcher, one should worship her at every festival.
But at the conclusion of the ritual work, having firmly established [the deity] as before, one should then invoke it into the kūrca and worship it daily according to the rules. || 73 ||
In the absence of the *kautuka*, worship should be performed upon a piece of gold;
in the absence of the *kautuka* everywhere, however, it may be on a piece of gold.
This [practice] should last for one month in the case of a water-pot (*kumbha*), and likewise for six months in the case of a mirror (*darpaṇa*).
It is said that on a cloth painting [the deity remains] for one year, and on wood for twelve years;
beyond that, Hari will no longer take delight therein.
Alternatively, having placed a seat-grass (kūrca) upon the pedestal of the image and having invoked [the deity], one should worship. || 74 ||
The worship of a dilapidated image will lead only to misfortune;

therefore, one should quickly perform the rite of renewal (jīrṇoddhāra) according to the prescribed rules as soon as decay occurs, whether it concerns the preliminary consecration (kautuka), the copper image, or the image made of stone or wood. || 75 ||
When it is worn out, cut, split, broken into pieces, or likewise aged;
when it is deficient in measurement or has a hole—one should abandon that image and discard it.
When it is worn out, cracked, broken, split, or likewise aged;
when its dimensions are deficient or it has a hole—one should certainly abandon such an image.
Having wrapped the image in a cloth and cast it into a body of water,
one should fashion an image according to the prescribed rite using the application of beeswax.
Having obtained the image as before, one should install it again according to the prescribed rite;
no regard for time should be made, and one should perform this rite swiftly. (79)
The primary limbs (mahāṅga) are designated as the throat,
belly, head, chest, forearms,
thighs, shanks, eyes, nose, lips, and palate. (80)
The ears, the fingers, the limbs, and the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth are called the secondary limbs (upāṅgas); likewise, the crown, ornaments, and garments are mentioned.
The wise know that the conch and discus, the head-discus, the weapons such as the lotus feet, the pedestal, the radiance, and the parasol are the secondary limbs (pratyaṅga).
The play-stick and the bamboo pole are the minor limbs on the body of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, the Āṣāḍha staff is designated as a minor limb on the dwarf (Vāmana).
Having performed the fire-oblation for peace, one should abandon an image that is deficient in its limbs, as well as the marriage-thread (kautuka);
in the case of a copper image deficient in its secondary limbs, one should likewise act with devotion. || 84 ||
The method for the kautuka-saṃskāra:

Having projected the Śakti into the Dhruva [pole star] and performed the union with a corresponding object, one should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, the Viṣṇusūkta, and Vaiṣṇava hymns. || 85 ||
Being composed, one should offer oblations with the eighty-eight [mantras] beginning with "īṅkāra," and having offered with the Rātrisūkta, one should again offer with the Jayādya mantras.
Then, having performed the purification of the image (bimbaśuddhi), one should likewise carry out the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Regarding the statement on the suitability for rejoining: even if a single limb is missing, one should not abandon it; such is the teaching. || 87 ||

One should perform the reconnection (sandhāna) [of the rosary] upon the crown, ornaments, clothing, nails, or the hair of the body; or upon the discus or conch; or when the head-discus is missing. || 88 ||
If the weapon of the stone [liṅga] is broken, one should provide a weapon made of metal;
some wise men say that for a copper [liṅga], the joints of the limbs should be repaired. || 89 ||
Regarding the discarding of the image:

if the golden or silver image should become defective in its limbs, one should not discard it; rather, having joined it with metal of equal quality, one should restore it to its original state step by step.
When other signs of failure appear during the joining process, or when a limb is similarly defective, one should perform the rejoining in due order;
likewise, when the image has moved or has become detached from its pedestal. || 91 ||
In the case of wheels made of cloth and similar materials, one should ensure a firm joining at the points where lines and holes meet, as well as in instances of cutting or splitting. || 92 ||
One should have it made as before, likewise joined with an equal amount of metal according to the rules;
as previously, at the conclusion of the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one installs it again in due order.
Even for an image made of copper, one must certainly perform the restoration of missing parts such as the ears, nose, and fingers; of this there is no doubt. (94)
Even if its secondary parts are deficient, one should discard that [vessel] made of stone or wood;
for if it is cracked even by the measure of one or two barleycorns here and there, it is indeed unfit.
One should fashion each respective limb with even a mere line; [the image should be] neither too large nor lacking in proportion, and it may be made of gold or silver. || 96 ||
Having collected that [image] just as one would with iron, at the conclusion of the propitiatory fire-offerings (śāntihoma),
one should perform the rite of rejuvenation according to the procedure for beeswax.
Having performed the opening of the eyes and so forth, one consecrates [the image] in due order;
as for a gem-encrusted image, one should merely take up its form. (98)
There should be no moving of an image that is free from defects,
especially when that flawless image is being worshipped; moreover,
one should not have another image made merely out of concern for the weight of the metal.
If he should do so out of ignorance, the king and the kingdom will perish;
therefore, having discarded the image according to the prescribed rule if it is decayed or has missing or extra limbs— || 100 ||

If one is capable, one should have it made with superior materials; that is the best case. However, if the image (kautuka) previously worshipped suffers a loss of limbs or other defects, [the following applies]. 101.
Having quickly projected that power (śakti) into the permanent image (dhruvabera), the one skilled in the ritual procedures should then fashion a new image and install it. 102.

Having first established the image itself upon the pedestal of curiosity (the kautukapīṭha) for the purpose of bathing, or else the festive image (autsavam) or the strength-image (baliberam), from the permanent image (dhruvāt); || 103 ||
Having invoked [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the daily worship;
having fashioned the *kautuka* (protective thread) as before and having established [the deity] therein, one should worship it. || 104 ||
One should establish the bathing, the festival, the offerings, and the worship in their proper places.
When the bathing and the festival are omitted, the worship with a golden *kūrca* serves as a substitute for the ritual image; indeed, in that case, the *kūrca* must be made of gold.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and invocation (samāvāhana), one should worship while meditating as before; this is the procedure for when the image has been stolen by thieves:
"If the image has indeed been carried away by thieves or even by enemies... (106).
Furthermore, for as long as one continues to fashion the image, for that duration of time,
one should indeed invoke [the deity] with devotion into a piece of gold and worship it.
Having fashioned the image as before, the wise one should perform its consecration;
in that case, there are no alternative options if the two goddesses have been carried away by the God of Gods.
Having fashioned the two goddesses according to the rules and installed them as before,
one should perform the marriage ceremony according to the previously mentioned injunctions.
"If one performs the offering in the perpetual fire, or if there is an invocation from the *dhruva* vessel, one should not perform the marriage rite"—such is the instruction of the ancestors. (110)
If the Lord of Gods has been carried away from there without his two goddesses, one should fashion an image of the God in accordance with the two goddesses, following the prescribed ritual. (111)
Having performed the invocation (āvāhana) for Dhruva and others, and having led forth the eternal fire (nityamagni),
one should perform the installation (pratiṣṭhā) again according to the very sequence prescribed for installation, after having led forth the eternal fire. || 112 ||
These two alone are the goddesses of the Lord; one should not conceive of others as goddesses.
For those who possess that power, there is prior consecration; one should not perform the rite of marriage.
Even if a new image has been installed, if it is seen to have been stolen again,
one should install a worldly (laukika) image accompanied by mantras and worship it.
Otherwise, if one were to act differently, the king and his kingdom would perish;
for the Lord of Gods remains fixed, as do those two goddesses who are deprived of limbs. (115)
O ascetics, even though the Lord's limbs were deficient while those two goddesses remained present,
they properly placed the respective power residing in each of their forms into the pitcher.
Having installed [the deity] in the temple of the child and performing the daily worship,
one should act according to the nature of the two gods or according to the nature of the Lord of Gods.
One should fashion it with materials of the same proportions and form as before and install it in due order;
one should not make the principal image larger than its original measurements.
One should have the two goddesses fashioned from an equal amount of metal, and never from more;
whatever image is free from defects, that is said not to be discarded.
Having perpetually maintained the sacred fire in the sacrificial hall and the fire-pits,
and having ritually dismissed that very Śakti, he should properly install her within the water-pot.

One should perform the consecration as before, but one should not perform a marriage ceremony there. If she is capable and has already been consecrated, no further rite of consecration should be performed again. (121)
When all the deities remain in the form of male icons, upon the destruction of a female icon, there is the destruction of the male icon, or else [the destruction] of the female [icon]. || 122 ||
This general rule has been declared regarding the act of rejoining [the sacred fire]. Furthermore, concerning the praise of the fruit for the one who performs the rejoining:
the fruit for the one who performs the rejoining shall be double that which is rooted in the original [act]. || 123 ||
He obtains all desires, becomes renowned and wealthy, and, liberated from all sins, enjoys pleasures upon the surface of the earth. || 124 ||
And when mobile beings are hidden away or when there is fear of an enemy army,
for as long as they remain there, one should indeed stay there for that same duration until their rescue.
Having invoked [the deity] with devotion upon the pedestal and meditated upon the God, one should worship Him;
then, having lifted those images, one should purify them with a purifying substance. || 126 ||
One should bathe the deity with water-pots according to the extent of one's means;
having performed the Mahāśānti oblation, one should also cause the Puṇyāha recitation to be proclaimed.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give them a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
one should honor them according to the rule and properly present the oblation.
And when mobile [images] have been concealed, or when the worship of stationary [images] has been deficient,
one should again perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) according to the circumstances of that time.
Furthermore, one should perform the consecration again by means of the path of re-consecration for a beautiful image endowed with auspicious marks that is being worshipped in the home. (130)
If it conforms to the fixed image (dhruvabera) and likewise to the requirements of the village, and if it has been obtained for the purpose of the festival procession or for the ritual bathing; 131.
Or, for the sake of perpetual festival, one should install and worship [the deity] there,
having placed the Śakti residing within that image into the solar orb.
The wise one, having invoked [the deity] from the *dhruva* vessel into that [other vessel], should establish it as before;
or else, having properly placed that very *śakti* into the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Having established the worldly [fire] there, one should invoke it into the water-pot and other vessels and worship it;
indeed, during the installation of the worldly [deity], one offers oblations into the worldly fire.
This alone would be the distinction; everything else would be the same for those gods who desire a form and those who do not desire one in their abode. (135)
They are well-established and worshipped upon pedestals, in niches, and on door-panels, as well as in the various implements of worship, in vessels, in vehicles, and on seats. (136)
Having been invoked and worshipped for a long time at ponds, wells, embankments, and the like, they deserve the rites appropriate for a new building during the construction of a temple. || 137 ||

Therefore, with every effort, whatever has been consecrated through mantra should be performed in its entirety at the beginning of new works and according to the procedure for the restoration of dilapidated temples. || 138 ||
Having performed the consecration at the conclusion of the new work, one should indeed perform it once again;
or, having taken up new materials, one should carry out the installation.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation regarding Renovations," in the section on Rituals (Kriyādhikāra) within the *Bhṛguproktā Saṃhitā*, the sacred scripture of the Lord belonging to the illustrious Vaikhānasa tradition.
Oṃ.
Chapter Twenty-four.
There is atonement for neglecting worship and for opening the doors;
hereafter I shall declare the atonement for the omission of worship.
[This applies] before sunrise in the morning for the temple of the Deity, and before sunset in the evening, as well as during midday.
If the opening of the door is deficient, one should then open it quickly.
Having sprinkled water around the fire in the perpetual sacrificial pit or on the hearth,
one should offer oblations with clarified butter to Varuṇa, the Sun, and the deities of the quarters.

The Vaiṣṇavas should perform the ritual again with the six mantras. If the materials for worship, such as water, flowers, and so forth, have already been brought together for the collection of substances, they should be used even without mantras.
Or, if one consecrates it in the Ālaya, one should recite that mantra twice;
if it has been brought by other threads, one should perform the consecration three times.

In the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, one should have it taken by Kṣatriyas and others whose arms are marked with the conch and discus; if these are unavailable, then by those who follow the subsequent [castes].
One should perform the recitation of the four Vedas and other texts six times over again and again;
furthermore, one should have the nails, hair, and so forth shaved at every change of the moon (parvan).
Wearing clean garments, having bathed, and likewise having cleansed their teeth and nails,
[they should perform] the rite dedicated to Śrī and Viṣṇu when the lamps are absent— that is, when the twilight lamps have failed.
Having offered the oblation to Agni once, one should provide double the number of lamps;
if the perpetual lamp is extinguished, one should perform one hundred and eight sacrifices.
A lamp made with wicks produced from the stalks of white lotuses shall be most dear to all the gods. (10)
The gift of a lamp with the finest ghee from a Kapila cow is indeed supreme;
a lamp whose flame rises to a height of eight finger-breadths is called the best.
Having prepared a wick from threads produced from the lotus stalks mentioned previously,
the middle [wick] should have a flame one finger-breadth high when fed with cow's ghee.
A lamp prepared with oil, provided with a wick made of cotton, is considered inferior;
its flame should be three finger-breadths high, or as high as is available.
A lamp fashioned with camphor wicks is the most excellent of all;
[the merit] is diminished if the sweeping and so forth are omitted, and likewise if the sweeping is deficient, or even if the smearing of the floor is deficient.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the *āpaḥ*, *hiraṇya*, and *pavamāna* mantras, one should smear [the area].
This applies when the cleansing of the faded floral offerings has been neglected, as well as when the ritual sprinkling has been omitted. || 15 ||
If one is unable to perform the consecration of the image, one should worship Vaiṣṇava, Vaiṣvaksena, and Vāruṇa, and then pay homage to the Lord of Gods.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water infused with kusha grass and having discarded the previous garment, one should clothe the Lord of Gods with another washed cloth. || 17 ||

If the consecration of the image (bimbābhiṣeka) is omitted, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava and Vāruṇa rites; if the ritual placement of flowers (puṣpanyāsa) is omitted, or if the time has elapsed, then one must perform them again at that time.
Having performed the placement of the flowers with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī once more,
one should offer oblations ten times, and then offer oblations a hundred times with the [divine] names.
If the worship is deficient,
one should worship the deities residing in the inner sanctum, the lords of the gates, and the gatekeepers; however, if their worship is omitted, one should worship the principal deity alone.
Having honored them twice over, one should worship each with its respective mantra once;
however, if the worship is devoid of meditation, one should then worship with the Viṣṇusūkta.
Having meditated upon the deity with perfect concentration, he worships him again in due order;
likewise, whether the worship is performed according to the ninefold division or even in a single [form], it is done in that same manner.
Whatever may be deficient regarding the seat and other such items, one should specifically offer oblations for each of those deficiencies,
recollecting the Vaiṣṇava mantra and the Viṣṇugāyatrī.
Then, remembering with his intellect the God of gods— the all-pervading and imperishable—
he performed the brahman-oblation (brāhmaṃ huta), which is superior even to the offering of oblations when no such offering has been made.
Then, having offered the oblation pertaining to Prajāpati accompanied by that of Viṣṇu,
one should likewise present the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the sacrificial offering doubled in quantity.
If the side-dishes are deficient, one should sacrifice to Soma accompanied by Viṣṇu;
and if the ghee is deficient, one should offer oblations to the Vaiṣṇava deities along with Sāman and the others.
If the offering lacks curd, one should perform oblations with the Vaiṣṇava Yajus-mantras beginning with "yajur-ādyam";
if there is no mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), one should worship with the Śrī-mantra, which is Vaiṣṇava. || 27 ||
If one performs the daily oblation out of ignorance when the regular oblation has been omitted, one should offer an oblation to Kapālāgra;
furthermore, having offered oblations to Vaiṣṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, one should likewise perform the oblation.
If one is unable to maintain that perpetual fire without interruption,
one should either consign it into oneself by means of the *samidh* rite or deposit it elsewhere, and then perform the sacrifice day after day.

The mantra prescribed in the Śrīvaikhānasa Sūtra is traditionally taught for the rite of installation; likewise, it is used for the rite of de-installation. One should not perform any action in the fire without a mantra.
If worship is omitted at the proper time, or if the morning twilight worship (prātaḥ-sandhyā) is omitted, the penalty at midday shall be double; thereafter,
one should worship with the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauruṣa, and the Viṣṇu-sūkta hymns.
If the worship is omitted during the morning or midday, it should be performed twice as much in the evening;
however, if the worship is omitted for an entire day, one should offer oblations and then perform the worship again twice as much.
Having offered the oblations into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire,
he should thereafter worship the Vaiṣṇava mantras twenty-five times, each consisting of six measures (mātrās).
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas, one should feed the Brahmins;
this is prescribed for a single day, but on the second day it should be doubled.
In this manner, one should increase [the offerings] day by day until the end of twelve days;
once the twelve days have passed, thereafter, one should perform [the rite] in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
One should worship with the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauruṣa, and the Viṣṇu-hymn (Viṣṇusūkta) one hundred times;
then, one should bathe [the deity] again with forty-eight jars.
Having worshipped and offered a great oblation or an abundant one, he should present it;
he should give animals to the preceptor and again feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 37 ||
If the temple should be deficient by one month, then one should likewise arrange the sacrificial fires,
such as the Āhavanīya and others, starting from the east.
Having meditated upon the Lord of Gods in his mind twenty-one times for each, as well as for the two goddesses, the two sages, the [mantra] of Viṣṇu, and that of Garuḍa; || 39 ||
In each respective oblation, one should offer what is to be poured together with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
having bathed the deity according to the rules with one hundred and eight jars.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas, after first counting the days for which the worship was deficient. || 41 ||
One should offer the materials for the daily worship to the Lord of Gods;
one should perform it in this manner every month, and in two months, it shall be twofold.
In this manner, one should increase [the number] until the end of the year;
thereafter, when the year has passed, one may perform it with eight thousand or even hundreds of jars.
Having bathed the Lord of Gods, and having prostrated and obtained his permission,
one should give gold, animals, land, and so forth, as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
Then, having offered the great propitiatory oblation (mahāśānti) into the fire of lotuses while recollecting the deity,
he should take up a thousand lotuses while reciting the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī.
Having immersed [the image] again and again, one should indeed offer oblations with the ghee of Kapila;
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the consecration once more.
In the same way, when worship is deficient, an expiation is prescribed;
this is stated to be common for other deities as well. (47)
If the bali offering is omitted, or if the morning sandhyā rite is omitted, the fault becomes double at midday; thereafter,
one should worship Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Soma, and Prajāpati.
If the offering is omitted during the morning or midday, it becomes double [the penalty] at evening;
however, if the bali-offering is omitted for a single day in the aupāsana fire, [the same applies]. 49.
One should offer oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta combined with the previously mentioned mantras;
thereafter, one should raise up the deficient bali according to the procedure stated before.
This is prescribed for a single day; for two days, it should be doubled.
One should increase it up to twelve days, even if the twelfth day has already passed.
In the fire of the fire, he offers oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, followed by the Viṣṇusūkta, and then those connected with the Supreme Self, beginning with the syllable "Om. || 52 ||
Having bathed the image and the *kautuka* (the marriage-thread) with seven jars,
and having offered the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*), one should gradually raise the ritual offerings (*balis*).
In this very manner, one should perform [the rite] until the end of the month;
if it should be deficient by a month in the eastern great sacrificial fire (āhavanīya), [the following applies].
One should recite the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas one hundred and eight times;
meanwhile, one should offer oblations into the Sabhya-kuṇḍa for all the deities.
After bathing the deity with one hundred and eight jars,
he should then diligently give twenty-five cows, dedicating them to the deity.
Having offered the great oblation, one should present the bali-offerings in their proper sequence;
in this very manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should perform this for the duration of a year.
If that sacrificial fire falls or is touched by those unfit to touch it who defile the Vedic tradition,
one should offer the oblation as before and worship the Lord of the Forest (the Fire) once again.

Having raised the bali offering, if there is an obstacle, one should offer a sacrifice to the Sun conjoined with Mercury as before, and then commence the ritual according to the prescribed rule. || 59 ||
If the strength is deficient, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite twenty-one times;
if the vessel is broken, worn out, or lacks the proper dimensions, one should perform it one hundred times.
The Vaiṣṇava Pauruṣa Sūkta, then the Viṣṇu Sūkta, followed by the Pāramātmika, the syllable Om, and likewise the Raudra [Sūkta]. (61)
For his pacification, one should offer oblations with mantras associated with Sūrya and Agni, those associated with the five Varuṇas, and with the Jayā and Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
In the event of excessive wind or excessive rain, having propitiated Hari as before,
one should perform a circumambulation of the inner sanctum while accompanied by the *dhruva* and *kautuka* [rites].
Having constructed a landing platform in the middle, one should offer a bali-oblation before Śrībhūta,
and likewise offer the parivāra-bali surrounding the Lord of Gods.
Some say that one should offer [the food] having reached each respective place;
however, when the time for the *annabali* has arrived, if the prepared food is not available, [one should proceed with what is at hand]. || 65 ||
One should offer the arghya and bali as before, or even just flowers;
furthermore, one should worship the solar and Vaiṣṇava deities ten times in the perpetual fire.
Outside the enclosure of the Ālaya, on the left side which has been designated,
and at the designated site for the sacrificial offering (balipīṭha), one should place that [offering] to the right.
At the time of the circumambulation with the offering (bali), if there is an absence of musical instruments, one should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta;
and if there is an absence of dance and song, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇusūkta.
Having offered oblations accompanied by the ringing of a bell,
one should perform the circumambulation with the ritual offerings while reciting the Śākuna Sūkta together with the Svasti Sūkta.
When a corpse has fallen within a boundary of fifty bow-lengths, or when a corpse lies upon a single path,
one should avoid the worship and the offering of oblations to the God of gods.

If one should perform it out of ignorance, having consecrated [the image] with the Buddhas, and having offered oblations to the gods and others, one should worship and present [the offering]. || 71 ||
When the corpse of a Kṣatriya or others is within sixty, seventy, or eighty days [of death],
one should perform the rite of pacification for the corpse of one born in the natural order (anuloma), as well as for a Śūdra, as previously stated.

If the worship is performed on another site, it shall not lead to any fault for the deity. If there is contact with the untouchable, or if the priest has been touched by other twice-born men who are impure, one should consecrate him with pure water.
If the jar has been touched by seven Kṣatriyas, one should bathe Hari with them;
likewise, if it has been touched by a Vaiśya, one should bathe him with twenty-four jars.
One should perform the peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma) and feed the brahmins according to one's ability;
likewise, in the event of contact with a Śūdra, one should bathe with one hundred and eight [mantras].
Then, having performed the Mahāśānti rite, he should also feed the Brāhmaṇas;
if he has been touched by those of lower castes (anuloma), he should perform the expiation prescribed for a Śūdra.
If touched by Brahmins who are impure due to being left-overs (from a meal), a Śūdra should perform the expiation prescribed for a Śūdra;
but if touched by Brahmins who are in a state of ritual impurity (āśauca), he should perform the expiation prescribed for a Śūdra.
But when [the image] is touched by those [defilements] in the reverse order, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water and other elements;
then, for seven days, one should offer oblations into the fire of lotuses while reciting the Mahāśānti mantra.
One should perform the consecration again according to the very sequence prescribed for consecration;
however, upon contact with a Tantrika, one should cause the expiation prescribed for the inverse order to be performed.
Those Tantric traditions that are not rooted in the Vedas are subverters of the Vedas;
one should never offer sacrificial oblations (havis) touched by anyone other than Brāhmaṇas who are cooks [for such rites]. 80.

If, however, out of delusion one should give [the offering] to a Vaiṣṇava even once, he should perform a sacrifice with those Brahmins who have eaten leavings or are impure, or with Kṣatriyas, or indeed with Vaiśyas. || 81 ||
If the food offered has been touched by those who are impure, one should sprinkle it with pure water;
having offered oblations to Viṣṇu ten times, one should then offer the other [food].
If it has been touched by Brahmins, Śūdras, or those born of anuloma unions who are subject to ritual impurity,
one should report it— whether out of ignorance or knowledge— with the most inferior of water-pitchers.
Having bathed [the deity], then having offered the śānti oblation and worshipped, one should present the offering;
however, if one should present the sacrificial food (havis) that has been touched by those who act in reverse order, [the rite is flawed]. || 84 ||
One should bathe the deity with forty-eight jars, perform the Mahāśānti oblation, and present abundant offerings. || 85 ||

Whether at the time of bathing the Lord of Gods, or at the time of worship, or during the offering—those who act contrary to the sacred order, heretics, the fallen, and those who revile the Vedas [are excluded]. (86)

If those who have abandoned their vows and broken their boundaries should, out of delusion, see [the offering], or if they should see the sacrificial oblation (havis), one should offer it to the Lord of the Gods. || 87 ||
Having bathed the Lord of Gods with pure waters for his pacification,
and having worshipped him at the conclusion of the peace-offering (śānti-homa), one should present abundant offerings.
Furthermore, if water or flowers that have been consecrated with mantras for the purpose of worship are touched by anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, one should discard them and fetch others.

Alternatively, having sprinkled [the water] with consecrated waters (prokṣaṇas) and placed it in another vessel, one should perform the mantra-consecration as before and worship with that very [water]. || 90 ||
If [the vessel] is likewise touched by Brahmins who are impure due to food remnants,
or touched by Brahmins in a state of ritual impurity (āśauca), one should discard that substance and take up another.
But if it has been touched or even seen by those born in the inverse order (pratiloma),
or by Śūdras, or by those who are impure, or by a woman in her courses, one should discard it.
Clarified butter, curd, milk, honey, or even water that has been touched by a woman who has recently given birth must never be accepted for the sake of the gods. (93)
If one should offer those [impure things] to the God of gods out of ignorance,
one should bathe him with pure water, perform an oblation, and worship him with a rite for peace.
A flower that has been touched must be discarded, as must other items such as fruit;
however, if one does not discard them out of greed, one should offer a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and perform a consecration.
Worship of Viṣṇu without mantras, as well as worship at an improper time, brings about the destruction of the village, famine, and disease. || 96 ||
Therefore, with every effort, especially at the proper times, one should worship Viṣṇu with mantras; such is the instruction of the ancestors. 97.
When all the seers (ṛṣis), meters (chandas), and presiding deities (adhidevas) of the various mantras are unknown, one should remember that the meter is Anuṣṭubh. 98.
Having remembered in general that Antaryāmī is the seer (ṛṣi) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the deity, one should worship the Supreme Person. 99.
Devotion is of eight kinds;
I shall describe this eightfold devotion toward the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow:
affection for his devotees and rejoicing in their worship of him. (100)
Devotion to hearing discourses on Him, transformations of the voice, eyes, and limbs [upon hearing them], constant remembrance of Him, and the avoidance of hypocrisy for His sake. (101)
That state of being the sole remainder is eternal, and it does not depend on anything else;
for this is indeed the eightfold devotion which exists through that commonality.
One should choose that very person as the preeminent worshipper, and not any other officiant.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation in Daily Worship," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for bathing,
which is the remedy for the fault incurred when the bathing of Viṣṇu is performed without first offering the sprouts. (1)
If the offering of the sprouts is omitted,
one should worship the six mantras of Brahmā and the others during the ritual service; likewise,
whether the worship with the forms (mūrtis) of Jayā and the others is deficient or even excessive, [the rite remains valid].
One should worship the mantra and each of its deities twenty times.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
he should first fill the vessels with flowers or even with white rice grains.
Having thus resolved upon the sprouts, one should bathe Hari again;
even if the dimensions of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth are deficient or excessive.
One should worship the mantras and the deities of Viṣṇu twenty times;
however, in the absence of earthen bowls (pālikās), one may instead offer them in shallow dishes (śarāvas). || 5 ||
If one should construct a bathing hall with measurements either less or more than the prescribed standard,
for each Vaiṣṇava temple, O Daitya, there shall be a hundred and eight [penances].
One should perform the final bath for the Ālaya in the north;
however, one who desires prosperity should do so in the east, while one who desires liberation should do so in the south.

One desiring water should perform it in the western quarter; one desiring all desires, in the quarter of Śaṅkara (the north); however, one should not perform it in the southeastern, southwestern, or northwestern quarters.
If one should perform [the rite] in that very same place, one should again perform the ritual bathing;
one should worship the mantras of the guardians of the quarters and the Vaiṣṇava mantra twenty times.
If the number of jars is either less or more than the prescribed measure,
one should offer oblations to Viṣṇu and Brahmā, accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Having offered the oblations separately, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should take [the vessel] endowed with auspicious marks;
for if it lacks a cloth, or is entirely without a cloth, there would be a great fault arising from the deficiency of the cloth and other such requirements.

One should honor the preceptor with garments and worship the Vaiṣṇava Śrī-mantra. At the arches and other such structures, if the arches are defective, one should worship the two door-keeper mantras (Dauvārika mantras).
Having become the respective lord of each door, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite;
in cases where the kūrca and other implements are deficient in measure, the Vaiṣṇava rite should be joined with the Brāhma rite.
Having offered oblations to Sūrya sixteen times, one should perform the rite with the proper characteristics;
and in each row where the measure is deficient, one should worship Paṅktīśa.
One should offer oblations with the Paṅktīśa mantra, which is Vaiṣṇava and composed of the five elements.
Mitra, the guardian of the celestial chariot, is celebrated as Paṅktīśa. || 15 ||
In a pit, in earthen mounds,

or in a pit lacking the prescribed dimensions, one should offer oblations to the Earth and other deities; or, when the aforementioned locations are unavailable, one may perform them using whatever materials are at hand.
One should perform oblations dedicated to the Earth-deity, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
or else, having constructed a pit in the western part of the bathing hall.
Having placed that [vessel] at the head of the row, or for the purpose of depositing the ritual substances,
one should arrange the materials, such as clay and the rest, in their proper places within the row.
After the bathing with clay and other substances, one should place a pitcher filled with pure water and wrapped in cloth and so forth upon a pedestal of grain in the center.
Some say that after reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one should perform the ceremonial bath;
and one should cause the bathing-pit to be constructed with stone or brick.
One should construct a pedestal (pīṭha) one cubit in height according to the rules for the base (adhiṣṭhāna);
if it is above the surface of the base, it may include a platform, a railing, and so forth, up to the top of the dais.
The Elder said that one should not make a floor for the *talopuri*;
above that, one should cause a cavity to be made according to the rules for the *aupāsana* fire.
Having constructed a pedestal one cubit in height from the wood prescribed for sacrifice,
and having installed it in the middle of the row, one should pour a stream of water to its north.
Having bathed the deity [there], some say that one should bathe him in that pit;
then, for the purpose of the daily consecration, likewise to the north of the pavilion.
Having thus established the Lord, one should bathe him together with the two goddesses;
meanwhile, one should prepare a pit measuring one cubit in length and breadth.
One should perform the rite for each of the seats individually, starting from the east and so on, according to the rules for the aupāsana fire, adding two additional verses. || 26 ||
In a height of one cubit, the face shall be one-sixth;
the height of the neck shall be one-third, and the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) shall be two parts.
A depression is prescribed for that [fire] just as for the domestic (aupāsana) fire;
some indeed say that this hollow is for the purpose of daily ablutions. || 28 ||
If one should construct mountains [as models] from a mountain or similar source using a measurement that is either deficient or excessive,
he should offer oblations to Agni and Viṣṇu, ending with the Vyāhṛtis for each individual case.

In the absence of grains, one should offer either all kinds of grains or exclusively barley; or, having added as much grain as is available beyond the measure of *vrīhi*, one should perform the worship. || 30 ||
For the pacification of that [obstacle], one should offer oblations to Vāyu, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
or, in the absence of sprouts, one may use previously grown sprouts instead. || 31 ||
One should offer oblations to that deity, as well as to Viṣṇu and Soma;
for if one performs auspicious rites with either a deficient or excessive measure, they produce only inauspicious results.
One should worship Indra and Viṣṇu along with the Mahāvyāhṛtis; however,
if the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are deficient in the prescribed application, the wise man [should perform the rite] with pañcagavya alone.
One should worship each of the Raudra and Vaiṣṇava mantras twenty times;
one should bring the excellent ghee from a tawny cow and curd from a red cow. (34)
Likewise, one should take the milk from a white cow, the dung from a black cow,
and also the urine from a cow with the color of a pigeon's neck.
If those of the described colors are not available, one may proceed with whatever is at hand;
or else, one should perform that conjunction using the very mantras previously mentioned.
When the conjunction of the five substances has been performed without the mantra,
one should touch [the mixture] with the hand and recite the mantra prescribed for the conjunction twice.
Among the principal substances, milk should be taken, excluding that of cows, goats, and buffaloes;
however, if one takes either goat's or buffalo's milk, one may bathe [the deity] with it. || 38 ||
One should offer the Pauruṣa Sūkta, and after that, the Viṣṇu Sūkta;
then, once each, the Aṅga-homa beginning with the syllable Om for the Supreme Self.
One should take ghee that has been freshly heated, possesses a golden luster, and is properly cooked;
however, if worms, insects, moths, or the like are seen in it, then it is not fit ghee.
Having purified it with a cloth, kindled it, and sprinkled water over it, he should bring it back again, while touching it with Vaiṣṇava mantras and those beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. || 41 ||
One should offer oblations with mantras from the Sāmaveda and others, as well as with those dedicated to Viṣṇu;
and one should bathe that God of gods with mantras, endowed with devotion.
If, however, honey is lacking, one should instead fetch water while recollecting the honey;
then, having offered it with a Vaiṣṇava mantra beginning with the Ṛgveda verses, thereafter—
One should bathe the God of gods while reciting the previously mentioned mantra; pure, thick, faultless curd of pleasing appearance should be taken. (44)
One should offer oblations of spoiled curd with the Vaiṣṇava Yajus-mantras and so forth,
and one should also offer the Vyāhṛtis and the Vaiṣṇava mantra beginning with "ato devā".
With the mantra "śānno devī," one should offer twenty oblations each into the milk;
and when the fragrance is lacking, one should indeed offer oblations to its presiding deity along with Viṣṇu.
If unbroken rice grains are unavailable, he should take whatever is available;
having offered oblations according to the Ṛṣi, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Soma rites, he sprinkles [the disciple] with water.
Having taken the fruit according to what is obtained with the Saumya and Vaiṣṇava mantras,
one should cast the tip of a blade of kuśa grass there at the end of the vyāhṛtis in the absence of kuśa.
Having offered oblations to the Ṛṣis, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Aindras, one should proceed;
or, in the absence of gems and precious waters, one may use gold alone.
Then one should worship the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Brāhma, and the Raudra hymns.
If the recitation is deficient, however, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava and Brāhma sacrifices as a substitute for the recitation. || 50 ||
Having offered the Pauruṣa Sūkta and thereafter the Viṣṇu Sūkta,
one should scatter śāli rice grains, or, in the absence of such grains, other medicinal herbs.
One should worship again with meritorious flowers, ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, using mantras dedicated to Āditya, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
in the absence of meritorious flowers, one should use the *dhātṛ-mantra* along with those dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having performed the expiation once, one should collect whatever materials are available;
in the absence of fragrant powders, [one should use] the Cakramantra for the fragrant powders and the Sarvaṣṇava [mantra].
One should likewise rub [the body] with a powder of uśīra and mudga.
When none of the various decoctions or powders are available, one should take the bark of the aśvattha tree for the purpose of the decoction.
Having offered oblations to Varuṇa and Viṣṇu, he should rub [the body] again with that very [substance].
If there is no greed for the water of the sacred ford, he should collect water from other sacred fords or even from a non-sacred source. || 55 ||
One should indeed recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra ending with the Vyāhṛtis once;
however, in the absence of medicinal herbs, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava mantra conjoined with the Raudra.
Having offered the oblation and taken [the remains] as available, one should cleanse with the previously mentioned mantra;
in the absence of all perfumes, one should instead take sandalwood.
Having offered oblations to Indra and Viṣṇu, and thereafter to the Vyāhṛtis, one should wipe [the vessel] with a clean cloth if a *plota* is unavailable;
otherwise, with another washed cloth. || 58 ||
Having offered oblations to Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, one should perform the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
the mantra "Tvaṣṭṛ is the lord of forms" is cited as the Tvaṣṭṛ-mantra. (59)
In the absence of root-fragrance, one should collect the tips of *dūrvā* grass as a substitute for root-fragrance;
having offered oblations to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, accompanied by those dedicated to Prajāpati. || 60 ||
If there is no acquisition of minerals, one should perform the rite with all kinds of minerals such as cinnabar or realgar;
having offered oblations with the Durga-sūkta and the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should proceed with that.
One should apply red arsenic (jātihiṅgulika) to the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and the lips;
and one should apply yellow orpiment (haritāla) and realgar (manaśśilā) to the ornaments and garments.
Collyrium is prescribed for all the limbs, or else for both the eyelashes;
or it may be applied to the eyes, the mouth, or indeed everywhere.

One should indeed adorn [the image] with these very elements according to their proper places. In the case of an ornament or a misplaced ornament, one should perform the Daurga and Vaiṣṇava sacrifices.
If ornaments are not obtained, one should offer oblations with mantras dedicated to Skanda and Viṣṇu;
likewise, when materials have been extracted in error, or when materials have been extracted through delusion or negligence. || 65 ||
Having offered oblations to that deity and twenty-one to Viṣṇu,
[one should act] when the breaking of the pitcher or similar incidents have occurred— such as when the pitcher has been broken, touched by Śūdras and others, or likewise defiled. || 66 ||
Taking another pitcher, one should fill it completely as before;
touching it, one should recite the Vauṣṇava mantra and the mantra dedicated to that deity one hundred times.
And he should offer oblations dedicated to that deity twenty-four times;
furthermore, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations to Viṣṇu and to Brahmā.
If worms,
insects, or moths fall upon substances,
one should always avoid that substance and procure another. (69)
Having offered a hundred oblations to that deity, one should bathe the Lord of Gods again;
or likewise, for the sake of pacifying all defects, during the ritual bathing.
One should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta and then the Viṣṇusūkta;
furthermore, one should offer eighty-eight oblations beginning with the syllable Om for the sake of the Supreme Self.
Then the Śrīsūkta, the Rātrisūkta, and thereafter the Durgāsūkta; these, along with the five Vāruṇa hymns and the Vaiṣṇava hymns beginning with the Jayā, [should be recited].

One should worship the presiding deities of the ritual substances and the deities of the *jaya* and other offerings through their respective forms. This applies when the intended ablution has been obstructed,
when the planned ablution has been omitted, during eclipses, at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and at the solstices (*ayana*).
On a single day, the wise practitioner should offer oblations for great pacification into a fire of lotuses;
he should bathe the deity with double the number of jars according to the prescribed rite.
In this very manner, having performed the growth ceremony, one should cause the ritual bathing to be carried out;
however, one should not perform the bathing while the Lord of Gods has been anointed with oil.
If [the image] has been smeared with oil, there should be no bathing;

rather, having first performed the release of the oil, one should perform the bathing again. If, however, through delusion, a practitioner should bathe [the image] without performing the release of the oil, [there is a fault]. (76)
That shall be an "Asura-bath" for the pacification of that fault;
having performed a propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa) once, one should likewise bathe [the image] again.
If one should bathe [the deity] together with the two goddesses, O Asura, that would be improper;
even in that case, one should bathe the Lord of Gods separately, concluding with the peace-offering (śānti-homa).
For the *beras* that are without specific distinctions, whether they are accompanied by the Goddess or not,

the ritual bathing (*snāpana*) and the *baliberam* must indeed be performed without the Goddess. If one performs the festive bathing (*autsavasnāpana*), it must likewise be performed without the Goddess.
If one performs the festival bath, however, one should perform it without bathing [the image] with the two goddesses.
There too, at the conclusion of the ritual bathing, one should perform the rite together with the two goddesses;
when the bathing is performed in conjunction with the goddesses, the wise man should cause it to be done as previously described.
And here, in the Bali section, is the twenty-sixth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for festivals; now, regarding the expiation for a festival,
[it applies] when the cloth is deficient in measurement, and likewise for the flagstaff.
If there is a deficiency in the characteristics of the banner-cloth and so forth, or if it is devoid of the proper marks, or if the work of painting is inverted,
one should worship the deity of the Garuda-banner one hundred and eight times with the Gāruḍa mantra.
Once the letters have been clearly articulated, one should then perform the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta),
especially in the case of touching that which is untouchable, or when the consecration (pratiṣṭhā-saṃskāra) of the banner has been performed.
If it is touched by Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas, one should bring it back after sprinkling it with water;
likewise if it is touched by Brāhmaṇas who are impure from eating leftovers, or by Śūdras.
Having sprinkled [the site] with seven jars, one should offer oblations to Dhvaja and Garuḍa twenty-seven times; this applies even when kings are defiled by food-leavings or impurities.
Having sprinkled with twenty-four jars, one should perform double the worship;
in the case of contact with a merchant, one should perform double the bathing and the fire-oblation.
If it is touched by those who have eaten leftovers, by the impure, by Śūdras, by those of inverse birth (pratiloma),
by a woman in her courses, or by a woman who has recently given birth, then the water-pots must be purified with eight hundred kusa-grass blades.
Having performed the bathing, one should perform the previously mentioned fire-oblation (homa) twice as much;
then, as before, one should again perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the deity of the banner.
If one is touched by someone of the same caste through natural order (anuloma), the penance is as stated for a Kṣatriya;
if touched by one called an Abhiṣikta, one should perform the expiation prescribed for a Vaiśya.
In the case of contact with others who are not of a lower order, one should perform the expiation prescribed for a Śūdra;
however, where no expiation has been mentioned, it should be determined by distinguishing between the castes and classes.
One should perform the prescribed expiation according to that very sequence;
in all cases, one should effect purification by means of the circumambulation with fire and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
When the flagstaff is inverted during the time of hoisting the flag— when the flag is thus upside down—
one should perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) and offer one hundred and eight oblations into the fire for the sake of the flag.
Having likewise performed the Gāruḍa rite and sprinkled [the flagstaff] with seven jars,
and having worshipped it and offered the ritual food (naivedya), one should again hoist the banner.

Having performed this in the event of the breaking of the staff, as well as the breaking of the banner, and likewise the breaking of the supports for the poles, one should collect another in the same manner. || 14 ||
In the event of the flagstaff falling or similar incidents, one should worship the Gāruḍa and Vaiṣṇava deities;
having sprinkled it with consecrated waters, one should thereafter properly re-erect the flagstaff there.
In the event of the destruction or breaking of the banner, one should offer oblations to the fire-god, to Garuḍa,
and likewise to the banners of Indra and Viṣṇu, and then have that very banner restored.
Having invoked Garuḍa there, one should again mount him upon the banner;
however, one should not perform the circumambulation of the village nor the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali). || 17 ||
When the remaining days have been completed, one should lower that banner.
However, if the banner-lifting ceremony was omitted, the deities of the world-protectors [must be worshipped]. || 98 ||
One should worship the Prājāpatya, the Raudra, and the Viṣṇu-sūkta in their proper sequence;
however, one should not perform the hoisting of the flag on the same day or on two consecutive days.
Some say that one should not perform [the rite] even on the festival day of Dinatrāya;
and regarding the faults mentioned and those not mentioned, there is an expiation for the banner as well.
One should worship the Dhvaja and the Gāruḍa again ten times when the festival of time is obstructed,
or when it is performed annually [but irregularly], or when the festival of time has been neglected or abandoned.
In the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, the festival lasts for as many days as there are [syllables] in the Mahāśānti mantra;
for that many days, one should offer oblations with devotion. || 22 ||
One should joyfully give as many cows along with their calves as there were [days],
or else one may give the wealth that constitutes the value of the festival.
Having bathed [the deity] with one hundred and eight jars,
having worshipped with all ritual services, and having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis), || 24 ||
Having performed a great worship, he should also cause the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) rite to be recited;
and having praised the Lord of Gods with the Viṣṇusūkta and the Puruṣasūkta.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the festival once again;
some say that one should properly conduct the festival twice as grand. || 26 ||
This is recorded as the expiation for the sacrifice of worship with a physical image:
if the preceptor is pregnant at the time of the hoisting of the flag. || 27 ||

If the Great Festival of the Sacred Thread (pavitra) is performed every year during the great festival, it is declared that the daily rite has been accomplished; thus, there is no need for the initiation of conception (garbhadīkṣā).

O twice-born ones, the husband of a pregnant woman who is also his preceptor should perform the rites of sprinkling and other such duties, as well as other obligatory rites, starting from the third month of her pregnancy.
"One should not perform the ancestral Śrāddha meal nor the sesame oblation (tilahoma); such indeed is the rule.
[One should avoid] bathing in the Sindhu river, performing Śrāddha at Gayā, shaving, and carrying out the deceased."
One should not undertake the climbing of mountains; such is the rule.
However, one may do so after having increased the merit for each successive year. || 31 ||
On a low day, or likewise on a single [specific] day of that festival of time, one should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta and with the six Vaiṣṇava [hymns]. || 32 ||
With the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, with the Brāhma mantras, and also with the Aindra and Vaiṣṇava mantras, [he worshipped] the forms of the attendants residing in that temple. || 33 ||
Having bathed [the deity] with water-pots and worshipped him thoroughly, one should present the offerings;
then, in the very same sequence previously described, one should perform the festival once again.
Having increased [the merit], one should practice thus day by day, day by day;
having celebrated the festival of the past, one should again perform the remainder. || 35 ||
Some perform the festival twice daily; others do so when the day is deficient. When the single-time festival is omitted, one should perform the previously mentioned oblation (homa). || 36 ||
One should likewise celebrate a festival and perform the remaining rites as previously prescribed;
when the deity has mounted the vehicle at the time of wandering through the streets. (37)
During a chariot procession, when faults are apprehended;
during a quarrel, the shedding of blood, or a great portent; when a person has died;
and when the wheels of the chariot become stuck, resulting in the death of men. (38)
Having wandered through the remaining path in a clockwise direction, and having entered the temple and descended the Lord of Gods; || 39 ||

O Lord, having bathed [the image] according to the rules with seven jars, the learned man should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). || 40 ||
In particular, one should offer mung-bean rice to the Lord;
having recited the mantra of forgiveness, one should also perform a prostration. || 41 ||
O best of sages, listen as I proclaim the types of mantras for forgiveness;
[whether an offense was committed] through ignorance, greed for wealth, passion, hatred, or negligence. || 42 ||
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by me, or by my sons, or even by my kinsmen. (43)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the preceptor, the priest, the devotees, or the attendants. (44)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the king, or by the king’s servants, or even by his ministers. (45)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the village leaders, the villagers, or even the guardians of the village. (46)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by the singers, the dancers, or likewise by the players of musical instruments. (47)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed by me, born of ignorance, regarding worship performed without mantras. (48)
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever fault I have committed through my actions performed according to the prescribed rules, beginning with prostrations and ending with the dismissal. 49.
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever offense has been committed;
I offer to you leaves, flowers, fruits, and water according to my ability. (50)
O Janārdana, please accept this offered oblation;
I do not know how to perform the invocation, nor do I know how to perform the dismissal.
In deed, thought, or word, there is no other refuge for me but you;
you move within all beings, you are the witness, the Lord of the universe. 52.
O Lord, in whichever of the thousands of wombs I may enter, may my devotion to You, the Infallible One, remain forever undeviating. (53)
The god is both the giver and the enjoyer; the god is this entire world.
Since the god triumphs everywhere, you yourself are indeed the god. 54.

O Lord of the World, even for Brahmā and the other gods, it is impossible to perform worship according to the prescribed rules in a manner free from the defects of deficiency, excess, or contradiction.
How much less so for us, men of little knowledge and unstable minds? Therefore, whatever lack of splendor has arisen during our daily worship— || 56 ||
O Viṣṇu, by this worship may everything be peaceful for us,
through these offerings performed by me day after day under the guise of ritual service.
"O Supreme Person, forgive all these transgressions;
thus, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should pray for complete expiation. (58)
"I do not know the portion for the worship; you are my refuge, O Supreme Person.
Having thus praised him and entered the sacrificial hall, they danced. || 59 ||
The method for the peace-offering (śānti-homa): Having established the Pauṇḍarīka fire, one should offer oblations of clarified butter in due order,
reciting the Vaiṣṇava, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Then one should offer oblations of the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
one should also offer oblations beginning with the syllable "IṂ" and perform the Vāstu-homa.

One should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) in the event of falling raindrops and the like, as well as along the pathway; one should also sprinkle [the area] according to the prescribed rule during the festival of the God of Gods when it is drenched by raindrops. || 62 ||
Likewise, having brought the image, covered it with another cloth,
dressed it, performed the great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti), and offered oblations, one should bathe it with one hundred and eight [pots of water].
Combined with *bhārata* rice and mixed with half a *dhara* of sesame seeds, along with three *niṣkas* of gold and betel leaf once more. || 64 ||
Having made the offering at the time of the festival, one should perform the prescribed expiation;
likewise, if the worship and other rites for the God of gods and the two goddesses are deficient by twice the amount, whether in the evening, in the morning, or during the festival.
If the oblation is doubled while the worship is deficient, or if the worship is doubled while the oblation is deficient,
one should offer the Vaiṣṇava and Viṣṇu-sūkta mantras there four times over.
Having performed worship with various oblations, one should duly offer four times as much;
if the oblation is deficient by two parts, there is a loss for those who do not depart [from their duty].
Having honored them with double [the usual] devotion, one should offer double [the usual] gifts;
for it is the injunction that when the festival-circle is deficient, one must not perform a festival that lacks the circle. || 68 ||
Or else, for the sake of a festival, one should have that [image] made for those who do not depart;
some say that one should request a discus and a *balibera* [offering vessel]. (69)

When the requested rite is completed, one should lead [the deity] back to its former abode; having established it there and performed the propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa), one should install it in its original place. || 70 ||

Having invoked [the deity] into the vessel and the flowers for the pacification of obstacles, one should properly perform the rite; however, if the fire-oblation (homa) was omitted, one should offer twice as much according to the prescribed rule.
If the worship of the deities residing in the water-pot (kumbha) is deficient,

or if the worship of the deities residing in the water-pot is performed only in the evening and morning, or if even one among the eleven ritual offerings (upacāras) is omitted during that worship; || 72 ||
One should cause the performance of the expiation prescribed for the deficiency in worship;
furthermore, one should again perform sacrifice to the deities stationed in the jars by means of their names.
Having worshipped again with double the intensity, one should offer double the oblation.
This applies when the water-pot is touched by those who should not be touched, or when the pot is touched by dogs, crows, and other such impure beings. || 74 ||
Having performed the expiation prescribed for the installation, one should bring another water-pot;
[this applies] when the worship of the Anapāyins is deficient, or when the sacrifice of the Viśāna, Pāyipaṅkti, and Sānta deities is omitted in the sacrificial pavilion.
But if the worship is inferior, he should offer oblations into the fire of that direction with those mantras;
if there is the threefold fire (tretāgni), he should sacrifice in the Āhavanīya fire for one who is tranquil.
One should offer oblations for all [the fires] in the Sabhya fire when arranging the single fire;
having worshipped it twofold, one should present the offerings twofold as well. || 77 ||
One should perform the penance in this manner for each day that has passed;
provided, however, that the fire is not the perpetual (nitya) one—that is, if the fire other than the perpetual fire is brought into the sacrificial pit. || 78 ||
Therefore, a festival is fruitless; hence, having perpetually established the fire and offered oblations, one should perform twice as many homas and then celebrate the festival again.
From the day of the consecration until the end of the festival, one should maintain the sacred fire without interruption;
for if the village and the army are diminished,
so too shall the deities perish along with their respective images.
One should also offer oblations to Vaiṣṇava, ending each with the Vyāhṛtis;
thereafter, having given the village offering (bali), one should perform the festival once again.
The wise man should construct the assembly pavilion for chewing the betel-leaves in the intermediate directions or the cardinal directions;
he should arrange it facing east or facing south.
The supreme instructor should fashion [the image] according to the divisions of five cubits and so forth;
having installed the deity there, he should worship it in due order with water for the feet and other offerings.
One should cause entertainments such as dance and song to be performed before his face according to the prescribed rite, and one should offer a handful of flowers at his feet.
Otherwise, in the event of a failure in duty, both the king and the kingdom perish;
therefore, with every effort, one should act in accordance with what has been stated. || 85 ||
Regarding the possible defects that may arise at the time of the circumambulation of the offering (balibhramaṇa):
