"If, at the moment of the circumambulation of the offering, a Caṇḍāla or a woman who has recently given birth should enter by mistake, one should immediately lead [the image] to the temple of Cakrādi. (86)
Upon the conclusion of the *cakra* rite, having separately bathed the *viśa*, the *bali*, and the *bera* with seven jars of water, one should likewise sprinkle the *bali*.
One should perform one hundred and eight offerings with the mantras of Cakrī, Īśa, and Amita, as well as with Vaiṣṇava mantras, and with the two mantras for Bali and Rakṣaka. || 88 ||

Having purified the pathway with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having offered the remaining oblation (śiṣṭabali), one should then complete the ritual once again. || 89 ||
During a festival, when a corpse falls upon a street, one should purify the street on all sides by means of the circumambulation with fire and the five products of the cow.

Having offered the bali-oblation with the mantras of the world-protectors as before, and having performed the fire-sacrifice, one should arrange the festive offerings and other rites as previously prescribed. || 91 ||
If death occurs within that village boundary, one should quickly remove that corpse, perform the previously mentioned expiation, and carry out the remaining rites. || 92 ||
One should never bring a corpse alone into the presence of Keśava;
for if it were brought there, it would lead to the destruction of both the village and the sacrificer.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying those defects, one should have the Vāstu-homa performed;
and there, the wise man should likewise perform the Śānti and the Mahāśānti by means of oblations.
Even for one devoid of ornaments,
having fed the Brahmins, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor,
as well as golden ornaments and garments of various colors. || 95 ||
If the temple ornaments are deficient, one should indeed worship with the Śrīsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns, using many fragrant substances, flowers, and especially garlands. || 96 ||
If the decoration of the deity is deficient, one should recite the Mahīsūkta and the Vaiṣṇava hymns;
likewise, if the chariot, the chariot-stand, the swing, or even the palanquin is deficient [in its adornment]. || 97 ||

A wise man should not perform a festival for the God of gods when the ornaments are inferior, nor when the sacrificial offering is deficient, nor when the offering is doubled [in excess], nor when it is deficient. || 98 ||
If the vehicle or its ornaments are deficient, one should worship Vaiṣṇava and Gāruḍa;
but if the banner is missing, one should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava banner-mantra.
If it is devoid of other attendants and lacks dancing and singing, [the rites] of Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu [are prescribed];
but if it lacks the white umbrella and so forth, those of Soma, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa [should be performed]. || 100 ||
If the ritual implements are inferior, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava Śrī-mantra;
but if it is devoid of perfumes and incense, one should worship the Bārhaspatya mantra along with the Vaiṣṇava.
One should perform the oblation with the mantras of the Ṛṣis, accompanied by the Brāhma-mantras;
however, if the lamp is extinguished, one should offer oblations with the Saura, Āgneya, and Vaiṣṇava mantras.
If the hymn of praise is omitted, one should offer oblations to the deities of the directions along with Viṣṇu;
if the preceptor and others are deficient, one should offer oblations to Bṛhaspati along with Viṣṇu.
One should perform the oblation with the mantras of the Ṛṣis, accompanied by the Brāhma-mantras;
for in the festival, in the consecration, and likewise in the ritual bathing and other rites, the dignity of the preceptor is paramount.
In the absence of a Guru, one should perform everything for those seeking other goals;
however, in the absence of a teacher as prescribed, one should not undertake the festival of Hari.
For he gathers the meaning of the scriptures and establishes it in right conduct;
therefore, the instructor of all duties is called the Ācārya. || 106 ||
Having become one with the inferior retinue, one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta along with the Vaiṣṇava hymns;
with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should perform oblations in the inferior circumambulation of the abode.
If the bathing of the deity is deficient or omitted, one should offer the water-mantra associated with Viṣṇu and the Vāruṇa mantra;
then one should bathe the deity again as before.
Regarding the absence of the fault of touch during a festival:
"Those people who have come there for the purpose of attending Viṣṇu’s festival are all equal to Brahmins, even those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) and the like. (109)
Therefore, contact with one who is untouchable does not result in fault for him who bathes during the festival of the God of gods for the sake of that touch. 110.
The ancestors dwelling in heaven certainly fall into hell if the conclusion of the festival is devoid of ritual offerings,
if worship at the end of the festival is omitted, and likewise if the sacrificial oblation (havis) is lacking. || 111 ||
Having offered that Vaiṣṇava mantra, one should worship it twice;
one should offer double the sacrificial oblation, and having prostrated, say, "Forgive me."
At the conclusion of the expiation, however, one should perform the remaining rites as before.
If there is a delay during a festival, or if the time has passed, one should offer oblations and [feed] a hundred Vaiṣṇava Brahmins.
One should offer the Mindā oblations, perform the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise worship;
having begun the festival in the morning at the desired time, it should be concluded at midday. || 114 ||
In the evening, after the evening worship and before one watch (yāma) has passed, let it be completed;
or [the morning rite] may be performed from the time of the morning ritual until evening, or even only in the evening.
If the secondary [rite] is deficient, one should perform the secondary expiation;
likewise, if the primary [rite] is deficient, one should perform the primary [expiation]; such is the teaching of the ancient sages. || 116 ||

If the two offerings (balis) fall, or even if the two offerings fall, having likewise worshipped the two offerings again, and having properly worshipped the Lord of Gods and offered the sacrificial oblation (havis), [one should proceed]. || 117 ||
Having worshipped the guardian of the offering, one should offer gold into the two fires;
having propitiated the offering according to the rite, one should then raise up another.
If the image has fallen—
that is, if the image has collapsed on the ground— one should quickly lift it up again,
bathe it with pure water, pay homage to it, and worship it.
Having praised the Lord with the Viṣṇusūkta and the Ekākṣara-sūkta and others,
and having consecrated him with twenty-four jars, || 120 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] and offered [the oblation], one should indeed offer a hundred oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire;
having praised [Viṣṇu] with the "viṣṇornuka" hymns and others, one should perform the festival in due order.
Once the image has fallen upon the ground, one should bathe it with its respective mantras or with the forms of its respective deities, for those who are peaceful and never depart.
For the pacification of that fault, the Vaiṣṇavas, having performed the rite with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, should worship that Lord of Gods and conduct a festival. || 123 ||
When the pedestal is separated from the vehicle, when the image falls upon the pedestal, or when the image is separated from the pedestal;
when the pedestal is broken, as well as its radiance, umbrella, weapons, ornaments, and so forth.

Having perceived the power (śakti) residing within that image and having deposited it into the water-vessel (kumbha), one should perform the purification of the image by joining together those parts that are broken or fallen away. || 125 ||
Having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should perform the ceremonial bathing;
and having performed the Mahāśānti sacrifice, one should perform the consecration once again. || 126 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] and offered [the oblation], one should perform the festival once again;
and if the image has fallen or is missing a limb,
one should install a *śakti* within it if it is stable.
Having performed the ritual for the abandonment of the worn-out image and having dismissed it,
one should then fashion a new image and install it according to the prescribed rules.
The instruction is that one should commence and perform the festival once again;
then, the remainder of the festival may be performed either with curiosity or with worship. 129.
Some say that one should perform a festival and have an image fashioned;
one should act in this very same way for Cakrin, Viśa, Amita, and the others.
One should offer oblations a thousand times with the aforementioned mantras and the [mantras of the] Mūrtis;
and whenever there is a collapse of vehicles, one should perform the Gāruḍa-homa.

In the event of the collapse of the chariot, the stage, or other structures, one who is skilled in the ritual procedures should perform oblations to the Brahman and Viṣṇu deities and have those [structures] repaired as before. || 132 ||
In the event of the downfall of singers and others, or upon the fall of the singer and the dancer, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for Śrīdevī;
likewise in the case of agitation, reviling, or cursing of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the preceptor (ācārya). || 133 ||
If there is a killing by anyone, having offered oblations with fourteen mantras belonging to the Ṛṣis and six belonging to Viṣṇu, one should again set the ritual into motion.
If someone kills them, one should perform oblations with fourteen verses of the sages (ārṣaka) and six verses dedicated to Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇava), and then cause the ritual action to proceed again.
In the event of the falling of lamp-vessels and the like, as well as the extinguishing of lamps, one should worship with the Āgneya and Vaiṣṇava [mantras].
And in the case of the falling of incense and other offerings, one should worship with the four Bārhaspatya [mantras]. || 135 ||
In the event of the falling of chowries and the like, or by anyone setting them on fire, as well as in the case of the falling of those who hold them or of fans; || 136 ||
Having worshipped Māyāsaṃhlādinī, Kiṣkindha, and Sundara,
as well as the deity Vāyu, one should perform a Vaiṣṇava fire-oblation (homa).
In the event of contact with fire or similar damage to the banner, or when the banner falls or is consumed by fire, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava banner.
In the case of a quarrel among devotees, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, one should worship both the Brāhma and the Vaiṣṇava [forms].
In the event of the collapse of musical instruments, players, and so forth, one should worship Nandīśa;
having offered oblations to the Brahman, Vaiṣṇava, and Saura [fires], one should commence the ritual action.
In a quarrel among those seeking wealth,
in a quarrel involving the shedding of blood,
and when a person has died due to other portents— all that indeed [is to be known].
Having thoroughly purified all of that during the Vāstuhoma and the consecration ceremony, [one should proceed].
One should offer oblations with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Vaiṣṇava hymn, and the Pauruṣa hymn in sequence,
as well as with the mantras of the assembly (pariṣad) and the gaṇas, while recollecting the God of gods.
And with mantras, oblations are offered into the fires that are the limbs of the festival;
likewise, one should bind the *kautuka* (protective amulet) for the sake of the sacred bathing (*tīrtha*) during the first part of the night, when the binding of the *kautuka* has been performed.
However, due to negligence, one should not fail to bind on the protective amulet (pratisara) in the morning;
having offered oblations with the Vāruṇa and Vaiṣṇava mantras, as well as the mantra of the deity of that particular day.
Having performed the binding of the *pratisarā*, one should likewise cause it to be done again; however,
if the bed is deficient or if the deity's seat there is deficient, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for the two goddesses.

If one should perform the festival even in the absence of a festival for the sake of a rite of wonder, the binding of the protective thread (kautuka) must take place immediately at the end of the morning twilight worship. || 145 ||
Having performed the festival and the pilgrimage, one should perform [the rite] immediately;
there is a special rule for the equinoxes and so forth, as well as for the equinox, the solstices, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 146 ||

If that [festival] is the ritual bath (bhṛtha) of the festival, then having performed the immediate tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka), one should properly carry out both the festival and the pilgrimage (tīrtha) at the appropriate time. || 147 ||
If it should be the time of the Tīrthakas in the past, one should offer oblations with the Vāruṇa, Skanda,
and Viṣṇu-sūktas, and then perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford.
The time for the sacred bath (tīrtha) should be at midday or during the forenoon endowed with auspicious qualities.
In the case of a bath at the end of the sacred site that is deficient [in merit], the deities of the directions along with Viṣṇu [should be worshipped].
Having offered oblations with the Viṣṇu-sūkta, one should perform the bathing ceremony again;
indeed, when the Mahāhavis offering is deficient, it should be performed by the Vaiṣṇavas using the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
He offers oblations with both the Vaiṣṇava and the Prājāpatya hymns;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods once again, he indeed presents the great offering.
Having offered praise with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and Vaiṣṇava hymns, he should place flowers at the feet [of the deity] while reciting those mantras ending with "Forgive me. (152)
There is an absence of impurity during the initiation for a festival;

however, for the sake of a festival or for the installation of the deity, once the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) has been performed previously, [impurity lasts] until the conclusion of each respective rite. || 153 ||
One should know that there is no impurity for a teacher, whether it be due to birth (sūtaka) or death (pretaka);
for one who has been formally chosen [as officiant], there is no impurity except upon his own death, nor indeed after the commencement of those respective rites.

"The instruction of the ancestors is that [the period lasts] until the conclusion of each respective rite; and Kṣatriyas and others shall likewise observe the impurity prescribed for their caste in every respect. (155)
For them, there is no selection accompanied by mantras, nor is there initiation from another;
this applies even to Śūdras who are devotees, as well as to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. (156)
For those engaged in the service of the gods, there is no lightening of the period of impurity at all.
O best of sages, if one desires to perform the worship of the incarnations, it is the festival of the incarnations [that must be observed]. (157)
The wise man should likewise cause the festival of the five preceding [incarnations] to be celebrated,
as well as the festival of Kalkin and the remaining four.
And for them as well, one should raise the banner marked with the fish;
this is a specific initiation for the purpose of a festival, or else for the purpose of the deity's consecration. || 159 ||
If there are obstacles to the festival or the day by means of such things as disturbances in the kingdom, great portents, or the affliction of fear from famine;
When those days have passed, the king’s kingdom perishes;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause [the rites] to be performed on the days specified.
If the king desires a festival on those days at midnight,
the rite of shaving is prescribed for both the preceptor and the officiating priests.
"Even at midnight, the rite may be performed," so said Śātātapa;
"there shall be no fault in a rite for the gods"—such is the teaching of the ancient sages.
During the festival of the deity, or specifically above that sacred site,
one should duly perform the festival of the Goddess according to the prescribed injunctions. || 160 ||
First, one should perform the rite of granting fearlessness to the Lord of the Gods, and afterwards worship the two Goddesses;
for their festival, one should perform the offering of sprouts separately for each.
In the first part of the night, having especially worshipped the Lord of Gods,
one should place the marriage-thread (kautuka) upon rice in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
Having properly performed the circumambulation, one should carry— either on the head or on a shoulder-pole— the village or the monastery itself, adorned with ornaments.
Having renounced [the ritual] before the deity, having touched [the child] at the conclusion of the auspicious day (puṇyāha),
and having tied the protective cord (pratisara), he should look upon [the child] and likewise lay him down on the bed.
Having worshipped the deity in the morning and established him in the pavilion for the assembly, having bathed him, worshipped him thoroughly, and offered abundant food, || 165 ||
Having adorned [the image] with garments and various ornaments, one should properly perform another festival as prescribed for festive occasions. (166)
Having bathed [the deity] once more and worshipped it thoroughly, one should offer [the offerings];
on the following day, one should likewise offer the splendor of ornaments.
Having performed the ritual application and the festival, and having bathed [the image] as before,
one should worship it thoroughly, present the offerings, and then install it in the seat of the living soul (jīvasthāna).
One should perform a festival for those four [deities] according to the sequence of their descent, in whichever temple the daily worship of these descents is performed. (169)
There, following the sequence of descent, one should perform the festival without haste;
thus, through various forms, the practice proceeds through those successive stages.
If one desires to perform worldly festivals with devotion, one should perform everything in this very manner, beginning with the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 171 ||
Even when worldly festivals are being performed,
one should always perform [the ritual] at evening and morning before the image during the festival.
The prohibition of festivals is indeed different;
however, when a festival for the gods of gods is already being performed, one should not perform another festival. || 173 ||
And there shall be no fault regarding other matters pertaining to the site during the festival;
for when the banner of Viṣṇu has been raised there, it is indeed for the sake of the festival.
However, until that final conclusion, the wise man should not perform the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration);
rather, he should preserve all its constituent parts and merely install them. 175.
Prohibition of other festivals in the village:
In that village, one should not perform any festival for human beings. (176)
A festival for Viṣṇu on another day is not at all a cause for fault;
however, his lunar festival has been defiled by the festival of Agni. (177)
Prohibition against villagers leaving for elsewhere:
When the banner of Viṣṇu has been raised specifically for the sake of the festival, all the inhabitants of that village [must remain] until before the concluding bath of the festival. || 178 ||
Otherwise, if diseases depart from the house, they will certainly not affect those living outside the village or its premises. (179)
If the primary focus were the ritual procedure of the festival itself, I shall explain the specific details here; listen, O best of sages! (180)
One should decorate the sacrificial hall and have an altar constructed in its center;
having placed one water-pot there, one should likewise place Garuḍa to its east.
Having arranged the vehicle in the south and the discus itself in the west,
and Viṣvaksena in the north, according to the prescribed rite.
Having likewise invoked the two goddesses into the pitcher and worshipped them,
one should worship the deities of their retinue upon the pedestal according to the prescribed rite.
In this very manner, according to the ritual injunctions, day after day at morning and evening,
one should arrange those respective fires on the eastern side of the pitcher-altar.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is as stated in the *Khila* section.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement in Great Festivals," in the section on Rituals (*Kriyādhikāra*) within the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu, the venerable *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*.
Oṃ.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: Expiation for Entering a Place Where Untouchables Have Entered.
Hereafter, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall proclaim the expiation, the expiation.
[One should not eat] with Caṇḍālas, those born from a woman after childbirth, menstruating women, outcasts, and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma). || 1 ||
Once they have entered the womb-chamber and likewise touched the image,
one should then perform a great propitiatory rite for seven nights by offering oblations into the fire of lotus-wood.
Having performed the ritual immersion in water for both mobile and immobile objects,
and having likewise performed the purification of the fixed [image], one should perform the consecration once again.
If the image is likewise touched by Śūdras or those born of the anuloma castes,
one should bathe it with one hundred and eight jars of water and perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once again.
Upon the entry of dogs, cocks, boars, or jackals,
and likewise upon touching them, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
Furthermore, one should perform the consecration again by means of the path of re-consecration;
however, if a Caṇḍāla or similar person has entered during the first enclosure, [the rite must be repeated].
Having performed the Vāstuhoma, he offers the Śāntihoma;
likewise, he should bathe the deity with one hundred and eight jars.
In the second enclosure, there should be a bath with one hundred and eight [offerings];
having offered the pacifying oblation, it is likewise done with twenty-four [offerings] in the third.
Having caused [the altar] to be strewn with grass and having worshipped it with water-jars, one should present the offerings;
if it is in the fourth enclosure, however, one should offer twenty-one Vaiṣṇava [oblations].
Having offered oblations and caused [the image] to be bathed with seven jars, one should worship it;
however, if it is the fifth [image], one should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite ten times.
Having offered oblations and caused [the deity] to be bathed with five jars, one should worship [him];
one should sacrifice twenty times to the deities of the respective assemblies according to their specific types.
Even at the sixth enclosure, having bathed [the deity] with seven jars according to the rule, one should cause the declaration of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited.
If, however, it is desired that all movement occurs on the seventh enclosure,
Bhṛgu stated that there is no fault in their entering onto the path.
If they are inside the inner apartments, one should perform their bathing with water;
but if they are outside, one should do so a hundred times with the respective Vaiṣṇava mantra.
"Having performed the oblation, one should cause [the image] to be bathed with seven jars; this is the instruction.
Purification by means of the circumambulation with fire and the five products of the cow is proclaimed for all cases. (15)
One should never worship that God of gods in a dwelling situated in the reverse order near a temple, even if it be a great one. || 16 ||
If it should adhere to the rampart, a great calamity will arise;
then there will be great fear for the kingdom, the sacrificer, and the village. || 17 ||
Having removed it very quickly according to the prescribed rule within seven nights,
and having performed a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) with oblations, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) once again.
Within a distance of one hundred daṇḍas, there shall be dwellings for those born in the inverse order;
and for Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas, one should designate a location more than one krośa away.
Now the expiation for death within the womb-chamber shall be declared;
furthermore, one should perform whatever has been prescribed regarding the entry of Caṇḍālas and others. || 20 ||
If it is in the first enclosure, it is declared to be exactly so;
likewise in the case of death occurring outside in the halls attached to the hall. || 21 ||
In the same way, at the time of death, one should perform the Mahāśānti sacrifice once;
having strewn the ground and worshipped the deity with water-pots, one should present the offerings.
Having taken it out of ignorance, he runs toward a well containing a corpse within;
yet, if he should worship with that and even offer the cooked oblation (havis), [it is not accepted]. || 23 ||
Having offered one hundred Vaiṣṇava oblations accompanied by the "yad devā" hymn, and having bathed [the image] with water-pots, he should worship it and present the offerings. || 24 ||
Regarding the burning by fire of pavilions and the like, the tradition of the ancestors holds that if it occurs otherwise [than prescribed], there is great fault;
this applies to the pavilion, the city gate, and likewise to the water-shed. (25)
Having performed a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) upon a fire-disaster, one should bathe Hari;
likewise in the case of the burning of garments and such, or a fire in the inner sanctum (garbhālaya), or the burning of a cloth, a garland, or an ornament.

If a divine image is touched by fire, or if there is contact with fire upon the image, one should quickly remove that [image] and perform a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) for seven nights, along with bathing it with scented water. || 27 ||

Furthermore, having performed the re-consecration and worshipped [the deity] thoroughly, one should present the offerings. In the event of the destruction of the image by fire, or when the image is destroyed by a fire that has consumed it, one should remove that image from its shrine. || 28 ||

Having performed the Mahāśānti rite for one month, and having again purified the womb-chamber with the circumambulation of fire and the five products of the cow, and having smeared it [with cow dung], || 29 ||
Having taken up another image, one should again perform the rite of installation;
a wooden or earthen image that has been overtaken by smoke should be worshipped [only] by others.

If one abandons even a beautiful mountain that is overtaken by flames, then, just as the space within a jar dissolves into the universal space when the jar is broken, [so too does the individual soul merge]. || 31 ||
Likewise, when the fire has been extinguished, the power remains pervading the entire universe;
having established the station of the planet in the fire of Brahmā and likewise in the abode.

Having offered the Mahāśānti oblation into the lotus-fire, he also performs the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti) by offering oblations there into the fire-pits for each respective planet in the eight directions.

Having offered the five elemental oblations into the central fire with the mantra dedicated to each respective deity, and having approached the image while reciting "Obeisance to Brahman," [one should proceed]. (34)
Having uttered "Namo vāce," one should recite [the mantra] while touching the water in the jar;
then, by means of sprinklings, one should circumambulate the village in a clockwise direction and sprinkle it. || 35 ||
Having bathed the deity with water-pots and worshipped him thoroughly, one should present the offerings;
thereafter, until the final re-installation, one should worship him daily upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
If the image has been touched by a snake,
or if there is contact with a snake upon the image, or when entering the inner sanctum,
one should purify the garments, garlands, and other offerings, and then consecrate them with pure waters. || 37 ||
One should perform the purification for the permanent image (dhruvabera) as previously prescribed for the consecration;
if the image is touched by food remnants or other impure things, one should act as stated before. || 38 ||
In the event of contact with those who lack qualification, Brahmins, or others, one should bathe the Lord with two, three, or four times as many jars respectively;
however, upon contact with a prostitute, one should bathe the Lord with eight hundred jars.
With forty-eight kings who have been consecrated,
and with officiating brahmins who are pure and have performed their ablutions, one should perform the consecration upon that which has been touched by them.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, an anointed kṣatriya should behave in every respect like a brāhmaṇa,
even upon touching one who has committed a mortal sin or when he is under royal authority.
O ascetics, one should perform the expiation according to the rules as prescribed in reverse order when there is the destruction of the image,
or when the single-liṅga (ekabera) has become worn out, or when it is deficient in its limbs, according to the Ekaberakalpa.
One should procure a wooden image according to one's means and with due honor; having invoked the deity into it, one should worship him in the place of the child. || 43 ||
Having installed one of those two in the abode of the child and worshipped it, one should perform the re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā) after restoring it as it was before. || 46 ||
If there is fear of thieves, enemies, and the like regarding either a single stone or metal [image], it is improper to perform worship there;
rather, one should install a stone image there instead.
"One should fashion [the deity] out of iron, wood, or stone; such is the injunction.
In the event of the collapse of the site of the inner sanctum, or when anthills and the like arise upon the site of the inner sanctum... (48)
Having established the pitcher according to the previously mentioned procedure and having invoked [the deity] therein,
one should indeed offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Vaiṣṇava mantras along with the [deity's] forms.
Having installed [the deity] in the pavilion of the face within the locations prescribed for the abode of the child,
one should perform the daily worship there and make the site firm.
One should again invoke the deities into the image, the water-pot, and so forth, by means of the rite of installation;
one should worship the deities residing in the inner sanctum around the water-pot.
In the case of a permanent image (dhruvabera) especially when it is afflicted by the aforementioned defects,
one should quickly construct a children's temple (bālālaya) in the prescribed location according to the rules.
If the secondary alternative (anukalpa) involves even a slight fault, one should not construct a house for the child;
rather, having properly placed the power (śakti) residing within that [child] into a water-pot (kumbha). || 53 ||
Taking the pitcher and the image from the middle line toward the south—either in the pavilion, in the intermediate space, or even in the garland-hall. || 54 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) there according to the prescribed rule, one should worship until the end of twelve days;
but after twelve days, one should prepare the fire-pit for the child. || 55 ||
One should prepare the sacrificial hall facing the direction of the child's lethargy,
as well as the bed-altar, the five fire-pits, and the surrounding enclosure.
Having prepared either one or the sabhya fire-altar on the eastern side of the bed-altar on the previous day,
and having performed the evening twilight worship (sandhyā), || 57 ||
Then, to the north of the child’s dwelling, one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice;
one should purify the child’s chamber with the circumambulation of fire and the five products of the cow. || 58 ||
And everywhere in the sacrificial hall, he should again cause the proclamation of an auspicious day;
then, at the conclusion of the night worship, having worshipped the God of gods.
Having offered the oblation according to the rite and having prostrated with the words "Forgive me," one should then perform the sequence for the installation of the shrine of the Child (Bāla),
and having established the perpetual fire, one should perform the Āghāra libation in the sacrificial pits.
Having consecrated the jar as before, one should place it well upon a pedestal of grain in front of the deity, within the space between the two Yamas, and pray as previously described.
Having installed the deity in the pitcher according to the prescribed rite, starting from the permanent image (dhruvabera),
[one should likewise install] the deities situated within the womb-chamber (garbhālaya), the lords of the doors, and the door-keepers.

One should visualize the deities seated upon the steps within the water of that jar, as well as the celestial chariot; and if it is old, one should likewise visualize the four [guardians], such as the Yakṣas.
And some [say that] the deities of the assembly being worshipped on the pedestal;
having taken up the image of Kumṛbha, they bathe it and place it upon a white elephant.
Having bathed him with seven jars and likewise bound the protective cord (pratisara),
and having laid him down, he praises the office of the Hotṛ priest at the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
Then, having summoned the deities residing in the Ālaya as before,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter and perform the sacrifice according to the sequence of invocation.
One should worship the attendants all around the sacrificial hall and perform the rite of oblation (homa) according to the very sequence prescribed for the installation ceremony.
Having recited the *pariṣan-mantras* with the *vyāhṛtis*, he indeed offers oblations into the *dākṣiṇāgni*;
and even without [the other two fires], he performs the *sabhyahoma*, which is the offering to all the deities.
One should pass the remainder of the night in due order with dances, songs, and instrumental music;
then, having bathed in the morning according to the prescribed rules, one should likewise recite the hymns (sūktas).
One should likewise construct the pedestal for the image in a temple of Brahmā or a childhood abode;
however, on a pedestal in a movable zodiac sign, one should especially perform the rite of jewel-depositation (ratnanyāsa) without [other elaborate preparations]. || 70 ||
Having placed a water-pot in front, one should set it down properly upon a pedestal of grain;
then, from that very pot, one should invoke [the deity] into the kautuka-vessel, as well as into the utsava and arcā images.
Having invoked the deities residing in the womb-chamber, the lords of the gates, the gatekeepers, and the deities situated upon the steps, each in their respective place; 72.
Having proclaimed an auspicious day and having worshipped according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer the five kinds of oblations and constantly perform worship according to the injunctions.
One should not perform the two rites of invocation and dismissal in the temple of the Youth (Kumāra).
Having brought the fire into the permanent hearth, one should perform the daily oblation.
In the dwelling of the child (the temple), one should arrange a bathhouse and so forth, as well as a hall for drinking water and likewise a chamber for bathing; furthermore,
a hall for the collection of flowers and a pavilion for the gathering of ritual materials.
The wise one should likewise have the sacrificial hall, the place for the flagstaff, the altar for the spirits, and the kitchen constructed as before in the first enclosure.
If, however, there is a Bhūtapīṭha and likewise a Dhvaja in the second enclosure,
one should construct them facing the Bālalaya according to the prescribed rule.
If one should cause [the mandala] to be made entirely around the third enclosure, this alone would be the distinction; everything else is as described in the Khilokta.
The Expiation for the Mixing of Tantras:
Hereafter, I shall explain the expiation for the mixing of tantras.
The tantra of Viṣṇu is declared to be twofold: indeed, the Saumya (northern) and the Āgneya (southern).
The Vaikhānasa, Pāñcarātra, Vaidika, and Tāntrika [traditions] follow in sequence;
of these two [the first two], the Vaikhānasa is superior, bestowing both worldly and otherworldly fruits. (80)
The Tantric Pāñcarātra, however, is secondary and bestows only worldly results;
its ritual procedure is rooted in the Vedas, yet it is characterized by Tantric initiation (dīkṣā). || 81 ||
The Pāñcarātra is also declared to be of two kinds: pure and mixed.
The Bhāgavata is said to be the pure [Pāñcarātra], while the other is the [mixed] Pāñcarātra.
A Sūta or a Sāttvata should perform the worship according to the pure path;
those who have abandoned the sacred thread, as well as Brahmins and others who have been initiated, are worshippers of the mixed [path]. || 83 ||
The rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (niṣeka) for them were enjoined in various respective Tantras;
these arose from the state of the Vedas having become fragmented in former times due to their disappearance.
Those who have reached the further shore of the Veda call that the Vaikhānasa branch;
the Lord himself taught that Vaikhānasa branch at the very beginning.
He who is known by the name Vikhanas, and likewise as Vaikhānasa,
spoke this Sūtra to the sages, making them fully understand the Dharma.
Following his authority, the sages composed many sūtras;
some of them, in the form of Smṛti, proclaim the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life.

Then, at the conclusion of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), being unwearied, one should perform the constant worship of Viṣṇu in the evening and morning; that indeed constitutes the worship of all the gods.
Thus has the concise mode of worship been declared in the Vaikhānasa Sūtra;
its exposition by the sages, however, is extensive in every respect. (89)
This extensive application has been explained out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds by Kāśyapa, Atri, myself, and Marīci. (90)
This very injunction of the Vaikhānasa tradition, being rooted in those sūtras, is the prescribed rule;
having installed [the deity] according to the Vaikhānasa rite in accordance with the rules, [one should proceed]. (91)
But when the arcane ritual is performed with a mixture of the Pāñcarātra system, the village, the patron, the king, and the kingdom perish. (92)
Having performed a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) for one fortnight to pacify that fault,
he should feed at least five hundred Brahmins there.
One should install [the deity] again according to the Vaikhānasa rite and worship it in all villages and dwellings that are suitable for habitation. || 94 ||
One should not worship Nārāyaṇa, the God of gods, according to the Pāñcarātra system;
one should worship him for the sake of all prosperity according to the Vaikhānasa rite. 95.
Outside the village, in a secluded place, on a riverbank, in a forest, or on a mountain,
one should worship according to the Vaikhānasa or Pāñcarātra method.
Having installed [the deity] according to the Pāñcarātra rite and in accordance with the prescribed rules, if the worship being performed for one month is deficient in its offerings; 97.
If one desires the entry of this gentle [deity] according to the Pāñcarātra or the Āgneya [tantras], one should perform it with devotion; that will become gentle. || 18 ||
One should offer oblations for seven nights in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice performed with great solemnity;
then, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give them sacrificial fees according to one's ability. || 99 ||
One should perform the recitation of the respective mantras for the rites such as the examination of the ground,
and one should also offer the prescribed oblations for the rites beginning with the opening of the eyes.
One should perform the ritual consecration in water for mobile [images] as previously described;
one should carry out the purification prescribed for a permanent image (dhruvabera) upon the permanent image itself. 101.
Having installed [the deity] again according to the Vaikhānasa rite in due order, one should cause all the rites beginning with worship to be performed by that same method. || 102 ||
If one desires the entry of this gentle deity into the pure worship, one should perform a great propitiatory oblation for one fortnight, and the remainder as before. (103)
"Having established [the deity], one should cause worship and other rites to be performed; this is the instruction even for uninterrupted worship in mixed village sites and the like. (104)
"One should install and worship [the deity] according to the Vaikhānasa rite;
however, if through ignorance there occurs a mixture with cruel rites such as those of the Śaivas," (105)
Having performed the great peace rite (mahāśānti) for a month and having fed a thousand Brahmins, one should install [the image] with a propitiatory rite (saumya) and worship it thoroughly. || 106 ||
"For the atonement of all other gods' violation of their tantric commitments, this very procedure is prescribed; such is the teaching of the Primordial Ancestor. (107)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement regarding Contact with the Untouchable and the Mixture of Tantras," in the section on Ritual Practice (*kriyādhikāra*) of the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium (*saṃhitā*) proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Om. The twenty-eighth chapter.

O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the purification and consecration of the vessels—the nine constituent parts of the worship of the vessels; having performed that, one should practice it correctly. || 1 ||

Indeed, for vessels made of metal intended for the Arghya offering, as well as for the vessel for the oblation, and likewise for the vessels for sipping water (ācamana) and those for the feet-washing water (pādya). || 2 ||

Indeed, [one should prepare] vessels for bathing, invocation, and offerings, as well as a vessel for the bali-oblation, and vessels for the purpose of waving the lights (nīrājana), and two vessels for incense and lamps. || 3 ||
Of the thousand-streamed vessel, of the vessels marked with the conch and the lotus, of iron jars and the like, and likewise of those with three legs; || 4 ||
Having fashioned these [images] with their characteristic marks, one should purify them with water and clay;
then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, one should likewise perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place [the vessel] upon a seat of grain;
having invoked the respective deities and worshipped them, one should present the offerings.
Varuṇa is the presiding deity of the four vessels beginning with the invocation-vessel;
as for the conch-shells, the deities for their worship have already been mentioned.
Soma is the presiding deity of the vessels for the arghya water;
Bhānu is the lord of the oblation vessels; and Bṛhaspati is the presiding deity of the incense vessel. || 8 ||
The vessel for the purposes of illumination and lustration (rājanā) is declared to be the Śrī;
however, in the case of the thousand-stream vessel, the Prakṛti is situated within the pericarp.
On the eight petals are the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvaryāṇi), and there also the four Vedas;
the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, are to be worshipped on the vessels marked with the conch and the lotus.
One should invoke the presiding deities of the bell as previously described,
and likewise those of the vessels, the water-pots, and the three-legged stands.
One should worship the presiding deities of all vessels as they have been described: the five great elements (mahābhūtas), the aggregate (skandha), and the Lord of the Vessel (kalaśādhipa). || 12 ||
I shall describe the consecration of beds, seats,
and vehicles, as well as the ritual preparation for beds, couches, thrones, chariots, and stages. (13)
Having constructed the palanquins and the vehicles according to the prescribed rule,
and having established the domestic fire (aupāsana), he should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.
Having purified [the site] as before with the fire-circumambulation and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should [install] Dharma, Jñāna, Aiśvarya, and Vairāgya separately. 15.
The presiding deities of beds, seats, vehicles, and feet are as follows:
Śeṣa is the lord of the bed, and Dharma alone is the lord of the seat.
Garuda is the presiding deity of all vehicles;
once the pitcher has been properly prepared, one should indeed meditate upon those respective lords.
Having bathed it with seven jars and placed it upon grain,
one should tie a protective cord (pratisara) to its foot, first on the eastern side and then on the southern.
Having invoked those respective deities at the conclusion of the duties of the Hotṛ priest,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter, having poured out the clarified butter in the same order as the invocation.
One should worship the mantras dedicated to each respective deity one hundred and eight times;
having invoked them with their respective forms, one should invoke their respective presiding deities as prescribed.
Having worshipped the deity with the eightfold offerings, one should then place [the image] upon it;
one should worship it on the seat, during the procession, and perform circumambulation of the temple.
One should likewise cause [the deity] to rest upon the bed and worship according to the prescribed rite;
one should also purify all other vessels as is appropriate.

Those born from the inverse unions of the castes, such as the Sūtas and others; heretics, the fallen, atheists, those who have broken the bounds of conduct, and likewise those who revile the Vedas. || 23 ||
Those afflicted with foul diseases, as well as those who revile their preceptors, are unable even to look upon the worship of the God of gods or the offering of the oblation. || 24 ||
Therefore, one should not construct a door that is covered by a curtain;
furthermore, one should avoid the proximity of those who have committed great sins.
Therefore, one should prepare a curtain cloth equal in width and height to the door;
for if one should worship without having covered the door with a curtain, [the rite is flawed]. (26)
Having offered oblations to the two deities of that day and having performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice with the Vyāhṛtis,
one should bathe the deity with divine water, worship it, and present the offering.
If one should perform worship without first worshipping the presiding deity of the ritual materials, one should offer oblations to the deities of those specific items,
and then worship the Vaiṣṇava deities with the Vyāhṛtis.
Having performed the worship of the presiding deities of the materials, one should worship with those very same [materials];
when the prescribed time has been fully completed, one should indeed perform the sealing of the door.
If, out of delusion, one does not lock the door at the end of the twilight period, then for the pacification of that fault incurred by opening it at an improper time: || 30 ||
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava, the Pauruṣa, and likewise the Viṣṇu-sūkta— each addressed to the presiding deity of its respective twilight— one should perform the binding.
The morning twilight has Indra as its presiding deity; the midday [twilight] has the Sun as its presiding deity;
likewise, the evening twilight is proclaimed to have Varuṇa as its presiding deity. (32)
If, out of delusion, one does not offer the oblation at the time of the eclipse or even before the eclipse begins once it has been cooked, [the following occurs].
The entire world is indeed afflicted by calamities such as mental anguish and physical disease;
[one should recite] the Vaiṣṇava and Viṣṇukta mantras, as well as those dedicated to the planetary deities.
Regarding the specific rules for renovation:
having offered oblations, bathed the Lord of Gods, and worshipped Him, one should present [the offerings], especially in the case of single-sloped vimānas and those of human proportions. || 35 ||
Likewise, when making a replacement for images that have been removed or have become dilapidated,
if one makes them larger than the original measurement, it does not cause any fault.
One should likewise expand this all around in accordance with the proportions;
that which was previously a structure of clay should be constructed using bricks and other materials.
Likewise, one should cause it to be performed after first expanding [the site] around the temple;
this applies also to the work of repairing dilapidated walls. || 38 ||
Alternatively, if one desires the increase of earthen objects,
one should cause it to increase on all sides, or likewise in the eastern and northern directions.
If there should be a village street in front, one should leave a space on three sides;
likewise, for the halls and pavilions, one should leave space on both sides and in front.
One should especially cause the house to expand toward the east or the north;
one may also extend the kitchen toward the north or even toward the east.
If there is a narrowness on one side due to rivers, oceans, or mountains, one should expand it on the other sides; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (42)
If there is an increase toward the south-west, there will never be security;
one should not construct walls, pavilions, and the like, nor draw boundary lines for the enclosures. (43)

In all pavilions and similar structures, whether constructed from inferior materials, the most excellent preceptor may cause them to be made either smaller or larger [than the prescribed dimensions]. || 44 ||
If one should cause the primary substance to be made deficient or excessive through ignorance, the sacrificer perishes. || 45 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform it as before;
or else, one may do so in the north of the kitchen or facing toward it. || 46 ||
Regarding the construction of a pond and other features:
one should construct a pond facing the temple.
One should determine the dimensions of the pond by means of a cord and clear away the ground starting from the length. (47)
One should perform the calculation of the *āya* and so forth using only the extended [length];
one should not determine the lunar day and the weekday by means of the width—such is the instruction. (48)
Having taken half of that circle, one should perform the measurement for the length and other dimensions of the well;
then, in front of all the pleasure gardens and service buildings, one should construct a large pond.
Now, O best of sages, I shall describe the consecration of ponds,
wells, and tanks, including their embankments made of stone, brick, and other materials.
Having firmly fixed [the pillars] in their positions along with the arrangement of the steps,
one should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice once ten days have passed.
Having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), one should purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having wrapped the jar with a thread, it should be filled with water from a flowing stream.
It was radiant with holy waters from sacred fords, golden tortoises, and fish;
it was provided with bundles of kuśa grass and unbroken grains of rice, and adorned with auspicious flowers. || 53 ||
Having established [the image] upon a seat of grain and having wrapped it with a pair of cloths, one should mutter the two sections of the *anuvāka* beginning with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā. (54)
Having uttered "Namo vāce," having recited "Śanno vātaḥ," and having said "Āpo vā idam," as well as with the mantras beginning with the Vedas; || 55 ||
Having consecrated that pitcher with mantras, one should worship Varuṇa within it;
then, having recited "Āpo vā idam," one should [offer] that water from the pitcher once again.
The preceptor should pour [the water] into ponds, wells, and tanks while facing east;
having done this, he may then use the water for his ritual activities.
Otherwise, if one should act in such a manner, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed the Mahāśānti rite once by means of oblations, one should perform the consecration again. (58)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Purification of Vessels," in the section on Ritual Practice within the *Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu. Om.
The twenty-ninth chapter.
The Ritual for Great Peace:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for great peace,
which pacifies all defects and removes the fear of all diseases.
It bestows all that is desired, is most excellent, and destroys all inauspiciousness;
it grants longevity and health to the performer, and provides peace, nourishment, and happiness. || 2 ||
In all cases of great calamities, a great rite of pacification (mahāśānti) is prescribed;
one should perform the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, complete with its characteristic features, facing the Ālaya fire.
Then, in the south or in the southeast, or even in the kitchen itself, having adorned it on all four sides with full water-pots, sprouts, and banners; || 4 ||
With plantains and kramuka fruits, and with hanging strings of pearls, [the house shall remain fragrant] for a month, a fortnight, seven days, or even three days. || 5 ||
Alternatively, having resolved upon a single day, one should determine the gravity or lightness of the faults and perform oblations for a corresponding number of days in sequence.
At the conclusion of the Āghāra offerings, when the Vaiṣṇava and Pauruṣa Sūktas have been well-offered,
one should then offer the Rudra-sūkta and subsequently perform the oblations for Dhātṛ and the other deities in their proper order.
Having uttered "Namo vāce" and having recited "Śanno vāta," one should likewise recite the six Vaiṣṇava mantras beginning with "Nārāyaṇāya vidmahe. || 8 ||
With clarified butter, with sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter, with fuel-sticks smeared with ghee,
and with groats, parched grain, sesame seeds, and cakes mixed with clarified butter, in due order.
Having bathed the deity with water-pots and worshipped him thoroughly, one should present the offerings;
the best oblation is performed at the three times of day, while that which omits the night is middling.
If it is performed in the evening and is deficient, it is proclaimed as the lowest;
however, a wise man should offer all the previously mentioned substances in the highest form.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter and cooked rice mixed with clarified butter in sequence at the middle [time];
or, in the case of the lowest [grade], with clarified butter alone, either in the forenoon or at midday.
The Elder Brother declared: "In the highest [form], the ritual bath is constant; in the middling, worship alone; and in the lowest, the fire-oblation alone. (13)
One should maintain the fire without interruption until the conclusion of the rite;
having performed the final oblation at the completion, one should feed the Brahmins.
Atiśānti should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him in the presence of the deity;
for when it is joined with the [mantra] beginning with "yad devā," it is traditionally known as Atiśānti. || 15 ||
If a general pacification (sāmānyaśānti) is joined with the presiding deities of the nine planets, it is called "the one named Adbhuta" (adbhutāhvayā);
if that [Adbhuta] pacification is further joined with [rites such as] Jaya and others, it is simply termed a "general pacification."
The pacification of portents (utpātaśānti) is performed with one hundred oblations using either the twelve-syllable or the eight-syllable mantra,
or likewise with the "viṣṇornuka" verses and others; thus it is called the pacification of portents.
The *śānti* (pacification) rite, or the *mahāśānti*, is said to consist solely of one hundred [mantras] dedicated to Viṣṇu; however,
when it is accompanied by the deities and others, it is called the *mahāśānti*.
Thus, the six pacifications have been declared, which dry up all defects;
one should perform the pacification for minor defects, and indeed everywhere with the Vaiṣṇava rites.

Having offered the two oblations of remorse and having recited the interrupted Gāyatrī dedicated to Viṣṇu, as well as the mantra "śanno mitra" and those beginning with "viṣṇornuka," [he should proceed]. || 20 ||
Eighty-eight [oblations] for Viṣṇu, the bestower of well-being, and likewise for Sarveśvara;
for Viṣṇu the protector of all, and also for the Soul of All.
And for the sake of the self of all gods, likewise for the self of all Vedas,
for the self of the sages, and for the maintenance of yoga.
Likewise, for the sake of establishing everything, there are ten [names] beginning with the word Viṣṇu;
however, in this context, everything is employed by means of the word Viṣṇu.
And likewise to Nārāyaṇa, and again to the Primordial Self,
and similarly to the Self of all gods, and likewise to him in the form of Indra.
To the Lord of Saṃyamana, to the Lord of Enjoyment,
likewise to the Bestower of All Satisfaction, and to the Infinite Self, in due order.
"To Brahmeśānātman," "to Prajāpati," and "to Anantaśayana"— these are the ten [names] beginning with Nārāyaṇa.
"To Puṇyanārāyaṇa," likewise "to the Lord of the Thirty-three," and "to the one who reclines on the banyan leaf," and likewise "to the dweller in the banyan seed."
Likewise, saying "to Pādārcis" and again "to the one in the form of a child," and having said "to the one whose form is illusion," he spoke "to the Awakened One."
To the one who is the body of all empowerments, to the one who is the excellence of all,
and to the one who stands at the summit— these are the ten [qualities] beginning with the "arrows of merit."
To the child, who has the form of a child, and likewise to the one who reclines on the leaf of the banyan tree;
to the Truth, who is established in truth, and furthermore to the one whose very self is truth.
Having said, "Salutation to the eternal Truth," and remembering the God of gods, [he spoke]:
"For all is indeed Truth; in Truth is Truth established."
With this very [formula] ending in the dative case, [one should worship] Sarvalokapravartine,
and likewise Satyātmadevāya and again Satyamodāya.
Meditating upon the God of gods as the embodiment of the staircase of truth, [he prays:
"O You who are Truth, whose self is Truth, and who arise from the foundation of Truth, grant me the ten [perfections]."
To the Person (Puruṣa), likewise to him who is praised as the Person, and in due order to him who has been studied by the Person,
and again to the one who bestows nourishment (puṣṭi).
Uttering "To the Self of Puruṣa" and "To the Puruṣa of Puruṣas," and thereafter [saying] "To the Friend of the World" and "To the Support of the World."
And [the offering is made] to the one who sets the world in motion, and likewise to the cause of the world;
to the four persons, and again to the one whose essence is the play of Viṣṇu.
"Having spoken thus for the sake of the joy of the world, for the welfare of the world, and likewise for the destruction of all thorns, [he said: 'For one who sports upon the stages [of yoga]...'"

One should say "kāya" (to whom), "kasmai" (to which), "katamasmai" (to whichever), "sarvasmai" (to all), and likewise "viṣṇave" (to Viṣṇu); and one should likewise say "viṣṇave" (to Viṣṇu) for one who is hostile to the mantra.
Having said "to the one of constant form," and also "to the one whose self is concealed," [he said] "to the one who causes great joy" and "to the bestower of all auspiciousness."
For the destruction of the inauspicious, for the accumulation of the auspicious,
and for merit— having offered [oblations] thus, others such as the word "merit" (puṇya) follow.
Having offered oblations to Balorjita, while recollecting the God of gods,
as well as to Jayasamṛddha and Kāmāndajanana;
Having said "to Sarvānanda," and after that "to Samṛddha," having said "to Śrīvidhāna," and [to] "Brahmasandruhaṇa."
Having said "and for the sake of the abode of excellence," one should subsequently worship [the deity] for the prosperity of the world,
for the marvelous, and for that which is without beginning or end.
Likewise with "of immeasurable majesty," likewise with "for ultimate benefit," and with that same [word] ending in the dative case,
as in "the foundation of all."
For the sake of the support of all the world and for the sake of bringing auspiciousness to all the world,
these eighteen [deities] are proclaimed and described as "the Satisfiers of All."
One should employ Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Puṇyanārāyaṇa,
and likewise Puṇya— each ending in the dative case— as separate [names].
Alternatively, one should offer eighty-eight oblations with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
wherein the number eighty-eight is prescribed along with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
There, one should not offer eighty-eight oblations with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
rather, there is the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma). O you whose wealth is austerity, listen as I now describe that limb-oblation.
Then, uttering "to the head," "to the two eyes," and "to the two ears," the wise one should offer oblations to the two nostrils, the two lips, and the teeth.
To the tongue, to the throat, to the chest, and to the two arms respectively;
and likewise to the two sides of the torso, to the two hands, to the nails, and to the belly.
Likewise, oblation is offered to the hips and the thighs, and also to the shanks;
then to the hair, to the crown, and again to the discus.
Then, after saying "To Śaṅkha, to Cakra, to Gadā,
to Śārṅga, and to Asī," let an oblation be offered to Ambara.
He indeed offers oblations to the ornaments, to the radiance, and to the parasol,
having sacrificed with the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to the teeth," while recollecting each respective object.
The oblation for the Crown-Garland and so forth: first to the Crown-Garland, then to the Divine One, and thereafter to the Supreme;
then to the All-Supreme, to the All, to Viṣṇu, and to the Sovereign Lord.
One should subsequently offer oblations to the head with the mantras "tvaṃ yajñapuruṣāya," to the Praṇava, to Viṣṇu, and likewise to Prabhaviṣṇu.
"To the divine one, to the excellent bearer"—to whom [is this addressed]?
After that, [it is] "to him alone, to Viṣṇu," and indeed "to the one who crushes all obstacles."
Having said "To Dhruva" and "To Viṣṇu for the forehead," [he should offer] to the two eyebrows with "To the intermediate space," and likewise to the one who is the self of the vital breaths.
While reciting "Into the two ears" and "Into the two wings," he offers oblations;
and while reciting "Into the limbs of the eyes" and "Into the two eyes," he is tormented.
Recalling each of those limbs— the two pupils of the eyes, the two outer corners, the two blue lotuses (the eyebrows), the two arms, and the two cheeks— [he meditated].
He offers to the nostrils and to the two nostril-pits;
he offers to the two ears, to the two testicles, to the teeth, and also to the two cavities of the belly.
Then one should offer oblations to the lower lip, to the upper lip, and thereafter to the tongue; then to the beautiful face, and again to Viṣṇu in the palate.
By means of the two jaws, the two earlobes, the two umbrellas, and the backbone.
Let it be offered to Grīvāya, to Kanakāya, and likewise to Supragrīvāya;
let it be offered to Kaṇṭhanālāya, to Kaṇṭhāya, and to Karṇanālāya.
Having offered oblations to the head with "Dyauḥ," and likewise to the protector of the sky,
to the one who is the basis of all, and to the refuge of the vital breaths;
One should offer oblations for the sake of the hair and the head to the dweller in merit;
and for the sake of the arms, the continuity of the quarters, and the protector of all kṣatriyas.
For the dissolution of all vital breaths from all places and bodies,
and for liberation from all sufferings.
To the protectors from the suffering of all worlds,
to the throats and neck-pipes, and thereafter to the bulbous roots (kanda).
Speaking thus, he [offered] from the backbone, the head, the body, and likewise from the eight arms,
from the bones, the elbows, and similarly from the little fingers,
from all the nails, and from the tendons.
From the collarbones, to the region of the cheeks, and also from the roots of the sides.
Then one should offer oblations to Pārśvābhyām, to Urase, to Hutāśanāya, and thereafter to Bhallāṭāya;
then to Urasyāya, to Śirasyāya, and to Bāhumuktāya.
Then, let oblation be offered to the heart, to the lotus, and to the mind; thereafter, to the intentions from the thoughts, and to the volitions from the intentions.
To Tarka, to those who dwell in logic, to Mati, and to the Powerful One;
to Kīkasa, to those who dwell in the bones, to Sūrya, and to Viṣṇucakṣus.
To Vāma, to Somanetra, to Viṣṇu, and to Prabuddha;
to Atala, to Adilā, to Mahābīja, and to Mahātman.
Having offered to the Self (ātman), the wise man should likewise offer to the Universal Self (sarvātman) for the sake of all gifts to the worlds, as well as for their pervasion and satisfaction.
One should offer oblations to Yama, who is of a non-manifest form yet identical [to all], and who is the essence of all;
one should offer them at the binding of the vital breath.
Recalling each respective limb, he offers oblations from the head;
likewise, he offers oblations from the pores of the skin and from the intestines.
One should offer oblations to the one whose form is the intestines and to the movement of the intestines;
furthermore, to the day, to the eternal throat, and to the eternal bond.
To the one who is the means of binding, fettering, and confinement; to the one with slow-moving breasts;
and to the one whose intellect rests upon his flanks, [offering salutations] from the vital points, the secondary vital points, and the joints.
Let oblations be offered to Sampatti, to Kumārī, to Puṇḍarīkā, to Nābhi,
to Hṛllasā, and to Nāsā.
One should offer oblations while recollecting him as Ārdrāya Vartitāya;
let there be an offering to Aniruddhāya Dṛṣate Vatsalāya.
Likewise, [he should offer] to the liver and spleen, and similarly to Mukunda;
then to Nyasta, to Varāya, and after that to Urvara.
Likewise, while reciting "for the binding of the belly" and "by means of the two channels," [he should touch] the waist-cloths,
the bodily substances, and again the bladder and the testicles.
For procreation, for the progenitors, and indeed again for the hips;
for the loom-stand, for the bamboo frame, and for those who uphold the lineage.
Having uttered "To Prajāpati," let it be offered with "and to Viṣṇu";
while pronouncing "To Śukra, to those who dwell in light, from the two thighs."
It is offered from the veins, from the joints of the bones, and from the openings;
having offered from the skin and the bones, one should thereafter offer again.
Having spoken thus regarding those who feed on form, those who feed on excrement, and those who feed on the chest,
he likewise addressed those who feed on blood, those who wear red garments, and those who feed on fat.
One should offer oblations to Jīva, to the breast, and again to the bone and marrow; then to those who dwell in the marrow, and again to the head.
One should offer oblations to the element itself, to the elements, and also to the forms of the elements;
one should also offer to the secondary elements while uttering the words "the ribs and the skin."
Let it be offered to Sarvarūpa for the neck, to Dhanada, to the Self of Wealth,
to Sarveśvara, to Yajña, and to Puruṣa.

Where the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma) is prescribed in rites such as the opening of the eyes (akṣyunmeṣa) and so forth, one should perform the oblation in that very manner; such is the instruction of the ancient teachers.
The highest [offering] is devoid of "svāhā" and so forth for the sake of the form of equality of all;
the middle is devoid of "svāhā" and so forth for the sake of the garland on the head; and the lowest is likewise devoid of them.
Regarding the stated offering of the eighty-eight limbs, one should perform each separately with the word "svāhā" at the end;
likewise, regarding the stated offering of the crown, garland, and so forth, one should perform each separately with "svāhā" at the end.
However, other wise ones explain the offering of the crown, garland, and so forth in another way.
Beginning with "from the two eyebrows" and ending with "one should offer oblations for the pacification of faults," this is declared to be the general expiation common to all.
To the one who wears a crown garland, to the divine one, to the one adorned with jewels, to the most excellent one,
to the one who is supreme over all, to the all-encompassing Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord.
And for the crown, the hair, and likewise for the uṣṇīṣa;
for the head, the mouth, the forehead, the two ears, and also the two eyebrows.
Then from the two outer corners of the eyes, from the eyes themselves, and immediately from the eyelashes;
then from the two banners, and to the Light, and to the one whose form is light.
Then one should offer oblations from the two cheeks, from the two jaws, likewise from the two nostrils,
from the two ear-lobes, from the two lips, and from the teeth.
To the tongue and the fine mouth, to the chin and the lower lip,
to the throat and the neck, and to the cervical vertebrae.
From the collarbones, from those which have the form of collarbones, likewise from the shoulders,
from the two arms, from the two upper arms, and from the elbows.
From the forearms, from the palms, and likewise from the fingers;
from the joints and from the nails, and likewise for the heart.
And likewise for the two breasts, the two sides, the belly, and the navel;
for the nape of the neck, the channels, and the row of the spinal column.
To the hips for progeny, for generation, and likewise for the bladder;
to the bladder and the testicles, to the two thighs, and to the knees.
From the shanks, from the ankles, from the heels and the feet,
from the toes, the joints, the nails, and likewise from the ligaments.
May there be prosperity from the joints, from the body hairs, and indeed from the hair-pores;
likewise from the vital organs, from the protective margins of the vital organs, from the offering-chambers, and from the vessels.
And from skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—
indeed, from those forms that are white— and for the sake of the most brilliant splendor.
From the elements, or from the forms of the elements, and from the words, and from the syllable;
and from the sounds, and then immediately to the mind and the intellect.
Immediately after that, one should say "svāhā" to the mind accompanied by the word *ahaṃkāra*,
and then utter the lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) preceded by the words "heart" (*hṛt*) and "vital breath" (*prāṇa*).
Wind and the individual soul (jīva), the living self (jīvātman), having been proclaimed for the sake of truth;
likewise the formless one, as well as knowledge (jñāna) which is the very nature of knowledge;
the infinite objects of knowledge and the knower, bliss, and the manifest itself.
The unmanifest is the prāṇa; the self of prāṇa is followed by apāna and vyāna.
He is the out-breath and the equalizing breath, the great one and the Great Self;
he is the self and the non-self, the universal soul of all, and the supreme beyond.
Likewise, for the Supreme Self, for whomever it may be,
and indeed for everyone, he likewise [bestowed] his head, his discus, and his conch.
The syllable "pāda" is for the major limbs, likewise for the secondary limbs, and for all the minor limbs; the utterance "puruṣāya" is for the Person.
Regarding the definition of hymns (*sūkta*):
the *Viṣṇu-sūkta* is exemplified by the six mantras beginning with *viṣṇornuka*;
the hymn beginning with *jātavedase* is exemplified as the *Drauga*.
The Śrīsūkta is proclaimed as "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm";
the Bhūsūkta, which brings auspiciousness to all the worlds, begins with "bhūmirbhūmnā".
The hymn beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha" is cited as the Brahma-sūkta;
the hymn beginning with "omāsaścarṣaṇī" is considered the Sārasvata-sūkta.
Having said, "O Rudra, be gracious to us," and speaking, "Praise the Renowned One," and also,
"O most bountiful, most auspicious one— you who are worthy— sustain [us]."
Having recited "O Agni, you are Rudra," and also "The King of you [all]," the Rudrasūkta is declared by means of these six mantras as well.
The Installation of the Balipīṭha:
I shall now describe the installation of the balipīṭha in brief.
Its height is prescribed to be equal to that of the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra). || 21 ||
Whether it be long or wide, in the center of the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra),
the height is declared to be seven parts out of ten.
When the total height is divided into twenty-seven parts, two parts are to be known as the pedestal (pādukā), and four parts as the base (jagatī). || 23 ||
The *kumuda* should be known to have three parts, and the *paṭṭikā* should be one part;
they say the *kaṇṭha* is six parts, while the *bala* and *kampas* are two parts each. (24)
One-fourth and one-eighth of a part is for the *agravartikā*;
two and a half parts is for the lotus flower (*padmapuṣpa*), and one and a half parts is for the lotus bud (*padmāpuṣpaka*). || 25 ||
Having understood it thus, one should designate each respective portion;
three parts should be measured by the span of a hand, or more than three hands.
Or even more than five cubits, it is prescribed to be made in front of the gopura;
in the center, however, the ground should be made with a measurement of four tālas. || 27 ||
One should cause this excellent, comfortable seat to be turned around if one desires to see the master; otherwise, the destruction of the village will occur. (18)
Alternatively, the wise man should have it constructed in the middle portion of the causal area,
duly observing the respective directions in the four quarters according to the rule.

Having thus performed the rite according to this procedure, one should indeed cause the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) to be carried out for the first enclosure and the others, according to their respective order, starting from the mouth and the length.
Having divided the fourth part into three sections starting from the first, [he placed] the Akras,
Śaṅkhas, and Dhvajins, as well as the Yūthanāthas, Pākas, and Arjunas.
The fourth enclosure consists of mental factors (*caitta*); some say that one should place two and three [deities] in the second and third [enclosures], as well as six and eight in the fourth.

If it is merely a veil of qualities (guṇāvaraṇa), one should fashion a banner in the first part of the third [section], and in the second, a leader of the herd (yūtheśa) and a destroyer of the senses (akṣahan). || 33 ||
If it is for those residing in the intermediate quarters, one should especially fashion the discus, conch, and banner in the third part, as well as Bhūteśa.
If it is only one unit in size, one should divide the area in front of the principal pavilion into four parts and arrange it in the third part.
Alternatively, having determined the width of the entrance outside the gateway (gopura),
one may arrange all [the deities] there, or only the leader of the host (yūtheśa).

Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and likewise the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), and having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the "unveiling of the eyes" (akṣimocana). || 37 ||

Having displayed the cow and other [emblems], and having bathed them again with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), each with its own respective mantra.
Having consecrated the aupāsana fire, either to its east or to its south,
one should prepare the water-pot according to the prescribed rite as before, up to the conclusion of the āghāra oblations.
Having bathed him with seven jars of pure water, one should sprinkle him with the consecration rite and also tie the protective amulet (kautuka) around his neck in a clockwise direction.
Having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest and performed the invocation, one should offer oblations of clarified butter;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations with that Vaiṣṇava mantra, [one should proceed]. || 41 ||
In the morning, having invoked [the deity] upon the seat and worshipped it thoroughly, one should present the offerings;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains as before.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the consecration of Garuḍa, the supreme installation of Suparṇa.
One should perform the installation either in the standing posture or in the case of the primary image (mūlabera) itself, which is in the standing posture. (43)
Whether on a seat or a bed, or whether sitting or standing—if these should be reversed, both the king and the kingdom perish. (44)
In the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Hasta, Svātī, Punarvasu, the birth-star of the sacrificer, or indeed the star of the king. || 45 ||
Therefore, one should offer the sprouts before that day; and after the offering of the sprouts, having gathered the materials as previously described, [one should proceed]. 46.
Aiming for the ritual of opening the eyes (akṣimocana), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the forenoon;
having performed the oblation for the limbs (aṅgahoma), one should likewise offer the oblation for the forms (mūrtihoma).
Having offered oblations ten times with the mantras "śatadhāra" and "kadāpisṛja," he then performed the opening of the eyes with those two.
Then, having performed the concluding oblation (antahoma) and having prostrated before the Sun,
one should perform the impregnation of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other rites during that afternoon.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in cow’s urine, cow dung, and water infused with kuśa grass;
or else, the wise one should perform it in a vessel containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Before the installation and other rites, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) at night; having performed the sacrifice to the earth (bhūmiyajña), one should likewise cause the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) to be carried out. || 51 ||
Having again prepared the bed-altar according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should then establish the Dakṣiṇāgni fire on the southern side of the altar.
Some say that one should have the *aupāsana* fire established;
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, one should then perform the purification of the ground.
Having established the jar upon the altar of light and performed its consecration as before,
one should bathe it with seven jars and wipe it dry with a cloth.

Having adorned them with garments and other ornaments, and having placed them upon the bed-altar, and having tied the protective cord (pratisara), one should cause them to lie down upon the beds. || 55 ||
One should perform all this with those very same two mantras;
