having strewn grass around the Dakṣiṇā fire, let oblations be well-offered to its presiding deity.
O mortal, having invoked Him according to the sequence of the Hotṛ's duties, let the oblation be offered;
thereafter, one should worship with one hundred and eight recitations of the Garuḍa-mantras.
One should worship with mantras beginning with the Sāmaveda, joined with Vaiṣṇava rites;
then one should pass the remainder of the night with dances, songs, and instrumental music.
Then at dawn, the righteous-souled one, having bathed together with the architects,
should perform the depositing of jewels when the auspicious moment has arrived.
Taking the divine pitcher, he should enter the temple again,
either when the white-colored [portion] is full or on the black side.
Either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure,
one should then place [the image] in the center of the pavilion accompanied by mantras.
Having honored the preceptor with gold, cattle, and land,
one should likewise honor the installers with garments, ornaments, and earrings.
Thus, one endowed with faith and devotion should install the image;
thereby there shall be prosperity for one's lineage as well as for one's mounts. (63)
He attains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. After this, I shall further describe the installation of Viṣvaksena and the supreme establishment of Śānti.

Having fashioned an image endowed with the [proper] characteristics, one should perform the installation correctly on a previously mentioned auspicious lunar mansion, during the bright fortnight, on a favorable day. (65)
Having fashioned the image with all its characteristic marks and having dismissed the artisan,
one should perform the Vāstu-homa and the subsidiary Homa, offering oblations with the protective mantras.
One should worship Viṣvaksena with two mantras, Viṣṇu, and the Vyāhṛtis;
then, by means of those two mantras, one should perform the ritual release of the eyes, beginning from the right.
One should prepare the infusion of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth in their proper sequence;
and having constructed a sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā) facing that temple.
In the middle of that, one should construct a bed-altar (śayyavedi) measuring one and a half times the size of the image;
and one should establish the aupāsana fire either to the east of it or at its very front.
Having prepared a bathing pit on the south as before,
one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and likewise carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) either on the evening before or on the preceding day,
one should then lift up the deity who has undergone the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and bathe him.

Having prepared the pitcher according to the prescribed rite, having invoked [the deity] there with mantras, having bathed it with seven pitchers, and having worshipped it with the eight forms; || 72 ||
Then, at the conclusion of the tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka), he should have her lie down upon the bed;
having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest, invoked [the deity], and offered the portions, he should perform the oblations of clarified butter.
Abandoning the worship of all other gods, one should practice the study of the Vedas;
one should perform one hundred and eight sacrifices with the mantras of Viṣvaksena.
Having offered oblations with the Vaiṣṇava Mūrtimantra as well as with the Gāyatrī,
and having performed the principal homa, he should spend the night after making further offerings.
Having concluded the morning rites, having invoked [the deity], and having worshipped [him], one should present the offering;
one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and the others in the presence of the deity.
Having specially prepared a sacrificial hall for all the retinues in front of their respective abodes, during their installation; || 77 ||
One should arrange the bed-altar in the middle of that [space] and the fire in front of it;
this is the prescribed sequence, though the mantra alone is what distinguishes it. (78)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with each respective mantra accompanied by the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
and having performed the installation and invocation, one should worship [the deity] daily according to the prescribed rules.
Having fashioned an image with all the proper marks, endowed with seven hoods, and resembling Aniruddha— the infinite lord of all nāgas who is established in infinity— [one should worship it]. (80)
Either in the first enclosure, or even in the second enclosure, or near Vāmalūru, or even outside the city gate; || 81 ||
Having determined the site and gathered the necessary materials,
thereafter one should perform the rites beginning with the sowing of sprouts and ending with the consecration as prescribed.
Having established [the deity] with the mantras of the remaining deities or else with that specific hymn (sūkta),
one should worship it daily according to the rules by the gentle path.
Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, Pitāmaha, and Anādiveṣṇava—these five, as well as the sages Śaṇḍa and Viṣṇu, are also Vaiṣṇavas. 84.
And likewise, the installation of the three— Suparṇa, Śānta, and Ananta— has now been described by me in brief.
The foundation of Vikhanas and that of Brahmā have been declared by me to be threefold, yet the installation is performed separately;
and for the deity within the inner sanctum, the officiant is considered to be the priest.
The procedure for the installation of the three-fold form (trimūrti) as well as the two-fold form (dvimūrti),
including that which takes place within the mandala, has been fully explained by means of the Mūrti-mantra.
However, having been excellently described as being primarily established separately, I shall now fully declare the installation of the sage Vighana. 88.
On the right side of the God, in the vicinity of the Goddess Śrī, [he is] gentle, bearing a conch and a discus, and likewise possessing four arms. (89)

Having installed one who carries the triple staff (tridaṇḍa), whose mind is intent on the worship of Viṣṇu, upon a tortoise-seat (kūrmapīṭha), one should worship him daily according to the prescribed rules. || 90 ||
One should perform everything correctly, as in the installation of the God of Gods, whether at the site, in the primary image (mūlabera), or on the throne or the bed. || 91 ||
One should always consider him as being seated and endowed with ascetic power;
if the opposite should occur, it will lead to the destruction of the king and his kingdom.
In the three later [asterisms], in Rohiṇī, Hastā, Svātī, or Punarvasu;
in the asterism of the sacrificer, or indeed in the asterism of the king. || 93 ||
Therefore, one should offer the sprouts prior to that day;
and after the offering of the sprouts, having gathered the materials as before, [one should proceed].
With the aim of the "unloosing of the eyes" (akṣimocana), one should perform the oblation in the forenoon;
having performed the oblation for the limbs (aṅgahoma), the oblation for the forms (mūrtihoma) should then be offered.

Having offered oblations a thousand times with the mantra "ato devā-idaṃ viṣṇu," the wise man, having performed the opening of their eyes by means of those two [mantras], should perform the final oblation at the conclusion.
Having performed either three or four consecrations according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should offer the bali oblation as before.
Before the day of the consecration, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) at night;
having performed the sacrifice of the ground (bhūmiyajña), one should also cause the circumambulation with fire (paryagni) to be carried out. || 98 ||
Having again prepared the bed-altar according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should establish the *śrāmaṇa* fire on the eastern side of the bed-altar.
Having consecrated either the domestic fire (aupāsana) or, according to some,
the sacrificial fire (āhavanīya) with mantras for an auspicious day, one should then perform the purification of the ground.
Having established the water-pot upon the bathing altar and consecrated it as before,
one should bathe [the deity] with seven jars and wipe [him] dry with a cloth.
Having adorned them with garments and other ornaments, and having placed them upon the bed-altar, and having tied the protective thread (pratisara), one should lay them down upon the beds. || 102 ||
One should perform all this with the same two mantras as before;
having strewn grass around the Śrāmaṇa fire, let oblations be well-offered to Viṣṇu.
The Hotṛ priest, having invoked [the deity] through the sequence of the Hotṛ-mantras and by means of that very form, should perform the oblation.
Now, the forms [of the deities] will be described in their capacity as the most excellent of worshippers. (104)
Having invoked the one who bears a triple staff, who is devoted to austerity, whose eyes are like lotuses,
and who is beloved by Hari, one should offer oblations with the four forms.
Otherwise, the forms [of the deities] will be described as door-keepers;
however, at the time of their separate installation, one should perform the rite together with the Goddess.
Except for the hanging thread (pralamba-sūtra) and the śrīvatsa mark, it should be fashioned like Viṣṇu;
that is declared to be the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. || 107 ||
His wife was renowned by the supreme ṛṣis as Divyā;
and [he had two sons], Viṣṇupriya and Suta, as well as Viṣvaksena’s friend.
And likewise Kalpasūtrakṛt, Śrāmaṇa, Agnipriya, and Paratattvapravaktā—these he worshipped with five forms in successive order. (109)
If they are to be worshipped as primary deities separately,
one should worship their forms one hundred and eight times with the two original Vaiṣṇava mantras.
One should worship with the mantra "Yo vedādih paramah," joined with the Vaiṣṇava [mantra], either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times. || 111 ||
The preceptor should spend the remainder of the night with dances, songs,
and instrumental music in the presence of the God of gods, assuming the form of the most excellent worshipper.
In the form of a gatekeeper, he is located at the southern side of the second door;
alternatively, if he is in his distinct primary form, he is likewise situated between Yama and Agni.
Whether bearing the conch and discus or even devoid of those two, that omnipresent Lord is called the gatekeeper by the wise. (114)
He who holds the conch and discus is proclaimed as being manifest elsewhere;
whether in the inner sanctum or outside, he should be installed facing north. || 115 ||
One should place the face of the King of Gods (Indra) on the southern side of the door;
having installed him with the Dhruva-sūkta, one should touch him with the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
Having honored the preceptor with devotion through gifts of cows, land, gold, and so forth, one should also worship the consecrators and others with garments, ornaments, and earrings. (117)
He who, endowed with devotion, performs the installation of the Supreme Guru shall attain the prosperity of the Vedas and the success of meritorious deeds. || 118 ||
Having attained all his desires, he goes to the world of merit by means of these two mantras: "ato devā" and "idaṃ viṣṇu". (119)
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the rules with the sixteen types of service, acting as the primary worshipper, one should [offer] those things presented to Him.
Having worshipped with garlands, perfumes, incenses, lamps, oblations, and so forth,
one shall attain the state of union at the end of the body.
One should perform the offering for a Vaikhānasa exactly like the offering to Viṣṇu;
and during the installation of a gatekeeper, one offers oblations dedicated to that deity.
On the southern side of the door, the Sthānaka is well-established;
it is proclaimed that its presiding deity is the mantra "avaikhānasāya. || 123 ||
This [universe] persists in its threefold form specifically by the command of Viṣṇu;
and that account has been told at great length in the section on Etymology (Nirukta-adhikāra). 124.
The Characteristics of the Fuel and Other Materials: I shall describe the characteristics of the fuel for all ritual acts.
[Fuel that is] thorny, hollow, dry, infested with worms, or covered in ants—[is to be avoided]. (125)
One should avoid that which is short, long, thin, thick, or has two joints; likewise, one should avoid that which has missing skin, is burnt, or is old. || 126 ||
Likewise, on a tree inhabited by flocks of birds, on a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), as well as in a temple, in a cremation ground, and likewise on barren soil; || 127 ||

One should avoid [reciting] in a dilapidated dwelling, at the root of a tree, in the company of a woman recently delivered or one who is impure from childbirth, during sexual intercourse, while sleeping, or when one is afflicted by illness. || 128 ||
A thorny branch and one that is hollowed out are said to cause total destruction;
if it is dry, there will be the loss of a brother, and if it is bitten by insects, there will be confusion of the mind. || 129 ||
In the case of ants and the like, a short skin-defect on the belly brings about fever;
one should know that a long one leads to death, while a thin one brings affliction and fear. (130)
A thick [line] is said to bestow poverty; one with two joints brings disease from sin;
if there is a cutting of the skin, it causes misfortune; and if it is burnt, it results in a disorder of the humors (sannipāta).
If [the image] is in an ancient temple, there will be the loss of sons and even the destruction of knowledge;
likewise, if it is in a bird sanctuary, there is the destruction of the mother and father. (132)
A site born from a cremation ground destroys one's lineage; one situated on saline soil brings about the loss of the kingdom;
and one located near a dilapidated dwelling causes diseases of the head. || 133 ||
If one is touched by a woman in the state of postpartum impurity (sūtaka) or by those under ritual defilement (āśauca), there will be the destruction of wife and sons;
if one is touched during sexual intercourse, there will indeed be affliction by disease in the tree.
One who dies during sleep meets his end peacefully, whereas one afflicted by illness faces danger from thieves;
however, one who is free from these defects and endowed with all auspicious marks [attains the highest state]. || 135 ||
[One should use wood] from the Palāśa, Bilva, and Śamī trees, as well as from the Khadira;
likewise, that produced from the Aśvattha, Vaṭa, Plakṣa, and Udumbara trees. || 136 ||
They know that the Śāntika hand is twelve finger-breadths long;
the Aindra is thirteen finger-breadths, and the Ārṣaka is eighteen finger-breadths. || 137 ||

That which measures fifteen finger-breadths in length is said to be for malevolent rites (ābhicārika). Regarding the rite of inciting hatred (vidveṣa), it is determined that the ring finger is the prescribed measure. || 138 ||

Such enclosing sticks (paridhis) are prescribed as being equal in length to the stated measurement; likewise, fuel-sticks (samidhs) originating from the banks of rivers or ponds are free from defects.

The *darbha* grasses used for the rite of strewing (*paristaraṇa*) should have their tips intact, be without internal nodes, and be neither too thick, nor too thin, nor too short; they should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length. 140.
The purifier (pavitra) is declared to be twelve finger-breadths in length;
the ritual broom (kūrca) used for the act of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is said to measure one cubit.
But in the absence of even the two officiating priests, one should place two bundles of kusha grass (kūrca), each an aratni in length, on the two sides for the Brahman and the Soma.
The tip of all the *kūrca* bundles should be four finger-breadths long;
the knot is said to be two finger-breadths, and the remainder should be fashioned as the hanging portion.

Then, for the purpose of purification during the sacrifice, a Veda-seat (vedī) was constructed, shaped like a calf's knee and measuring one pradeśa in height, fashioned from a hundred blades of darbha grass.
One should fashion a protective ring from two blades of *darbha* grass that have no internal pith;
its tip should be four finger-breadths long, and the knot should be one finger-breadth.
It is said that the root [of the herb] is two finger-breadths long; one should prepare it according to the rule.
Having placed it on the ring fingers, one should perform all ritual acts.
"One with unpurified hands should not perform any ritual act; such is the injunction. (146)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Balipīṭha and the Performance of the Mahāśānti," in the section on Ritual Practice (Kriyādhikāra) within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The thirtieth chapter.
Thereafter, the installation of the ten incarnations will be described.
Previously, I have already explained both the conceptualization of the incarnations together in one place and their conceptualization in separate shrines. (1)
If they are within a single inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should divide it into sixteen parts and arrange four parts for Aniruddha in the center.
Alternatively, O best of sages, one may represent Viṣṇu alone, whether seated or standing,
having set aside two portions in front for the sake of the door.
In the remaining ten parts, one should arrange the portions for the fish and other [deities];
whichever specific location has been assigned for each in the arrangement of the squares.
Having conceived that state as being composed of equal portions, one should establish and worship those various forms which are differentiated by their distinct states.
One should bring the descents face-to-face with the primary [teachings] in their proper order;
their characteristics were previously explained at length in the *Khila*.
One should perform each [rite] as supreme, joined with the permanent *kautuka* (sacred thread);
or else, having established the *kautuka*, one may perform it alone upon the prescribed spot.
Some say that one should worship after invoking the Primordial Form (Ādimūrti),
because Aniruddha is traditionally held to be the recipient of the tenth parts.
This is declared to be the middling [method]; the inferior [method] is certainly only that which consists of the fixed [mantra].
Having placed [the deity] upon a seat in front and having invoked it, one should worship it. || 9 ||
One should fashion those measures either equal to the primary image, or up to the limit of the ears, or else up to the limit of the arms. || 10 ||
In the consecration of the five forms, when the arrangement of Puruṣa and the others is performed, this alone shall be the authoritative measure; one should not perform anything additional.
The Brāhmaṇa is the authority for the five heroes and for Garuḍa;
he is equal to Vāsudeva, or even superior up to his arms, but not beyond that.
If the image of the ten incarnations is intended merely for curiosity, the wise man should divide the height of the original form and the *dhruva* by three. || 13 ||
Having set aside one part, two parts constitute the height for the most excellent type of image;
three parts and two parts constitute the height for the medium type of image.
Dividing each of those [intervals] into nine parts, one should determine twenty-seven elevations (tuṅga) as before, starting from the lowest single part. || 15 ||
If it should be merely for the sake of curiosity, one may arrange [the image] in a place of worship;
one should worship immeasurably those who take away the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) from them on all sides.
One should fashion the vehicles of Aniruddha all around the central area of Vainateya using nine squares. || 17 ||
Having thus performed the rites of aversion, one should again begin the installation;
one should then prepare the site for the pedestal within the sacrificial hall in due order.
One should arrange three paces in the eastern direction along the outer perimeter,
and likewise one pace each in the southern and other directions for the purpose of the doors.

From the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa), one should consecrate the principal fires for the Matsya and other [deities] in their respective directions, according to the sequence of the ten parts.
Having prepared the pit and the sacrificial altar as prescribed, the rites beginning with the opening of the eyes are performed after the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 21 ||
Even without the rites for all the deities and the supreme self, one should arrange the consecration, festivals, and so forth, as before. || 22 ||
Their principal mantras and likewise their various forms have already been described by me; everything else is just like that of Hari.

One should perform the invocation for the ten parts beginning with the primary form, starting from Dhruva; because this Dhruva is partless (niṣkala), one should perform it using the names of the auspicious knots (kautuka).
If it should be otherwise, one should worship with the names beginning with "Dhruva":
Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Rāma, and likewise Kṛṣṇa. || 25 ||
One should properly place it in the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) to the south or north, or one may place it in the intermediate space, or even in the dance pavilion (nṛttamaṇḍapa). || 26 ||
Having constructed a hall for their installation and having prepared a place for the excellent food,
one should arrange the hall for Vāmana facing the south.
To its south or east, one should prepare a space for Rāghava;
or, having placed [the image] for Nṛsiṃha on the left, one should do so to its left or in the east.
For the sake of Kṛṣṇa, one should construct a sacrificial hall extending from east to west;
having caused a bed to be made there in the western part, [one should place it] in front of that.
One should designate the primary fire and a bathing pit in front of it;
then, at the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, one should prepare a water-pot as previously described.

Having performed the ceremonial bathing, the mounting of the bed, the recitation of the Maitra hymn, and everything else in its entirety according to the previous procedure in the principal fire; || 31 ||
One should worship [the deity] one hundred and eight times with the respective principal mantras;
having bathed in the morning according to the rules, one should enter the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa).
Having placed Varāha and Rāma on the right, and likewise Nārasiṃha on the left, and Kṛṣṇa to his left. || 33 ||
Having installed Vārāha and Nārasiṃha in the front pavilion,
or having installed Kṛṣṇa and Rāma in the intermediate space, one should worship them.
To the south, one may install Nārasiṃha, provided it is not devoid of its vehicle; this applies to a single-liṅga temple (ekabera-vimāna) in both the inner sanctum and the front pavilion.
If there should be a lack of space to perform the festive installation ceremony,
one should place the image in the outer part of the front pavilion once that pavilion has been constructed.
Having installed [the deity] in the prescribed location for the festival, one should worship it;
the worship of the primary images of others is performed with the sixteen forms. (37)
This alone would be the distinction; everything else is like that of Hari.
Or else, the Fish and the Tortoise [images] should be in the center of the sanctum.
Having installed Varāha and the others, one should arrange them in the eight directions;
one should also separately perform the rites for Dhruva and Kautuka in front.
O ascetics, O best of sages, listen as I shall briefly describe the installation of the five heroes, the re-establishment of the five heroes, and their worship. (40)
The worship of the five primordial deities beginning with Vāsudeva, together with Viṣṇu and Brahmā, is declared as the "Worship of the Nine Heroes. (41)
O you whose wealth is austerity, this [mantra], whether joined with *annaprajāpati* or devoid of it, bestows nourishment upon all worlds and brings about the success of all sacrifices. 42.
This worship of the five heroes indeed increases the Vedas and the Vedic way of life;
it bestows all sovereignty upon men and grants liberation as well as all spiritual perfections. || 43 ||
It may be the Nadīviśāla, the Aṣṭāṅga, the Somacchanda, the Catuḥsphuṭa,
or the Sarvatobhadraka, or even in the form of a Gopura (gate-tower).
Having constructed it with one or two stories according to the prescribed rule,
one should make the ground solid on the first level and establish [the structure] upon the second level.
When the height of the son of Vasudeva is one-eighth less than the width of the womb, the rise of Saṅkarṣaṇa is thirty-three daṇḍas plus one. || 46 ||
Balabhadra, created by the divine powers, was indeed taller than Vāsudeva;
Pradyumna’s height reached as far as the very limit of Vāsudeva’s ears.
Nasya, Stanau, Āsāna, and Ucca are Rukmiṇī; Sāmba is indeed [the next]; Aniruddha is declared to be after Hikkā of Vāsudeva. || 48 ||
One should fashion the lotus-seated Brahmā with a height equal to that of Vāsudeva;
one should fashion Viṣṇu in their midst as the collective form of them all.

One should perform [the rite] for the stationary, the moving, and likewise for both the stationary and the moving, either together with Śrī and Bhūmi or without them, according to the prescribed rule.
One should establish the five [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva in the human position;
likewise, one should place Vāsudeva himself to the north of the Brahma-thread.
The dark-complexioned, two-armed Lord, endowed with the conch and discus, whose eyes were as long as lotuses, and whose face resembled the serene moon. || 52 ||
The god wearing yellow garments and adorned with all ornaments;
and on his right, the goddess Rukmiṇī, dark-complexioned and radiant in red garments.
She was adorned with fish-shaped earrings and a sacred thread,
wearing a circular earring on her right ear and a shark-shaped earring on her left.
The right foot is drawn back and the left foot is firmly planted;
the left hand is extended and the right hand likewise displays the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā). || 55 ||
Alternatively, one should place her holding a divine lotus with her right hand,
and on her right side, one should fashion Baladeva.
One should depict him as white-complexioned and two-armed; with his right hand he bestows boons and fearlessness, while his left hand is raised; he is adorned with all ornaments. (57)
On the right side of the wall, however, [one should place] Brahmā, with a golden luster, two-armed, with his left hand on his hip and his right hand granting fearlessness. || 58 ||
One should place [the image] facing north, adorned with all ornaments;
to the north of Vāsudeva is Pradyumna, standing with two arms.
One should fashion [the deity] resembling the dark green of a ripening crop, adorned with all ornaments,
with the right hand granting fearlessness and the left resting upon the hip.
Leaning against the northern wall, he stands with Ambā, two-armed, facing south, dark-complexioned, and adorned with all ornaments. (61)
One should visualize the right hand as granting boons (varada) and the left hand resting on the hip;
and to the east of that, one should fashion Aniruddha, who has the luster of coral.
His right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), while his left hangs down along the hip;
indeed, his two hands are exactly like those of Sāmba, facing toward the south.
One should fashion Viṣṇu in the center using the very best of the ten parts;
the stationary [deities] in the divine portion, and the moving [deities] in the Brahma-square.
A stationary structure is declared to have a height equal to that of Vāsudeva, provided it is entirely mobile according to the measurement favorable to all. 66.
One should place the *kautuka* (sacred thread) before each of the five heroes;
the *kautuka* should take on the same form as the *dhruva* [thread], which is its specific form.
While there is curiosity among all [regarding whom to bathe], one should nevertheless bathe Viṣṇu alone during the festival,
specifically the four-armed Viṣṇu.
One should fashion Annaprajāpati from the east of Aniruddha;
one should make him in the form of a living being, with either two arms or four arms. (69)
One should worship the thirty-three gods all around in the inner sanctum;
the twelve Ādityas on the eastern wall and the Rudras on the southern wall.
In the west are the eight Vasus, and in the north, the two Nāsatyas, in due order;
on the southern side of the door are those bearing swords, spears, arrows, and bows.
One should worship the ten weapons: the mace (gadā), the sword (khaḍga), the conch (śaṅkha), the Śārṅga bow, the shield (kheṭaka), the goad (aṅkuśa), and the lotus (padma). || 72 ||
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) on all sides, as well as Prahlāda, who is the embodiment of knowledge,
and the twelve Ādityas and eleven Rudras in their proper order.
One should depict the eight Vasus, the two Nāsatyas, and the four Jyotiṣas in order on the eastern wall; below them, on the plinth, one should place the Pāṇḍavas facing outward.
The wise practitioner should visualize the five divine heroes, each endowed with their respective emblems, facing north and south respectively, against the eastern wall.

This alone would be the distinction; everything else—such as the months, fortnights, lunar mansions, auspicious moments (muhūrta), and astrological configurations—is exactly like that of Hari. || 76 ||
Having offered the sprouts, he should likewise collect the ritual materials;
he should then prepare the sacrificial hall, the five fires, and the Pauṇḍarīka altar.
One who is devoid of the *aupāsana* fire should place [the image] to the south of the *dakṣiṇāgni*; likewise, one should place the image of Annamūrti to the north of the *āvasathya* fire.
One should perform all the rites, such as the opening of the eyes and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), as previously described.
Having extracted the deities who have entered into the preliminary consecration, one should perform their ritual bathing (abhiṣeka). || 79 ||
Having adorned [the image] according to the rules, one should perform a circumambulation of the village;
then one should place it upon a seat in the south-western corner of the sacrificial hall.
Having prepared the ritual jar for each of them individually as before, and having adorned it, worshipped it, and tied on the *pratisarā* amulet; 81.
Having laid him down upon his bed, he should teach him the Vedas in due order,
after praising the office of the Hotṛ priest between Vāsudeva and Viṣṇu.
In the Āhavanīya fire of Rāma, in the Dakṣiṇa fire of Pradyumna, and likewise in the Gārhapatya and Āvasathya fires of Sāmba; || 83 ||
The *hautra* ritual should belong to Aniruddha and the *brāhmaṇa* portion to Prajāpati;
having invoked them as before, the *hotra* rite should be performed in the *aupāsana* fire. (84)
Having offered oblations of clarified butter after having ascertained [the proper time], and having worshipped all the gods,
he should strew grass around the assembly fire of Vāsudeva according to the prescribed rule.
The Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, the Śrīsūkta, the Mahīsūkta, together with the five Vāruṇa hymns. || 86 ||
Accompanied by the root-homa and the sāman-chants, and endowed with the [proper] deities and so forth, he offers a thousand oblations while meditating upon the God. || 87 ||
One should sacrifice there once again, indeed with Viṣṇu in mind;
having offered to all the deities, one should sacrifice to Vaiṣṇava three times more.
Having offered the Mindā oblations and the Picchinna oblation, and having performed the Pravāhaṇa rite, he likewise offered the Puruṣasūkta into Rāma’s Āhavanīya fire. (89)
Then, one should offer the Viṣṇu-sūkta and the Brāhma-sūkta to Pradyumna on the south,
and again offer the Vaiṣṇava-sūkta to Sāmba in the Gārhapatya fire.
At the domestic fire (āvasathya), one should worship Aniruddha with the single-syllable mantra and others,
as well as with the two Rudra-mantras, while recollecting the God with devotion.
The officiating priest, having performed the eight-fold rite, should offer oblations in the final [sections] and so forth;
he should sacrifice in the Āhavanīya fire, performing the Jaya and other offerings once each.
Then, having consecrated the Pauṇḍarīka fire according to the prescribed rite,
he placed a lotus soaked in cow's ghee within it while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should offer the supreme self-oblation;
then, having dismissed the other fires, he should dismiss the sabhyāgni and the pauṇḍarīkāgni.
Ruru should pass the remainder of the night with dances, songs, and instrumental music;
then, having bathed in the morning, he should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra and perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā).

Then, after performing the *śānti-homa* according to the prescribed rite, he should release the *pauṇḍarīka* [offering] at the end of the homa, and then perform the other rites as before upon the pedestal of worship (*arcā-pīṭha*).
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him in the presence of the deity;
having strewn grass around the Sabhya fire, one should worship with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra. || 97 ||
Having performed the oblation, he should establish the Sabhya fire to the south for the daily homa;
meanwhile, the Ācārya should carry the principal pitcher on his head in front.
The attendants of that deity should proceed carrying the jars while chanting propitiatory hymns;
having recited the Śākuna Sūkta, the Śākuna priest should perform the circumambulation of the temple.
Then, having entered within and placed [the image] in the seat of the Jīva,
the Preceptor, while mentally meditating upon Hari, should mutter the Ātmasūkta.
Having performed the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) and the placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa) upon the image as before,
[one should do so] for all [deities] beginning with Rāma, accompanied by their respective initial syllables.
Meditating with his mind upon the inward-turned activity [of consciousness] and upon Viṣṇu, the highest of the high,
he proceeded in due order from Vāsudeva down to Rukmiṇī.
Having invoked Viṣṇu in the center, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
the wise practitioner should then invoke Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others in their proper order.
The deities residing in the womb-chamber, the lords of the gates, the gatekeepers,
the world-protectors of the celestial palaces, and likewise their successive retinues.
Having invoked [the deities] from the pitcher of Vāsudeva in due order,
one should likewise meditate upon all of them together in a single pitcher, excluding Viṣṇu.
Having invoked Vāsudeva, one should then invoke [the other deities] in sequence;
having caused the priests to recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula as before, together with the installers.
One should offer honey, milk-rice, and other such foods to Rāma and the others;
one should give an offering of mung-bean flour to Brahmā, and pure food to Prajāpati.
One should perform the mūrtihoma in the perpetual fire-pit according to the prescribed rules;
having completed the rites ending with the offering of oblations and the festival, one should perform the ritual bathing at night.
Thereafter, one should indeed commence the festival according to the sequence prescribed for festivals;
one should give gold, cattle, land, and so forth as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is like that of Hari.
Regarding the installation of the five heroes, the specification of their locations is:
at the edge of a village, at the edge of a city, at the edge of a mountain, or within a forest. (110)
On the banks of rivers or oceans, in a secluded place, or elsewhere,
having established the five-fold vidyā-yāga here, one should worship it.
The Method of Worshiping the Five Heroes:
Hereafter I shall explain the worship of the most excellent Five Heroes.
The worshipper, having risen at dawn, bathed, and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana), [should proceed]. 112.
Having satiated the gods and others with water and having recited the prayers as before,
he should then enter the temple and circumambulate it according to the prescribed rule.

Having performed all the rites, such as opening the doors and so forth, as previously described, and having gathered all the ritual materials while discarding the withered offerings (nirmālya), [he should proceed]. || 114 ||
Having cooked the sacrificial offerings and side-dishes according to the prescribed rule,
he should bathe Vāsudeva while again reciting the mantra "iṣe tvā" and others.
Having bathed Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rite with the Puruṣasūkta,
one should bathe Balabhadra with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Having bathed Pradyumna with the Viṣṇu-sūkta and Sāmba with Vaiṣṇava hymns,
one should bathe Aniruddha with the Ekākṣara and other sūktas.
One should worship Brahmā and Prajāpati with the two Brāhma-mantras, and [the deities] with the names of the three enclosures of Vāsudeva Viṣṇu. || 118 ||
One should also place flowers for the other deities according to their forms;
having worshipped the deities of the door and so forth, one should enter again inside.
Seated facing north upon a seat with one knee bent,
he should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and likewise invoke [the deity] from the Pole Star (dhruva).
In the case of Viṣṇu’s mobile [liṅga], there is no invocation nor dismissal;
likewise for the single-form (ekabera) [liṅga] of Viṣṇu, the specific procedure therein shall now be described.
Having first worshipped the image with its eight forms prior to the consecration, and having likewise performed the oil massage and bathed it again as before; || 122 ||
Having adorned and installed [the image], one should worship it with the eight forms.
I shall now explain the specific details regarding the worship of Balabhadra and the others.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to Rāma with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
then, having recited "hiraṇyagarbha," one should likewise offer the arghya oblation.
The sipping of water (*ācamana*) for Pradyumna is prescribed with the mantra "yoge yoga";
while saying "idamāpaḥ śivā" and "iha puṣṭim," he offers the respectful oblation (*arghya*). (125)
Then, during the worship of Sāmba, one should perform the offering of the oblation;
having recited "samāne vṛkṣe," one should again offer water for sipping (ācamana). 126.

The *arghya* offering is performed with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, and the oblation (*havis*) with the verse beginning "samāvavarti. The oblation, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the *arghya* for Aniruddha are as before.
One should worship those headed by Saṅkarṣaṇa with offerings ending in mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa),
and likewise Brahmā and Prajāpati with the two Brāhma-mantras.
One should worship Viṣṇu and Vāsudeva with thirty-two forms;
all these forms have already been described by me in the Khila section.
For those who have no physical forms, worship is performed by means of their names;
this is the sole wonder of the five heroes when it occurs. (130)
At that time, however, addressing him as Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa,
speaking of Pradyumna and Sāmba, and calling him Aniruddha— || 131 ||
Then, having invoked [the deities] with the five [syllables] and worshipped them according to the rule,
one should install the deities upon the five [elements] at the conclusion of the worship, according to the rule.
Thus has been briefly described the worship of the five heroes;
all other matters not mentioned here should be performed in the same manner as for Viṣṇu. || 133 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Ten Incarnations and the Five Heroes," in the section on Rituals within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The thirty-first chapter.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the general expiation, the universal atonement for all;
for worship performed according to the rules is impossible even for Brahmā and the other gods to accomplish.
Or what [need is there to speak] of those humans of unsettled minds, whose hearts are attached to sense objects and whose consciousnesses are carried away by the senses? || 2 ||
Regarding faults that were unknown during rites such as worship,
and regarding faults that were known yet disregarded during rites such as worship—
whether through delusion, greed, or negligence— (3)
For the sake of pacifying each respective fault,
one should perform the general expiation at the conclusion of each respective twilight (saṃdhyā) with the Vaiṣṇavas using the Viṣṇu-sūkta.
One should also [worship] with the Puruṣasūkta, as well as the Viṣṇugāyatrī, with the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable [mantras], and also with "namo brahmaṇe. (5)
Having offered flowers at the feet [of the deity], one should propitiate them, saying, "Forgive me.
At the conclusion of the night worship, however, one should do so with a hymn beginning with the single-syllable [Om].
Having praised [Viṣṇu] with the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, one should offer a handful of flowers;
this should be done at the end of the month, or on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), or likewise under the Śravaṇa asterism.
Therefore, one should perform the rite of offering the sprouts on the day prior;
having especially worshipped the Lord of Gods during the preceding night.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation and likewise tied the protective amulet (pratisara),
and having laid down the Lord of Gods, one should then bathe according to the prescribed rite in the morning.
At the conclusion of the morning twilight, having performed the circumambulation of the village and having established the Lord of Gods in the bathing pavilion, [he should proceed].
Having bathed [the deity] with forty-eight jars,
one should fashion a lotus out of rice grains, possessing eight petals and a pericarp.
Having installed the deity within that [image], one should worship it with seats and other offerings;
or one should present a great oblation or abundant food according to one's capacity. || 12 ||
Having offered water for drinking and water for sipping, one should present mouth-perfume;
at that very time, the wise one should perform the worship of the image as before. || 13 ||
And having sprinkled the perpetual fire with oblations to the gods and others, to Viṣṇu,
with the Puruṣasūkta and likewise with the hymn beginning "viṣṇornuka".

Then one should worship with clarified butter and with sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter, ending with the Vyāhṛtis, using the Jayā and other mantras, as well as the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras and the mantras of the forms of the assembly (pariṣanmūrtis). || 15 ||
One should worship one hundred and eight times with the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras,
and likewise offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) using the previously mentioned mantras.

Having established [the image] in the place of the Jīva and having prostrated with the words "Forgive me," one should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and his predecessors in the presence of the deity.
Whatever deficiency has occurred during the year in the daily or occasional worship,
for the sake of pacifying all those defects, one should indeed perform it in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the aforementioned worship for the pacification of the faults acquired throughout the year, or for the sake of spiritual power.

Some of the best of sages desire that the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) be performed during the conjunction of the Śravaṇa asterism with the twelfth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the offering of the *pavitra* for the sake of the *pavitrāropaṇa* rite of Hari—
whether it be for daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or annual worship (*saṃvatsarārcana*).
Whatever faults may arise, whether through ignorance or even through knowledge, they are undoubtedly pacified by the Pavitrāropaṇa alone. || 22 ||
It pacifies all defects, grants the fulfillment of all desires,
bestows long life and health upon the performer, and brings about the success of all sacrifices.
One should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite for Viṣṇu for the sake of all peace, especially during the bright fortnight of the month known as Mārgaśīrṣa. || 24 ||
The proper time is on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, or under the asterism Śravaṇa,
during the months of the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), or likewise on the fifth day of Viṣṇu. || 25 ||
One should perform [the rite] for the poet in the month of Āśvayuja on the full moon day of Āśvayuja,
and also on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight during the six months dedicated to Śambhu.
On the twelfth day, it is prescribed for the Sun; on the sixth, it is proclaimed for Skanda;
and in the month of Kārttika, it is for Durgā on the ninth day under the asterism of Kṛttikā.

One should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) on the fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight, or alternatively, during the dark fortnight, or under the asterisms of Uttarāphalgunī or Uttarāṣāḍhā.
Therefore, one should perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third day prior to that [main] day. || 29 ||
After the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇaka), one should also collect the ritual materials;
one should prepare the pavilion for the purificatory rite (pavitramaṇḍapa) either in front of the deity or to its south.

Or else, having prepared a place there in the bathing hall according to the prescribed rite, [one should adorn it] with archways, full water-pots, and banners of plantain trees and areca palms. || 31 ||
Having adorned the four gates and both pillars with canopies, banners, garlands, and wrappings around the pillars; || 32 ||
With hanging strings of pearls, or with flowers, or with garlands of darbha grass, with networks of golden tinkling bells, and with wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) adorned with jewels; || 33 ||
Having decorated the entire interior and having smeared it with cow dung, one should offer many lamps, adorned with five-colored [garlands]. || 34 ||

In its center, having measured four cubits or three cubits in each of the four directions, and having established the location for the pedestal by means of cords extending eastward and northward; || 35 ||
Regarding the conceptualization of Mount Meru and the rest: in the center of that [space], there should be one Mount Meru with a height of one cubit;
surrounding it are the eight principal mountain ranges (kulācala), each of which is less than a quarter of its size.
Surrounding that, there are sixteen squares, each reduced by one-third;
these indeed are the stations of the eight [deities] beginning with Indra and those beginning with Śiva.
With four lines of ten [squares] each, one forms a square on the outside;
within these are the seven oceans and six islands, beginning with Śāka. (38)
Therein, Mount Meru has a golden luster, appearing white, yellow, black, and reddish;
likewise, there are the pairs beginning with Himācala and the eight principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). || 39 ||
White, yellow, black, dark, red, blue, white, and crimson—
these should be diligently arranged in the sixteen squares outside of that.
Having meditated upon Jambūdvīpa and the others, one should likewise place the salt ocean outside them, and then Śākadvīpa, which resembles the dark green of grain, outside that as well.
The white Ocean of Milk is in the realm of Brahmā; beyond that is Kuśadvīpa, then the yellow Ocean of Clarified Butter, and likewise the blue Krauñcadvīpa.
The white ocean of curd-water is joined with Śālmalīdvīpa;
the honey-colored ocean, having a golden-yellow luster, is joined with Gomedadvīpa. || 43 ||
Some [oceans] are an ocean of sugarcane juice, some are white and joined with lotuses;
there is an ocean of pure water, a red one, and likewise the Lokāloka mountain.
Having thus prepared the mandala-circle with colors produced from modifications of minerals, or with flower-pollen, or even with powdered leaves; || 45 ||
Having ensured that all these [mantras] are joined with their respective seed-syllables (varṇa) without confusion,
one should recite them after fasting on the previous day and bathing at the three periods of the day.
The purificatory substance for the Dhruva-vessel and the others should be made of gold weighing no less than one niṣka each;
for the two goddesses, it should be half that measure, and likewise for the members of the assembly.
One should fashion a single thread for Viṣṇu that covers the surface of the ankle;
this is called the *buddha-sūtra*, and it is unique to Hari. (48)
If he is unable [to do so], he should instead prepare a woven thread and arrange it;
if he prepares a woven one, he should then fold it three times.
The method for preparing the purifier (pavitra) is as follows:
two persons should stand facing the east, while one stands facing them;
reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, he should increase [the length of] the cord by one [loop] at the upper right.
Having tripled that [measurement], one should again increase it by one part on the upper left;
then, having placed it in a clean location, one should likewise place earth upon it.
Having placed the two hands together, struck them, and folded them triple, one should fashion it; this is called the *yajñopavīta*. Now, the thread for the knot is described.
One should fashion the forms of Puruṣa and the others with one thousand and eight, half of that, or a hundred, or even half of that again.
One should fashion the retinues of the two goddesses with half that [measurement];
for the best and other [sizes], it should extend to the ankles, the knees, or the thighs.
One should fashion an odd number of knots with threads of the five colors mentioned;
having performed all this during the day and having observed the evening twilight (saṃdhyā) worship, [one should proceed].
The Deposition of Substances:
Having fashioned the pavilion of the three worlds, one should perform the deposition of those substances;
and one should place all the purificatory offerings upon the summit of Mount Meru.
One should place the materials for the eightfold offerings upon the eight great mountain ranges (kulācala),
and one should place auspicious objects upon the eight positions of the world-protectors (lokapāla).
Woven garments, upper cloths, and so forth; the elements, as well as ornaments... [and] sacrificial oblation, water. 58.
The purifiers, beginning with Puruṣa, are located on the Kulaparvatas starting from the east.
One should place the Kapila and other [deities] in the corners, starting from the southeast;
likewise, one should place the threads for the attendants within sixteen divisions of that area.
One should place [the vessels] upon new cloth on each of the mountains mentioned,
and likewise, filled with their respective substances, upon all the oceans.
One should place eight jars for each [deity], wrapped with threads,
filled with grains such as *āḍhaka* and others, and covered separately with upper cloths.
One should place those ablution jars on the outer continents;
one should worship Viṣṇu in the east, outside the Cakravāla mountain range.
One should worship the curved sword and the arrow on the right;
having worshipped Paṅktīśa in the west, one should especially worship him on the left as well. || 64 ||
One should worship the discus, the sword, and the arrow on the right;
having worshipped Paṅktīśa in the west, one should especially worship [the remaining weapons] on the left.
The conch, the shield, the Śārṅga bow, as well as the Kaumodakī mace;
the umbrella, the pair of chowries, the mirror, and likewise the banner. || 65 ||
One should install them without confusion in the corners beginning with the northeast;
the commencement of the festival, the bathing ceremony at the conclusion of the night worship, or the festival itself [should take place]. 66.
Having lifted [the image] from the pedestal with the mantra "Paraṃ raṃ ha," and having recited the Svastisūkta, he, adorned with all ornaments, should proceed to the crossroads.

Having placed [the image] on the western seat of the mandala, having worshipped it with the eight forms, having offered the sacrificial food, and likewise having bound the protective thread (pratisara); || 68 ||
As before, one should have the deity cast in shadow and teach him the Vedas in due order;
then the officiant, having worshipped the presiding deities of the ritual materials, should perform the rites according to the prescribed rules.
One should fashion a lotus mandala with its proper characteristics to the east of the [main] mandala;
as for the method of oblation there, having established the perpetual fire and having sprinkled water around the fire.

One should perform oblations with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru) using Vaiṣṇava mantras; having praised the office of the Hotṛ priest, invoked the gods, and worshipped them as before.
Having offered clarified butter oblations after the ritual determination, one should worship them on all sides with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and the Pauruṣasūkta.
One should offer oblations with the Śrīmahīsūkta combined with the five Vāruṇa hymns;
having also offered with the Jayā and other [mantras], one should likewise [offer] to the deities and others.
Then there is a thousand oblations dedicated to all the deities,
the two *mindā* oblations for broken rites, and after that, the *padmahoma*.
One should likewise offer oblations with the Pārāyaṇika-mantras joined with the syllable *īṃ*, as well as the Rātrisūkta and the Sārasvata-sūkta.
Likewise, one should recite the Brahma-sūkta beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," as well as the two Rudra-mantras together with the Viśvajit-sūkta.
Having uttered "Namo vāce" and recited "Śanno vāta," and having completed the fire-oblation at night while keeping the God of gods in mind; || 77 ||
Having bathed in the morning, one should then perform one's duties according to the prescribed rules;
having removed the flowers offered to the deity, one should also clean away the remains of the offering (nirmālya). || 78 ||
Having established the deity in the northeast within a pavilion above the mandala as before,
one should bathe him after worshipping with the eight services (aṣṭopacāra) and with salt and other substances. || 79 ||
Reciting "iṣe tvorje tvā," one should bathe [the image] with all substances;
having recited the Puruṣasūkta, one should consecrate it with pure waters.
Then, having wiped [the image] again with a cloth, one should place it upon the previous seat;
all rites such as the internal bath and so forth should be performed for a single-liṅga (ekabera) form.
Having first adorned [the deity] with garments, upper cloths, ornaments, and minerals as is appropriate, and having worshipped it with the eight forms using the previous mantras.
Having performed the touching of the thread with the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka,
one should perform the investiture of the purifier (pavitrāropaṇa), which is scented with camphor and other fragrances and possesses a delightful aroma.
With the very same mantra mentioned previously, one should offer [the oblation] to the God with devotion;
one should separately offer that excellent [oblation] to the forms [of the Lord], such as Puruṣa and the others. 84.
Regarding the number of purifiers (pavitra):
one for Viṣṇu, and likewise one for each of those [other deities] is considered middling;
if there is a single thread for all of them, they declare that to be inferior. || 85 ||
One should offer a knotted thread and a sacred thread (nivīta) with devotion to the God;
in this same manner, one should likewise provide a thread for all [the deities], beginning with Dhruva.
One should give a thread-garment (nivītaka) to all the female deities;
in this manner, it should be given to all, preceded by the sounding of conch shells and musical instruments. 87.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods with the eightfold offerings according to the prescribed rite, one should present abundant sacrificial oblations such as milk-rice and the like. || 88 ||
Having offered water for drinking and sipping, as well as betel-leaf mixed with camphor,
the preceptor should perform an offering of flowers with hymns and prostrate himself with the five limbs.
Having slowly performed a circumambulation of a village or a grove adorned with all ornaments, one should place [the image] in a place inhabited by living beings.
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and those who preceded him in the presence of the deity;
however, in the middle [case], one should perform it without the maṇḍala of the three worlds.
One should place the sacred threads upon new cloth on the grain-seat;
one should offer oblations in the perpetual fire-pit with the *pauṇḍarīka* flower, excluding the *anila* (wind) mantra.
The declaration of the fruit of the Pavitrāropaṇa rite is as follows:
for the lowest class of devotee, the ritual bath with pure water alone shall suffice.
Thus, he who performs the Pavitrāropaṇa of Hari with devotion [attains the supreme goal]. || 93 ||
One obtains all that is desired and gains the fruit of all forms of giving;
liberated from all sins, one becomes renowned and attains prosperity. 94.
Having obtained the fruit of worshiping for a year, he shall attain union (sāyujya). That mortal who wears this thread, which has been used by the God of gods, [attains this]. || 95 ||
If there be worship at home, especially during the performance of the fire-oblation (homa), one obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
One should worship in the domestic fire (aupāsana) even without [invoking] all the deities or the Supreme Self,
and without any of the ritual exclamations beginning with "īṃ".
For the gods beginning with Brahmā, one should recite their respective mantras one hundred and eight times;
likewise, the Jayā hymns, the Kūṣmāṇḍa verses, and the Pañcavāruṇa hymn.
One should offer the Mindā oblations and the Vyāhṛtis even if they have been interrupted;
this alone shall be the modification, while everything else remains as before.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Preparation of the Pavitra," in the section on Rituals (Kriyādhikāra) within the *Śrīvaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
The thirty-second chapter.
O wise ones, hereafter I shall proclaim the procedure for the worship of the Śamī tree. On the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Proṣṭhapada, || 1 ||
Having entered the temple and bowed down to the Lord,
one should perform the ritual bathing according to the procedure prescribed for bathing.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods equally with various garments and ornaments, and having mounted him upon a horse equipped with all manner of missiles and weapons; || 3 ||
When evening has arrived, the wise man should lead the Lord of Gods, accompanied by parasols and chowries and provided with all musical instruments. || 4 ||
In whatever place the Śamī tree stands, the deity goes to that very spot;
having adorned the area all around the Śamī tree according to the prescribed rite. || 5 ||
The learned man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited and should perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa);
furthermore, he should smear the area in front of the deity with cow dung.
Having adorned it with colored streaks and other ornaments, one should sprinkle it with purified water;
then, having installed the Śārṅga bow and likewise the arrow in that place.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the presiding deities of the Śārṅga bow:
having invoked Viṣṇu, Rudra, Brahmā, and likewise Varuṇa.
One should worship the presiding deities of the arrows, the discus, and likewise the conch; as well as the mace-bearer, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow.
One should worship Vahni, the presiding deity of the Śamī tree, there;
likewise, one should worship the deities of the eastern branches of the tree and the Rākṣasas on the southern side.
The Piśācas in the west, and Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the north—
having invoked these deities, the wise man should worship them in this very order.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings, the worshipper, being of a well-pleased mind and full of vigor, should take up a bow and present fruits and other offerings.
With the mantra "dhanvanā gā," the wise man should cause the bowstring to sound;
with the mantra "yāta iṣuḥ śi," he should fix the arrow upon the bow.
With his discus he should cut down the yakṣas and other lords in the east, and the rākṣasas in the south;
likewise, with his mace he strikes the piśācas situated in the western direction.
And with the *asinā* mantra, one strikes at the north, as well as Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
one should discharge four arrows in the four directions around the tree. || 15 ||
One should discharge an arrow called Śārṅga at the top of the tree;
then, taking up other arrows once again, one should sprinkle them with purified water.
Having established [the deity] before the god and caused him to perform a prostration, he should then take up the deity and lead him toward the village. || 17 ||
Having performed the circumambulation of the temple, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
having bathed [the deity] with warm water and seated him upon the throne.
Having offered the great oblation, one should likewise offer betel-leaf;
he who performs this with devotion is liberated from all sins. || 19 ||
One obtains all desires and attains union with Viṣṇu.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the Kṛttikā-lamp and the characteristics of the Kṛttikā-lamp. (20)
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform worship with lamps;
having entered the temple and bowed down to the Lord of Gods.
Having bathed the God together with the two Goddesses according to the prescribed rite, and having adorned the Lord of Gods with various garments and ornaments, [he worshipped Him]. || 22 ||
Having especially offered rice mixed with sesame, milk-rice, cakes, and parched grain, one should present mouth-fresheners. || 23 ||
Having placed the god upon the vehicle together with his two queens, accompanied by umbrellas and chowries, and provided with all kinds of musical instruments. || 24 ||

At the conclusion of the twilight worship (sandhyā-pūjā), the wise one should also lead [the deity] along the path, either to the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) or even to the third enclosure (tṛtīyāvaraṇa). || 25 ||
Either in the fifth enclosure or likewise in the seventh,
one should properly establish a palmyra tree in the middle of the path.
Likewise, the coconut, or else the kaitaka, the betel nut, and also the bamboo;
some say it is the agastya.
Having fixed these [parts] upon the wood and having made them firm with effort,
[the height of the pedestal] should be equal to that of the vimāna, or even one-third greater.
Or even more than half, or indeed more than three-quarters;
or likewise less by a quarter, and similarly less by half.
The lowest [size] is three-quarters less than that, having the same measurement as the lamp-pillar;
it should extend ten cubits all around the lamp-staff. || 30 ||
Having fashioned a covering with circular pieces shaped like gate-towers (gopura), one should move about;
one should cover it entirely from the base to the top with palm leaves.
One should encircle it with waves, garlands of *darbha* grass, and archways;
having adorned it with flowers and perfumes, one should wrap it with a new cloth.
Having performed the *puṇyāha* rite according to the rules, one should also cause the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) to be performed;
O best of sages, I shall now describe the presiding deities of the great lamps.
One should then invoke it by those names: Baḍabāmukha, Kālāgni, Pralayānala, and Mahādīpa.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings, one should also present parched grains (lājā);
[the vessel] may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. || 35 ||
Having properly filled the vessel with cow's ghee and other such substances, one should place five wicks in the four cardinal directions starting from the center. || 36 ||
Now hear the sequence of presiding deities for the auspicious thread and the lamp:
Bahurūpamukha, Kālāgni, and likewise Pralayānala. (37)
Having invoked Jātavedas as the great lamp into the five [fires] and having worshipped them with the eightfold offerings (aṣṭopacāra), one should also offer parched grain (lāja).
The priest, with a well-pleased mind and adorned with all ornaments, should lift up the lamp with both hands while reciting the mantra: "O Viṣṇu, [this is] for you. (39)
For the welfare of the entire world, [he should worship] from the head down to the feet;
and for the prosperity of that village, from the forehead down to the end.
Having circumambulated it three times each, from the eyes down to the feet, for the increase of the king and the kingdom, and for the auspiciousness of all; || 41 ||
Then, taking the lamp, he should proceed very slowly;
having performed three circumambulations, he should set it down carefully on the tip of his staff.
Having taken four wicks, one should cast them in the four directions;
and with the mantra "This is your source," one should place [the lamp] upon the great lamp. || 43 ||
When the great lamp has been ignited, one should repeatedly bow to the Lord of Devas;
by the fruit of beholding the lamp, all sins are destroyed, and both lifespan and fame increase. || 44 ||
By beholding that lamp, one shall immediately attain all desires;
upon the extinguishing of that lamp, the wise man should lead the Lord of Gods away.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having installed the deity in the place of life, one should worship the Supreme Being (Puṣottama). 46.
Having offered an abundance [of food], one should indeed offer mouth-perfume;
he who thus performs this excellent Kṛttikā-lamp with devotion— || 47 ||
One who desires a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom; one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth;
one who desires prosperity shall attain it, and he shall likewise enjoy long life and fame. (48)
One attains all sovereignty and shall achieve union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. Next, I shall describe the sequence of festivals for the offering of fragrant oil during the month of Jyeṣṭha. || 49 ||
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has duly arrived, on a day joined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism,
one should especially procure fragrant oil during the Viṣṇu-portion [of the day].
I shall now proclaim that sequence; listen, O best of sages!
Having prepared the sacrificial hall, fully equipped with all ornaments. (51)
Having caused the Sabhya and Pauṇḍarīka fires to be established according to the prescribed characteristics, on the day preceding that [main] day, or on the third or even the fifth day; || 52 ||
One should begin the placement of the ritual seed-syllables (aṅkura) either on the seventh or the ninth day;
having performed the foundational oblation (āghāra) according to the rules, all subsequent rites should then be carried out.
The physicians, however, should cause a depression to be made on the ground at the northern side, measuring four tālas in width and likewise in depth. || 53 ||
One should place a vessel with a capacity of two droṇas in a low spot;
one should firmly set the vessel in the low spot with the mantra: "Bhūḥ, for stability. (55)
Those which arise from Malaya aloe-wood, from Devadāru wood,
or from any other perfumed wood— these indeed are fit for the gods.
Having collected the guggulu and having ground each substance separately,
one should place the materials into the vessel while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
Then, having covered it with a shallow dish, one should smear it all over with clay;
one should then place cow-dung and pieces of wood upon it. || 58 ||
One should cook it over a mild fire until the appearance of oil;
having cooked it with skill and effort, one should extract the oil immediately. (59)
The merchant should throw various items that have been soaked in decoctions into it;
then, having purified the oil, he should place that vessel securely upon a grain-mat.
One should wrap it with a thread using the very mantra already mentioned;
then, having likewise worshipped the ancestors, Soma, and the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati).
Having invoked them into the oil, one should worship them with offerings up to the arghya;
likewise, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Narasūkta.
Having recited the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī one thousand and eight times,
the preceptor should go quickly to the vicinity of the sabhyāgni fire.
It should be two tālas in width, circular, four aṅgulas in height, shaped like a tortoise, and fashioned from wood such as bilva. || 64 ||
In the consecration of images, during festivals, and in all rites such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship,
one should remain established upon a tortoise-seat (kūrmapīṭha) as prescribed for every undertaking.
Then, composed and with a serene mind, he should offer oblations into the sacrificial fire;
for a rite performed without the tortoise-seat (kūrmapīṭha) shall be fruitless.
One should offer oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, and likewise the Narasūkta— those dedicated to all the deities as well as those pertaining to the Supreme Self.
Having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, one should perform the concluding oblation (antahoma).
Then, having sprinkled water around the fire, one should offer the Mahāśānti in the proper sequence.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the wise practitioner should perform the concluding homa;
having placed the fire into the vessel of meditation or a conch-bowl, he should proceed.
Before applying the oil as an ointment, one should transfer the fire onto the *dhruva* stick;
then, one should honor the attendant with garlands, garments, earrings, and other such gifts.
O best of sages, having wrapped his head with a new cloth and having carefully placed that oil vessel upon his head; || 71 ||
Gradually, having come together with all musical instruments,
adorned with every ornament, and accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas.
Having circumambulated the pathway, one should place [the offerings] before the Lord;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods with everything up to the arghya offering, and having prostrated, [one should proceed]. || 73 ||
One should recite the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇu-sūkta, and the Nara-sūkta in succession;
then the preceptor should quickly anoint the deity with oil.
In the same manner, one should smear the two goddesses here with their respective mantras;
one should smear all the members of the retinue with their respective mantras.
The preceptor, having gone quickly to the vicinity of the festival deity, should cleanse the armor while reciting the mantra "parilikhitam. || 76 ||
When the armor is worn out or broken, a craftsman should perform its repair;
having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should purify it with water. || 77 ||
Having recited "viṣṇornu ka" and so forth, one should again don the armor;
having made it firm as before, one should carefully purify it with effort. || 789 ||
Having bathed the deity with a thousand jars according to the prescribed rite,
and having worshipped the god as before by means of the ritual for the propitiation of the ancestors (Nṛtyapūjā).
One should offer a great oblation, or an abundant quantity of milk-rice (pāyasa), and bow down to Puruṣottama with the mantra "Forgive me. (80)
Having made the sound of the Veda (brahmaghoṣa), one should give the teacher's fee (ācāryadakṣiṇā);
one should perform [the rite] on the day, in the fortnight, in the month, and likewise in the year.
Whatever form [one contemplates], one should meditate upon it in that same way and apply it to the images;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause the protection of the images to be performed. || 82 ||
On the festival of Kārttikī, likewise on the festival of Jyeṣṭhā, on the festival of Āṣāḍhī, and likewise on the festival of Śrāvaṇī. || 83 ||
Likewise, during the festival of Caitra and on the occasion of an eclipse,
ten thousand [offerings] are prescribed for the festival of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
During the festival of the God of gods, an eclipse does not cause any defect;
indeed, one should perform the consecration even during an eclipse or in times of fear. || 85 ||
Thus, he who performs this rite with devotion for the destruction of disease shall attain all his desires and obtain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. || 86 ||
The Expiation for Faults in Domestic Worship:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for faults in domestic worship. If the morning worship is omitted, the evening worship must be performed with double the usual care. (87)
In the evening when [the fast] is broken, and likewise in the morning, until the limit of twelve days,
the wise man should increase the amount in this very same manner, doubling it daily.
Having worshipped [the deity] and offered [the oblation], one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas. Om.
Chapter Thirty-three.
The Ritual for Bathing with the Five Nectars (Pañcāmṛta):
Now follows the bathing with the five nectars, which is dear to the God of gods,
performed on the five days of Viṣṇu, as well as during the two solstices and the two equinoxes.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, especially during the Vyatīpāta yoga,
at the conclusion of a consecration, at the end of a festival, and for the sake of all-encompassing peace.
The consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), which brings delight to the God of gods,
is performed after properly smearing the ground in front of the deity with cow dung.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) here two cubits in length and breadth, using either barley or rice,
one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus.
Above the lotus, one should scatter flowers or tulasī;
the wise man should inscribe the Praṇava in the center of the lotus-shaped figure.
One should write the eight-syllable mantra on the petals starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
then, having collected the water-pots, the Guru should wrap them with thread.
The five nectar-substances—
molasses, milk, curd, ghee, and honey— all combined together,
are to be known as the *pañcāmṛta*, which is dear for the purpose of bathing the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should indeed fill the five consecration jars with nectar;
one should place water mixed with molasses well within the center of the lotus.
One should place a jar filled with milk upon a lotus petal in the east;
one should place a jar filled with curd upon a petal in the south.
One should place the vessel of curd in the west and honey in the north;
likewise, one should place the secondary bathing substances (upasnāna) on the petals starting from the southeast.
From the center to the northeast, likewise at the secondary bathing place (upasnāna),
one should worship Āditya, the two Aśvins, Rudra, and the Vatsaras.
One should invoke the five winds, starting with the eastern one, in the middle and the other directions;
then, having taken up the God of gods, one should establish him in the west.
The wise one should worship with water for the feet and other offerings according to the prescribed procedure for bathing, reciting "Somaṃ rājā" and then "Śanno devī" in sequence. (14)
Reciting "iṣe tvorje tvā" and "agna āyāhi vīta," and having uttered "agnim īḷe," the wise man should bathe the Lord of Gods.
Having recited "The four waters," one should perform the complete ritual bathing;
thus is the supreme five-nectar bath (pañcāmṛta-snāna), which brings about all peace. (16)
It generates prosperity for the king and the kingdom and bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
Hereafter, O Hari, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 17.
Upon the rice, in front of the deity, on a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should draw an eight-petalled lotus and place the Praṇava in its center. || 18 ||
One should place the eight-syllable mantra on the petals starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
then, having adorned that lotus with kuśa grass, flowers, and other offerings, one should likewise [place it] upon it.
Regarding the characteristics of the five products of the cow:
the best milk is from a tawny (kapilā) cow, curd is recommended from a white cow, ghee should be taken from a red cow, and likewise, cow dung from a black cow. (20)
The cow’s urine should be from a blue-colored cow; the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) bestow auspiciousness.
One-quarter prastha of ghee is prescribed, and curd is said to be twice that amount.
It is said that the milk should be three parts, the cow dung four parts, and the cow urine six parts;
one should properly mix these five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Cow-dung that has fallen [to the ground] is excellent, as is cow-urine that has not fallen;
milk should be taken while it is warm from the udder, and likewise ghee that is freshly heated.
And curd that has not passed its time and is unspoiled—this is the characteristic of cow-derived products.
In the middle square is cow urine, in the eastern [square] is curd, and in the southern [square] is ghee.
One should place milk in the west and cow dung in the north in due order;
likewise, one should place scented water in the southeast and sour gruel in the southwest.
In the northwest one should place yellow pigment, and in the northeast water with *kuśa* grass;
having thus arranged them in this sequence, one should worship the presiding deities.
The presiding deities are declared to be as follows:
the Ganges is said to be in cow urine, the Yajurveda in curd, the Sāmaveda in clarified butter, and the Ṛgveda in milk. || 27 ||
Then one should worship Atharvan in a cow-dung with the eight forms; the cow-urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, and the curd with the mantra "adadhikrā vṇe. (28)
Having said "ājyam śukram asi," one uses clarified butter; with "āpyāyasva" indeed is milk; with "gandhadvārām" cow-dung; and with "devasya tvā" the water of kuśa grass. || 29 ||
Having thus consecrated [the image] in sequence with mantras beginning with the four Vedas, one should perform the method of bathing;
one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and purify it thoroughly with sour gruel (āmla). || 30 ||
With yellow fragrances and the mantra "Sinīvālī," and with sweet,
cool water and the mantra "Bhūrānile," one should indeed worship Hari with the Narasūkta.
Having bathed [the image] and adorned it with garments and ornaments, one should offer [the food];
that which remains from the consecration, or indeed that nectar consisting of the products of the cow.
Having caused [the deity] to consume [the offering], one is liberated from great sins and minor sins;
having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, one shall attain union (sāyujya). || 33 ||
