The preparation of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the purpose of purification is that which is employed for the sake of purifying the body, the temple, and so forth. (34)
Upon the entry of a charioteer, a Sāttvata, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, or others [into the temple],
one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sprinkle the temple with it.
Having collected the five products of the cow, one should fill five vessels with them.
Then, having smeared the courtyard of one's own house with cow dung, one should have a sixteen-petaled lotus and a colored mandala (raṅgavallī) fashioned in its center. || 37 ||
And taking a bell-metal vessel filled with half-a-droṇa of rice, one should draw a lotus in its center, provided with five petals. || 38 ||
One should place vessels of the five products of the cow upon those petals;
having established clarified butter in the center, one should pour curd into the eastern [vessel]. || 39 ||
The wise man should place the milk in the south, the cow dung in the west, and the cow urine in the north, in that order.
In the clarified butter, one should place the Sāmaveda; in the curd, the Ṛgveda;
in the milk, the Atharvaveda; and in the cow dung, Skanda himself. || 41 ||
One should worship Śarva and the gods, as well as the presiding deities (adhidevas), with cow's urine;
and having recited "ājyam aśukram asi," one should take up sixteen portions. || 42 ||
Having recited "dadhikrāvṇo" and cast that curd into the fire, one should take up triple the amount of milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva. || 43 ||
With the mantra "Gandhadvārām," one should place four parts of cow dung and six parts of cow urine into that [water] while reciting the Gāyatrī. || 44 ||
Having recited "The purifier of the forest," one should then unify the fivefold [substances].
I shall now state the form-mantra (mūrti-mantra) of the presiding deity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 45 ||
One should worship with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), Śiva, Īśa, and the Unmanifest;
and having recited the Viṣṇu-sūkta, as well as "Rudramanyam" and "Tryambakam. || 46 ||
Having recited "aṇoraṇīyān" and likewise "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should sprinkle the entire temple with these sprinkling mantras and the [relevant] Anuvākas. || 47 ||
Having recited "aśanno devī," one should consume [the mixture] and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) three times;
having thus drunk the pañcagavya, one becomes purified—this is certain. || 48 ||
The wise man should drink that five-fold cow-product (pañcagavya) offered by the preceptor for the purpose of consecration, for festivals, or indeed for any other purpose.

Born in the lineage of the Vaikhanasas, endowed with the sacraments beginning with the impregnation rite (niṣeka), possessed of the aforementioned characteristics, excellent, and endowed with knowledge. || 50 ||
One should choose as the supreme preceptor either a householder skilled in ritual action, or a celibate student, or even a forest-dweller.
The instruction is that one should have the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) and other such rites performed;
the teacher, the forest-dweller, and the student may perform them when the master has died.
There would be no fault even for those two, according to the ancient teaching;
however, one who has paid the teacher's fee should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) three times.
The declaration of the fruit is that by drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in this manner, one is liberated from all sins;
this should be done from the day of commencement onwards, following the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇaka).
Regarding the statement that there is no impurity for those who have been initiated:
"If impurity should specifically occur in the midst of a ritual," (55)
Purification occurs through bathing alone; having bathed, one should perform one's duties—this applies to those who have been initiated, those observing vows, ascetics, and celibate students. (56)
For them, there shall be no impurity regarding water, like a lotus leaf;
even one who is consecrated for a sacrifice [is exempt], yet a man with only one son [must observe it] upon the death of his mother, father, or guru.
Having performed the purificatory rites and returned to the hall, he should perform the rites for the gods;
once the rites for the gods are completed, he should then perform the rites for the deceased.
Upon the completion of the rites for the deceased, one should perform the rites for the gods;
however, the rites for the gods should come first, and the rites for the deceased immediately thereafter.
Śātātapa declared that this must be performed day after day;
even if the death of the preceptor should occur in the midst of the rites for the gods.
At the time of the departure of the vital breath, having released the protective binding and having bound it upon his sons and others, he should swiftly proceed with the ritual action.
If his sons and others are not available, he should bind [the offering] in the hand of a deity;
otherwise, having invited another worthy person, he should complete the remainder of the rite. || 62 ||
One should not perform the binding while engaged in any ritual action;
however, if a person of deluded intellect binds it in the hand of another out of ignorance, [the following occurs]. 63.
That action is declared to be fruitless and brings destruction to the king and the kingdom.
Hereafter, I shall describe the procedure for the pure bath of Hari; I shall explain the ritual for the pure bath of Hari. 64.
For the purpose of consecration in the mandala, one should install the God of gods either in the outer pavilion with stairs or for the sake of the ritual bathing itself.
Or else, one should perform the ritual consecration (abhiṣeka) in an assembly pavilion;
having smeared the square pavilion with cow dung. (66)
Adorned with fivefold groups [of ornaments], with canopies and pillar-wrappings, and with hanging strings of pearls and hanging garlands of flowers. || 67 ||
Having decorated it on all sides with banners and flags,
and having placed the poor everywhere within it, he covered the interior with a canopy.
Having placed a firm seat and being well-composed, the worshipper,
having prostrated before the Lord of Gods with the words "Bhuḥ prapadye" and having sought His permission, [should proceed].
Having lifted [the image] from the pedestal with the mantra "paraṃ raṃ ha," the four [priests] should recite the Svasti-sūkta as well as the Śākuna-sūkta. (70)
Having brought it accompanied by the sound of a conch shell, one should place it here upon the seat;
having placed it with the mantra "apratadviṣṇustavate," one should remain composed.
Performing the ritual service with a graceful gesture,
one should offer flowers at the feet while reciting "namo nārāyaṇāya.
Then, having offered water for the feet and water for sipping according to the previously mentioned procedure, [one should proceed].
One should perform the cleaning of the teeth with the mantra "annādyāya," and by that same [mantra], one should likewise perform the purification of the tongue and the rinsing of the mouth. (73)
Having again given water for sipping and wiped [the face] with a cloth, and having offered mouth-perfume, and having bowed down and obtained permission; || 74 ||
Having covered that back portion of the deity from the neck downwards,
the Guru, permeated by that same state of being, stands behind the deity.
Then, reciting the mantra portions beginning with "ato devā" and "somaṃ rājānam," he should perform an anointing with oil and bind his hair once again. || 76 ||
Having wrapped [the head] with a fragrant garland and washed his hands,
he should then anoint [his body] with oil from the forehead down to the feet and massage it.
One should rub the body of the deity with rice flour or sandalwood paste.
The times for offering oil and other substances are prohibited on the eighth, the ninth, the fourteenth, and the day of the full or new moon.
Likewise, one should avoid the application of ointments and the cleaning of the teeth;
then, having approached the deity at the bathing altar as before, [one should proceed]. (79)
One should properly place him facing east, or indeed with his face toward the moon;
having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, and having bowed down and obtained his permission. (80)
One should purify with an acidic substance using the mantra "parilikhita";
by that same [mantra], one should also perform the cleansing of the hair with *āmalaka* and other such ingredients. || 71 ||
Having said, "The four waters," one should bathe [the deity] again with water;
having said, "Salutation to Varuṇa," one should bathe [the deity] with water and flowers.
Having smeared the limbs of the deity with turmeric while reciting "Sinīvālī," one should bathe him with fragrant water while saying "Bhūrānilaya."
Having again given water for sipping (ācamana), he should likewise give a garment and an upper cloth,
and he should also give a sacred thread while reciting the respective mantra.
Having placed the two purifiers upon the ring fingers of the other's hands,
he should worship him with the eight services and praise him with the Vedas in due order.
The procedure for the thousand-stream ablution is performed with water poured from vessels marked with the conch and lotus,
using the "thousand-stream" vessel while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
Having bathed [the image] thereafter with the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, and then with the respective mantras of the two goddesses, or indeed with their individual mantras; || 87 ||
Having bathed it and applied sandalwood paste, and having wiped it with a cloth,
the knower of mantras should cover it with a fine, washed piece of cloth.
Having arranged the upper garment, one should also purify the ornaments;
then, having offered water for sipping again, one should place flowers at the feet.
Then, having taken up the image, one should place it upon a seat as described before;
the manner of its adornment is with a fine silk cloth provided with a variegated girth-belt.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods so that he is pleasing to the eye and the mind, and having released the *alakabandha* (the hair-tuft) and offered incense as is appropriate; || 91 ||
One should also adorn [the deity] with an upper garment, a sacred thread, and ornaments;
having worshipped with seats and other offerings, ending with the lamp and the water for sipping (ācamana).

According to the procedure prescribed for daily worship, one should employ mirrors and other implements according to the rules, and likewise address the physical forms as if they were kings, using their respective mantras.
Having performed the *mātrādāna* and offered the *madhuparka*, one should then prepare a square mandala with the mantra "athāvanīda. (94)
Having prepared a washed leaf here and spread it with its tip pointing eastward or northward,
one should place a leaf made of plantain upon it, with its tip pointing either eastward or northward.
One should wash or sprinkle the vessel of the oblation with the mantra "ā mā vājasya";
one should worship Sūrya, the lord of the oblation, at its side. || 96 ||
Having sprinkled it with clarified butter while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā," and having cast the oblation into it while reciting "amṛtopastaraṇam asi," [he should proceed]. || 97 ||
Having placed fruits such as those accompanied by jaggery, or curd, or even milk,
therein while recollecting [the Lord] with the Gāyatrī mantra, saying "To the Lord of Devas," || 98 ||
Around that very [altar], in the directions starting from the east and so forth, in due order,
one should offer four oblations of milk-rice and four oblations of pure rice.
Having taken [the substances] with five vessels, one should place them upon three feet;
having recited "yatte susīma," one should indeed pour clarified butter (ghṛta) into them.
Having touched [the food] with the *Annasūkta*, he should again offer water for sipping (*ācamana*), having recited "That of his...
(*tad asya priyam*) and uttered "A beautiful being, self-existent" (*subhūḥ svayaṃ*). || 101 ||
One should offer an abundant oblation to Viṣṇu with devotion;
one should offer a second and a third oblation without the recitation of mantras. || 102 ||
The officiant should offer as much food as is necessary to satisfy his mind,
even if the sacrificial oblations are placed in the four directions and above on three pedestals.

One should offer the images of Puruṣa and the others with their respective mantras, having performed the fire-oblation according to the rules with clarified butter and clarified butter mixed with sacrificial porridge (caru). || 104 ||
Having offered sweet, cool water with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," one should present it five times using a vessel filled to the capacity of a prastha. || 105 ||

Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should present mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa), as well as cakes (apūpa), flattened grains (pṛthuka), parched grain (lāja), and fruits such as plantain (kadali) and others. 106.
Having offered coconuts with the eight-syllable mantra itself,
and having again given water for sipping (ācamana), one should present the mouth-freshener (mukhavāsa).
Having circumambulated the temple, he should then place [the image], adorned with all ornaments, at the seat of life (jīvasthāna) while reciting: "Thou art Bhūḥ, bhaḥ. (108)
Without royal honors and likewise without abundant sacrificial offerings, having established [the deity], worshipped him, and offered the fivefold oblation. || 109 ||
One should install the deity upon the pedestal of the image; this is declared to be the middle [method].
And at the conclusion of the daily consecration, one should establish the deities there as well.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, and having indeed performed the cleansing of the teeth,
one should show a mirror and present mouth-perfume.
Having anointed [the image] with oil, purified it with sour liquids and other substances, and consecrated it,
one should smear its limbs with turmeric and then bathe it with perfumed waters.
Having worshipped with the eightfold offerings and bathed [the image] as before,
one should install it in the seat of life (jīvasthāna) and cover it with a cloth as before.
Having worshipped with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with the lamp and the water for sipping (ācamana),
one should offer pure food as the sacrificial oblation (havis) to the deity while reciting the mantra.
Having given water for drinking and water for sipping, one should offer mouth-perfume;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else remains as before.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Five Nectars Bath, the Five Products of the Cow, and the Ritual for the Pure Bath," in the section on Rituals within the *Śrī-Vaikhānasa Bhagavacchāstra*, the compendium proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Oṃ.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the consecration of the Cow-gift (Godā), the supreme installation of the Cow-gift,
which is meritorious, pleasing to Viṣṇu, and bestows the fruits of all desires. || 1 ||
Formerly, in the meritorious forest of Vṛndāvana, there was a woman born from a portion of the Goddess of the Earth,
endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu and desiring the enjoyments of Viṣṇu.
Having become a two-armed human woman, she herself attained Hari;
she is especially renowned on the earth by the name Godā. || 3 ||
Having attained union with Viṣṇu at the end, she became his constant companion;
O best of sages, listen as I describe the procedure for her installation.
The month, lunar mansion, lunar day, weekday, and so forth have already been declared by me;
on the day as specified, one should perform the rite preceded by the sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 5 ||
Having diligently performed the collection of materials and other preliminary rites,
one should carry out everything according to the prescribed procedure for the consecration of the Earth Goddess.
On the second day, one should perform the opening of the eyes, as well as the Vāstuhoma and other rites,
and also the three-fold consecration (adhivāsa) for the purpose of purifying the image.
The Pauṇḍarīka is the principal fire; one should perform the remainder as previously described.
Having placed the water-jars upon the altar, one should likewise place them upon a heap of grain as before.
One should place images weighing five niṣkas within them;
having inserted the nine gems, one should carefully wrap them with cloths.
Then, joined with meditative concentration (dhyāna), one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) into the jars;
having worshipped the eight Apsarases, beginning with Jayā, one should present the offerings.
Having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka) as before, he should have her lie down upon the bed;
then, having performed the worship of all the gods, he should cause her to study the Vedas.
Having strewn the sacrificial grass for the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, one should perform the recitation of the *hautra* formulas;
and at the time of the *hautra* recitation, one should also perform the invocation with the [divine] forms.
They know her as Godā, Vasumatī, Lakṣmīsakhī, and Viṣṇusatī;
one should perform the oblation in all the sacrificial pits according to the previously mentioned procedure. 13.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations using these two earth-mantras;
this alone shall be the distinction, while everything else should be carried out as previously described.
The preceptor should pass the remainder of the night with dance, song, instrumental music, and the like;
then, at dawn, the righteous one should raise the Goddess from her seat with the recitation of mantras.
Having bathed [the deity] with the previously mentioned jars and adorned it with garments and other ornaments,
the knower of mantras, having performed the placement of gems and so forth, should join it to the pedestal.
Having strengthened it with lime, the preceptor, acting as the sacrificer’s priest, should take the pitcher upon his head and proceed to the village or the temple itself. || 17 ||
Having led [the image] around by way of circumambulation, one should cause it to enter the temple;
then, having honored the preceptor according to the prescribed rite with garments, ornaments, and earrings.
One should give the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which brings pleasure to the Goddess;
when the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has arrived, one should perform the formal invocation (āvāhana).
One should perform everything as before using the two earth-mantras;
having worshipped with the ritual services, or with abundant great sacrificial offerings (mahāhavis). || 20 ||

Having offered it according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the chanting of the Veda (brahmaghoṣa) to be performed; one should also cause a thousand Brahmins to partake of the meal and the giving of the ten gifts to be carried out. || 21 ||
Thus, he who performs the installation of the cow with devotion and without haste shall attain all desires and reach union with Viṣṇu. || 22 ||
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the consecration of sandals (pādukā-pratiṣṭhā), the supreme installation of sandals;
having fashioned them with the proper characteristics from materials such as gold, silver, copper, and so forth. || 23 ||
Having had sandals made that were worthy of the feet of the God of gods, adorned with jewels, endowed with every auspicious mark, and exceedingly beautiful; 24.
The patron, in particular, having caused the installation of the sandals upon the feet of the God of gods according to the scriptures and in due order, [should proceed]. (25)
The performer shall undoubtedly obtain all desires;
otherwise, there can certainly be no pleasing of the God of gods.

Therefore, the performer, having first performed the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the selection of the preceptor (ācāryavaraṇa) and so forth, should joyfully cause [the rite] to be performed according to his capacity and then bestow [the gifts]. || 27 ||
One should perform the entire selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) as prescribed for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā);
then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice with three gold niṣkas, [one should proceed]. || 28 ||
Having invoked the Vāstupuruṣa and performed his purification, one should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) according to the previously stated procedure. || 29 ||

Having prepared the pitchers according to the prescribed rite with gold weighing one niṣka each, they should be individually endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and separately equipped with the five weapons.
Having fashioned the actual form of the sandals from three *niṣkas* of Vaiṣṇava gold, the wise one should place them into the middle of the pitcher.
Having performed the ritual bath with seven jars according to the prescribed characteristics, having offered the *āghāra* oblation according to rule, and having praised the *hautra* therein; || 32 ||
Having invoked the remaining [deities] along with their presiding deities through the [respective] forms (mūrtis), having offered oblations of clarified butter, and having prepared the bed; || 33 ||
One should worship one hundred and eight times with the Vaiṣṇava hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Pauruṣasūkta, and indeed with the remaining pair of mantras.
Likewise, having offered the mantra of the guardians of the directions twenty-eight times,
and having also offered oblations to Jaya and the others, beginning with the deities of the city and so forth— 35.
Having performed the fire sacrifice and completed it, and having passed the remainder of the night,
one should perform the morning bath and other duties, and then enter [the ritual] during the auspicious hour (muhūrta).
Then, with joy, one should offer a cake made of black gram at the feet of the God,
or present an abundant great oblation (mahāhavis) to the Lord of Gods.
Thus, the man who performs the installation of the sandals with devotion shall attain all sovereignty and completely cast off all sin.
Having obtained the fruit of all forms of giving, one enjoys the fruit of proximity, by means of drawing forth power with the aim of rejuvenation. (39)
One should perform all rites according to the procedure for a dilapidated image.
Hereafter, I shall explain the installation of devotees—the ritual for the consecration of devotees. (40)
One should imagine a Brāhmaṇa, either with matted hair or a topknot,
with palms joined in reverence, absorbed in meditation, and with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose.
One should fashion a Kṣatriya endowed with a crown, a Vaiśya with hair tied up in a topknot,
and Śūdras, Anulomas, and others with tufts of hair on their heads.
Or else, even those who are shaven-headed and intent on meditation upon the Blessed One should see the Lord of Gods in whatever form they [meditate upon], and thus take on that very appearance.

One should fashion the twice-born according to the method described for the eight *tālas*, and having caused the *śūdras* and others to be made according to the rule, using the middle [measure] alone. (44)
The measurement for devotees, for the permanent image (dhruvabera), and likewise for the two goddesses, has already been stated according to the requirements of the permanent image. || 45 ||
Having thus fashioned the image of the devotee, one should again perform the consecration ceremony.
Asuras, Vidyādharas, gods, sages, and likewise humans—whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or even those of the lowest castes [may do so]. || 47 ||

In the temple of Viṣṇu, the worship of the images of the devotees should be performed by those endowed with devotion for each respective deity, bearing their specific emblems, and being solely intent upon them.
Whether during the northern course of the sun or the southern, one should act with haste under an auspicious constellation and lunar mansion, especially during the bright fortnight. || 48 ||
Having taken hold of a stable zodiacal sign, or when both [the Moon and the Sun] are in an auspicious rising,
one should offer the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) in sequence starting from the day prior to that.
On the third day, one should perform the opening of the eyes by means of an artisan;
then, one should formally select a preceptor who possesses the characteristics previously described, following the prescribed sequence.
In front, or on the right, or on the left, in a delightful place,
one should construct a pavilion, a gabled hall, or a water-shed according to the prescribed rules.
Having prepared the sacrificial pit for the domestic fire (aupāsana), one should perform the foundational oblation (ādhāra);
and having offered the ancillary oblations (aṅgahoma) together with the five great sacrifices (pāñcamahāyajña). || 52 ||
Then, having performed the opening of the eyes, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
[this should be done] at a river, or a pond, or a large well, or even in a cauldron.
Having indeed consecrated that image, one should perform the purification of the physical form;
one should then prepare the sacrificial hall endowed with the characteristics previously described. || 54 ||
Having adorned it with canopies and the like, beautified with all ornaments,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center, measuring one and a half times the size of the image.
In the east, one should prepare the Āhavanīya fire-pit as before;
in the north, for the purpose of the Vāstu-homa, according to the previously stated injunctions.
Having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagni), one should perform the sprinkling with ritual purifications;
having offered the Āghāra oblation as before, accompanied by the mantra dedicated to Viṣṇu. || 57 ||
One should cause the consecrated image to enter the sacrificial hall and perform the worship of the water-pot according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should meditate upon that specific form, especially within the water-pot;
having bathed the image with five jars, one should purify it with care.
Having spread out the five garments, one should place it together with the water-pot;
having adorned it with clothes and other ornaments, one should worship it with the eight forms.
There, having recited the "Puṇyāha" formula and tied on a protective amulet (pratisara),
one should then cause the image to lie upon the bed with its head toward the door.
One should provide an upper garment and worship as far as the lamp;
having sprinkled water around the fire, the *mūlahoma* is then offered.
Then, having offered eighty-eight oblations accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
one should perform one hundred and eight sacrifices with the eight-syllable mantra.
One should worship each of those forms with its respective mantra one thousand and eight times,
and pass the remainder of the night in due order with dances, songs, and instrumental music.
Again at dawn, the righteous-souled one, having bathed according to the prescribed rules for bathing,
raised the reclining image, bowed to it, and paid his respects.
Having first adorned it with garlands, one should worship it with the eight forms; then, having performed the concluding oblation, one should cause it to enter the inner sanctum.
The disciple, having first offered water, should present the five jewels and gold as a fee for the preceptor at the place of the seat.
When the auspicious moment had arrived, the preceptor, accompanied by the patron,
took the earthen pitcher and the image, and circumambulated the temple.
Having placed and established [the deity] in the seat of the individual soul (jīvasthāna) upon the aforementioned pedestal,
one should mutter the Ātmasūkta and then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the respective seed-syllables (bīja).
One should place the seed-syllable consisting of the first letter of that name, encircled by the syllable Oṃ;
having joined it with the mantra of its form at the conclusion of the root-mantra.
Having invoked the power (śakti) from the pitcher, one should summon it onto the head of the image;
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and perform the proclamation of well-being (svasti).
Having worshipped with all the previously mentioned forms and having offered the oblation,
one should cause the remnants of that offering to be given to his devotees.
And all those things not specifically mentioned should be performed with the Mūrtimantra,
during the consecration, the festival, and likewise during the daily fire-oblation.
Likewise, for the installation of the retinues and the devotees, the Guru should utter "svāhā" at the end [of the mantra] for the devotees and their attendants. || 74 ||
Having uttered "Salutation to Viṣṇu," one should offer oblations for all [deities];
one should thus worship Viṣṇu, the inner controller (antaryāmin), in all the offerings. || 75 ||
Those who have gone to the abode of Viṣṇu, as well as his attendants,
all his devotees and servants, are permeated by the form of Viṣṇu.
Thus spoke the Lord Brahmā in former times to all the sages;
having heard that, all the sages questioned the Grandfather.
"O Brahman, O Lord, how can the attendants be of the nature of Viṣṇu?
Thus addressed, the Creator spoke to those sages concerning all the worlds.
Listen, all you sages, to that which you inquire about:
because his nature is to pervade the universe, he is designated as Viṣṇu. (79)
Therefore, one should visualize Viṣṇu along with his attendants, such as Śrī and others;
at the end of the mantra for each attendant, the wise practitioner should utter their respective names.
If one does not perform [the rite] with each respective name, Lord Hari may become angry;
therefore, having carefully observed the scripture, one should offer it to Viṣṇu.
In plowing, in the inspection of the land, in reporting the herds of cows, in the gathering of stone and wood, and also in the preparation of beeswax. || 82 ||
Likewise, during the flowing of molten metal, at the daily rites, at the installation of the two goddesses, at their marriage ceremony, and at the installation of devotees; || 83 ||

At the Jayantī festival, during the ritual bathing, at the emergence of honey from an anthill, upon the occurrence of quarrels and the like, and during the Vāstu-homa and its subsidiary homas; || 84 ||
In the opening of the eyes and likewise during the three consecrations (adhivāsana),
in these twenty rites, the Śrāmaṇaka fire is to be employed.
Alternatively, having offered oblations in the Āhavanīya fire, one should perform the rite separately;
some maintain that the Śrāmaṇa and Āhavanīya fires are interchangeable. (86)
O wise ones, he who thus performs the worship of the devotees with devotion brings peace to the village and bestows prosperity upon the devotees. (87)
